conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.back: Consider postpartum thyroiditis (destructive release) — check TFTs and TPO antibodies, treat the thyrotoxic phase with propranolol (not antithyroids), and monitor for a subsequent hypothyroid phase.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.front: What is the organising principle for pelvic & vaginal infections?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.back:
Discharge character + upper vs lower tract:
  • BV = thin grey fishy (not an STI)
  • trichomonas = frothy yellow-green (STI)
  • PID = ascending infection with pain, fever and cervical excitation → treat empirically to protect fertility.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.front: What is pelvic inflammatory disease (PID)?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.back: Infection and inflammation of the upper female genital tract — uterus (endometritis), fallopian tubes (salpingitis), ovaries (oophoritis) and surrounding peritoneum — usually from an STI ascending from the endocervix.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.front: Why is the classic sign of PID cervical motion tenderness?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.back: Because infection ascends from the endocervix upwards, so moving the inflamed upper-tract structures (on cervical motion) hurts — 'cervical excitation'.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.front: What is the examinable essence of managing PID?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.back: A LOW threshold to treat empirically (don't wait for confirmation, as the cost of missing it is high) plus knowing the antibiotic regimens.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.front: What is the most common causative organism of PID?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.back: Chlamydia trachomatis — often asymptomatic and insidious.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.front: Which organism causes more severe PID?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.back: Neisseria gonorrhoeae.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.front: Which organisms besides chlamydia and gonorrhoea cause PID, and why is metronidazole included?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.back: Mycoplasma genitalium (increasingly recognised) and anaerobes/Gardnerella/endogenous flora — the anaerobic involvement is why metronidazole is included.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.front: List the risk factors for PID.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.back:
• Non-barrier contraception/not using condoms
  • multiple/new sexual partners
  • young age (<25)
  • previous PID or STI
  • and recent instrumentation including IUD insertion (risk highest in the first ~3 weeks after fitting).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.front: What are the symptoms of PID?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.back:
• Lower abdominal pain (typically bilateral)
  • deep dyspareunia
  • abnormal vaginal/cervical discharge
  • abnormal bleeding (intermenstrual, postcoital, or menstrual irregularity)
  • fever
  • and dysuria.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.front: What are the examination findings in PID?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.back: Cervical motion tenderness ('cervical excitation') — the classic sign — plus adnexal/pelvic tenderness, cervicitis, and purulent discharge.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.front: What investigation must always be done in a sexually active woman with pelvic pain?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.back: A pregnancy test (β-hCG) — to exclude ectopic pregnancy, the must-not-miss differential.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.front: What swabs/tests are used in suspected PID?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.back:
• A NAAT endocervical/vulvovaginal swab (chlamydia and gonorrhoea)
  • a high vaginal swab (BV, candidiasis, trichomoniasis)
  • and microscopy (absence of pus cells makes PID unlikely)
  • CRP/ESR are often raised (supportive).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.front: What is a useful microscopy rule-out for PID?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.back: The absence of pus cells on microscopy of a vaginal/endocervical swab makes PID unlikely.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.front: Is PID a clinical or laboratory diagnosis?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.back: A clinical diagnosis — investigations support it, but a negative swab does not exclude it, so treat empirically on clinical suspicion.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.front: What is the first-line (BASHH) treatment regimen for PID?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.back:
• IM ceftriaxone 1 g single dose
  • oral doxycycline 100 mg BD for 14 days
  • oral metronidazole 400 mg BD for 14 days.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.front: What is the second-line (fluoroquinolone) regimen for PID?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.back:
• Oral ofloxacin 400 mg BD for 14 days
  • metronidazole 400 mg BD for 14 days (or moxifloxacin 400 mg OD for 14 days, particularly for suspected M. genitalium).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.front: Why are fluoroquinolones now second-line for PID (BASHH/MHRA)?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.back: Following MHRA safety advice about disabling tendon, muscle, joint and neurological effects, so the ceftriaxone-based regimen is preferred first-line.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.front: When should quinolones be avoided in PID?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.back: If there is a high risk of gonococcal PID (partner has gonorrhoea, severe disease, contact abroad) — because of high quinolone resistance in gonorrhoea.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.front: How is an IUD managed in a woman with PID?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.back: In mild PID the device can usually be left in situ; consider removal in severe cases or if there is no improvement in 48–72h. If it is removed, consider emergency contraception where there has been unprotected intercourse in the preceding 7 days.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.front: What general measures accompany antibiotic treatment of PID?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.back:
• Analgesia
  • rest
  • avoiding intercourse until BOTH she and her partner(s) have completed treatment (otherwise she is simply reinfected)
  • and referral to GUM for specialist management and contact tracing/partner treatment.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.front: When is inpatient/IV treatment indicated in PID?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.back:
• A surgical emergency that cannot be excluded
  • severe disease
  • a tubo-ovarian abscess
  • pregnancy
  • failure of oral therapy
  • or inability to tolerate oral treatment.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.front: List the complications of PID.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.back:
• Tubo-ovarian abscess (may need drainage)
  • infertility (tubal scarring, risk rising with each episode)
  • ectopic pregnancy
  • chronic pelvic pain
  • and Fitz-Hugh-Curtis syndrome (perihepatitis).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.front: What is Fitz-Hugh-Curtis syndrome?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.back: Perihepatitis — RUQ pain from liver-capsule inflammation with 'violin-string' adhesions — a classic complication of chlamydial/gonococcal PID.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.front: What is bacterial vaginosis (BV)?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.back: An overgrowth of anaerobic bacteria in the vagina caused by loss of the protective lactobacilli — the commonest cause of abnormal vaginal discharge in women of reproductive age. It is NOT a sexually transmitted infection but a disturbance of the vaginal flora.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.front: What is the core mechanism of BV?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.back: Healthy lactobacilli produce lactic acid keeping the pH acidic (<4.5) and suppressing other bacteria; when lactobacilli are lost, the pH rises (alkaline), favouring overgrowth of anaerobes — chiefly Gardnerella vaginalis.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.front: Is bacterial vaginosis a sexually transmitted infection?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.back: No — it is a disturbance of the vaginal flora (loss of lactobacilli)although sexual activity can disrupt the flora.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.front: How does BV discharge differ from candida and trichomonas?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.back:
• BV: thin, white/grey, homogenous, fishy odour, pH >4.5, minimal itch, not an STI.
  • Candida: thick white 'cottage cheese', no odour, normal pH, prominent itch, not an STI.
  • Trichomonas: frothy yellow-green, offensive odour, pH >4.5, itch/soreness, an STI.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.front: List the risk factors for BV.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.back:
• Multiple/new sexual partners (sexual activity disrupts flora)
  • excessive vaginal cleaning/douching
  • recent antibiotics
  • smoking
  • and a copper IUD.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.front: What are the clinical features of BV?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.back: ~50% are asymptomatic; otherwise a thin, white, homogenous discharge coating the vaginal walls, with a fishy odour (often worse after sex/menstruation, as alkaline semen/blood raises pH) and NO significant itching or soreness.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.front: Why is the fishy odour of BV worse after sex or menstruation?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.back: Because alkaline semen and menstrual blood raise the vaginal pH, releasing the fishy amine odour.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.front: What is the whiff test?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.back: Adding potassium hydroxide (KOH) to the discharge releases a fishy amine odour — a positive whiff test.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.front: What are Amsel's criteria for diagnosing BV?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.back:
Diagnose BV if ≥3 of 4 are present:
  • thin white homogenous discharge
  • vaginal pH >4.5
  • clue cells on microscopy
  • and a positive whiff test.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.front: What are clue cells?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.back: Vaginal epithelial cells stippled with adherent bacteria, giving a 'granular/moth-eaten' cell border — the microscopy hallmark of BV.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.front: What is the laboratory alternative to Amsel's criteria for BV?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.back: The Nugent score / Hay-Ison Gram-stain grading.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.front: What are the complications of BV outside pregnancy?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.back: An increased risk of acquiring STIs (including HIV) from the raised pH and loss of protection, and post-procedural infection (e.g. after termination/surgery).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.front: What are the pregnancy-related complications of BV?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.back:
• Miscarriage
  • preterm birth
  • preterm prelabour rupture of membranes (PROM)
  • chorioamnionitis
  • low birth weight
  • and postpartum endometritis (a uterine infection — not endometriosis).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.front: Does asymptomatic BV usually need treatment?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.back: No — usually not. Treat if BV is found before a gynaecological procedure such as termination of pregnancy or IUD insertion.Pregnant women should NOT be screened for, or routinely treated for, asymptomatic BV: treating it does not reduce preterm birth (NICE).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.front: What is the first-line treatment for BV?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.back: Oral metronidazole 400 mg twice daily for 5–7 days.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.front: What are the alternative treatments for BV?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.back:
• Metronidazole 2 g as a single oral dose (aids adherence but slightly less effective)
  • or intravaginal metronidazole 0.75% gel one applicator at night for 5 nights
  • or clindamycin 2% cream one applicator at night for 7 nights.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.front: What advice is given about metronidazole and alcohol?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.back: Avoid alcohol during and for ~48h after metronidazole, because of a disulfiram-like reaction (nausea, vomiting, flushing)— the exam-safe answer, even though newer evidence questions the mechanism.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.front: What key preventive advice reduces BV?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.back: Avoid vaginal douching, soaps and shower gels inside the vagina, as these disrupt the protective flora.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.front: Should sexual partners be treated in BV?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.back: No — treating male partners does not reduce recurrence, so partners are not routinely treated.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.front: How is BV managed in pregnancy?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.back: Treat symptomatic BV (given adverse outcomes) with oral metronidazole 400 mg BD for 5–7 days (avoiding the high-dose 2 g single regimen) or topical treatment; metronidazole is considered low-risk in pregnancy.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.front: How common is recurrence of BV?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.back: Common — approximately 50–70% within a year; consider avoiding triggers and, in some, suppressive regimens.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.front: What is trichomoniasis, and what organism causes it?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.back: A sexually transmitted infection caused by Trichomonas vaginalis — a flagellated protozoan parasite (not a bacterium). It classically causes a frothy yellow-green discharge with a 'strawberry cervix'.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.front: Why does it matter that trichomonas is a true STI (unlike BV)?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.back: Because it requires partner treatment and contact tracing (referral to GUM), whereas BV is a flora disturbance and partners are not treated.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.front: How do trichomonas, BV and candida differ in pH and STI status?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.back:
• Trichomonas: pH >4.5, an STI (treat partners).
  • BV: pH >4.5, not an STI.
  • Candida: pH <4.5 (normal), not an STI.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.front: Contrast the discharge in trichomonas, BV and candida.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.back:
• Trichomonas: frothy, yellow-green, offensive/fishy, with itch.
  • BV: thin, white/grey, fishy, minimal itch.
  • Candida: thick, white, curdy, no odour, prominent itch.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.front: Describe Trichomonas vaginalis and its transmission.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.back: A motile, flagellated protozoan (parasite) spread by sexual contact; it infects the vagina, urethra and paraurethral glands in women, and the urethra in men. Incubation is ~4–28 days.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.front: What proportion of trichomonas infections are asymptomatic?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.back: Up to ~50% (a reservoir for transmission); men are usually asymptomatic.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.front: What are the clinical features of trichomoniasis in women?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.back:
• Frothy, yellow-green discharge with a fishy/offensive smell
  • vulval itching/soreness
  • dysuria
  • dyspareunia
  • and a 'strawberry cervix' (colpitis macularis) — punctate cervical haemorrhages, highly specific but rarely seen.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.front: What is a 'strawberry cervix'?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.back: Punctate cervical haemorrhages (colpitis macularis) seen in trichomoniasis— highly specific but rarely observed.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.front: How does trichomoniasis present in men?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.back: Usually asymptomatic; it may cause urethral discharge/discomfort, dysuria, or balanitis.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.front: How is trichomoniasis diagnosed in women?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.back:
• Vaginal pH >4.5
  • a charcoal swab from the posterior fornix → microscopy (wet-mount) showing motile flagellated trophozoites
  • NAAT is the most sensitive test and increasingly first-line (same sample as chlamydia/gonorrhoea).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.front: How is trichomoniasis diagnosed in men?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.back: With a urethral swab or first-catch urine (NAAT is the most sensitive test).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.front: Why is a Pap (cervical) smear not used to diagnose trichomonas?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.back: Trichomonas may be an incidental finding on a Pap smear, but the Pap is not a diagnostic test (false positives/negatives) — confirm with a proper test.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.front: What is the first-line treatment for trichomoniasis?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.back: Oral metronidazole 400–500 mg twice daily for 5–7 days.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.front: What is the alternative treatment for trichomoniasis, and its caveats?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.back: Metronidazole 2 g single oral dose — but the 7-day course is generally preferred (especially in HIV), and the single dose is less favoured/avoided in pregnancy.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.front: What advice about alcohol accompanies metronidazole for trichomoniasis?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.back: Avoid alcohol (disulfiram-like reaction) during and shortly after treatment.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.front: Why must sexual partners be managed in trichomoniasis?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.back: Because it is an STI — partners must be treated and contact-traced, with GUM referral (the key contrast with BV, where partners are not treated).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.front: What additional screening is recommended in trichomoniasis?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.back: Screen for other STIs (co-infection is common — chlamydia, gonorrhoea, HIV); a test of cure is done if symptoms persist.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.front: What are the associations/complications of trichomoniasis?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.back: Increased HIV transmission risk, and adverse pregnancy outcomes — preterm birth and low birth weight.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.front: How is trichomoniasis treated in pregnancy?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.back: Oral metronidazole 400–500 mg twice daily for 5–7 days (avoiding the high-dose 2 g single regimen); topical/gel treatment is not effective for trichomonas.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.front: Give the reflex clinical picture of trichomoniasis.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.back: Frothy yellow-green offensive discharge with vulval itch, pH >4.5, ± a strawberry cervix → charcoal swab/NAAT → oral metronidazole + treat partners/contact-trace.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ov.front: What is ovarian torsion?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ov.back: A gynaecological surgical emergency in which the ovary (usually with the fallopian tube — 'adnexal torsion') twists around its supporting ligaments, cutting off its blood supply and threatening ovarian viability.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ov.front: What is the exam essence of managing ovarian torsion?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ov.back: Suspect it clinically, image with ultrasound, and operate promptly — and don't be reassured by normal Doppler flow.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ov.front: On which two ligaments does the ovary twist in torsion?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ov.back:
• The infundibulopelvic (suspensory) ligament (carrying the ovarian vessels)
  • and the utero-ovarian ligament.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ov.front: Explain the venous-first mechanism of ovarian torsion.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ov.back: Twisting first occludes the low-pressure venous and lymphatic drainage → ovarian congestion and oedema (enlargement); as swelling worsens, arterial inflow is compromised → ischaemia → infarction.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ov.front: Why can arterial Doppler flow still be present in early/partial ovarian torsion?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ov.back: Because venous obstruction precedes arterial compromise (the venous-first sequence), so arterial flow may persist early — the key diagnostic trap.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ov.front: In whom does torsion of an ovarian mass vs a normal ovary typically occur?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ov.back: Torsion with a mass/cyst (~85–95%) occurs in adults with an ovarian cyst/dermoid/tumour (a mass acts as a lever point; ~5 cm is a classic size). Torsion of a normal ovary occurs in prepubertal girls (longer ligaments, mobile ovaries).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ov.front: What is the risk-factor logic for ovarian torsion?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ov.back: Anything that enlarges the ovary or makes it more mobile predisposes to torsion.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ov.front: List the risk factors for ovarian torsion.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ov.back:
• Ovarian cyst/mass (the biggest — especially dermoid cysts and cysts ~5 cm+)
  • OHSS/ovulation induction (enlarged ovaries)
  • pregnancy (corpus luteum cyst, ligament laxity)
  • reproductive age
  • prepubertal girls (long ligaments)
  • and previous torsion.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ov.front: What is the cardinal presenting feature of ovarian torsion?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ov.back: Sudden-onset, severe, unilateral lower abdominal/pelvic pain — often colicky/intermittent (if it partially twists and untwists) then constant.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ov.front: What associated symptoms and signs occur in ovarian torsion?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ov.back:
• Prominent nausea and vomiting (vagal/peritoneal)
  • pain radiating to the flank/groin
  • adnexal tenderness ± a palpable mass
  • and possibly low-grade fever and mild leukocytosis.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ov.front: Give the classic stem for ovarian torsion.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ov.back: A young woman with sudden severe unilateral pelvic pain and vomiting, and a known ovarian cyst → ovarian torsion until proven otherwise.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ov.front: What investigation must ALWAYS be done first in suspected ovarian torsion, and why?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ov.back: A pregnancy test (β-hCG) — always — to exclude ectopic pregnancy, the must-not-miss differential.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ov.front: What is the first-line imaging for ovarian torsion, and its findings?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ov.back:
Pelvic ultrasound with Doppler — showing
  • an enlarged, oedematous ovary (commonest finding) ± an underlying cyst/mass
  • peripherally displaced follicles (stromal oedema pushes the follicles to the rim)
  • a 'whirlpool sign' (twisted vascular pedicle)
  • and free pelvic fluid.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ov.front: What is the #1 diagnostic trap in ovarian torsion imaging?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ov.back: Doppler flow may be NORMAL or present in up to ~50% of torsions (venous obstruction precedes arterial), so normal Doppler does NOT exclude torsion.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ov.front: How is the definitive diagnosis of ovarian torsion made?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ov.back: At surgery — if clinical suspicion is high despite equivocal imaging, proceed to diagnostic laparoscopy.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ov.front: What is the definitive treatment of ovarian torsion?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ov.back: Prompt surgery, usually laparoscopy, to visualise and untwist (detort) the ovary.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ov.front: Why is ovarian conservation (detorsion) preferred even if the ovary looks ischaemic?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ov.back: Because intra-operative visual assessment of viability is highly inaccurate (only ~18–20% of 'necrotic-looking' ovaries are truly necrotic; blackened ovaries frequently recover follicular function), so conserving preserves fertility.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ov.front: What adjunctive procedures accompany detorsion in ovarian torsion?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ov.back: Cystectomy (remove an underlying cyst at the same time, once detorted) and oophoropexy (fixing the ovary) — for recurrent torsion or torsion of a normal ovary with long ligaments.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ov.front: When is oophorectomy indicated in ovarian torsion?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ov.back: For a frankly necrotic/non-viable ovary or a suspicious mass (possible malignancy), particularly in postmenopausal women.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ov.front: Why is timing critical in ovarian torsion?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ov.back: Because the sooner detorsion happens, the greater the chance of salvaging the ovary.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ov.front: Which key differentials overlap with ovarian torsion?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ov.back: Appendicitis, ectopic pregnancy, and ovarian cyst accident (rupture/haemorrhage) — with ectopic being the must-not-miss one (hence β-hCG first).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.front: What is antenatal care, and why is its schedule high-yield?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.back: The structured programme of monitoring throughout pregnancy that keeps mother and baby well, screens for complications and prepares for birth. Its schedule and checks are a fixed, examinable framework — booking bloods, scans, supplements, and 'what's checked when'.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.front: How many antenatal appointments are recommended for uncomplicated pregnancies (NICE)?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.back: 10 for nulliparous women and 7 for parous women.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.front: What happens at the booking appointment (~8–12 weeks)?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.back:
• Lifestyle advice
  • BP
  • urine dipstick
  • BMI
  • and booking bloods (ideally by 10 weeks).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.front: When is the dating scan, and what does it establish?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.back:
At 11⁺²–14⁺¹ weeks —
  • to confirm dates
  • exclude multiple pregnancy
  • and determine chorionicity.
The combined test is offered at the same scan if accepted.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.front: When is the combined test done, and what does it measure?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.back: At 11⁺²–14⁺¹ weeks, at the dating scan — screening for Down's, Edwards' and Patau's syndromes using nuchal translucency + βhCG + PAPP-A. Women booking too late for it, or in whom nuchal translucency cannot be measured, are offered the quadruple test at 14⁺²–20⁺⁰ weeks (Down's only).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.front: When is the anomaly scan performed?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.back: At 18–20⁺⁶ weeks.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.front: What is checked at the 28-week appointment?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.back:
• BP, urine, symphysis-fundal height
  • a second anaemia and antibody screen (Hb <10.5 → iron)
  • and the first anti-D dose if RhD-negative.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.front: What happens at the 34-week and 36-week appointments?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.back:
• 34 weeks: routine care, second anti-D, and birth-plan discussion.
  • 36 weeks: check presentation and offer ECV if breech, plus breastfeeding/vitamin K/baby-blues information.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.front: What are the booking bloods?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.back:
• FBC
  • blood group & Rhesus status
  • red-cell antibodies
  • haemoglobinopathies
  • hepatitis B
  • syphilis
  • HIV
  • and a urine culture.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.front: Which screening test has been removed from the booking blood panel?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.back: Rubella screening (it is no longer part of the booking bloods).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.front: What is the folic acid recommendation in pregnancy?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.back:
• 400 micrograms daily from before conception to 12 weeks (reducing neural tube defects)
  • 5 mg (high dose) if BMI ≥30, epilepsy medication, personal or family history of NTD, coeliac disease, diabetes, thalassaemia trait, or sickle cell disease.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.front: Which women should take high-dose (5 mg) folic acid?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.back:
Those with
  • obesity
  • epilepsy (on antiepileptics)
  • a personal/family history of NTD
  • coeliac disease
  • diabetes
  • or thalassaemia trait.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.front: What is the vitamin D recommendation in pregnancy?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.back: 10 micrograms daily for ALL pregnant women (note the unit is micrograms, not mg).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.front: Is iron routinely offered in pregnancy?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.back: No — iron is only given if the woman is anaemic.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.front: Why is high-dose vitamin A avoided in pregnancy?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.back: It is teratogenic — avoid high-dose vitamin A (>700 mcg) and avoid liver (very high in vitamin A).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.front: How is blood pressure monitored antenatally, and what triggers referral?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.back: BP at every appointment; refer a woman >20 weeks with new BP ≥140/90 within 24h, and same-day for ≥160/110.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.front: What happens to blood pressure physiologically in the first half of pregnancy?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.back: It FALLS (vasodilation + increased volume), returning to baseline by term — so a rising BP is abnormal.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.front: When are fetal movements discussed, and what advice is given?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.back: After 24 weeks; women are advised to report reduced fetal movements.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.front: From when is symphysis-fundal height plotted, and what does a small measurement prompt?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.back: From 24 weeks, at each appointment; a small SFH prompts a growth scan.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.front: When are anti-D doses given antenatally in RhD-negative women?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.back:
• Either a single dose of anti-D 1500 IU IM at 28 weeks
  • or 500 IU IM at 28 and 34 weeks.
Separately, a potentially sensitising event (ECV, antepartum haemorrhage, abdominal trauma, invasive testing) needs anti-D within 72 hours regardless.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.front: What is labour, and how is it diagnosed?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.back: The process of expelling the fetus, placenta and membranes — diagnosed by regular, painful uterine contractions producing progressive cervical change (effacement and dilatation).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.front: How is true labour distinguished from false labour/Braxton Hicks?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.back: Braxton Hicks are irregular contractions (~every 20 min) with NO progressive cervical change → reassure and, if term and well, send home. True labour has progressive cervical change.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.front: What are other signs of labour besides contractions?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.back:
• A 'show' (blood-stained mucus plug)
  • and rupture of the membranes.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.front: Describe the first stage of labour and its phases.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.back:
From onset to full dilatation (10 cm).
  • Latent phase: up to ~4 cm — slow, irregular painful contractions with cervical effacement/early dilatation.
  • Active/established phase: from ~4 cm — regular contractions dilating the cervix ~0.5–1 cm/hour to full dilatation.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.front: Describe the second stage of labour and its phases.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.back:
From full dilatation to delivery of the baby.
  • Passive phase: full dilatation before/without an urge to push.
  • Active phase: active pushing → delivery.
The mechanism of labour (cardinal movements) occurs here.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.front: Describe the third stage of labour.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.back: From delivery of the baby to delivery of the placenta and membranes.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.front: What is active management of the third stage, and its benefit (NICE)?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.back: A prophylactic uterotonic (IM oxytocin 10 IU) + controlled cord traction + delayed cord clamping — it reduces the risk of postpartum haemorrhage.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.front: What is physiological management of the third stage, and when is it used?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.back: No drugs and spontaneous delivery of the placenta — only if the birth is uncomplicated and the woman chooses it.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.front: List the cardinal movements of labour in order.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.back: Engagement → descent → flexion → internal rotation → extension → restitution → external rotation → expulsion.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.front: What is engagement and flexion in the cardinal movements?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.back:
• Engagement: the head enters the pelvic brim.
  • Flexion: chin to chest, presenting the smallest diameter of the head.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.front: What is internal rotation and extension in the cardinal movements?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.back:
• Internal rotation: the occiput rotates anteriorly.
  • Extension: the head delivers under the symphysis pubis (crowning).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.front: What is restitution and external rotation?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.back:
• Restitution: the head realigns with the shoulders.
  • External rotation: the shoulders rotate to the anteroposterior position.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.front: What is a partogram?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.back: A graphical record of labour progress (cervical dilatation vs time), contractions, fetal heart and maternal observations; a 'flag' is raised when progress crosses the alert/action line.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.front: How is the fetal heart monitored in low-risk vs high-risk labour?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.back:
• Intermittent auscultation in low-risk labour
  • continuous CTG if there are risk factors or concerns.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.front: What are the '3 P's' of failure to progress in labour?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.back:
• Power (inadequate uterine contractions — the commonest cause, correctable with oxytocin)
  • Passage (the pelvis — cephalopelvic disproportion)
  • and Passenger (the fetus — size, malposition/malpresentation).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.front: What is the commonest cause of failure to progress, and how is it corrected?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.back: Inadequate uterine contractions ('Power') — correctable with oxytocin.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.front: What analgesia options are available in labour?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.back: Non-pharmacological measures → Entonox → epidural.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.front: What rate does the cervix dilate in the active first stage?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.back: Approximately 0.5–1 cm per hour.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.front: How is delay in the established first stage of labour defined?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.back: Less than 2 cm of cervical dilatation in 4 hours — or slowing progress in a parous woman.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.front: How is delay in the active second stage defined in a NULLIPAROUS woman?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.back: Suspect delay after 1 hour of active pushing, and diagnose it after 2 hours.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.front: How is delay in the active second stage defined in a PAROUS woman?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.back: Suspect delay after 30 minutes of active pushing, and diagnose it after 1 hour — half the nulliparous times.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.front: What happens once delay in the second stage is diagnosed?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.back: Senior review, and consideration of assisted vaginal birth (ventouse or forceps) or caesarean, depending on the station, position and fetal condition.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.front: When is the third stage of labour prolonged?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.back:
• If it is not completed within 30 minutes of the birth with active management
  • or within 60 minutes with physiological management.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.front: What should happen if physiological management of the third stage becomes prolonged?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.back: It is converted to active management. The same applies if there is haemorrhage or if the woman requests it.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.front: Why does a prolonged third stage matter?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.back: It means a retained placenta, and the uterus cannot contract down properly around it — so the risk is postpartum haemorrhage.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.front: Give the three delay thresholds of labour in one line.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.back:
• First stage: less than 2 cm in 4 hours.
  • Second stage: 2 hours of active pushing if nulliparous, 1 hour if parous.
  • Third stage: 30 minutes with active management, 60 minutes with physiological.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Mu.front: What is a multiple pregnancy, and why is it high-risk?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Mu.back: A pregnancy carrying more than one fetus (most commonly twins). It is high-risk across the board — higher rates of nearly every obstetric complication (preterm birth, growth restriction, pre-eclampsia, PPH) plus, for monochorionic types, dangerous shared-placenta complications. Rates have risen with IVF and older maternal age.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Mu.front: What is the single organising concept that determines the risk profile of a multiple pregnancy?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Mu.back: Chorionicity (how many placentas) — NOT zygosity — because it decides whether the babies share a circulation.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Mu.front: What is the difference between zygosity and chorionicity?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Mu.back: Zygosity (identical vs non-identical) is the underlying biology; chorionicity + amnionicity (how many placentas and sacs) is the clinically decisive classification, as it determines whether the babies share a circulation.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Mu.front: Describe dizygotic twins and their chorionicity.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Mu.back: Two ova fertilised by two sperm (non-identical); they are ALWAYS DCDA (2 placentas, 2 sacs). They make up ~2/3 of twins.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Mu.front: Describe monozygotic twins and what determines their chorionicity.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Mu.back: One fertilised ovum splits (identical); the TIMING of the split determines chorionicity — they can be DCDA, MCDA, or MCMA.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Mu.front: What are the three chorionicity types, their placenta/sac count, and risk?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Mu.back:
• DCDA (2 placentas, 2 sacs, no shared circulation — lowest risk)
  • MCDA (1 placenta, 2 sacs, shared circulation — TTTS/TAPS risk)
  • MCMA (1 placenta, 1 sac, shared circulation — cord entanglement, highest risk).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Mu.front: Why is the monochorionic group the dangerous one?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Mu.back: Because a shared (mono)placenta means a shared circulation, allowing complications like twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome (TTTS), TAPS and (for MCMA) cord entanglement.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Mu.front: When and how is chorionicity best determined?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Mu.back: Best assessed before 14 weeks on first-trimester ultrasound (a key reason for the early dating scan), as the membrane junction is clearer then (NICE).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Mu.front: What is the lambda (λ)/'twin peak' sign, and what does it indicate?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Mu.back: A thick membrane (4 layers) with a wedge of placenta between the sacs at the junction — indicating a DICHORIONIC pregnancy.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Mu.front: What is the T-sign, and what does it indicate?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Mu.back: A thin membrane (2 layers) meeting the placenta at a right angle with no wedge — indicating a MONOCHORIONIC pregnancy.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Mu.front: List the risk factors for (dizygotic) twins.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Mu.back:
• Previous twins
  • family history (maternal side)
  • increasing maternal age
  • multigravidity
  • assisted conception (IVF/ovulation induction — the biggest modern driver)
  • and ethnicity (higher in Afro-Caribbean, lower in East Asian populations).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Mu.front: What are the maternal complications of multiple pregnancy?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Mu.back:
• Anaemia
  • pre-eclampsia/pregnancy-induced hypertension
  • gestational diabetes
  • hyperemesis (higher β-hCG)
  • antepartum and postpartum haemorrhage (overdistended uterus → atony)
  • and polyhydramnios.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Mu.front: What is the dominant fetal risk in multiple pregnancy?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Mu.back: Preterm birth — about 60% of twins deliver before 37 weeks; also growth restriction, malformations and higher perinatal mortality.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Mu.front: What is twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome (TTTS)?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Mu.back: A monochorionic complication where unbalanced blood flow across placental anastomoses leaves the donor twin hypovolaemic (anaemic, oligohydramnios, growth-restricted — the 'stuck twin') and the recipient twin hypervolaemic (polycythaemic, polyhydramnios, cardiac overload/hydrops).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Mu.front: Describe the donor and recipient twins in TTTS.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Mu.back:
• Donor: hypovolaemic — anaemic, oligohydramnios, growth-restricted (the 'stuck twin').
  • Recipient: hypervolaemic — polycythaemic, polyhydramnios, at risk of cardiac overload/hydrops.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Mu.front: How is TTTS treated?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Mu.back: Fetoscopic laser ablation of the shared communicating placental vessels.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Mu.front: What is TAPS?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Mu.back: Twin anaemia-polycythaemia sequence — a chronic, subtler haemoglobin imbalance between monochorionic twins.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Mu.front: Why do MCMA twins deliver early by caesarean?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Mu.back: Because of the risk of cord entanglement (both twins in a single sac).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Mu.front: What antenatal care/supplements are recommended in multiple pregnancy (NICE)?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Mu.back:
• Early ultrasound to confirm the diagnosis, determine chorionicity and date
  • consultant-led care with more frequent visits
  • FBC at 20–24 and 28 weeks to detect anaemia (iron/folic acid only if indicated, NOT routinely)
  • aspirin 75–150 mg daily from 12 weeks for pre-eclampsia prophylaxis
  • and serial growth scans.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Mu.front: What is the surveillance schedule for monochorionic vs dichorionic twins?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Mu.back:
• Monochorionic twins: fortnightly ultrasound from 16 weeks with amniotic-fluid/Doppler assessment to screen for TTTS/TAPS/sFGR (refer to fetal medicine).
  • Dichorionic twins: less intensive scanning (~4-weekly growth).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Mu.front: What is the planned timing of birth for uncomplicated DCDA, MCDA and MCMA twins?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Mu.back:
• DCDA: 37+0 weeks
  • MCDA: 36+0 weeks
  • MCMA: 32+0 to 33+6 weeks (by caesarean, due to cord-entanglement risk).
Triplets ~35 weeks. Offer antenatal corticosteroids if delivering preterm.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Mu.front: When can vaginal birth be offered in twins, and what is required?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Mu.back: If twin 1 is cephalic, vaginal birth can be offered — with 2 obstetricians present, continuous CTG, and epidural often advised.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Mu.front: When is caesarean indicated for twins?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Mu.back: If twin 1 is non-cephalic (breech/transverse), or for any MCMA pregnancy (always caesarean).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Mu.front: Why is prophylactic oxytocin used at delivery of twins?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Mu.back: Because the overdistended uterus carries a high PPH risk (atony), so active third-stage management with prophylactic oxytocin is used.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: How is heavy menstrual bleeding (HMB) defined?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Excessive menstrual loss that interferes with quality of life — defined by IMPACT, not millilitres (the old '≥80 mL' figure is obsolete).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: Why is the term 'dysfunctional uterine bleeding (DUB)' obsolete?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Because HMB is a symptom; the cause is classified with PALM-COEIN rather than labelled DUB.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What does the PALM part of PALM-COEIN represent?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back:
The STRUCTURAL causes:
  • Polyp (endometrial/cervical)
  • Adenomyosis
  • Leiomyoma (fibroids)
  • and Malignancy & hyperplasia

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What does the COEIN part of PALM-COEIN represent?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back:
The NON-structural causes:
  • Coagulopathy (e.g. von Willebrand)
  • Ovulatory dysfunction (PCOS, perimenopause, thyroid)
  • Endometrial (primary endometrial dysfunction)
  • Iatrogenic (copper coil, anticoagulants)
  • and Not otherwise classified

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What examination findings suggest fibroids vs adenomyosis as a cause of HMB?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: A bulky, irregular ('knobbly') uterus suggests fibroids (Leiomyoma); a tender, boggy, symmetrical uterus with dysmenorrhoea suggests adenomyosis.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: Which cause of HMB is suggested by heavy bleeding since menarche plus easy bruising?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Coagulopathy (e.g. von Willebrand disease).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: Which cause of HMB is suggested by irregular cycles and hirsutism?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Ovulatory dysfunction (e.g. PCOS).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What symptoms in HMB should prompt exclusion of malignancy?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Intermenstrual, postcoital, or postmenopausal bleeding. Postmenopausal bleeding at age 55 or over is an urgent suspected-cancer (2-week-wait) referral; consider the same pathway under 55. Persistent intermenstrual or postcoital bleeding warrants hysteroscopy and endometrial biopsy.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: When should a physical (including pelvic/speculum) examination be done in HMB?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Before all investigations or before fitting an LNG-IUS; the exception is a low-risk history with a non-LNG-IUS treatment, which can start without examination.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What blood test should be done for ALL women with HMB, and when?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: A full blood count for all women, in parallel with starting treatment, to detect anaemia.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: When is coagulation testing (e.g. for von Willebrand) indicated in HMB?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Only if the history suggests it — HMB since menarche and a personal/family bleeding history.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: Which tests are NOT done routinely in HMB (NICE)?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back:
• Serum ferritin is not routinely tested
  • routine female-hormone testing is not done
  • and thyroid function is tested only if there are other thyroid signs

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: When is outpatient hysteroscopy indicated in HMB?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: When submucosal fibroids/polyps or endometrial pathology are suspected — e.g. persistent intermenstrual bleeding or cancer risk factors.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: When is transvaginal ultrasound or endometrial biopsy used in HMB?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Transvaginal ultrasound for larger structural abnormality; endometrial biopsy if cancer/hyperplasia is a concern (persistent intermenstrual bleeding, or age ≥45 with treatment failure).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What is the first-line treatment for HMB (NICE)?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: The LNG-IUS (Mirena) — if there is no pathology, fibroids <3 cm not distorting the cavity, or adenomyosis, and long-term use is acceptable. It is the most effective medical option and the clear first choice.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What non-hormonal options treat HMB?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back:
• Tranexamic acid 1 g orally three times daily for up to 4 days of bleeding (an antifibrinolytic with no cycle effect — avoid in active or previous VTE)
  • or NSAIDs such as mefenamic acid 500 mg three times daily or naproxen, which reduce bleeding AND dysmenorrhoea
Neither provides contraception.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What hormonal options treat HMB if the LNG-IUS is declined?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: The combined oral contraceptive pill, or cyclical oral progestogens (norethisterone 5 mg three times daily, days 5–26). Note that cyclical norethisterone is NOT a contraceptive — only the LNG-IUS and the COCP also provide contraception.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What surgical/procedural options exist for HMB?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back:
• Endometrial ablation (family complete, not if future fertility desired)
  • hysteroscopic removal of submucosal fibroids/polyps
  • uterine artery embolisation or myomectomy (fibroids, fertility-sparing)
  • and hysterectomy (definitive but a last resort)

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: Why is endometrial ablation unsuitable for women wanting future fertility?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Because it destroys the endometrium, so it is only used when the family is complete.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: Give the overall management sequence for HMB.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Physical exam → FBC (not routine ferritin/hormones/TFTs) → LNG-IUS first-line; else tranexamic acid/NSAIDs or COCP/cyclical progestogens → surgery (ablation/hysterectomy) if medical treatment fails and family is complete. Treat the underlying cause and any anaemia. Only the LNG-IUS and COCP also provide contraception.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What is dysmenorrhoea, and what does the approach hinge on?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Painful menstruation — the commonest cause of school/work absence in adolescent girls. The approach hinges on separating primary (no pathology → treat symptomatically) from secondary (a pelvic disease is causing it → find and treat the cause).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What is the mechanism of primary dysmenorrhoea?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: The endometrium releases prostaglandins (especially PGF2α) → myometrial contractions and uterine ischaemia → cramping pain. This is why NSAIDs (prostaglandin-synthesis inhibitors) are first-line and so effective.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: How does the onset of primary vs secondary dysmenorrhoea differ?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Primary: young, 6–12 months after menarche. Secondary: older (20s–30s+), often after years of pain-free periods.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: How does the pain timing differ between primary and secondary dysmenorrhoea?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Primary: pain with or just before the period, lasting 1–3 days. Secondary: often begins days before, persists through and after the period, and may occur at other times.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What associated features suggest secondary (rather than primary) dysmenorrhoea?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back:
• Deep dyspareunia
  • menorrhagia
  • intermenstrual/postcoital bleeding
  • and subfertility
examination may be abnormal (mass, tenderness, fixed uterus).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What examination findings are expected in primary vs secondary dysmenorrhoea?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Primary: normal examination. Secondary: examination may be abnormal — a pelvic mass, tenderness, a fixed/retroverted uterus, or adnexal masses.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: List the secondary causes of dysmenorrhoea.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back:
• Endometriosis (classic — cyclical pain, dyspareunia, subfertility)
  • adenomyosis (boggy tender uterus, HMB)
  • fibroids
  • PID (especially new-onset in under-25s — chlamydia)
  • ovarian cysts
  • copper IUD (iatrogenic)
  • and cervical stenosis/outflow anomalies

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What key history points help distinguish primary from secondary dysmenorrhoea?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back:
• Age of onset relative to menarche
  • the timing/pattern of pain
  • associated symptoms (dyspareunia, HMB, intermenstrual/postcoital bleeding, subfertility, discharge/fever → PID)
  • impact
  • and contraception (copper coil)

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: When is a pelvic examination performed in dysmenorrhoea?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: In primary dysmenorrhoea it can be deferred (normal); if secondary is suspected, perform an abdominal and pelvic (bimanual/speculum) examination for masses, tenderness, a fixed/retroverted uterus, and adnexal masses.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What investigations are used if secondary dysmenorrhoea is suspected?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back:
• Pregnancy test (exclude ectopic)
  • STI screen/high vaginal + endocervical swabs (PID/chlamydia, especially under-25s)
  • transvaginal ultrasound (fibroids, adenomyosis, cysts, endometrioma)
  • and laparoscopy (gold standard for endometriosis, though empirical medical treatment first is supported)

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: Are investigations needed for typical primary dysmenorrhoea?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: No — primary dysmenorrhoea needs no investigations if the history is typical.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What is the first-line treatment for primary dysmenorrhoea?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: NSAIDs (ibuprofen/naproxen) started from the onset of pain — they inhibit prostaglandins; paracetamol can be added.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What is the second-line (hormonal) treatment for primary dysmenorrhoea?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Hormonal treatment — the combined oral contraceptive pill (cyclical or extended/tricycling; check UKMEC), with LNG-IUS/progestogen as alternatives; NSAIDs and hormonal treatment can be combined if single agents are insufficient.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What non-drug measures help primary dysmenorrhoea?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back:
• Local heat
  • TENS
  • and gentle exercise

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: How is secondary dysmenorrhoea managed?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back:
Treat the cause — e.g.
  • endometriosis (analgesia → hormonal suppression → GnRH analogues → laparoscopic surgery)
  • PID (antibiotics)
  • fibroids/adenomyosis (cause-specific)
  • copper coil (consider removal/alternative)
refer to gynaecology if specialist workup is needed or symptoms are severe.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: Why is mefenamic acid now less favoured as the NSAID of choice?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: It is no better in efficacy, has a narrow therapeutic window, and carries a higher seizure risk in overdose — so ibuprofen/naproxen are preferred.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What is the key rule when dysmenorrhoea fails to respond to NSAIDs plus hormonal contraception?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Suspect a secondary cause (especially endometriosis) → investigate/refer.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What should new-onset pelvic pain/dysmenorrhoea in an under-25-year-old prompt consideration of?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: PID/chlamydia — with STI screening/swabs.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What is amenorrhoea, and how should it be approached?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Absence of menstruation — a symptom, not a diagnosis. Work backwards through the axis: hypothalamus (GnRH) → pituitary (FSH/LH) → ovaries (oestrogen) → endometrium → patent outflow tract. A break at any level causes amenorrhoea, and the FSH/LH pattern indicates where. Always exclude pregnancy first.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: Define primary amenorrhoea and its thresholds.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Menstruation never established — no period by age 15 (with normal secondary sexual characteristics) OR by age 13 (with none).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: Define secondary amenorrhoea and its thresholds.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Menstruation stopped after being established — for 3–6 months if previously regular, or 6–12 months if there was previous oligomenorrhoea.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What is the commonest cause of primary amenorrhoea, and its features?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Gonadal dysgenesis — Turner syndrome (45,X) → streak ovaries, high FSH/LH, and short stature.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: List the primary causes of amenorrhoea.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back:
• Gonadal dysgenesis (Turner syndrome, commonest)
  • androgen insensitivity syndrome (46,XY female phenotype)
  • outflow malformations (imperforate hymen, transverse septum, Müllerian agenesis/MRKH)
  • functional hypothalamic (anorexia)
  • congenital adrenal hyperplasia
  • and constitutional delay

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What must be excluded first in any secondary amenorrhoea?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Pregnancy (β-hCG) — also consider lactation and menopause.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What is the commonest pathological cause of secondary amenorrhoea?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: List the secondary causes of amenorrhoea.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back:
• Pregnancy/lactation/menopause (exclude first)
  • hypothalamic (stress, excessive exercise, low weight/anorexia → hypogonadotropic)
  • PCOS
  • hyperprolactinaemia
  • POI
  • thyroid disease
  • Sheehan's syndrome (pituitary necrosis after PPH)
  • and Asherman's syndrome (intrauterine adhesions after D&C)

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What blood tests are done first in amenorrhoea (after excluding pregnancy)?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: FBC, U&E, TFTs, and a coeliac screen; then the key hormones (FSH/LH, prolactin, testosterone) to localise the lesion.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What does a LOW FSH/LH (hypogonadotropic) pattern indicate?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: A hypothalamic/pituitary cause — stress, low weight, excessive exercise, Sheehan's, or a prolactinoma.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What does a HIGH FSH/LH (hypergonadotropic) pattern indicate?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: An ovarian cause — premature ovarian insufficiency or gonadal dysgenesis (Turner's).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: How is a raised prolactin interpreted and investigated?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Repeat it (stress and food falsely raise it) and review her medication — antipsychotics, metoclopramide and antidepressants are the commonest cause. If it is persistently raised with no drug cause, arrange a pituitary MRI.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What hormone pattern suggests PCOS in amenorrhoea?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Raised testosterone and a raised LH:FSH ratio.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: When is a karyotype indicated in amenorrhoea?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: If FSH is high — to confirm Turner's syndrome/gonadal dysgenesis.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What is the role of pelvic ultrasound in amenorrhoea?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back:
To check
  • whether the uterus and ovaries are present
  • assess the outflow tract
  • and look for polycystic ovaries

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: How is amenorrhoea from gonadal dysgenesis/POI managed?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: HRT — to develop/maintain secondary sexual characteristics and protect bone.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: How is hypothalamic amenorrhoea managed?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back:
• Weight restoration
  • reducing excessive exercise
  • managing stress/an eating disorder
  • and bone protection

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: How is PCOS-related amenorrhoea managed?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back:
• Weight management
  • cycle regulation (COCP/progestogen for endometrial protection)
  • and treatment of hyperandrogenism/subfertility

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: How is hyperprolactinaemia causing amenorrhoea treated?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: With a dopamine agonist (cabergoline or bromocriptine).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: How is amenorrhoea from outflow obstruction (e.g. imperforate hymen) or Asherman's managed?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Outflow obstruction → surgery; Asherman's syndrome → hysteroscopic adhesiolysis.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What is Sheehan's syndrome?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Pituitary necrosis following a postpartum haemorrhage, causing hypopituitarism (including amenorrhoea).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What is Asherman's syndrome?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Intrauterine adhesions (typically after a D&C) causing amenorrhoea, treated with hysteroscopic adhesiolysis.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: Which cause of hypothalamic amenorrhoea is classically 'the athlete'?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Low weight/over-exercise/stress → reduced GnRH → low FSH/LH (functional hypothalamic amenorrhoea).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What is premenstrual syndrome (PMS)?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Psychological, physical and behavioural symptoms in the LUTEAL phase (the ~2 weeks before the period) that resolve once menstruation starts. It is common (~40%), with ~5–8% severe; the severest form is premenstrual dysphoric disorder (PMDD).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What is the core concept underlying PMS?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Symptoms are triggered by normal cyclical ovarian hormone CHANGES (not abnormal levels) — susceptible women over-respond to the fluctuations. This is why suppressing ovulation (COCP, GnRH) and modulating serotonin (SSRIs) both work.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: How is PMS distinguished from a primary mood disorder by timing?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: PMS symptoms occur ONLY in the luteal phase, resolve with menstruation, and there is a symptom-free week after the period; a primary mood disorder is present throughout the cycle with no symptom-free interval.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What is the key teaching point about diagnosing PMS?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: PMS is defined by the cyclical pattern, confirmed PROSPECTIVELY (not by symptoms alone, as retrospective recall over-diagnoses it). If symptoms don't clear after the period, it is NOT PMS.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What is the difference between PMS and PMDD?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: PMS is the broad syndrome (physical + psychological + behavioural, in the luteal phase); PMDD is the severe, predominantly affective form — a formal psychiatric diagnosis (DSM-5/ICD-11).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: List the psychological, physical and behavioural symptoms of PMS.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back:
• Psychological: mood swings, irritability, depression, anxiety, tension
  • Physical: breast tenderness, bloating, headache, fatigue, cravings
  • Behavioural: poor concentration, sleep disturbance, withdrawal

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: How is PMS diagnosed (RCOG)?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: With a prospective symptom diary over 2 cycles — the DRSP (Daily Record of Severity of Problems) is RCOG-recommended — showing symptoms confined to the luteal phase with a symptom-free interval, while excluding other diagnoses.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: Which other diagnoses must be excluded when assessing PMS?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back:
• Depression/bipolar disorder
  • thyroid disease
  • and perimenopause

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What is done if the diagnosis of PMS is unclear?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: A 3-month GnRH-analogue trial (which switches off ovarian hormones); resolution of symptoms confirms it is ovulation-driven PMS.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What are the first-line management options for PMS?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back:
• Lifestyle measures (exercise, sleep, diet, reducing alcohol/caffeine) and CBT
  • a continuous drospirenone-containing COCP (e.g. Yasmin) to suppress ovulation
  • and SSRIs (citalopram/escitalopram) — continuous OR luteal-phase only — for moderate-severe PMS/PMDD

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What is distinctive about SSRI dosing in PMS?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: SSRIs can be given continuously OR only in the luteal phase (they have a rapid onset in PMS, unlike in depression).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What are the second-line options for PMS?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Higher-dose SSRIs (continuous or luteal), or transdermal oestradiol plus a progestogen (for endometrial protection).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What is the third-line (specialist) treatment for PMS, and its requirement?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: GnRH analogues — potent ovulation suppression producing a hypo-oestrogenic state, so they require 'add-back' HRT to protect bone and cardiovascular health; used only for severe/resistant cases.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What is the fourth-line (last resort) treatment for PMS?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Hysterectomy plus bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy (± HRT) — removing ovarian cycling; reserved for the most severe/resistant cases when the family is complete.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What other treatments may help specific PMS symptoms?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back:
• Spironolactone (for bloating/breast tenderness)
  • some evidence for vitamin B6 (pyridoxine)
  • and CBT throughout

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What is the underlying logic of the PMS treatment ladder?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: You are either suppressing ovulation (COCP → GnRH → surgery, escalating potency) or modulating serotonin (SSRIs) — the two mechanistic levers.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: Why is a symptom-free week after the period essential to the diagnosis of PMS?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Because PMS symptoms are confined to the luteal phase and resolve with menstruation; the absence of a symptom-free interval points to a primary mood disorder instead.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: Why do both ovulation-suppressing and serotonin-modulating treatments work in PMS?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Because PMS results from over-response to normal cyclical hormone changes — suppressing ovulation removes the trigger, while SSRIs modulate the serotonergic response to it.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What is menopause, and its retrospective definition?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Permanent cessation of menstruation from loss of ovarian follicular function — retrospectively defined as 12 months after the last period (average UK age ~51).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What is premature ovarian insufficiency (POI)?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Menopause occurring before age 40 — where the calculus flips so that HRT becomes a replacement (not just an optional symptom treatment).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What is the core hormonal mechanism of menopause?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Ovarian follicles deplete → oestrogen falls → loss of negative feedback → FSH and LH rise. Every symptom flows from oestrogen deficiency, and the high FSH is the biochemical fingerprint.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: Define perimenopause, menopause, postmenopause, POI and early menopause.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back:
• Perimenopause: the transition (irregular cycles + symptoms, up to 12 months after the last period)
  • Menopause: 12 months amenorrhoea
  • Postmenopause: after that
  • POI: menopause <40
  • Early menopause: 40–45

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: How is menopause diagnosed in a woman ≥45 with typical symptoms (NICE)?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Clinically — with NO blood tests, because FSH fluctuates and does not change management.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: When should FSH be checked in suspected menopause?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back:
Only if
  • the woman is 40–45 with symptoms
  • under 40 (POI)
  • or has atypical features

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: How is POI diagnosed?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Symptoms plus an elevated FSH (>30) on 2 samples taken 4–6 weeks apart.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: List the causes of POI.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back:
• Idiopathic (commonest)
  • iatrogenic (chemotherapy/radiotherapy/oophorectomy)
  • autoimmune
  • and genetic (Turner syndrome, Fragile X)

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What are the vasomotor and menstrual features of menopause?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Vasomotor: hot flushes and night sweats (the hallmark). Menstrual: irregular then absent periods. Note that contraception is still needed — for 2 years after the last period if under 50, 1 year if 50 or over, stopping at 55; HRT is not a contraceptive.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What genitourinary and psychological features occur in menopause?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back:
• GSM: vaginal dryness, dyspareunia, urinary frequency/urgency, recurrent UTIs
  • Psychological: mood/anxiety/low mood, 'brain fog', poor sleep, reduced libido

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What are the long-term health consequences of menopause?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Osteoporosis (fractures) and an increased risk of cardiovascular disease.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What non-hormonal options are used for menopausal symptoms?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back:
• Lifestyle measures (exercise, weight, reducing alcohol/caffeine/smoking)
  • CBT (now recommended for vasomotor symptoms and low mood)
  • SSRIs/SNRIs for flushes — but avoid paroxetine and fluoxetine in a woman on TAMOXIFEN, as they reduce its efficacy (use venlafaxine)
  • and topical vaginal oestrogen/moisturisers-lubricants for GSM

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What is the 'golden rule' of HRT regarding the uterus?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back:
• If the uterus is present → combined HRT (oestrogen + progestogen), as the progestogen protects the endometrium (unopposed oestrogen causes hyperplasia/cancer)
  • If no uterus → oestrogen-only HRT
  • Still having periods → sequential (cyclical) combined
  • postmenopausal (≥12 months amenorrhoea) → continuous combined
Before starting, exclude undiagnosed postmenopausal or unscheduled bleeding, current or past breast/oestrogen-dependent cancer, active VTE, active liver disease and untreated endometrial hyperplasia.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: Why is unopposed oestrogen dangerous in a woman with a uterus?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: It causes endometrial hyperplasia and cancer, so a progestogen is added for endometrial protection.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: When is transdermal HRT preferred over oral, and why?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: In women with VTE risk or BMI >30 — transdermal oestrogen does not raise VTE risk (no first-pass metabolism), whereas oral oestrogen does.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What are the main benefits of HRT?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Symptom relief and bone protection.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What is the breast cancer risk with HRT?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: A small increase with COMBINED HRT (duration-related, falling after stopping); oestrogen-only HRT carries little/no increase.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What are the VTE/stroke risks of HRT, and how does route affect them?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: VTE and stroke are raised with ORAL HRT but not with transdermal HRT.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: Should HRT be offered to prevent cardiovascular disease or dementia?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: No — HRT should NOT be offered for prevention of cardiovascular disease or dementia (NICE); it is for symptoms and bone protection.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What sex-steroid replacement is offered in POI, and until when?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: HRT or the combined oral contraceptive pill, until at least ~51 — replacing the oestrogen a young woman should have, protecting bone and cardiovascular health; the older-woman HRT-risk narrative does not apply.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: Why do women with POI still need contraception, and which option is contraceptive?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Because they may occasionally ovulate and rarely conceive; HRT is NOT contraceptive, but the COCP is.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What additional issues should be addressed in POI?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back:
• Fertility (e.g. donor eggs)
  • bone health (DEXA)
  • and psychological support

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: Give the reflex diagnostic and management summary for POI.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Menopause <40 → diagnose with FSH ×2 (4–6 weeks apart) → offer HRT/COCP until ~51 for bone and cardiovascular protection, with contraception still needed.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What is subfertility, and how common is it?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Failure to conceive after 12 months of regular unprotected intercourse — affecting ~1 in 7 couples. Both partners are investigated, organised around whether the problem is sperm, egg (ovulation), or the plumbing (tubes).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What proportion of couples conceive within a year, reframing subfertility?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Over 80% conceive within a year (and about half the rest in the second year) — most couples are subfertile (reduced, not zero fertility), so the workup is as much reassurance and timing as pathology.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What are the approximate proportions and core tests for the causes of subfertility?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back:
• Male factor ~30% (semen analysis)
  • ovulatory disorder ~25% (mid-luteal/day-21 progesterone)
  • tubal/pelvic ~20% (HSG/laparoscopy)
  • unexplained ~25% (all tests normal)

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: List the causes of male-factor subfertility.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back:
Low count/motility/morphology from
  • varicocele
  • cryptorchidism
  • mumps orchitis
  • Klinefelter's
  • obstruction
  • hypogonadism
