  • and drugs/heat/smoking

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: List the causes of ovulatory subfertility.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back:
• PCOS (commonest anovulation)
  • hypothalamic dysfunction (low weight/exercise/stress)
  • hyperprolactinaemia
  • POI
  • and thyroid disease

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: List the causes of tubal/pelvic subfertility.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back:
• PID (chlamydia — the big one)
  • previous ectopic/surgery
  • endometriosis
  • and fibroids/adhesions

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What preconception advice applies to a couple trying to conceive?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back:
• Folic acid 400 micrograms daily (5 mg if BMI ≥30, diabetic, on antiepileptics, or a previous neural tube defect)
  • stop smoking/alcohol
  • optimise BMI (~19–30; lose weight if ≥30)
  • and have intercourse every 2–3 days

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What is the core investigation for male-factor subfertility, and when is it repeated?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Semen analysis; repeat at ~3 months if abnormal (spermatogenesis takes ~74 days) — but repeat immediately if there is azoospermia or severe oligozoospermia.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What are the WHO reference values for semen analysis?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back:
• Volume ≥1.5 mL
  • concentration ≥15 million/mL
  • motility ≥40%
  • and normal forms ≥4%

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: How is ovulation confirmed biochemically?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: A mid-luteal progesterone taken 7 days before the expected period (day 21 of a 28-day cycle, adjusted for cycle length). A level above 30 nmol/L confirms ovulation; 16–30 is borderline and should be repeated.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What further blood tests are done if a woman's cycles are irregular?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back:
• FSH/LH (day 2–5)
  • prolactin
  • TSH
  • testosterone (for PCOS)
  • ± AMH (ovarian reserve)

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What are the tests for tubal patency, and what is done before instrumentation?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back:
• HSG (first-line)
  • HyCoSy
  • or laparoscopy + dye (if pelvic pathology)
Screen for chlamydia before any instrumentation.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: When should a subfertile couple be investigated, and when referred earlier?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Investigate after 1 year; refer earlier (before 1 year) if the woman is ≥36, there is a known cause, or a predisposing history (PID, cancer treatment, amenorrhoea, undescended testes).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What is the dominant prognostic factor in fertility?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: The woman's age.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: How is ovulatory subfertility due to PCOS managed?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back:
• Weight optimisation
  • ovulation induction with letrozole (increasingly first-line) or clomifene (± metformin)
  • gonadotrophins if oral treatment fails
  • and dopamine agonists (cabergoline/bromocriptine) for hyperprolactinaemia

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: How is tubal-factor subfertility managed?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Tubal surgery (for mild disease) or IVF, which bypasses the tubes and is often preferred for significant tubal damage.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: How is male-factor subfertility managed by severity?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back:
• Mild → IUI/IVF
  • severe → ICSI (intracytoplasmic sperm injection)
  • surgical sperm retrieval
  • or donor sperm

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What is intrauterine insemination (IUI), and its uses?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Placing prepared sperm directly into the uterus — used for mild male factor, same-sex couples, and donor sperm.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What are the steps of IVF?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Ovarian stimulation → egg retrieval → in-vitro fertilisation → embryo transfer.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What is ICSI, and when is it used?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Intracytoplasmic sperm injection — a single sperm injected directly into the egg, used for severe male-factor subfertility.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: How is unexplained infertility managed?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Do NOT offer clomifene/letrozole (no benefit); continue regular intercourse and offer IVF after 2 years.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What is the key complication of ovulation induction/IVF?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome (OHSS).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: Which infection is the leading cause of tubal-factor subfertility, and what precaution follows?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Chlamydia — screen for it before instrumentation (e.g. HSG).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What is ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome (OHSS)?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: An iatrogenic, systemic complication of fertility treatment — an exaggerated ovarian response to controlled stimulation. It is the most serious complication of ovulation induction/IVF (has caused maternal deaths); the central danger is a massive fluid shift plus a prothrombotic state → VTE.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What is the mechanism of OHSS?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Stimulated ovaries exposed to hCG (the trigger injection, or endogenous hCG of an early pregnancy) release VEGF → increased vascular permeability → fluid leaks into the 'third space'.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: How does the VEGF/fluid-shift mechanism explain the OHSS picture?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back:
• Third-space loss (ascites, effusions, oedema)
  • intravascular depletion (hypovolaemia, haemoconcentration, hypotension, AKI)
  • haemoconcentration + prothrombotic state → VTE
  • and ovarian enlargement (pain, torsion/rupture risk)

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: Why is OHSS described as hCG-driven, and why does pregnancy worsen it?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: OHSS is rare without hCG and worsens if pregnancy occurs, because endogenous hCG keeps the ovaries stimulated — 'late' OHSS is pregnancy-associated and more severe.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What are the features of MILD OHSS (RCOG)?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Abdominal bloating/discomfort and mild nausea, with ovaries <8 cm.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What are the features of MODERATE OHSS?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Moderate pain, nausea/vomiting, and ascites on ultrasound, with ovaries 8–12 cm.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What are the features of SEVERE OHSS?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back:
• Clinical ascites (± hydrothorax)
  • oliguria
  • haemoconcentration (haematocrit >45%)
  • hypoproteinaemia
  • and ovaries >12 cm

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What are the features of CRITICAL OHSS?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back:
• Tense ascites/large effusions
  • haematocrit >55%
  • WCC >25
  • oligo/anuria
  • VTE
  • ARDS
  • and organ failure

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: List the risk factors for OHSS.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back:
• PCOS (many follicles)
  • young age
  • low BMI
  • high antral follicle count/high AMH
  • previous OHSS
  • high follicle number/oestradiol during stimulation
  • hCG trigger + luteal support
  • and pregnancy

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: How does OHSS present?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back:
• Abdominal bloating, distension and pain (ovarian enlargement + ascites)
  • nausea/vomiting/diarrhoea
  • reduced urine output
  • shortness of breath (ascites/effusion)
  • and signs of VTE (including unusual sites such as upper-limb/neck veins)
It develops within days of the hCG trigger/egg collection, or later if pregnant.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What investigations are used in OHSS?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back:
• FBC (haematocrit for haemoconcentration/severity, WCC)
  • U&Es (AKI/electrolytes), LFTs, albumin, coagulation
  • ultrasound (enlarged ovaries, ascites)
  • CXR if respiratory compromise
  • and β-hCG (pregnancy predicts worsening)

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: Which conditions must be excluded when diagnosing OHSS?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back:
• Ovarian torsion
  • ovarian rupture
  • and ectopic pregnancy

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What is the general management principle for OHSS?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: It is usually self-limiting → supportive care while awaiting resolution; priorities are fluid balance, symptom control, and VTE prevention.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: How is mild-moderate OHSS managed (outpatient)?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back:
• Analgesia (paracetamol/codeine — avoid NSAIDs, as they may compromise renal function)
  • antiemetics
  • oral fluids to thirst
  • monitoring of symptoms/weight/urine output
  • safety-netting
  • and VTE risk assessment

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: How is severe/critical OHSS managed (inpatient)?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back:
• IV fluids to correct hypovolaemia with monitoring of fluid balance/U&Es/haematocrit
  • paracentesis for tense/symptomatic ascites
  • essential VTE prophylaxis (LMWH + stockings)
  • human albumin (plasma expander) in some
  • and HDU/ICU for critical cases

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: Why is VTE prophylaxis essential in OHSS?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Because OHSS is strongly prothrombotic (haemoconcentration) and kills via thrombosis — including at unusual sites (neck/arm veins) — and the risk often extends into pregnancy if she conceives.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What is the role of paracentesis in OHSS?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Draining tense/symptomatic ascites relieves pain and breathing and improves renal perfusion.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: When is surgery indicated in OHSS?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Only for ovarian torsion, rupture, or ectopic pregnancy — otherwise the fragile enlarged ovaries are left alone.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: How can OHSS be prevented?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back:
• Identify high-risk women (PCOS, high AMH)
  • use lower stimulation doses
  • antagonist protocols with a GnRH-agonist trigger instead of hCG
  • 'freeze-all' embryos (avoiding pregnancy hCG that cycle)
  • and cabergoline (reduces the VEGF effect)

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: Why is a GnRH-agonist trigger used instead of hCG to prevent OHSS?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Because hCG is the driver of OHSS; a GnRH-agonist trigger avoids the prolonged hCG stimulation, reducing OHSS risk.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What is the organising principle for medical disorders in pregnancy?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Pregnancy alters physiology and drug safety, so many conditions need screening (e.g. GDM), prophylaxis (VTE), or specific treatment — always weighing maternal and fetal wellbeing.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What is gestational diabetes (GDM)?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Glucose intolerance first recognised in pregnancy, driven by the insulin resistance that placental hormones (human placental lactogen, cortisol, progesterone) create to divert glucose to the fetus.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: How does maternal hyperglycaemia in GDM affect the fetus?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: It crosses the placenta, causing fetal hyperinsulinaemia and macrosomia → shoulder dystocia and neonatal hypoglycaemia. GDM is also a red flag for future type 2 diabetes.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What are the '5678' diagnostic thresholds for GDM on the 75g OGTT?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back:
• Fasting glucose ≥5.6 mmol/L OR
  • 2-hour glucose ≥7.8 mmol/L
— either value alone is diagnostic.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: How are women screened for GDM?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back:
With a 75g OGTT —
  • previous GDM: OGTT as soon as possible after booking and repeated at 24–28 weeks
  • any other risk factor: OGTT at 24–28 weeks.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: List the risk factors for gestational diabetes.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back:
• BMI >30
  • a previous macrosomic baby (≥4.5 kg)
  • previous GDM
  • a first-degree relative with diabetes, and
  • high-prevalence ethnicity (South Asian, Black Caribbean, Middle Eastern).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What is the 'glycosuria trap' in pregnancy?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: A trace of glucose on urine dipstick is NORMAL in pregnancy (increased GFR and reduced tubular reabsorption). Do NOT screen with urinalysis/fasting glucose/HbA1c — use the OGTT.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What is the first step for GDM diagnosed with a fasting glucose <7 mmol/L and no complications?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back:
A trial of
  • diet and exercise
  • adding metformin if targets are missed, and
  • insulin if glucose remains high.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What is the first step for GDM with a fasting glucose ≥7 mmol/L at diagnosis?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Immediate insulin (± metformin) — too high to wait for diet/exercise.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What is the approach when fasting glucose is 6.0–6.9 mmol/L with complications (macrosomia/polyhydramnios)?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Consider immediate insulin (± metformin).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: Within what timeframe should a newly diagnosed woman with GDM be seen, and what is taught?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Seen in a joint diabetes/antenatal clinic within 1 week, and taught capillary blood glucose self-monitoring.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: Outline the glucose-lowering ladder in GDM.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Diet + exercise first (fasting <7, no complications; review in 1–2 weeks) → metformin if targets not met → insulin if metformin insufficient, or first-line if fasting ≥7 (or 6.0–6.9 with complications).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What are the capillary glucose targets in GDM?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back:
• Fasting <5.3 mmol/L
  • 1 hour post-meal <7.8
  • 2 hours post-meal <6.4
  • and keep >4 mmol/L if on insulin (to avoid hypos).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What fetal surveillance is used in GDM?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Growth scans to detect macrosomia/polyhydramnios.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: When is delivery timed in GDM?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Timed delivery by ~40–41 weeks (elective birth offered no later than 40⁺⁶), earlier if on treatment or with complications.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What should happen to glucose-lowering treatment immediately after birth in GDM?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Stop all glucose-lowering treatment immediately after birth — GDM resolves with delivery of the placenta.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What neonatal monitoring is needed after a GDM pregnancy?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Monitor the neonate for hypoglycaemia (fetal hyperinsulinaemia persists briefly after birth).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What postnatal maternal follow-up is needed after GDM?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Maternal fasting glucose or HbA1c at 6–13 weeks postnatally, then annual HbA1c, given the high future risk of type 2 diabetes.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: Why is GDM a 'red flag' for the mother's future health?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Because it predicts a high risk of developing type 2 diabetes later, warranting ongoing surveillance.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: Which placental hormones drive the insulin resistance of pregnancy?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Human placental lactogen (hPL), cortisol, and progesterone.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What is intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy (ICP/obstetric cholestasis)?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: A liver disorder unique to pregnancy in which bile acids accumulate in the maternal circulation, causing intense itch (typically in the third trimester) that resolves after delivery. At high bile-acid levels it raises stillbirth risk.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What is the mechanism of harm in ICP?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Impaired bile flow raises serum bile acids, which are thought to cross to the fetus and, at high concentrations, trigger fetal cardiac arrhythmia/placental vasospasm → sudden stillbirth. The bile-acid LEVEL, not the symptoms, drives risk.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What is the cardinal (often only) clinical feature of ICP?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Pruritus — classically worse on the palms and soles and worse at night, with NO rash (only excoriations).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What is the severity classification of ICP by peak bile acids (RCOG)?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back:
• Mild: 19–39 micromol/L
  • moderate: 40–99 micromol/L
  • severe: ≥100 micromol/L.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: At what bile-acid level is the stillbirth risk significantly raised?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: ≥100 micromol/L (severe ICP) — this is the key threshold; mild ICP does not significantly raise stillbirth risk above background.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What is the paradigm shift in understanding ICP stillbirth risk?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: It was previously taught that ICP raised stillbirth risk in everyone; current evidence concentrates the excess risk at bile acids ≥100, so mild ICP is now managed much more conservatively.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What are the key investigations in suspected ICP?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Serum bile acids (the key diagnostic and prognostic test) and LFTs (transaminases ALT/AST often raised, using pregnancy-adjusted ranges — ALP rises physiologically so is not useful).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: How is the diagnosis of ICP arrived at?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: It is a clinical diagnosis — itch with raised bile acids — confirmed retrospectively by resolution after delivery. Pre-eclampsia/HELLP must be excluded, but a viral hepatitis or autoimmune screen and liver ultrasound are done only if the features are atypical or the biochemistry fails to resolve postnatally.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What is the significance of a normal ALP in interpreting LFTs in pregnancy?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: ALP rises physiologically in pregnancy (placental source), so it is not useful for diagnosing ICP; transaminases (ALT/AST) with pregnancy-adjusted ranges are used instead.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: Is ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA) routinely recommended in ICP, and why?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: No — randomised evidence shows it does not prevent stillbirth and has only limited/insignificant benefit on itch, so routine use is superseded (it may be considered on an individual basis).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What supportive measures are used for the itch of ICP?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Topical emollients (e.g. menthol in aqueous cream — safe, may soothe) and a sedating antihistamine (chlorphenamine) to help sleep, though the effect on itch is limited.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: When is vitamin K given in ICP?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Water-soluble vitamin K only if there is prolonged clotting or severe cholestasis (impaired fat-soluble vitamin absorption creating a bleeding risk).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: How is the timing of birth stratified by bile-acid level in ICP?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back:
• ≥100 (severe): planned birth ~35–36 weeks
  • 40–99 (moderate): ~38–39 weeks
  • <40 (mild): ~40 weeks.
Co-existing GDM/pre-eclampsia/multiple pregnancy prompts earlier delivery.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What monitoring guides delivery timing in ICP, and what is the limitation of CTG?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Serial bile acids and LFTs guide delivery timing; CTG is offered but cannot reliably predict or prevent the sudden stillbirth.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What is the postnatal follow-up for ICP?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Confirm resolution with an LFT/bile-acid check at ~4+ weeks; note the high recurrence (~45–90%) and a small increased lifetime hepatobiliary risk (gallstones).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What is the recurrence rate of ICP in future pregnancies?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: High — approximately 45–90%.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: Give the reflex clinical picture of ICP.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Third-trimester pruritus of the palms and soles with NO rash and raised bile acids, resolving after birth → measure bile acids and stratify delivery timing.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What are the bilirubin and jaundice findings in ICP?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Bilirubin is usually normal and clinical jaundice is rare — it is the bile acids that rise, and they are the earliest and commonest abnormality. Dark urine, pale stools, RUQ discomfort and fatigue may occur variably.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: Why is bile-acid-stratified delivery timing used rather than a flat 37–38 weeks?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Because stillbirth risk is concentrated at bile acids ≥100, so severe ICP is delivered earlier (~35–36 weeks) while mild ICP can be managed to ~40 weeks.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: Why is VTE important in pregnancy?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: VTE (DVT + pulmonary embolism) is a leading direct cause of maternal death; pregnancy is a major prothrombotic state, and diagnosis/prevention deliberately differ from the non-pregnant pathway.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: How does pregnancy fulfil all three arms of Virchow's triad?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back:
• Hypercoagulability (oestrogen raises clotting factors and lowers protein S)
  • stasis (uterine venous compression)
  • and endothelial injury (at delivery).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: When is VTE risk highest in pregnancy?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: In the third trimester and the puerperium (first 6 weeks) — the puerperium carries the greatest daily risk of all.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: When is every woman VTE risk-assessed?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back:
• At booking
  • on any admission
  • intrapartum, and
  • postnatally
— because the risk is dynamic (RCOG uses a cumulative risk-factor score).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: List the risk factors used in VTE risk scoring.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back:
• Age >35
  • BMI >30
  • parity ≥3
  • smoking
  • gross varicose veins
  • current pre-eclampsia
  • immobility
  • multiple pregnancy
  • IVF
  • family history of unprovoked VTE
  • thrombophilia
  • medical comorbidities (SLE, IBD, cancer), and
  • transient factors (hyperemesis/dehydration, OHSS, surgery, long-haul travel).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What is the thromboprophylaxis for a woman with a previous VTE?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: She is highest risk — LMWH throughout the antenatal period plus 6 weeks postnatal. The one exception is a single VTE provoked by major surgery, fully recovered, with no other risk factors: LMWH from 28 weeks.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What is the thromboprophylaxis for an antenatal risk score of ≥4?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: LMWH from the first trimester plus 6 weeks postnatal.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What is the thromboprophylaxis for an antenatal risk score of 3?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: LMWH from 28 weeks plus 6 weeks postnatal.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What is the thromboprophylaxis for a postnatal risk score of ≥2?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: LMWH for at least 10 days postnatal.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What is the anticoagulant of choice for VTE prophylaxis/treatment in pregnancy, and why?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Low molecular weight heparin (e.g. enoxaparin) — it does not cross the placenta. DOACs and warfarin are contraindicated (warfarin is teratogenic — fetal warfarin syndrome).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: When is anti-Xa monitoring used with LMWH in pregnancy?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Only at body-weight extremes (<50 or ≥90 kg) or in renal impairment — not routinely.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What thromboprophylaxis applies after a caesarean with additional risk factors or emergency caesarean?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Postnatal LMWH.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What mechanical/general measures support VTE prevention?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Anti-embolism stockings, mobilisation, and hydration.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: Why are D-dimer and the Wells score NOT used to diagnose VTE in pregnancy?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back:
• D-dimer rises physiologically in pregnancy (so is not useful), and
  • the Wells score is not validated in pregnancy.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: How is suspected DVT investigated in pregnancy?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Compression duplex ultrasound (DVT is more often left-sided/iliofemoral); if negative but suspicion remains, repeat on days 3 and 7.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: How is suspected PE investigated in pregnancy?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back:
• ECG and CXR first
  • if there are DVT signs, do a leg ultrasound first (avoids radiation)
  • otherwise a V/Q scan or CTPA, guided by the CXR.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: When should treatment be started in suspected VTE in pregnancy?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Start treatment-dose LMWH immediately on suspicion — do not wait for imaging, and do not delay for a thrombophilia screen.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: How long is LMWH continued when treating VTE in pregnancy?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: For at least 3 months AND until at least 6 weeks postnatal (whichever is longer).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: How is massive/life-threatening PE managed in pregnancy?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: With IV unfractionated heparin or thrombolysis.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What must happen to LMWH around labour/delivery?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Stop LMWH at the onset of labour or before planned delivery, to allow safe timing of regional anaesthesia.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: Give the reflex for suspected PE in a pregnant woman.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Start treatment-dose LMWH on suspicion, then investigate (ECG + CXR first, then leg ultrasound or V/Q/CTPA) — without using D-dimer or the Wells score.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What is hyperemesis gravidarum (HG)?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: The severe end of nausea and vomiting of pregnancy (NVP) — vomiting causing weight loss, dehydration and electrolyte disturbance. NVP is near-universal and benign; HG affects the ~0.3–3.6% who become genuinely unwell.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What drives hyperemesis gravidarum, and which states worsen it?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Elevated β-hCG — so it is worse in high-β-hCG states such as multiple pregnancy and molar/trophoblastic disease. β-hCG mimics TSH, so severe HG can cause transient biochemical hyperthyroidism.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: How is hyperemesis gravidarum diagnosed?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back:
• Onset before 16 weeks with no other cause
  • severe nausea and/or vomiting (vomiting is not required)
  • and an inability to eat or drink normally that strongly limits daily activities
Weight loss of ≥5%, dehydration and electrolyte imbalance support the diagnosis rather than being required for it.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What is the PUQE score, and its severity bands?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back:
A severity score for nausea duration + vomiting + retching over 24h:
  • ≤6 mild
  • 7–12 moderate
  • 13–15 severe
(the HELP tool is a newer validated alternative).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: When should another cause be sought rather than diagnosing HG?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: If vomiting starts after ~11–16 weeks, or with abdominal pain/fever/dysuria — search for another cause (UTI, gastroenteritis, molar pregnancy, thyroid/liver disease). HG is partly a diagnosis of exclusion.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: List the risk factors for hyperemesis gravidarum.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back:
• Multiple pregnancy
  • molar disease
  • nulliparity
  • obesity
  • a personal/family history of HG
  • and a female fetus (mostly reflecting higher β-hCG)

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What investigations are used in hyperemesis gravidarum?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back:
• Weight (vs pre-pregnancy)
  • MSU to exclude UTI
  • U&Es (hypokalaemia, hyponatraemia)
  • FBC (haemoconcentration)
  • TFTs/LFTs if indicated
  • and ultrasound to confirm a viable intrauterine pregnancy and exclude multiple/molar pregnancy

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What is the current RCOG position on ketonuria in hyperemesis?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Ketonuria is NOT an indicator of dehydration and should NOT be used to assess severity; use the PUQE score, weight loss, clinical dehydration and electrolytes instead.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What are the first-line antiemetics for HG?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back:
• Antihistamines (cyclizine/promethazine)
  • phenothiazines (prochlorperazine/chlorpromazine)
  • and doxylamine/pyridoxine (Xonvea)

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What are the second-line antiemetics for HG, and their cautions?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back:
• Ondansetron (counsel on a small first-trimester cleft-palate risk — benefit outweighs it)
  • metoclopramide (max 5 days — extrapyramidal/oculogyric crisis risk)
  • or domperidone

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What is used for refractory hyperemesis gravidarum?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Combination antiemetic therapy if a single agent fails, and corticosteroids for refractory cases.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What conservative measures help in nausea/vomiting of pregnancy?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back:
• Rest
  • small bland meals
  • ginger
  • and P6 acupressure

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What IV fluids are used in HG, and which are avoided?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Normal saline with potassium chloride to correct dehydration and hypokalaemia; NO glucose/dextrose fluids (they can precipitate Wernicke's in a thiamine-deficient woman).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: Why and how is thiamine given in admitted HG?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Thiamine is given to ALL women admitted with prolonged vomiting (oral 100 mg TDS or IV Pabrinex) BEFORE any dextrose, to prevent Wernicke's encephalopathy (confusion, ataxia, ophthalmoplegia).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What is the triad of Wernicke's encephalopathy that HG treatment aims to prevent?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back:
• Confusion
  • ataxia
  • and ophthalmoplegia

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: Why is VTE prophylaxis given during HG admission?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Because dehydration and immobility increase VTE risk, so LMWH prophylaxis is given while admitted.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What determines the setting of care in HG?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back:
• Mild → community oral antiemetics
  • ambulatory day-care if community treatment fails and PUQE <13
  • admit if she cannot tolerate oral fluids/antiemetics, has continued vomiting with weight loss, PUQE ≥13, or comorbidity

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What additional supportive measures are used in HG?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back:
• A PPI or H2-antagonist for reflux
  • and mental-health support

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: Why should an ultrasound always be performed in hyperemesis gravidarum?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: To confirm a viable intrauterine pregnancy and exclude multiple pregnancy and molar/trophoblastic disease (high-β-hCG states that worsen HG).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What is the recurring principle in managing substance use in pregnancy?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Support and substitution, not judgement or abrupt withdrawal — a judged woman disengages from antenatal care. It clusters with social vulnerability (a safeguarding lens).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: Which two substances break the 'just stop' rule because abrupt cessation is dangerous?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Opioids and alcohol/benzodiazepines — abrupt withdrawal is itself dangerous.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What is the guidance on alcohol in pregnancy?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Avoid completely — there is no safe threshold, and risk is dose-related.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What is the facial triad of fetal alcohol syndrome?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: A smooth philtrum, a thin upper lip, and small palpebral fissures — plus growth restriction and CNS/neurodevelopmental effects (microcephaly, learning disability).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: How are heavy/dependent drinkers managed in pregnancy?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: With supported detox, because abrupt withdrawal can cause seizures/delirium tremens; give thiamine cover.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What are the fetal effects of tobacco/smoking in pregnancy?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back:
CO and nicotine cause chronic fetal hypoxia and vasoconstriction →
  • growth restriction (low birth weight)
  • placental abruption
  • praevia
  • preterm birth/PPROM
  • miscarriage/stillbirth
  • and SIDS

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: How is smoking assessed and addressed at booking?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Ask about smoking and do a CO breath test at booking, and refer all smokers to Stop Smoking Services (opt-out).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What smoking-cessation pharmacotherapy is used or avoided in pregnancy?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Nicotine replacement therapy (NRT) — considered alongside behavioural support from the earliest opportunity, not held back until support has failed, and continued after birth if needed to prevent relapse. It is safer than continuing to smoke. Varenicline, bupropion and cytisinicline are all avoided in pregnancy and breastfeeding.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: How should opioid use be managed in pregnancy?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Do NOT attempt abrupt withdrawal (risks fetal distress, miscarriage, preterm birth); use opioid substitution with methadone or buprenorphine, maintained throughout via a specialist drug service.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: Why is abrupt opioid detoxification avoided in pregnancy?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Because it can cause fetal distress, miscarriage, and preterm birth.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What is neonatal abstinence syndrome (NAS), and its features?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Withdrawal in a neonate exposed to opioids (or benzodiazepines) in utero — high-pitched cry, jitteriness, tremors, poor feeding, sweating, diarrhoea, seizures (CNS + GI + autonomic features).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: How is neonatal abstinence syndrome assessed and treated?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Assessed with Finnegan scoring; managed with supportive care and weaning oral morphine if severe.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What are the fetal/maternal effects of cocaine in pregnancy?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back:
• Placental abruption (vasoconstriction)
  • fetal growth restriction
  • and maternal hypertension/stroke/MI
There is no substitution therapy — management is supportive/safeguarding.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What is the classic obstetric complication associated with cocaine use?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Placental abruption (from vasoconstriction).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What are the fetal effects of cannabis in pregnancy?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Growth restriction and neurodevelopmental effects.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What general principles apply to all substance use in pregnancy?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back:
• Non-judgemental engagement
  • a multidisciplinary team with safeguarding ('complex social factors')
  • screening for blood-borne viruses (hep B/C, HIV) in injecting users
  • and enhanced fetal growth surveillance

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: Which blood-borne viruses should be screened for in injecting drug users in pregnancy?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back:
• Hepatitis B
  • hepatitis C
  • and HIV

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: Is breastfeeding encouraged in women on opioid substitution?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Yes — breastfeeding is encouraged in women stable on methadone or buprenorphine.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: Which substances can a woman generally stop abruptly and which cannot?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back:
• She can stop tobacco, cocaine/stimulants and cannabis abruptly (with support)
  • opioids and alcohol/benzodiazepine dependence require supported/substitution management, not abrupt cessation

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What is Rhesus (RhD) disease / haemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn (HDFN)?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: An RhD-negative mother becomes sensitised to the RhD antigen on her RhD-positive baby's red cells; in a later pregnancy her anti-D IgG antibodies cross the placenta and haemolyse a subsequent RhD-positive fetus. It is now almost entirely preventable with anti-D prophylaxis.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: Explain the two-hit logic of Rhesus disease.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back:
• First exposure (a sensitising event — fetal RhD+ cells enter the maternal circulation) triggers a primary immune response producing maternal anti-D IgG (the current baby is usually unaffected)
  • A subsequent RhD+ pregnancy allows anti-D IgG to cross the placenta and haemolyse fetal red cells → HDFN

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: Why is the first affected pregnancy usually the second RhD-positive pregnancy?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back:
• Because the first RhD+ pregnancy causes sensitisation (making maternal anti-D), but the current baby is usually spared
  • the anti-D IgG then affects a subsequent RhD+ fetus

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: Roughly what proportion of the UK population is RhD-negative?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: About 15%.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What is the goal and tool in an RhD-negative woman who is NOT yet sensitised?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back:
• Goal: prevent sensitisation
  • Tool: anti-D immunoglobulin prophylaxis — which works only BEFORE sensitisation

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What is the goal and tools once a woman is already sensitised?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back:
Goal: monitor and treat the affected fetus. Tools:
  • antibody titres
  • MCA Doppler
  • and fetal (intrauterine) transfusion
Anti-D is useless once sensitised.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: Why is anti-D pointless once a woman is already sensitised?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Because anti-D cannot reverse existing sensitisation — once she has made her own anti-D antibodies, giving more is ineffective; prophylaxis is purely preventive.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What antenatal blood tests screen for Rhesus disease?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Booking bloods: ABO group, RhD status, and a red-cell antibody screen (all women); the antibody screen is repeated at ~28 weeks.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What is fetal RHD genotyping (cffDNA), and its benefit (NICE)?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Non-invasive testing of cell-free fetal DNA from ~11–16 weeks to determine the fetal RhD status; if the fetus is RhD-negative, anti-D is unnecessary (sparing ~40% of women).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What is the routine antenatal anti-D prophylaxis (RAADP) regimen?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back:
• Either a two-dose regimen (anti-D at 28 and 34 weeks, 500 IU each)
  • OR a single dose (1500 IU once at 28–30 weeks)

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: How does anti-D prophylaxis work?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: By passive immunisation — 'mopping up' fetal RhD+ cells before the maternal immune system reacts to them.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What postnatal anti-D is given, and when?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: If the baby is RhD-positive, anti-D is given to the RhD-negative mother within 72 hours of delivery.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: When should anti-D be given after a sensitising event, and at what doses?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back:
As soon as possible, within 72 hours. Dose:
  • 250 IU before 20 weeks
  • ≥500 IU from 20 weeks (guided by a Kleihauer test for larger bleeds)

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: List the sensitising events that require anti-D in an RhD-negative woman.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back:
• Delivery of an RhD+ infant
  • miscarriage, threatened miscarriage or ectopic pregnancy from 12⁺⁰ weeks
  • external cephalic version
  • antepartum haemorrhage
  • invasive procedures (amniocentesis, CVS, fetal blood sampling)
  • and abdominal trauma
Below 12 weeks, anti-D is NOT given for miscarriage, threatened miscarriage or ectopic pregnancy — whether managed medically or surgically.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What is the Kleihauer test and its purpose?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Acid is added to maternal blood: adult HbA is eluted while fetal HbF-containing cells resist and stay visible, quantifying the fetomaternal haemorrhage to size the anti-D dose (used from ≥20 weeks/for large bleeds).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What cord blood tests are done on every baby of an RhD-negative mother?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: FBC, blood group, and a direct Coombs test (DAT) — a positive DAT indicates maternal antibodies bound to the baby's red cells.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: What does a positive direct Coombs test (DAT) on cord blood indicate?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Maternal antibodies are bound to the baby's red cells (confirming immune haemolysis / HDFN).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: How is a sensitised pregnancy monitored?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: With serial maternal antibody titres and MCA (middle cerebral artery) Doppler — a raised peak systolic velocity indicates fetal anaemia (non-invasive).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: How is significant fetal anaemia from HDFN treated?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Intrauterine (fetal) blood transfusion.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: How is the neonate with HDFN managed, and what is the severe end?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Phototherapy, exchange transfusion, and IVIG; the severe end is hydrops fetalis.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: Which other red-cell antibodies also cause HDFN, and what is notable about Kell?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Anti-Kell and anti-c; Kell is notable because it suppresses erythropoiesis (as well as causing haemolysis).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.front: Give the reflex on when anti-D is/is not useful.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Me.back: Anti-D prevents sensitisation (given before/around exposure) but does nothing once a woman is already sensitised — then MCA Doppler and intrauterine transfusion are used.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.front: What is the organising principle for malpresentation/malposition?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.back: Determine presentation/lie near term and offer external cephalic version (ECV) where appropriate. Unstable/transverse lie and breech carry cord-prolapse and delivery risks — confirm presentation before labour.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.front: What is breech presentation, and how common is it at term?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.back: The fetus lies with its buttocks or feet (caudal end) presenting to the pelvis rather than the head — a malpresentation complicating ~3–4% of term deliveries. Breech babies have worse outcomes than cephalic babies regardless of delivery mode.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.front: Why is intervention for breech deliberately timed late?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.back: Because the fetus usually turns spontaneously to cephalic as the third trimester progresses (~25% breech at 28 weeks but only ~3–4% at term), so timing gives nature a chance first.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.front: What is the management pathway for breech in one line?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.back: Try to turn it (ECV) → if that fails, decide how to deliver (caesarean vs vaginal breech).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.front: Describe a frank (extended) breech.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.back: Hips flexed with knees extended (legs straight up, feet by the head) — the most common type.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.front: Describe a complete (flexed) breech.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.back: Both the hips and knees are flexed (as if sitting cross-legged).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.front: Describe a footling breech and its significance.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.back: One or both feet present first, with the buttocks higher. It carries the highest cord-prolapse risk and is a contraindication to vaginal breech birth.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.front: What is the natural history of breech presentation?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.back: About 25% of pregnancies are breech at 28 weeks but only ~3–4% at term — most perform a ~180° turn to head-down by ~36 weeks (a 360° turn would return it to breech).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.front: List the risk factors for breech presentation.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.back:
• Uterine abnormalities (malformations, fibroids)
  • placenta praevia
  • polyhydramnios or oligohydramnios
  • fetal abnormality (CNS malformation, chromosomal disorders)
  • prematurity
  • multiple pregnancy
  • and nulliparity.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.front: How is breech presentation diagnosed?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.back: Abdominal palpation (a hard ballotable head at the fundus, an irregular mass in the pelvis, fetal heart higher than expected), confirmed on ultrasound (which also assesses type, growth, liquor and placental position).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.front: How is breech managed before 36 weeks?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.back: Watch and wait — most turn spontaneously to cephalic.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.front: What is external cephalic version (ECV), and when is it offered?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.back: Manual manipulation of the fetus to a cephalic presentation, offered for persistent breech from 36 weeks (nulliparous) / 37 weeks (multiparous), generally performed at/near term (37+0).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.front: What is the success rate of ECV, and what improves it?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.back: Around 50% (higher in multiparous women; <5% revert). Tocolysis (terbutaline 250 micrograms subcutaneously) improves success. ECV reduces the caesarean rate. Give anti-D 500 IU IM to RhD-negative women afterwards, successful or not, with CTG before and after.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.front: Why is ECV performed where caesarean is available?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.back: Because there is about a 1 in 200 risk of needing an emergency caesarean immediately afterwards.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.front: List the contraindications to ECV.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.back:
• Caesarean already indicated for another reason
  • antepartum haemorrhage in the last 7 days
  • abnormal CTG
  • major uterine anomaly
  • ruptured membranes
  • placenta praevia
  • and multiple pregnancy (except delivery of a second twin).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.front: What is the recommended mode of delivery for a persistent breech at term, and why?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.back: Planned caesarean reduces perinatal mortality compared with planned vaginal breech, and is what most UK women choose — though the absolute risk is low either way (about 2 per 1000 with planned vaginal breech vs about 0.5 per 1000 with planned caesarean).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.front: Is vaginal breech birth ever an option, and what is an absolute contraindication?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.back: Yes — planned vaginal breech remains an option for selected women with an experienced attendant, but footling breech is a contraindication.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.front: Why do breech babies do worse regardless of delivery mode?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.back: Because the underlying cause of the breech (e.g. fetal abnormality, uterine anomaly) partly drives the poorer outcomes, independent of how the baby is delivered.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.front: What are the delivery-related complications of vaginal breech birth?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.back:
• Cord prolapse (especially footling — the presenting part doesn't fill the pelvis)
  • head entrapment
  • birth trauma
  • and hypoxia.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.front: Why must breech babies be screened for developmental dysplasia of the hip (DDH)?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.back: Because breech presentation is a major risk factor for DDH, so these babies need hip ultrasound screening.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.front: What is fetal lie, and what is normal?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.back: The relationship of the long axis of the fetus to the long axis of the uterus; the normal lie is longitudinal.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.front: Why does an abnormal (transverse/oblique) lie matter?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.back: Because you cannot deliver a transverse baby vaginally, and if the membranes rupture the cord (or an arm) can prolapse — an emergency. It is rare at term (<0.3%).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.front: What is the organising principle for abnormal lie?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.back: An abnormal lie is only a problem at term/in labour — before that it is usually transient and self-correcting. Management follows a timeline: watch early → intervene near term → prevent the cord-prolapse catastrophe.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.front: How is abnormal lie managed before 36 weeks?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.back: No management — most spontaneously revert to longitudinal; reassure.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.front: How is abnormal lie managed at ≥36–37 weeks (term)?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.back:
• Refer to the obstetric team
  • investigate for a cause
  • consider ECV
  • arrange elective admission to guard against cord prolapse
  • and plan delivery.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.front: Define transverse, oblique and unstable lie.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.back:
• Transverse lie: fetal long axis perpendicular (head one lateral side, buttocks the other; scapulo-anterior commonest).
  • Oblique lie: fetal long axis at an angle (head/buttocks in one iliac fossa).
  • Unstable lie: the lie keeps changing near term (classically the multiparous, lax uterus).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.front: List the risk factors for abnormal lie.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.back:
• Multiparity (lax uterus — classic cause of unstable lie)
  • polyhydramnios (fetus floats freely)
  • prematurity
  • multiple pregnancy
  • uterine abnormalities/fibroids/pelvic tumours
  • placenta praevia (blocks engagement)
  • and fetal abnormalities.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.front: What should an abnormal lie at term prompt a search for?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.back: An underlying cause — especially placenta praevia and fibroids/pelvic mass — as it is often not just chance.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.front: How is abnormal lie diagnosed?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.back: Abdominal examination (neither head nor buttocks at the fundus/pelvis; the fetus felt lying across; a high/absent presenting part), with ultrasound confirming the lie and looking for a cause.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.front: What is the key management step for transverse/oblique/unstable lie at term, and why?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.back: Elective admission from ~37 weeks — because labour or membrane rupture can happen any time, and an abnormal lie with ruptured membranes carries a high cord-prolapse risk; inpatient care allows immediate caesarean.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.front: What advice is given to a woman in the community with an abnormal lie near term?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.back: To present urgently if contractions start or the waters break.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.front: Can ECV be attempted for abnormal lie, and what limits it?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.back: It may be attempted to convert to cephalic (late pregnancy or early labour, if membranes are intact), but abnormal/unstable lie tends to revert, so ECV alone is often insufficient. Contraindications are as for breech.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.front: How is a persistent transverse/oblique lie delivered?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.back: Elective caesarean for a persistent abnormal lie, ECV failure/contraindication/preference; a persistent abnormal lie in labour requires immediate caesarean (a transverse baby cannot deliver vaginally).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.front: How is ruptured membranes with an abnormal lie managed?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.back: Expedite delivery by caesarean (high cord-prolapse risk).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.front: What is 'stabilising induction'?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.back: A specialist option for selected unstable lie — ECV to cephalic followed immediately by amniotomy and oxytocin, performed in theatre with caesarean standby.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.front: What is the major danger of abnormal lie, and when is it highest?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.back: Cord prolapse — because the presenting part does not fill the pelvis; the risk is highest at membrane rupture.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.front: What is the feared end-point of a neglected transverse lie?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.back: Obstructed labour leading to uterine rupture.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.front: Why should ARM (amniotomy) be avoided with a high/mobile presenting part in abnormal lie?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.back: Because it risks cord or arm prolapse at amniotomy.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.front: Which patient classically has an unstable lie?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.back: A multiparous woman with a lax uterus.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.front: What four interventions/complications does the 'labour interventions & complications' topic cover?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.back:
• Induction of labour
  • assisted (instrumental) vaginal birth
  • caesarean section
  • and perineal trauma (tears)
— each with clear indications, methods and risks, where consent, documentation, and anticipating complications (perineal tears, VTE, PPH) matter.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.front: What is induction of labour (IOL)?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.back: Artificial initiation of labour before it starts spontaneously — used when continuing the pregnancy poses more risk than delivering.It occurs in ~1 in 3 UK births.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.front: What single question governs the whole approach to induction of labour?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.back: Is the cervix ready? — assessed by the Bishop score, which dictates the method.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.front: What is the two-part core principle of induction of labour?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.back:
You cannot force labour on a closed, unfavourable cervix without ripening it first — so IOL is:
  • (1) ripen the cervix
  • then (2) stimulate contractions.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.front: What does the Bishop score assess, and what are its components?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.back:
Cervical readiness on vaginal examination. Components:
  • cervical dilatation
  • effacement/length
  • consistency
  • position
  • and station of the presenting part.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.front: What does a Bishop score of ≤6 indicate and imply?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.back: An unfavourable ('unripe') cervix — it needs cervical ripening first (prostaglandin or mechanical).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.front: What does a Bishop score of >6 indicate and imply?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.back: A favourable ('ripe') cervix — ready for amniotomy (ARM) plus oxytocin.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.front: List the indications for induction of labour.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.back:
• Prolonged pregnancy (commonest — offer at 41–42 weeks to reduce stillbirth)
  • prelabour rupture of membranes at term (reduce infection)
  • maternal conditions (pre-eclampsia/hypertension, diabetes, obstetric cholestasis)
  • fetal growth restriction/concerning surveillance
  • intrauterine fetal death
  • and twin/complicated pregnancy.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.front: What is a membrane sweep, and when is it offered?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.back: An adjunct (not formal IOL) offered from ~39–41 weeks to promote spontaneous labour.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.front: What is the standard first-line agent for cervical ripening (Bishop ≤6)?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.back: Vaginal dinoprostone (PGE2) — as a tablet/gel/controlled-release pessary;low-dose oral misoprostol (25 microgram) is an alternative.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.front: When are mechanical methods (balloon catheter/osmotic dilator) used for induction, and their advantage?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.back: When pharmacological ripening is unsuitable (hyperstimulation risk, previous caesarean); they cause less hyperstimulation than prostaglandins.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.front: What is the method of induction when the cervix is favourable (Bishop >6)?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.back: Amniotomy (ARM) plus IV oxytocin (Syntocinon), titrated to about 4 contractions per 10 minutes.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.front: Why is ARM ± oxytocin not the primary method on an unfavourable cervix?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.back: Because an unripe cervix must first be ripened (with prostaglandin or mechanical methods); ARM ± oxytocin is reserved for a favourable cervix.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.front: What monitoring is used during active induction of labour?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.back:
• Bishop score before and during
  • continuous CTG during active induction (prostaglandin/oxytocin) to detect fetal distress and hyperstimulation
  • and watching contraction frequency on oxytocin.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.front: What is uterine hyperstimulation, the key IOL complication?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.back: Excessive contraction frequency/duration reducing placental perfusion and causing fetal distress (rarely uterine rupture).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.front: How is uterine hyperstimulation managed?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.back:
• Stop/remove the inducing agent (remove the pessary, stop oxytocin)
  • consider tocolysis (terbutaline 250 micrograms subcutaneously)
  • continue continuous CTG
  • and escalate.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.front: List other complications of induction of labour.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.back:
• Failed induction (→ re-attempt ripening or caesarean)
  • cord prolapse at amniotomy (especially with a high presenting part)
  • more instrumental/caesarean delivery
  • postpartum haemorrhage (atony after prolonged oxytocin)
  • infection (prolonged ROM)
  • and often more painful labour than spontaneous.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.front: What is the oxytocin contraction target during induction?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.back: About 4 contractions per 10 minutes.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.front: When is induction offered for prolonged pregnancy, and why?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.back: At 41–42 weeks, to reduce the risk of stillbirth.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.front: List the contraindications/cautions to induction (favouring caesarean).
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.back:
• Placenta praevia, vasa praevia, cord presentation
  • transverse/abnormal lie or malpresentation
  • previous classical (vertical) caesarean or significant uterine surgery
  • and active primary genital herpes.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.front: Why are prostaglandins used cautiously with a previous caesarean scar?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.back: Because of the uterine-rupture risk; mechanical methods (balloon) are often preferred in this situation as they cause less hyperstimulation.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.front: Why does amniotomy risk cord prolapse, especially with a high presenting part?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.back: Because rupturing the membranes with a high, poorly-applied presenting part can allow the cord to descend below it (cord prolapse).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.front: What is a caesarean section, and the two frameworks that dominate it?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.back: Delivery through incisions in the abdominal wall and uterus rather than vaginally. Two frameworks dominate: the urgency categories (1–4, how fast to deliver) and the anatomical layers crossed;VBAC (whether she can deliver vaginally next time) sits around it.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.front: What defines a Category 1 caesarean and its decision-to-delivery target?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.back: An immediate threat to the life of the mother or baby ('crash'); delivery within 30 minutes.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.front: What defines a Category 2 caesarean and its target?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.back: Maternal/fetal compromise that is not immediately life-threatening; delivery within 75 minutes (though acute fetal compromise is pushed toward 30 minutes where possible).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.front: What defines a Category 3 caesarean?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.back: Delivery is needed but mother and baby are stable — no fixed time, but expedited.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.front: What defines a Category 4 caesarean?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.back: Elective (planned, no urgency) — timed to suit the mother and service.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.front: List the triggers for a Category 1 caesarean.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.back:
• Suspected uterine rupture
  • major placental abruption
  • cord prolapse
  • fetal hypoxia
  • and persistent fetal bradycardia.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.front: What is the nuance about the 75-minute Category 2 target?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.back: 75 minutes is the Category 2 audit standard, but for confirmed/suspected acute fetal compromise, delivery is pushed toward 30 minutes where possible.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.front: What is a lower segment caesarean section (LSCS), and why is it preferred?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.back: A transverse incision in the lower uterine segment (~99% of caesareans) — it has a lower future-rupture risk, less bleeding, and better healing.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.front: What is a classical caesarean, its indications, and its key drawback?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.back: A longitudinal (vertical) upper-segment incision — used for very preterm delivery, some transverse lie, anterior praevia/accreta, or obstructing fibroids. It has a higher future rupture risk and contraindicates VBAC.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.front: Which abdominal muscle is NOT cut during a caesarean, and how is it handled?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.back: The rectus abdominis — it is not cut but separated and pushed laterally after opening the linea alba.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.front: List the anatomical layers crossed in a caesarean (in order).
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.back: Skin/fascia → anterior rectus sheath (incised) → rectus abdominis (separated, not cut) → transversalis fascia → extraperitoneal connective tissue → peritoneum → uterus (with the bladder reflected inferiorly off the lower segment before the uterine incision).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.front: List the maternal indications for caesarean section.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.back:
• Previous caesarean (especially classical)
  • maternal request
  • obstructing fibroids
  • active primary genital herpes
  • and cardiac/medical disease.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.front: List the fetal indications for caesarean section.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.back:
• Breech
  • transverse/abnormal lie
  • fetal compromise
  • and a twin pregnancy with a non-cephalic first twin.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.front: List the placental indications for caesarean section.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.back:
• Placenta praevia (the placenta covering the internal os — the grade I–IV and major/minor terms are no longer used)
  • placenta accreta
  • and vasa praevia.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.front: List labour-related indications for caesarean section.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.back:
• Failure to progress
  • cord prolapse
  • and previous severe shoulder dystocia.
HIV is an antenatal planning decision rather than a labour indication: vaginal birth is supported at a viral load <50 copies/mL, caesarean is considered at 50–399, and recommended at ≥400 or if the load is unknown.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.front: When is planned VBAC appropriate?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.back: At ≥37 weeks with a single previous lower-segment caesarean.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.front: When is VBAC contraindicated?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.back: With a previous uterine rupture or a previous classical (vertical) scar.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.front: What is the main serious risk of VBAC, and its approximate absolute risk and success rate?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.back: Uterine rupture (higher than with elective repeat caesarean but low in absolute terms, ~0.5%); VBAC success is ~72–75%.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.front: How does induction/augmentation affect VBAC?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.back: It raises the risk of uterine rupture, so prostaglandins are used cautiously.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.front: List the intra-operative and post-operative complications of caesarean.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.back:
Intra-operative:
  • haemorrhage
  • bladder/bowel/ureteric injury
  • incision extension.
Post-operative:
  • infection (wound, endometritis, UTI)
  • VTE (thromboprophylaxis needed)
  • and ileus.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.front: What are the future-pregnancy risks after a caesarean?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.back:
• Uterine rupture
  • placenta praevia/accreta (scar implantation)
  • repeat caesarean
  • and adhesions.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.front: What neonatal complications are associated with caesarean?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.back: Transient tachypnoea of the newborn, and iatrogenic prematurity if the dates are wrong.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.front: Why does placenta praevia/accreta risk rise with each caesarean?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.back: Because of scar implantation — the placenta can implant abnormally over the uterine scar, increasing the risk with each successive caesarean.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.front: What is a perineal tear, and what determines its grade?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.back: A laceration between the vagina and anus during vaginal delivery. The grade is defined by which structure the tear reaches — skin → muscle → anal sphincter → rectal mucosa — and the grade dictates where and by whom it is repaired.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.front: Describe a first-degree perineal tear and its management.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.back: Injury to skin/superficial tissue only, with no muscle involvement. It often heals without suturing if the skin edges are well opposed; suture it if they are not, or if it is bleeding.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.front: Describe a second-degree perineal tear and its management.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.back: Injury to the perineal muscle but NOT the anal sphincter; sutured on the ward.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.front: Describe a third-degree perineal tear and where it is repaired.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.back: Injury involving the anal sphincter complex (external anal sphincter ± internal anal sphincter); repaired in THEATRE.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.front: Describe a fourth-degree perineal tear and where it is repaired.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.back: Injury involving the anal sphincter complex PLUS the rectal (anorectal) mucosa; repaired in THEATRE.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.front: What is OASIS?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.back: Obstetric Anal Sphincter Injury — third- and fourth-degree tears. Everything below the sphincter (1st/2nd degree) is repaired on the ward; sphincter involvement or beyond goes to theatre.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.front: What is the RCOG subclassification of third-degree tears?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.back:
• 3a: <50% of the external anal sphincter (EAS) thickness torn
  • 3b: >50% of EAS thickness torn
  • 3c: both EAS and internal anal sphincter (IAS) torn

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.front: What is the rule if you are unsure about the grade of a third-degree tear?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.back: If in doubt, classify it HIGHER.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.front: What is a 'buttonhole' tear, and why is it a trap?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.back: A tear of the rectal mucosa with an INTACT anal sphincter — it is NOT a fourth-degree tear/OASIS but a separate entity, documented separately.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.front: What is the strongest risk factor for OASIS?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.back: Being a primigravida/first vaginal birth (OASIS ~6% in primips vs ~1.7% in multips).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.front: List the risk factors for perineal tears/OASIS.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.back:
• Primigravida (strongest)
  • large baby (macrosomia)
  • precipitate labour
  • shoulder dystocia
  • instrumental delivery (especially forceps > ventouse)
  • prolonged second stage
  • and occipito-posterior position

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.front: Which instrumental delivery carries a higher OASIS risk, forceps or ventouse?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.back: Forceps carries a higher OASIS risk than ventouse.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.front: How is a third- or fourth-degree tear (OASIS) repaired?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.back: In theatre, under regional/general anaesthesia, by a trained clinician. For a full-thickness external anal sphincter tear, end-to-end or overlap repair are equivalent; for a partial-thickness tear (all 3a and some 3b) an end-to-end technique must be used, since overlap requires a complete tear to mobilise the ends. The internal anal sphincter is repaired separately, end-to-end.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.front: What is the post-OASIS management?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.back:
• Broad-spectrum antibiotics
  • laxatives (to reduce dehiscence — NOT a routine bulking agent)
  • physiotherapy
  • a digital rectal examination after repair
  • and perineal-clinic follow-up (to discuss future delivery mode)

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.front: Which laxative approach is used after OASIS, and what is avoided?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.back: Laxatives are given to reduce wound dehiscence; a routine bulking agent is NOT used.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.front: What type of episiotomy is used to help prevent OASIS, and its angle?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.back: A mediolateral episiotomy (~60° from the midline, NOT midline), where indicated — it reduces OASIS, especially in instrumental delivery.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.front: What other measures help prevent perineal trauma during crowning?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.back: Perineal support ('hands-on') with a warm compress during crowning, and controlled delivery of the head.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.front: What is the OASI Care Bundle?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.back: The national quality initiative aimed at reducing obstetric anal sphincter injuries.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.front: List the short-term complications of perineal tears.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.back:
• Bleeding
  • infection
  • wound dehiscence
  • pain
  • and urinary retention

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.front: List the important long-term complications of perineal tears.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.back:
• Faecal urgency/incontinence
  • flatus incontinence
  • dyspareunia
  • perineal pain
  • rectovaginal fistula (with 4th-degree tears)
  • and psychological impact

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.front: What is the feared long-term complication of OASIS?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.back: Faecal incontinence.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.front: What is assisted (operative) vaginal birth?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.back: Using a ventouse (vacuum) or forceps to help deliver the baby's head in the second stage of labour. It sits between spontaneous vaginal birth and caesarean — shortening a second stage that has become unsafe, while avoiding the extra morbidity of a caesarean at full dilatation.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.front: What are the fetal and maternal indications for assisted vaginal birth?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.back: Fetal: suspected fetal compromise (an abnormal CTG). Maternal: delay in the second stage, or maternal exhaustion.
