There is also a group in whom pushing (Valsalva) should be avoided — maternal cardiac disease, severe hypertension, myasthenia gravis, or spinal cord injury.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.front: What does the FORCEPS mnemonic stand for?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.back:
The prerequisites for assisted vaginal birth:
  • Fully dilated cervix
  • OA position (and above all the position must be known)
  • Ruptured membranes
  • Cephalic presentation
  • Engaged head
  • Pain relief adequate
  • Sphincter (bladder) empty

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.front: How engaged must the head be before an assisted vaginal birth?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.back: No more than 1/5 palpable abdominally, with the station at or below the ischial spines.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.front: What should happen if one of the FORCEPS prerequisites is not met?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.back: The birth should be by caesarean section. The prerequisites are not negotiable — attempting an instrument without them risks serious maternal and fetal injury.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.front: Why must the fetal position be known before an assisted vaginal birth?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.back: Because instrument placement depends on it, and misplacement causes injury. If the position is uncertain on vaginal examination, ultrasound should be used to determine it.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.front: Besides the FORCEPS prerequisites, what else must be in place?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.back:
• Informed consent
  • an appropriately experienced operator
  • adequate facilities
  • a clear plan if the attempt fails
  • and neonatal resuscitation available

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.front: When should an assisted vaginal birth be attempted in theatre rather than the delivery room?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.back: When failure is more likely — a mid-cavity or occipito-posterior position, a suspected large baby, or a high maternal BMI. This is a 'trial' in theatre so that caesarean can follow immediately if it fails.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.front: Compare ventouse and forceps for success and maternal trauma.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.back: Ventouse is more likely to fail but causes less maternal trauma (fewer third/fourth-degree tears). Forceps has a higher success rate but causes more maternal trauma and is the leading instrumental risk factor for OASIS. In short: ventouse spares the mother, forceps spares the baby.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.front: Which neonatal injuries are associated with ventouse?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.back:
• Cephalhaematoma
  • retinal haemorrhage
  • neonatal jaundice (from a resolving cephalhaematoma)
  • and — the dangerous one — subgaleal haemorrhage

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.front: Which neonatal injuries are associated with forceps?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.back:
• Facial nerve palsy
  • facial bruising and marks from the blades
  • and skull fracture

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.front: What is the rule about ventouse in preterm birth?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.back: Ventouse should be avoided below 32 weeks and used with caution between 32⁺⁰ and 36⁺⁰ weeks, because of the risk of subgaleal and intracranial haemorrhage. Forceps is the preferred instrument at preterm gestations.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.front: What is the golden rule about using two different instruments?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.back: Do NOT use sequential instruments. Swapping from a failed ventouse to forceps sharply increases the risk of intracranial and subgaleal haemorrhage. If the first instrument fails, the next step is caesarean, not another instrument.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.front: When should an attempt at assisted vaginal birth be abandoned?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.back: If there is no descent with each pull, or if the baby is not delivered after three contractions/pulls by an experienced operator. Abandoning early and moving to caesarean is the safe decision, not a failure.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.front: What is a subgaleal haemorrhage, and why is it dangerous?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.back: Bleeding between the epicranial aponeurosis and the periosteum. That space crosses suture lines, so it can accommodate the neonate's entire blood volume — the baby can exsanguinate. It occurs predominantly after ventouse.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.front: How does subgaleal haemorrhage present, and how is it distinguished from cephalhaematoma?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.back: Subgaleal: a boggy, fluctuant, spreading swelling that CROSSES suture lines, with pallor, tachycardia and shock. Cephalhaematoma: subperiosteal, does NOT cross suture lines, and is self-limiting. Any baby after a difficult or failed ventouse must be observed for subgaleal bleeding.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.front: What are the maternal complications of assisted vaginal birth?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.back:
• Obstetric anal sphincter injury (forceps more than ventouse)
  • vaginal and cervical trauma
  • postpartum haemorrhage
  • urinary retention
  • VTE
  • and pain

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.front: What antibiotic prophylaxis is given after an assisted vaginal birth?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.back: A single dose of prophylactic co-amoxiclav after every assisted vaginal birth — it roughly halves maternal infection and is now recommended (RCOG).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.front: What aftercare follows an assisted vaginal birth?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.back:
• A single prophylactic antibiotic dose
  • VTE risk assessment
  • bladder care with documented voiding
  • analgesia
  • and a debrief covering what happened and what it means for future births

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.front: What should a woman be told about future births after an assisted vaginal birth?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.back: That most women who have had an assisted vaginal birth go on to have a spontaneous vaginal birth next time. This should be covered in the postnatal debrief.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.front: What is the organising principle for intrapartum emergencies?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.back: Recognise the emergency and act on a rehearsed protocol. Cord prolapse and shoulder dystocia are the classic 'call for help now' scenarios — time-critical, needing immediate senior help.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.front: What is umbilical cord prolapse?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.back: An obstetric emergency where the umbilical cord descends below the presenting part AFTER the membranes rupture, exposing it to compression and cold — leading to fetal hypoxia, and potentially death or hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy within minutes.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.front: What are the two mechanisms by which cord prolapse harms the fetus?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.back: (1) Mechanical compression of the cord between the presenting part and the pelvis, and (2) cold/handling-induced arterial vasospasm — both cut off fetal blood flow.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.front: What is cord presentation, and how does it differ from cord prolapse?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.back: Cord presentation is when the cord lies between the presenting part and the cervix with INTACT membranes (a warning, not the emergency); cord prolapse requires RUPTURED membranes.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.front: Distinguish overt from occult cord prolapse.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.back:
Both occur with ruptured membranes.
  • Overt: the cord descends PAST the presenting part (into/through the cervix/vagina, may be visible).
  • Occult: the cord descends ALONGSIDE (not past) the presenting part.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.front: What is the classic clinical trigger to exclude cord prolapse?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.back: Sudden fetal bradycardia or an abnormal CTG immediately after the membranes rupture (especially after artificial rupture of membranes/amniotomy) → perform a vaginal exam to exclude cord prolapse.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.front: List the risk factors for cord prolapse.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.back:
• Abnormal lie/presentation (transverse/unstable lie, breech)
  • prematurity (small presenting part)
  • polyhydramnios (gush sweeps the cord down)
  • multiple pregnancy (especially the second twin)
  • high/unengaged presenting part
  • multiparity
  • a long umbilical cord
  • low-lying placenta
  • and iatrogenic causes (ARM with a high presenting part, balloon catheter, external cephalic version).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.front: How is cord prolapse diagnosed?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.back: A palpable cord on vaginal examination, or a visible cord at the introitus, after rupture of membranes; and/or a fetal heart abnormality (sudden bradycardia or variable decelerations), especially right after rupture of membranes.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.front: What is the overall goal of managing cord prolapse?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.back: Relieve cord compression and deliver immediately, while calling for senior obstetric, anaesthetic and neonatal help and preparing for immediate caesarean.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.front: How is the presenting part manually managed in cord prolapse?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.back: Manually elevate the presenting part with a gloved hand in the vagina, pushing it UP off the cord, and hold it continuously until delivery.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.front: What maternal positions relieve cord compression in cord prolapse?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.back: Knee-chest, face down — kneeling with the chest and head down on the bed and the buttocks elevated, which gives the greatest elevation of the presenting part. This is NOT the all-fours position. The alternative is exaggerated Sims/left lateral with the hips elevated (head-down).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.front: What is bladder filling in cord prolapse, and when is it useful?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.back: Instilling ~500 mL of warm saline via a Foley catheter to elevate the presenting part (empty it before delivery); useful if delivery or transfer is delayed.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.front: Why must cord handling be minimised in cord prolapse, and should the cord be replaced?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.back: Handling/cold provokes arterial vasospasm, worsening hypoxia; keep the cord warm/moist and do NOT forcibly replace it.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.front: What medication changes are made in cord prolapse?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.back: Stop oxytocin; consider tocolysis (terbutaline 0.25 mg subcutaneously) if there is fetal compromise and delivery is delayed.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.front: What is the default mode of delivery for cord prolapse, and the alternative?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.back: Category 1 emergency caesarean (deliver within 30 minutes); instrumental vaginal delivery if the cervix is fully dilated and delivery is imminent.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.front: How should cord prolapse be managed in the community (e.g. planned home birth)?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.back: Advise a knee-chest position by phone, call 999, and elevate the presenting part; midwives carry a Foley catheter for bladder filling.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.front: Which position is preferred for ambulance transfer of a woman with cord prolapse, and why?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.back: Exaggerated Sims (not knee-chest), because knee-chest is unsafe in a moving ambulance.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.front: What are the main complications of cord prolapse?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.back: Fetal hypoxia leading to hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy, cerebral palsy, or death; outcomes are worse with prematurity, congenital malformation, and delay in transfer (especially planned home births).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.front: Why does a high or unengaged presenting part predispose to cord prolapse?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.back: Because a poorly-applied presenting part leaves a gap through which the cord can descend below it.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.front: What is shoulder dystocia?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.back: An obstetric emergency where, after the head delivers, the anterior shoulder becomes impacted behind the maternal pubic symphysis and gentle axial traction fails to release it. It is a bony impaction, not a soft-tissue problem.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.front: What is the formal definition of shoulder dystocia?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.back: A vaginal cephalic delivery that requires additional obstetric manoeuvres after gentle axial traction fails (head-to-body delivery prolonged, classically >60 seconds).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.front: Why is shoulder dystocia time-critical?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.back: Once the head is out, the cord is compressed and the chest cannot expand, so the baby faces rapid hypoxia (~47% of shoulder-dystocia deaths occur within 5 minutes of the head delivering).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.front: Why does simply pulling harder fail (and harm) in shoulder dystocia?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.back: Because it is a bony impaction (shoulder vs pubic symphysis); manoeuvres work by changing pelvic geometry or rotating/reducing the shoulder diameter, whereas excessive/downward traction worsens it and causes brachial plexus injury.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.front: What is the 'turtle-neck' sign?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.back: The fetal head delivers and then RETRACTS back against the perineum, with failure of restitution and failure of the shoulders to deliver with routine traction — a sign of shoulder dystocia.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.front: List the risk factors for shoulder dystocia, and note about prediction.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.back:
• Pre-labour: macrosomia, maternal diabetes (most important associated factor), obesity/excess weight gain, previous shoulder dystocia (strong recurrence), post-dates.
  • Intrapartum: prolonged first/second stage, instrumental delivery, oxytocin augmentation.
However, prediction is POOR and most cases are unpredictable.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.front: What does the HELPERR mnemonic stand for?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.back:
• H – call for Help
  • E – Evaluate for Episiotomy
  • L – Legs (McRoberts')
  • P – suprapubic Pressure
  • E – Enter (internal rotation manoeuvres)
  • R – Remove the posterior arm
  • R – Roll (all-fours/Gaskin).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.front: What is the first-line manoeuvre for shoulder dystocia and how is it performed?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.back: McRoberts' manoeuvre — lay the woman flat, remove pillows, and hyperflex the hips (knees to chest) with an assistant each side. It rotates the symphysis upward to free the shoulder; ~90% effective and least invasive, so always first.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.front: How is suprapubic pressure applied in shoulder dystocia?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.back: An assistant applies suprapubic pressure over the anterior shoulder (downward and lateral, 'CPR-style') to push it under the symphysis, combined with McRoberts'.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.front: What is the role of episiotomy in shoulder dystocia?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.back: It does NOT relieve the bony impaction but creates room for internal (vaginal) manoeuvres.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.front: What are the internal rotation manoeuvres for shoulder dystocia?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.back: Rubin II (push the posterior aspect of the anterior shoulder toward the fetal chest) and Woods' screw (press the anterior aspect of the posterior shoulder, rotating the shoulders in the opposite direction to Rubin II, up to 180°), performed with a hand inserted vaginally.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.front: Why is delivering the posterior arm effective in shoulder dystocia?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.back: Sweeping the posterior arm across the chest and out reduces the shoulder diameter, freeing the impaction — it is a highly effective manoeuvre.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.front: What is the 'Roll' (Gaskin) manoeuvre?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.back: Moving the woman onto her hands and knees ('all-fours') and re-attempting delivery/manoeuvres.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.front: What must NEVER be done in shoulder dystocia, and why?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.back:
• Do NOT apply fundal pressure (worsens impaction and risks uterine rupture)
  • do NOT apply excessive/downward traction on the head (the main cause of brachial plexus injury — use only routine axial traction)
  • and discourage maternal pushing.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.front: What are the third-line/last-resort options if all manoeuvres fail?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.back:
• Cleidotomy (deliberate clavicle fracture)
  • symphysiotomy
  • or the Zavanelli manoeuvre (replace the head into the uterus and perform emergency caesarean).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.front: What is the Zavanelli manoeuvre?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.back: A last-resort manoeuvre in which the fetal head is replaced into the uterus, followed by emergency caesarean section.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.front: What are the main fetal complications of shoulder dystocia?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.back:
• Brachial plexus injury (Erb's palsy C5–C6 = 'waiter's tip', common and usually resolving; Klumpke's palsy C8–T1 = 'claw hand', rarer)
  • fractures (clavicle and humerus)
  • and hypoxia leading to hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy or death.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.front: What is Erb's palsy and its cause?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.back: A brachial plexus injury of C5–C6 producing the 'waiter's tip' posture; it is a common consequence of shoulder dystocia (often from excessive non-axial traction — downward or lateral) and usually resolves.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.front: What is Klumpke's palsy?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.back: A brachial plexus injury of C8–T1 producing a 'claw hand'; it is rarer than Erb's palsy.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.front: What are the main maternal complications of shoulder dystocia?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.back: Postpartum haemorrhage and perineal/third-fourth-degree tears (the main risks); also symphyseal separation/femoral neuropathy from McRoberts'.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.front: What must be documented after a shoulder dystocia?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.back:
• The time of head and body delivery
  • the manoeuvres performed and their order
  • which shoulder was anterior
  • cord gases
  • and the staff present (medicolegal importance).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.front: Which classic combination of factors is associated with shoulder dystocia, though most cases are unpredictable?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.back: Maternal diabetes and macrosomia (a large baby).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.front: What is the central goal of HIV management in pregnancy, and how effective is it?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.back: Preventing vertical (mother-to-child) transmission. With the full UK care bundle, vertical transmission is <0.5% (down from ~25% untreated).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.front: At what three points can vertical transmission of HIV occur, and which is the biggest risk?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.back:
• In utero (via the placenta)
  • intrapartum (exposure to maternal blood/secretions at delivery — the BIGGEST risk)
  • and postnatally (breastfeeding).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.front: Which single number drives HIV management decisions in pregnancy?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.back: The maternal viral load.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.front: What mode of delivery and neonatal PEP apply when maternal viral load is <50 copies/mL at ~36 weeks?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.back: Vaginal delivery is supported, and the low-risk infant usually receives zidovudine monotherapy (short course).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.front: What is advised when maternal viral load is 50–399 copies/mL at ~36 weeks?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.back: Consider caesarean delivery, with higher-risk (combination) neonatal PEP.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.front: What is advised when maternal viral load is ≥400 copies/mL at ~36 weeks?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.back: Planned caesarean is recommended, with higher-risk (combination) neonatal PEP.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.front: Why is an undetectable viral load (<50) the target in HIV pregnancy?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.back: Because it makes vaginal birth safe and minimises neonatal treatment; a detectable/high viral load shifts management toward caesarean and intensified infant prophylaxis.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.front: How is HIV screening offered in pregnancy?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.back: HIV testing is offered to ALL pregnant women at booking on an opt-out basis, alongside hepatitis B and syphilis screening; this universal screening underpins the low UK transmission rate.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.front: What should happen with a late-presenting or untested woman in labour regarding HIV?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.back: Urgent point-of-care HIV testing.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.front: Which pregnant women with HIV should take antiretroviral therapy (ART), and for how long?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.back: ALL pregnant women with HIV take combination ART, for life, regardless of CD4 count or viral load.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.front: How is ART managed for a woman already on effective treatment at conception vs newly diagnosed?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.back: If already on effective ART, continue it; if newly diagnosed, start ART as soon as possible to suppress the virus before delivery.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.front: Give a typical ART regimen used in pregnancy.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.back: Tenofovir + emtricitabine (or abacavir + lamivudine) plus a third agent, often dolutegravir.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.front: What determines the mode of delivery in HIV pregnancy?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.back:
The maternal viral load at ~36 weeks:
  • <50 → vaginal supported
  • ≥400 → planned caesarean
  • 50–399 → consider caesarean.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.front: When is an intrapartum IV zidovudine infusion used?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.back: If a caesarean is being done for viral-load reasons, or in higher-risk labour (detectable viral load).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.front: Which intrapartum procedures should be avoided if the mother is not virally suppressed?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.back:
• Fetal scalp electrodes
  • fetal blood sampling
  • and instrumental delivery.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.front: What neonatal post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) does an HIV-exposed infant receive, and when?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.back: Every exposed infant receives antiretroviral PEP within 4 hours of birth — zidovudine monotherapy (~2–4 weeks) if the mother is low-risk (<50), or combination PEP if higher-risk (detectable/unknown viral load).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.front: What is the UK default for infant feeding in HIV, and why?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.back: Formula feeding — it eliminates the breastfeeding transmission route.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.front: Under what circumstances does BHIVA support breastfeeding in HIV?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.back:
If strict criteria are met —
  • the mother is fully suppressed (<50)
  • has good adherence
  • is engaged with the MDT
  • and has monthly viral-load monitoring (mother and baby).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.front: How is HIV diagnosed in an exposed infant, and why not antibody testing?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.back: With HIV PCR (viral test), because maternal antibodies persist in the infant for about 18 months, making antibody testing unreliable early on.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.front: Which HIV transmission route does neonatal PEP primarily target, and which does formula feeding target?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.back: Neonatal PEP addresses residual intrapartum/in-utero exposure; formula feeding eliminates the postnatal breastfeeding route (while ART/viral suppression and delivery planning address the in-utero and intrapartum routes).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.front: What is chickenpox in pregnancy, and why does it threaten two patients?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.back: Primary infection with varicella-zoster virus (VZV) in a susceptible woman. It threatens the mother (varicella is far more dangerous in adults/pregnancy — pneumonia, hepatitis, encephalitis) and the fetus/neonate (fetal varicella syndrome or neonatal varicella).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.front: Why are most chickenpox exposures in pregnancy harmless?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.back: Because ~90% of UK adults are already immune, so danger is confined to the non-immune (seronegative) minority.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.front: How is VZV transmitted, and can shingles transmit it?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.back: It is highly contagious via droplets/contact; shingles can transmit varicella (chickenpox) to a non-immune person via vesicle contact.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.front: Why is the varicella vaccine contraindicated in pregnancy?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.back: Because it is a live (attenuated) vaccine.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.front: What is the first step when a pregnant woman is exposed to chickenpox?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.back:
Determine immunity:
  • prior chickenpox or 2 doses of vaccine → reassure
  • if no/uncertain history → check VZV IgG serology urgently, and if seronegative proceed to management.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.front: What is the management of a susceptible pregnant woman EXPOSED to chickenpox but with NO rash yet?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.back: Post-exposure prophylaxis — antiviral-first: oral aciclovir 800 mg QDS from days 7–14 after exposure (valaciclovir an alternative). If she cannot take oral antivirals, discuss immunoglobulin with virology; VZIG itself is withdrawn in the UK.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.front: What is the single most-tested trap about VZIG in chickenpox?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.back: VZIG is useless once the rash is out — it is a prophylactic, not a treatment. Established chickenpox is treated with aciclovir, never VZIG.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.front: How is a pregnant woman who has DEVELOPED the chickenpox rash managed?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.back: Oral aciclovir 800 mg five times daily for 7 days if within 24h of onset AND ≥20 weeks (caution/counsel if <20 weeks) — note this differs from the 800 mg QDS post-exposure regimen; IV aciclovir and admission for severe disease (pneumonia, neuro signs, dense rash). Immunoglobulin has no role once the rash is out. She should contact the GP by telephone, not attend in person, and avoid contact with pregnant women/neonates until lesions crust (~5 days).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.front: What reflects the UKHSA/RCOG shift in post-exposure prophylaxis for chickenpox?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.back: Antivirals (aciclovir days 7–14 post-exposure) are now the preferred PEP rather than VZIG — there is no significant difference in efficacy, and VZIG has since been withdrawn in the UK altogether. If oral antivirals cannot be used, immunoglobulin is discussed with virology.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.front: What are the serious maternal complications of varicella in pregnancy?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.back:
• Varicella pneumonia (a major cause of maternal mortality; risk rises with gestation, smoking, immunosuppression)
  • hepatitis
  • encephalitis
  • and rare death.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.front: What is the fetal risk of maternal chickenpox before 28 weeks (especially <20 weeks)?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.back: Fetal varicella syndrome (FVS) — a small overall risk (~1%).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.front: What are the features of fetal varicella syndrome?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.back:
• Skin scarring in a dermatomal distribution
  • limb hypoplasia
  • eye defects (chorioretinitis, cataracts, microphthalmia)
  • and neurological abnormalities (microcephaly, learning disability).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.front: What is the fetal/neonatal risk when maternal chickenpox occurs between 28 weeks and term?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.back: The fetus may develop shingles in infancy but is usually well at birth.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.front: What is the risk when maternal chickenpox occurs around delivery (−7 to +7 days)?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.back: Neonatal varicella — which can be severe or fatal, because the neonate is exposed before maternal antibody has developed/crossed.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.front: How is the fetus monitored after maternal chickenpox?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.back: Refer to fetal medicine; perform a detailed ultrasound about 5 weeks after infection to look for FVS features (amniocentesis only after skin lesions have fully healed).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.front: How should delivery be timed relative to a maternal chickenpox rash?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.back: Avoid delivery in the viraemic period; delaying about 7 days after the rash allows maternal antibody to cross to the fetus.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.front: What does a neonate receive when the maternal chickenpox rash falls in the risk window?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.back: Aciclovir plus IV varicella-zoster immunoglobulin, if the maternal rash appears from 7 days before to 7 days after delivery, or for a susceptible exposed neonate. VZIG itself has been withdrawn in the UK — an IV varicella-zoster immunoglobulin preparation is used (or normal IVIG if it cannot be sourced), and the antiviral is the backbone rather than the optional extra.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.front: Is breastfeeding encouraged in maternal chickenpox?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.back: Yes — breastfeeding is encouraged if the mother is well.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.front: How long should a pregnant woman with chickenpox isolate, and from whom?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.back: Until the lesions have crusted over (~5 days), avoiding contact with other pregnant women and neonates.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.front: Give the reflex first action for any pregnant woman exposed to chickenpox with an uncertain history.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.back: Check VZV IgG serology urgently to determine susceptibility before deciding on prophylaxis.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.front: Why does rubella in pregnancy matter, given the mother's illness is trivial?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.back: Because of the catastrophic teratogenic damage to the developing fetus (congenital rubella syndrome) — rubella is the archetypal teratogenic infection and the reason childhood MMR exists.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.front: What is the defining management fact about rubella in pregnancy?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.back: There is NO treatment and no way to protect the current fetus once the mother is infected — everything rests on prevention through pre-pregnancy MMR vaccination.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.front: What kind of virus is rubella, and how is it spread?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.back: A single-stranded RNA togavirus, spread by droplets, with an incubation of ~14–21 days.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.front: What is the fetal risk of rubella infection at <8–10 weeks?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.back: Up to ~90% of fetuses are affected — devastating, with multiple defects.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.front: What is the fetal risk of rubella infection at 11–16 weeks?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.back: Lower risk, with sensorineural deafness as the main defect.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.front: What is the fetal risk of rubella infection after 16–20 weeks?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.back: Congenital rubella syndrome is very low, and after 20 weeks congenital defects are essentially not seen.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.front: What is the classic triad of congenital rubella syndrome (CRS)?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.back:
• Sensorineural deafness (commonest single feature),
  • congenital cataracts, and
  • congenital heart disease (classically patent ductus arteriosus ± pulmonary artery stenosis).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.front: What is the commonest single feature of congenital rubella syndrome?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.back: Sensorineural deafness.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.front: Which congenital heart defects are classically associated with rubella?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.back: Patent ductus arteriosus (PDA) and pulmonary artery stenosis.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.front: List other (non-triad) features of congenital rubella syndrome.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.back:
• Microcephaly and learning disability,
  • a 'blueberry muffin' rash (dermal haematopoiesis — shared with CMV),
  • hepatosplenomegaly,
  • thrombocytopenia,
  • growth restriction;
  • also salt-and-pepper retinopathy, microphthalmia and glaucoma.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.front: Give the three classic congenital-infection triads.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.back:
• Rubella → cataracts + PDA + deafness;
  • CMV → periventricular calcification + sensorineural deafness + microcephaly;
  • Toxoplasmosis → hydrocephalus + intracranial calcification + chorioretinitis.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.front: How does maternal rubella present when symptomatic?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.back:
Often subclinical; when symptomatic —
  • a fine maculopapular rash (face → trunk),
  • characteristic postauricular/suboccipital lymphadenopathy,
  • low-grade fever,
  • malaise,
  • coryza,
  • and arthralgia.
It is mild and self-limiting.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.front: What happened to antenatal rubella susceptibility screening in the UK?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.back: It has stopped in England — the test does not protect the current pregnancy, may falsely reassure, and rubella is now very rare here. HIV, hepatitis B and syphilis screening continue.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.front: How is rubella diagnosed if clinically suspected in pregnancy?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.back: Serology — IgM (acute infection) and IgG (past infection/immunity); paired sera/avidity testing confirms timing; notify public health.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.front: What is the treatment for rubella in pregnancy?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.back: There is no antiviral treatment — management is supportive for the mother, with counselling on fetal risk.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.front: How is confirmed first-trimester rubella infection counselled?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.back: Refer to fetal medicine and discuss the high risk of congenital rubella syndrome, including the option of termination.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.front: Why can't the MMR vaccine be given during pregnancy, and when is it offered?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.back: MMR is a live vaccine, so it is contraindicated in pregnancy; non-immune women are offered MMR postnatally (avoid conception for 1 month; it can be given while breastfeeding).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.front: What is the population strategy to prevent congenital rubella syndrome?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.back: Childhood MMR (2 doses), and checking/vaccinating women of uncertain immunity before they conceive.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.front: How is a woman with rubella infection after 20 weeks counselled regarding CRS?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.back: Reassure — congenital rubella syndrome is essentially not seen after 20 weeks (defects are minimal after 16–20 weeks).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.front: Which rash feature is shared between congenital rubella and CMV?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.back: The 'blueberry muffin' rash (dermal haematopoiesis).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.front: What is Group B Streptococcus (GBS) and why does it matter in pregnancy?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.back: Streptococcus agalactiae — a gut and vaginal commensal carried by ~a quarter of pregnant women. It is harmless to the mother but is the leading cause of severe early-onset neonatal infection (sepsis, pneumonia, meningitis) in the UK.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.front: What is the single key intervention to prevent GBS neonatal disease, and when is it given?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.back: Antibiotics DURING labour (intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis, IAP) — to stop the baby being colonised as it passes through the birth canal. Timing is everything: GBS prophylaxis only works intrapartum, not antenatally.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.front: How does a baby acquire early-onset GBS disease?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.back: GBS lives in the maternal vagina/rectum, and the baby is exposed during vaginal delivery, leading to invasive disease in the first days of life.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.front: Contrast early-onset and late-onset GBS disease.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.back:
• Early-onset (<7 days, usually <24–48h): vertical spread from the maternal genital tract during birth, presenting with sepsis/pneumonia/respiratory distress, and preventable by intrapartum antibiotics.
  • Late-onset (7 days–3 months): environmental/postnatal contact, more often meningitis, and NOT preventable by IAP.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.front: Which type of GBS disease does intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis prevent?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.back: Early-onset GBS disease only — late-onset disease is not targeted by this strategy.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.front: Does the UK use universal GBS screening?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.back: No — the UK uses a RISK-FACTOR-based approach, offering IAP on risk factors rather than screening all pregnant women.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.front: Why does the UK not screen all pregnant women for GBS?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.back:
• Because most carriers' babies are born safely,
  • a late swab cannot reliably predict disease, and
  • screening everyone would give huge numbers of women unnecessary antibiotics (anaphylaxis and resistance risk).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.front: How does the US approach to GBS differ from the UK?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.back: The USA uses universal rectovaginal swab screening at 35–37 weeks, whereas the UK uses a risk-factor-based approach (a classic exam-comparison trap).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.front: Is the UK considering universal GBS screening?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.back: Yes — a UK cluster-randomised trial is evaluating whether to switch to universal screening rather than the current risk-factor-based approach.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.front: List the risk factors that warrant offering intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis for GBS (RCOG).
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.back:
• A previous baby with invasive GBS disease;
  • GBS detected in the current pregnancy (vaginal/rectal swab or GBS bacteriuria);
  • preterm labour (<37 weeks);
  • intrapartum fever ≥38°C (or suspected chorioamnionitis);
  • and prolonged rupture of membranes.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.front: How is GBS bacteriuria in the current pregnancy managed?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.back: Treat it at diagnosis (e.g. amoxicillin) AND offer intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis in labour.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.front: How is a woman with known GBS colonisation in a PREVIOUS pregnancy managed?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.back: Offer either IAP in this labour, OR testing (enriched culture medium, ECM) in late pregnancy with IAP if positive.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.front: How is a woman whose PREVIOUS baby had invasive GBS disease managed?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.back: Offer IAP in this labour — no swab is needed.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.front: What is the first-line intrapartum antibiotic for GBS prophylaxis, and its dosing?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.back: IV benzylpenicillin — a 3 g loading dose as soon as possible after labour starts, then 1.5 g 4-hourly until delivery.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.front: What GBS intrapartum antibiotic is used for non-severe penicillin allergy?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.back: A cephalosporin (e.g. cefuroxime).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.front: What GBS intrapartum antibiotic is used for severe penicillin allergy (anaphylaxis)?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.back: Vancomycin.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.front: Why is clindamycin no longer recommended for GBS prophylaxis?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.back: Because of rising GBS resistance to clindamycin.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.front: Is intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis needed for a planned caesarean with intact membranes before labour?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.back: No — there is no passage through the birth canal, so IAP is not required.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.front: How are neonates managed after GBS risk in labour?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.back:
'Adequate' IAP means an appropriate antibiotic given at least 4 hours before birth.
  • Babies who received adequate IAP and are well have routine observation;
  • babies with risk factors but inadequate or no IAP, or signs of infection, have observation ± investigation and antibiotics per neonatal early-onset sepsis pathways (NICE).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.front: Why should an MSU be sent antenatally in relation to GBS?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.back: Because GBS bacteriuria found on urine testing triggers both treatment at diagnosis and intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.front: What is the organising principle for hypertensive disorders of pregnancy?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.back:
Timing + proteinuria + organ features. New hypertension after 20 weeks:
  • without proteinuria/organ involvement = gestational hypertension
  • with proteinuria or organ dysfunction = pre-eclampsia
  • with seizures = eclampsia.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.front: What is pre-eclampsia?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.back: A multisystem disorder defined by NEW hypertension plus end-organ dysfunction (classically proteinuria) after 20 weeks of pregnancy.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.front: What is the unifying pathophysiological concept of pre-eclampsia?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.back: The placenta is the problem — abnormal spiral-artery remodelling → a poorly perfused, ischaemic placenta → release of anti-angiogenic factors → widespread maternal endothelial dysfunction → hypertension, proteinuria, oedema and multi-organ complications.This is why delivering the placenta is curative.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.front: What is eclampsia, and when can seizures occur?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.back: Pre-eclampsia plus a tonic-clonic seizure. Seizures can occur antenatally, intrapartum, or POSTNATALLY(a classic trap — pre-eclampsia does not end at delivery).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.front: What defines severe pre-eclampsia by blood pressure?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.back: Blood pressure ≥160/110 mmHg (with pre-eclampsia), or pre-eclampsia with severe features — an emergency.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.front: What are the severe/impending-eclampsia red-flag features?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.back:
• Severe frontal headache
  • visual disturbance (flashing lights/blurring)
  • epigastric or RUQ pain (liver-capsule stretch)
  • brisk reflexes/clonus
  • sudden facial/hand oedema
  • and reduced urine output.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.front: What is the diagnostic BP threshold for pre-eclampsia (NICE)?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.back: Hypertension ≥140/90 mmHg on two occasions after 20 weeks, PLUS at least one feature of proteinuria or organ dysfunction.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.front: How is proteinuria quantified in pre-eclampsia?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.back: A urine protein:creatinine ratio (PCR) ≥30 mg/mmol (or ACR ≥8); do not use a first-morning void to quantify it.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.front: List the organ-dysfunction features that (with hypertension) define pre-eclampsia.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.back:
• Renal (raised creatinine/proteinuria)
  • hepatic (raised transaminases ± RUQ/epigastric pain)
  • neurological (visual disturbance, severe headache, clonus)
  • haematological (thrombocytopenia, DIC, haemolysis)
  • and uteroplacental (fetal growth restriction).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.front: What is the role of PLGF-based testing in pre-eclampsia?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.back: Placental growth factor (PLGF) testing, between 20 and 36⁺⁶ weeks, helps RULE OUT pre-eclampsia in suspected disease. PLGF is pro-angiogenic, so a LOW level supports the diagnosis; a normal level makes pre-eclampsia within the next 14 days very unlikely.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.front: List the HIGH-risk factors for pre-eclampsia (any ONE → aspirin).
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.back:
• Hypertensive disease in a previous pregnancy
  • chronic hypertension
  • chronic kidney disease
  • diabetes (type 1 or 2)
  • and autoimmune disease (SLE, antiphospholipid syndrome).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.front: List the MODERATE-risk factors for pre-eclampsia (TWO or more → aspirin).
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.back:
• First pregnancy (nulliparity)
  • age ≥40
  • BMI ≥35
  • family history of pre-eclampsia
  • multiple pregnancy
  • and a pregnancy interval >10 years.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.front: What is the aspirin prophylaxis regimen for pre-eclampsia, and its indication?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.back: Aspirin 75–150 mg once daily from 12 weeks until birth (many use 150 mg at night; start before 16 weeks for maximal effect). Given for one high-risk OR two or more moderate-risk factors.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.front: What surveillance is used in a woman with diagnosed pre-eclampsia?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.back:
• Serial BP and urine PCR/dipstick
  • bloods (FBC — falling platelets worrying, U&Es/creatinine, LFTs, and coagulation/LDH/haptoglobin/blood film if HELLP suspected)
  • PLGF testing
  • and fetal surveillance (growth-scan ultrasound, umbilical artery Doppler, CTG).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.front: What is the definitive treatment of pre-eclampsia?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.back: Delivery of the fetus and placenta; all other treatment temporises to allow fetal maturity while keeping the mother safe. In pre-eclampsia, birth is offered at 37⁺⁰ weeks and initiated within 24–48 hours; earlier birth is expedited if BP is uncontrollable or the mother or fetus deteriorates.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.front: What is the first-line antihypertensive for pre-eclampsia/gestational hypertension?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.back: Labetalol (oral, or IV in severe disease).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.front: What is the second-line antihypertensive if labetalol is unsuitable (e.g. asthma)?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.back: Nifedipine; methyldopa is third-line.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.front: What is the target blood pressure in pre-eclampsia?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.back: ≤135/85 mmHg.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.front: Which antihypertensives are contraindicated in pregnancy, and why?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.back: ACE inhibitors and ARBs — they cause fetal renal damage and oligohydramnios(a classic trap).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.front: What is the drug of choice for eclamptic seizures, and its dual role?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.back: Magnesium sulfate — it both treats AND prevents eclamptic seizures (superior to diazepam/phenytoin), given in severe pre-eclampsia and eclampsia. Dose: 4 g IV loading over 5–15 minutes, then 1 g/hour for 24 hours (or 24 hours after the last seizure).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.front: What are the features and antidote of magnesium sulfate toxicity?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.back: Toxicity progresses from loss of deep tendon reflexes (first sign) → respiratory depression → cardiac arrest. The antidote is IV calcium gluconate; monitor reflexes, respiratory rate and urine output.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.front: How is an eclamptic seizure managed?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.back:
• ABCDE
  • protect the airway
  • IV magnesium sulfate (4 g loading dose over 5–15 minutes, then 1 g/hour for 24 hours; a recurrent seizure gets a further 2 g bolus)
  • control BP (IV labetalol/hydralazine)
  • then expedite delivery once the mother is stabilised.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.front: What is HELLP syndrome?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.back: A severe variant/complication of pre-eclampsia — Haemolysis, Elevated Liver enzymes, Low Platelets — presenting with RUQ/epigastric pain, nausea and malaise ± the pre-eclampsia picture; it risks liver haematoma/rupture and DIC.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.front: How is HELLP syndrome managed?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.back: Stabilise the mother and deliver.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.front: Why must BP monitoring and treatment continue postnatally in pre-eclampsia?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.back: Because the disease and seizures can worsen after delivery — pre-eclampsia does not end at delivery. Methyldopa must also be stopped within 2 days of birth (risk of postnatal depression) and replaced with an alternative.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.front: What should new hypertension BEFORE 20 weeks make you think of?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.back: Chronic (pre-existing) hypertension or another cause — or a molar pregnancy.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.front: What is gestational hypertension?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.back: New hypertension arising after 20 weeks of pregnancy WITHOUT proteinuria or organ dysfunction (the presence of which would make it pre-eclampsia).Also called pregnancy-induced hypertension.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.front: Why is gestational hypertension described as 'pre-eclampsia's antechamber'?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.back: Because up to a quarter (~15–25%) of women with gestational hypertension go on to develop pre-eclampsia, so it is defined as much by what you watch for as by what it is.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.front: How does gestational hypertension differ from chronic hypertension in timing and resolution?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.back: Gestational hypertension arises AFTER 20 weeks and usually resolves after birth (typically within 6 weeks); chronic hypertension is present before 20 weeks (or pre-pregnancy) and does not resolve. If BP is still raised at the 6–8 week postnatal review, look for a secondary cause.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.front: How does gestational hypertension differ from pre-eclampsia?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.back: Both are new hypertension after 20 weeks, but gestational hypertension has NO proteinuria and NO organ dysfunction, whereas pre-eclampsia has proteinuria or organ/uteroplacental dysfunction.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.front: What are the two 'negatives' that define gestational hypertension?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.back:
• No proteinuria (urine PCR <30 mg/mmol)
  • and no maternal organ or uteroplacental dysfunction.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.front: What are the diagnostic criteria for gestational hypertension (NICE)?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.back: New hypertension ≥140/90 mmHg after 20 weeks on two occasions, with no proteinuria (PCR <30) and no organ/uteroplacental dysfunction; severity graded as mild-moderate up to <160/110 and severe at ≥160/110.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.front: What is the key investigation at each visit in gestational hypertension, and why?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.back: Urine dipstick/protein:creatinine ratio — the key test to catch the transition to pre-eclampsia (the development of proteinuria).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.front: What surveillance is undertaken in gestational hypertension?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.back:
• BP monitoring (frequency scaled to severity)
  • urine dipstick/PCR at each visit
  • bloods (FBC, U&Es, LFTs) as indicated
  • PLGF-based testing if pre-eclampsia is suspected (20–36⁺⁶ weeks)
  • and fetal monitoring (growth scans/Doppler) if concern arises.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.front: What is the antihypertensive ladder for gestational hypertension?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.back:
The same as pre-eclampsia:
  • first-line labetalol
  • second-line nifedipine (if labetalol unsuitable, e.g. asthma)
  • third-line methyldopa
target BP ≤135/85.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.front: Which antihypertensives are contraindicated in gestational hypertension, and why?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.back: ACE inhibitors and ARBs — they cause fetal renal damage.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.front: What is the target blood pressure in gestational hypertension?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.back: ≤135/85 mmHg.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.front: What is the approach to timing of birth in gestational hypertension?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.back: Aim to continue to term where BP is controlled and there are no complications; deliver earlier if it progresses to pre-eclampsia or BP becomes uncontrolled.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.front: What happens to blood pressure postnatally after gestational hypertension?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.back: It usually normalises but must be monitored, with antihypertensive treatment weaned.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.front: What long-term health risk does gestational hypertension flag?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.back: A higher lifetime risk of chronic hypertension and cardiovascular disease — warranting long-term follow-up.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.front: Why does a hypertensive disorder in a previous pregnancy affect the next pregnancy?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.back: It is a high-risk factor for pre-eclampsia, so aspirin 75–150 mg from 12 weeks is indicated in any subsequent pregnancy.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.front: Give the exam framing for distinguishing the three hypertensive states by presentation.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.back:
• High BP first detected at 28 weeks with clear dipstick and normal bloods = gestational hypertension
  • the same BP with proteinuria or deranged LFTs/platelets = pre-eclampsia
  • high BP already present at booking (before 20 weeks) = chronic hypertension.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.front: How is severe gestational hypertension defined?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.back: BP ≥160/110 mmHg (mild-moderate is up to <160/110), graded as for pre-eclampsia.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.front: What proportion of women with gestational hypertension progress to pre-eclampsia?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.back: Roughly 15–25% (up to about a quarter).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: What are the four gynaecological cancers and their hallmarks?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back:
• Endometrial (postmenopausal bleeding, unopposed oestrogen)
  • ovarian (vague late symptoms + raised CA-125)
  • cervical (HPV, screened/vaccine-preventable, post-coital bleeding)
  • vulval (VIN/lichen sclerosus, elderly, vulval lump/itch/ulcer).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: What is the single highest-yield reflex in gynae-oncology?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: Postmenopausal bleeding is endometrial cancer until proven otherwise → urgent (2-week-wait) referral for transvaginal ultrasound ± biopsy.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: What is endometrial cancer and how common is it?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: A malignancy of the uterine lining — the commonest gynaecological cancer in the UK and the 4th commonest cancer in women. It is overwhelmingly a disease of postmenopausal women (peak 60s–70s).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: Why does endometrial cancer usually present at a curable stage?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: Because it announces itself early and loudly through abnormal (postmenopausal) bleeding, so it is usually diagnosed at an early, curable stage.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: What is the central through-line explaining Type 1 endometrial cancer risk?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: Unopposed oestrogen — oestrogen drives endometrial proliferation and progesterone opposes it, so anything raising the oestrogen-to-progesterone ratio raises risk.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: Describe Type 1 endometrial cancer.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back:
• ~80% of cases
  • oestrogen-dependent
  • endometrioid adenocarcinoma (grade 1–2)
  • precursor is atypical endometrial hyperplasia
  • typical patient is obese, peri-/postmenopausal
  • better prognosis
  • usually p53 wild-type.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: Describe Type 2 endometrial cancer.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back:
• ~20% of cases
  • oestrogen-independent
  • serous, clear cell, or carcinosarcoma histology
  • precursor serous intraepithelial carcinoma
  • typically older, thinner, often multiparous women
  • worse prognosis (aggressive, spreads early)
  • often p53-mutated (serous).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: Why does obesity increase endometrial cancer risk?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: Adipose tissue aromatises androgens into oestrogen, increasing unopposed oestrogen exposure — it is the biggest modifiable driver.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: List the reproductive risk factors for endometrial cancer.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: Nulliparity, early menarche, and late menopause — all increasing lifetime oestrogen exposure; also PCOS (chronic anovulation → unopposed oestrogen).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: Why does tamoxifen increase endometrial cancer risk (the 'tamoxifen trap')?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: Tamoxifen is anti-oestrogenic in the breast but pro-oestrogenic on the endometrium, so it protects against breast cancer but raises endometrial cancer risk.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: Which hormonal exposures increase endometrial cancer risk?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: Oestrogen-only HRT (without a progestogen, in a woman with a uterus) and tamoxifen; diabetes and hypertension also cluster with it.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: Which factors are protective against endometrial cancer?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back:
• The combined oral contraceptive pill
  • the Mirena/LNG-IUS
  • and pregnancy
smoking is anti-oestrogenic (the one context it 'protects' — never a recommendation).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: What hereditary syndrome predisposes to endometrial cancer, and its implication?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: Lynch syndrome (HNPCC) — lifetime risk up to ~40–60%. Consider it in younger patients; it prompts mismatch-repair (MMR) testing (now routine on biopsy) and colorectal cancer screening.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: What is the cardinal symptom of endometrial cancer?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: Postmenopausal bleeding (PMB) — over 90% present this way.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: How does endometrial cancer present in premenopausal women?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: Intermenstrual bleeding, or heavier/irregular menstrual bleeding; also abnormal discharge or (postmenopausal) pyometra, and in late disease pelvic pain and weight loss.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: What is the 2-week-wait referral criterion for suspected endometrial cancer (NICE)?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: Refer on the suspected-cancer pathway (seen within 2 weeks) any woman ≥55 with postmenopausal bleeding; consider a 2WW referral in women <55 with PMB.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: What is the role and cutoff of transvaginal ultrasound in the PMB pathway?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: TVUS measures endometrial thickness: ≤4 mm is reassuring (>99% negative predictive value); >4 mm warrants endometrial biopsy. Exception: in women taking tamoxifen the measurement is unreliable, so proceed to hysteroscopy ± biopsy whatever the thickness.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: What is the first-line tissue diagnosis in the PMB pathway?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: An outpatient Pipelle endometrial biopsy (a 'blind' aspiration sampler).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: When is hysteroscopy ± biopsy used in the PMB pathway?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: If the Pipelle sample is inadequate, there is a focal lesion (polyp/submucosal fibroid) to target, or bleeding persists despite a normal blind sample — allowing directed biopsy.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: Summarise the PMB triage pathway in one line.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: 2-week-wait referral → transvaginal ultrasound → if >4 mm, Pipelle biopsy → if inadequate or a focal lesion, hysteroscopy.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: What imaging is used for staging endometrial cancer once confirmed?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: MRI pelvis to assess myometrial invasion, and CT for distant spread.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: What is the surgical cornerstone of treatment for early-stage endometrial cancer?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: Total hysterectomy plus bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy (TH+BSO), typically laparoscopic, ± pelvic lymphadenectomy/sentinel node depending on stage and grade.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: What adjuvant therapies are used in endometrial cancer?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back:
• Radiotherapy (vaginal brachytherapy/external beam) for higher-risk early disease
  • chemotherapy ± radiotherapy for advanced/high-grade disease
  • and immunotherapy (dostarlimab or pembrolizumab with carboplatin-paclitaxel), guided by MMR/microsatellite status, in advanced/recurrent disease.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: What is the role of progestogens (high-dose oral or LNG-IUS) in endometrial cancer?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: A fertility-sparing option in selected young women with early, low-grade disease or atypical hyperplasia who wish to conceive; and palliative treatment for women unfit for surgery.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: How is atypical endometrial hyperplasia (the Type 1 precursor) managed?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: Total hysterectomy is definitive; the LNG-IUS/progestogen with surveillance is used if fertility is desired or the woman is unfit for surgery.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: What does the current FIGO endometrial staging incorporate beyond anatomical extent?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: Incorporation of histological subtype, lymphovascular space invasion (LVSI), and molecular classification (POLE-mutated, MMR-deficient, p53-abnormal, no-specific-molecular-profile) alongside anatomical extent — a shift toward prognostic/molecular staging.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: Why is ovarian cancer called the 'silent killer'?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: It is the leading cause of gynaecological-cancer death in the UK; it presents late with vague symptoms mistaken for IBS or ageing, so about two-thirds are diagnosed at an advanced stage — the mirror of endometrial cancer.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: What is the 'incessant ovulation' hypothesis of ovarian cancer?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: Each ovulation ruptures and repairs the ovarian surface; cumulative lifetime ovulations drive malignant transformation, so anything reducing lifetime ovulations is protective.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: Which cell of origin accounts for ~90% of ovarian cancers, and give examples?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: Epithelial tumours — high-grade serous (commonest), mucinous, endometrioid, and clear cell; typically in postmenopausal women (60s); the marker is CA-125.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: Where is high-grade serous ovarian cancer now thought to originate?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: From the fallopian tube fimbriae (not primarily the ovarian surface).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: Describe germ-cell ovarian tumours and their markers.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: About 5% of cases, in young women (teens–30s); examples include dysgerminoma, yolk sac tumour and teratoma; markers are AFP, βhCG and LDH.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: Describe sex cord-stromal ovarian tumours and their hormonal effects.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: About 5% of cases, any age; granulosa cell tumours (oestrogen → postmenopausal bleeding) and Sertoli-Leydig tumours (androgen → virilisation); markers include inhibin and oestrogen.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: What is a Krukenberg tumour?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: A metastatic tumour of the ovary (classically from a gastric — or breast — primary), characteristically bilateral with signet-ring cells.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: What is Meigs syndrome?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: The triad of a benign ovarian fibroma + ascites + pleural effusion, all of which resolve after removal of the tumour.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: List the risk factors that increase ovarian cancer risk.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back:
• Nulliparity
  • early menarche
  • late menopause
  • increasing age (postmenopausal)
  • BRCA1/BRCA2 mutations (biggest genetic driver)
  • Lynch syndrome
  • a family history of ovarian/breast cancer
  • and endometriosis (clear-cell/endometrioid subtypes).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: What is the biggest genetic risk factor for ovarian cancer?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: BRCA1/BRCA2 mutations (BRCA1 lifetime risk ~40%); Lynch syndrome also increases risk.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: Which factors are protective against ovarian cancer, and why?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back:
• The COCP (major, persisting years after stopping)
  • pregnancy/multiparity
  • and breastfeeding
— all reduce the number of lifetime ovulations.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: What persistent symptoms should raise suspicion of ovarian cancer (especially in women ≥50)?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back:
Persistent or frequent symptoms (particularly >12×/month):
  • abdominal distension/bloating ('clothes don't fit')
  • early satiety/loss of appetite
  • pelvic/abdominal pain
  • urinary urgency/frequency
  • change in bowel habit
  • weight loss
  • and fatigue.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: Why is new-onset 'IBS' in a woman over 50 a red flag?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: Because IBS rarely presents for the first time at that age, so new IBS-type symptoms in an older woman should prompt investigation for ovarian cancer.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: What are the late signs of ovarian cancer?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back:
• Ascites
  • a palpable pelvic/abdominal mass
  • pleural effusion
  • and bowel obstruction.
Ascites and/or a pelvic or abdominal mass that is not obviously fibroids means an urgent suspected-cancer referral straight away — do not wait for a CA-125.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: What is the first-line investigation in a woman with persistent possible ovarian-cancer symptoms (NICE)?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: Serum CA-125; if it is ≥35 IU/mL, arrange an ultrasound of the abdomen and pelvis.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: What additional markers should be measured in women under 40 with suspected ovarian cancer?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: AFP and βhCG, measured alongside the CA-125 to detect germ-cell tumours — not held back until a mass has been demonstrated.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: What is the Risk of Malignancy Index (RMI), and its referral threshold?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: RMI = U × M × CA-125. Refer to the gynae-oncology MDT if RMI ≥250.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: What are the components of the RMI?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back:
• U (ultrasound score: 1 point each for multilocular cyst, solid areas, bilateral lesions, ascites, intra-abdominal metastases → U=0/1/3)
  • M (menopausal status: premenopausal=1, postmenopausal=3)
  • and CA-125 (absolute value in IU/mL).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: Why is CA-125 non-specific, and what is its role?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back:
It is also raised in
  • endometriosis
  • fibroids
  • PID
  • menstruation
  • pregnancy
  • ascites of any cause and other cancers.
It is a triage and monitoring tool, not a diagnostic test.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: What imaging and staging system are used for ovarian cancer?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: CT abdomen/pelvis for staging, using FIGO staging (stage I confined to the ovaries → stage IV distant metastases).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: Summarise the NICE ovarian cancer pathway in one line.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: Persistent symptoms → CA-125 → if ≥35, ultrasound → calculate RMI → if ≥250, gynae-oncology MDT referral (add AFP + βhCG in women under 40). The short-circuit: ascites and/or a pelvic or abdominal mass on examination, not obviously fibroids, goes straight to an urgent suspected-cancer referral without waiting for CA-125 or ultrasound.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: What is the surgical management of ovarian cancer?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: Total abdominal hysterectomy + bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy + omentectomy with maximal cytoreduction ('debulking'); the goal is no visible residual disease (the strongest prognostic factor). Fertility-sparing surgery is possible in young women with early germ-cell or borderline/stage IA epithelial disease.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: What is the strongest prognostic factor in ovarian cancer surgery?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: Achieving no visible residual disease after cytoreductive ('debulking') surgery.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: What chemotherapy is used for ovarian cancer?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: Platinum-based chemotherapy (carboplatin) ± paclitaxel — adjuvant for most, or neoadjuvant in advanced disease.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: What maintenance therapies are used in advanced high-grade epithelial ovarian cancer?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: PARP inhibitors — olaparib if BRCA-positive, and niraparib/rucaparib in defined (HRD-dependent) settings; bevacizumab (anti-VEGF) in selected cases.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: What causes nearly all cervical cancer, and which types are most important?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: Persistent high-risk human papillomavirus (HPV) infection; types 16 and 18 cause ~70% of cases. Cervical cancer affects young women (peak 30s–40s) and is largely preventable by vaccination and screening.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: Explain the HPV oncoprotein mechanism in cervical cancer.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: HPV E6 inhibits p53 (the guardian of the genome) and E7 inhibits Rb (retinoblastoma suppressor); losing both tumour-suppressor 'brakes' allows uncontrolled cervical epithelial proliferation → CIN → invasive cancer.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: What are the two main histological types of cervical cancer and where do they arise?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back:
• Squamous cell carcinoma (~70–80%) arising at the transformation zone (squamocolumnar junction), best detected by screening;
  • and adenocarcinoma (~20%), glandular and arising higher in the canal, so harder to catch on screening.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: What is CIN and how do its grades differ?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back:
Cervical intraepithelial neoplasia — a pre-invasive precursor.
  • CIN I = dysplasia of the lower third (often regresses);
  • CIN II = lower two-thirds;
  • CIN III = full-thickness (carcinoma in situ), which is treated.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: What is the classic trap distinguishing CIN from dyskaryosis?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: CIN is a HISTOLOGICAL (biopsy) diagnosis; dyskaryosis is the CYTOLOGICAL (cell) term used on the smear result.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: List the risk factors for cervical cancer.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back:
• Persistent high-risk HPV (the cause),
  • smoking (independent risk and impairs HPV clearance),
  • immunosuppression (HIV, transplant),
  • early first intercourse/multiple partners/non-barrier contraception (HPV exposure),
  • long-term COCP use,
  • multiparity,
  • and non-engagement with screening.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: What is the biggest determinant of who develops cervical cancer?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: Non-engagement with (non-attendance at) cervical screening.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: Who is invited for NHS cervical screening, and at what interval?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back:
Women and anyone with a cervix aged 25–64.
  • Ages 25–49: every 5 years if HPV-negative (lengthened from every 3 years);
  • ages 50–64: every 5 years.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: What is HPV primary screening?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: The cervical sample is tested FIRST for high-risk HPV, and cytology is examined only if HPV-positive ('reflex cytology') — reversing the old cytology-first order.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: What is the action for a hrHPV-negative screening result?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: Routine recall (in 5 years, or 3 years if there was a recent prior HPV-positive result).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: What is the action for hrHPV-positive with normal cytology?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: Repeat the test in 12 months.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: What is the action for hrHPV-positive with abnormal cytology (dyskaryosis)?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: Refer for colposcopy.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: What happens if a woman is hrHPV-positive at 3 consecutive annual tests?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: She is referred for colposcopy regardless of cytology.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: Summarise the cervical screening algorithm in one line.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: HPV first → if negative, done → if positive, look at the cells → abnormal cells (or persistent HPV) = colposcopy.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: What is seen at colposcopy, and how are abnormal areas identified?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back:
