• Acetic acid turns abnormal areas white ('acetowhite');
  • iodine (Schiller's test) stains normal epithelium brown while abnormal areas do not take it up;
  • a directed biopsy confirms the CIN grade.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: What is the standard treatment for CIN, and its main future-pregnancy risk?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: LLETZ (large loop excision of the transformation zone); it carries a small increased risk of preterm birth in future pregnancies.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: What HPV vaccine is used, what does it cover, and who is offered it?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: The 9-valent HPV vaccine — covering HPV 16 and 18 (plus 31/33/45/52/58, and 6/11 for warts); offered to all children in school Year 8 (~age 12–13), both girls and boys.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: What is the current HPV vaccine schedule for the routine cohort?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: A single-dose schedule for the routine cohort; MSM up to 45 and immunocompromised people have separate schedules.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: Why is HPV vaccination given before sexual debut?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: To vaccinate before HPV exposure, giving maximum protective benefit.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: What are the symptomatic red flags of cervical cancer?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back:
• Abnormal bleeding — postcoital, intermenstrual, or postmenopausal (the classic triad);
  • blood-stained/offensive discharge;
  • dyspareunia;
  • and late features such as pelvic pain, leg oedema, ureteric obstruction/renal failure and fistula.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: What should be done for an abnormal-looking cervix (mass/ulcer/contact bleeding) on speculum?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: Urgent 2-week-wait referral (NICE) regardless of screening status — do NOT wait for a smear.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: How is cervical cancer investigated and staged once suspected?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back:
• Colposcopy + biopsy confirms invasive disease;
  • examination under anaesthesia (EUA), MRI pelvis (local/parametrial spread), and CT/PET for nodal/distant disease;
  • it is FIGO staged, incorporating imaging and nodal status.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: What is the management principle by stage in cervical cancer?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: Early disease → surgery; locally advanced disease → chemoradiation. Radical surgery and radiotherapy are not combined, to avoid stacking morbidity.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: What is a radical trachelectomy, and when is it used?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: Removal of the cervix with pelvic lymphadenectomy while preserving the uterus — a fertility-sparing option for early cervical cancer (stage IA2–IB1) when fertility is desired.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: What is a Wertheim's hysterectomy?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: A radical hysterectomy with pelvic lymphadenectomy, used for early cervical cancer (IA2–IIA) when fertility is not desired (± ovarian preservation).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: How is locally advanced cervical cancer (IB3/IIB–IVA) managed?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: Chemoradiation — cisplatin-based chemotherapy plus external beam radiotherapy and brachytherapy.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: How is metastatic (IVB)/recurrent cervical cancer managed?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: Palliative chemotherapy ± bevacizumab, with immunotherapy (pembrolizumab) in defined settings.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: What is vulval cancer, who does it affect, and the commonest type?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: A malignancy of the external female genitalia — rare, a disease of elderly women (peak 70s+); ~90% are squamous cell carcinoma (VSCC).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: What is the central organising concept ('two roads') of vulval cancer?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: It arrives by two separate routes — a younger HPV road and an older lichen-sclerosus road — and almost everything (age, precursor, p53 status, prognosis) follows from which road the patient is on.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: Describe the HPV-dependent road to vulval cancer.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back:
• Caused by high-risk HPV (mainly type 16);
  • the precursor is usual-type VIN (uVIN, now called vulval HSIL);
  • typically younger women (40s–50s);
  • p53 wild-type;
  • risk factors include smoking, immunosuppression and other HPV lesions (CIN);
  • slower progression.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: Describe the HPV-independent road to vulval cancer.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back:
• Caused by chronic inflammation — lichen sclerosus (± lichen planus);
  • the precursor is differentiated VIN (dVIN);
  • typically older women (70s+);
  • p53-mutated;
  • faster progression with much higher cancer risk.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: Which vulval cancer road is the more dangerous, and why?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: The HPV-independent (lichen sclerosus/dVIN) road — dVIN progresses faster (~2–3 years vs ~6–7), carries a much higher cancer risk, and is easily mistaken for a benign dermatosis.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: What is the VIN terminology trap?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: Usual-type VIN (uVIN, HPV-driven) is now often called vulval HSIL; differentiated VIN (dVIN, HPV-independent, lichen-sclerosus-associated) retains its name and is more dangerous.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: What is lichen sclerosus and its typical appearance?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: A chronic inflammatory dermatosis — intensely itchy white/porcelain atrophic ('cigarette-paper') plaques, in a figure-of-eight perianal distribution, with architectural loss (labial fusion, buried clitoris).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: What is the malignancy risk of lichen sclerosus, and via what precursor?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: About 4–5% lifetime risk of progression to vulval squamous cell carcinoma, via differentiated VIN (dVIN).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: How is lichen sclerosus managed, and why does treatment matter for cancer?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: Potent/ultrapotent topical steroids (e.g. clobetasol), which also reduce cancer risk, plus long-term surveillance; biopsy any non-healing/ulcerated/thickened area to exclude dVIN/cancer.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: How does vulval cancer typically present?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back:
• Vulval itching (pruritus, often long-standing especially on the lichen-sclerosus road);
  • a lump, ulcer or plaque (raised/warty/eroded);
  • bleeding, pain or discharge;
  • a non-healing sore;
  • sometimes an enlarged groin (inguinal) node.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: Why is vulval cancer often advanced at diagnosis?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: Presentation is frequently delayed through embarrassment, so it is often advanced by the time of diagnosis.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: What is the essential investigation for any suspicious vulval lesion?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: Biopsy — every suspicious vulval lesion, and any suspicious area within lichen sclerosus.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: Why should the whole lower genital tract be inspected in vulval cancer?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: Because HPV-related disease is often multifocal, so the cervix and vagina should also be checked.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: What is the referral pathway for an unexplained vulval lump/ulceration/bleeding?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: Urgent 2-week-wait referral (NICE).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: How does vulval cancer spread, and what is the dominant prognostic factor?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: It spreads via the inguinal (groin) lymph nodes, and nodal status is the dominant prognostic factor.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: How is uVIN (vulval HSIL) managed?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: Local surgical excision, or topical imiquimod in selected counselled women (after excluding occult invasion); laser in some cases.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: How is dVIN managed?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: Excision, treated more aggressively because of its high, fast progression risk, alongside optimising lichen sclerosus treatment.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: What is the cornerstone of treatment for invasive vulval cancer?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: Surgery — wide local excision (or radical vulvectomy for larger/multifocal disease) aiming for clear margins, extended to include adjacent dVIN/lichen sclerosus.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: How are the groin nodes managed in vulval cancer?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back:
• Sentinel lymph node biopsy for early unifocal tumours;
  • inguinofemoral lymphadenectomy if nodes are involved or the tumour is high-risk.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: When are radiotherapy/chemotherapy used in vulval cancer?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: Adjuvant radiotherapy ± chemotherapy for node-positive/high-risk disease, or primary chemoradiation for advanced/unresectable disease.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: How is each road of vulval cancer prevented/addressed?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back:
• HPV vaccination (9-valent) protects against the HPV-dependent road;
  • treating lichen sclerosus with steroids plus surveillance addresses the HPV-independent road.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: Give the reflex stem for vulval cancer.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back: An elderly woman with long-standing vulval itch who now has a lump/ulcer → vulval cancer until proven otherwise.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.front: Summarise the hallmark of each of the four gynaecological cancers.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.back:
• Cervical = young/HPV;
  • endometrial = obese/postmenopausal bleeding;
  • vulval = elderly/itch;
  • ovarian = late/silent.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fe.front: What is the definition of female genital mutilation (FGM)?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fe.back: All procedures involving partial or total removal of the external female genitalia, or other injury to the female genital organs, for NON-MEDICAL reasons. It has no health benefits, causes serious harm, is a form of child abuse and a human-rights violation, and is illegal in the UK.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fe.front: Does FGM have any health benefits or religious basis?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fe.back: No — it has no health benefits and no religious basis; it is culturally rooted and performed on girls (often young), causing physical and psychological harm.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fe.front: What are the three key threads in approaching FGM?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fe.back:
• (1) Classify it (WHO Types 1–4)
  • (2) know the legal framework (illegal under the FGM Act 2003, FGM Protection Orders, and the mandatory reporting duty)
  • and (3) manage the acute and long-term consequences (including deinfibulation for Type 3).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fe.front: Describe WHO Type 1 FGM.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fe.back: Clitoridectomy — partial or total removal of the clitoris and/or the prepuce.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fe.front: Describe WHO Type 2 FGM.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fe.back: Excision — partial or total removal of the clitoris and the labia minora, ± excision of the labia majora.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fe.front: Describe WHO Type 3 FGM.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fe.back: Infibulation — narrowing of the vaginal orifice with a covering seal (cutting and appositioning the labia, ± excision of the clitoris). It is the most extensive type.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fe.front: Describe WHO Type 4 FGM.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fe.back: All other harmful procedures to the female genitalia for non-medical reasons — pricking, piercing, incising, scraping, or cauterisation.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fe.front: Which type of FGM causes the most obstetric/gynaecological problems, and what may be needed?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fe.back: Type 3 (infibulation) — causing obstructed flow, intercourse and delivery problems; it may require deinfibulation (surgical opening).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fe.front: What are the acute complications of FGM?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fe.back:
• Severe pain
  • haemorrhage
  • shock
  • infection (including tetanus, HIV/hepatitis from shared instruments)
  • urinary retention
  • genital tissue injury
  • and death.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fe.front: What are the long-term complications of FGM?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fe.back:
• Urinary (recurrent UTIs, dysuria, obstruction/retention)
  • menstrual/gynaecological (dysmenorrhoea, haematocolpos, difficult examinations)
  • sexual (dyspareunia, reduced function)
  • obstetric (obstructed labour, perineal tears, PPH, need for deinfibulation)
  • and psychological (PTSD, anxiety, depression).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fe.front: What UK law makes FGM illegal, and what does it criminalise?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fe.back: The Female Genital Mutilation Act 2003 (amended by the Serious Crime Act 2015) — it is a criminal offence to perform FGM, to assist/arrange it, or to fail to protect a girl from it, including taking a girl abroad for FGM (extraterritorial).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fe.front: What is the maximum penalty for FGM offences in the UK?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fe.back: 14 years' imprisonment; there is also a separate offence of failing to protect a girl (under 16) from FGM.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fe.front: What is an FGM Protection Order (FGMPO)?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fe.back: A civil court order to protect a girl at risk of FGM — for example, by removing/surrendering her passport to prevent her being taken abroad.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fe.front: What legal protection exists for FGM survivors regarding identity?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fe.back: Lifelong anonymity for FGM survivors.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fe.front: What is the mandatory reporting duty for FGM (who and what)?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fe.back: Regulated healthcare professionals, social care workers, and teachers (England and Wales) have a PERSONAL duty to report KNOWN cases of FGM in a girl UNDER 18.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fe.front: What does 'known' mean for the FGM mandatory reporting duty?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fe.back: Either the girl DISCLOSES she has had FGM, OR you VISUALLY IDENTIFY physical signs of FGM in the course of your work.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fe.front: How and when is a case reported under the FGM mandatory reporting duty?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fe.back: Report to the POLICE — call 101 (999 if there is immediate risk); the statutory limit is within 1 month, but best practice is as soon as possible (ideally by close of the next working day).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fe.front: Does the mandatory reporting duty apply to girls 'at risk' or 'suspected' cases?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fe.back: No — it applies only to KNOWN cases in girls under 18; at-risk or suspected cases are managed with a normal safeguarding referral to children's services, not the police duty.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fe.front: Does the mandatory reporting duty apply when an adult (≥18) discloses FGM she had as a child?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fe.back: No — the duty applies only to girls under 18; an adult disclosure is managed via local safeguarding, considering risk to other girls.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fe.front: Does a disclosure by a parent/relative (not the girl herself) trigger the mandatory reporting duty?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fe.back: No — the mandatory police duty is not triggered by a third-party disclosure, though safeguarding still applies.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fe.front: Summarise the key decision on FGM reporting.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fe.back:
• KNOWN FGM (disclosed by, or visibly identified in, a girl under 18) → mandatory personal report to the POLICE (101) AND a safeguarding referral to children's social care — the police duty is IN ADDITION to normal safeguarding, never instead of it.
  • At risk/suspected/adult → safeguarding referral, but not the mandatory police duty.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fe.front: What are the principles of clinical management of a woman with FGM?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fe.back:
• Sensitive, non-judgemental, culturally-aware care
  • use professional interpreters (not family)
  • careful documentation
  • psychological support for trauma/PTSD
  • assess risk to other girls
  • specialist FGM services
  • and deinfibulation for Type 3.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fe.front: What is deinfibulation, and when can it be done?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fe.back: Surgical opening of a Type 3 infibulation — done antenatally, in labour, or when non-pregnant.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fe.front: Why must re-infibulation never be performed?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fe.back: Because re-closing (re-infibulating) after delivery is illegal in the UK.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.front: What is the organising principle for any reproductive-age woman with bleeding/pain and a positive pregnancy test?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.back: Exclude ectopic pregnancy. Use transvaginal ultrasound plus serial βhCG to locate the pregnancy and assess viability.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.front: What is an ectopic pregnancy and its commonest site?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.back: Implantation outside the uterine cavity — most commonly the fallopian tube (~95%, especially the ampulla). The tube cannot sustain the pregnancy, so it eventually ruptures, causing life-threatening intraperitoneal haemorrhage.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.front: What is the classic triad of ectopic pregnancy?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.back:
• Amenorrhoea (6–8 weeks)
  • unilateral lower abdominal pain
  • vaginal bleeding (dark/'prune juice')
However, presentations are commonly atypical.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.front: Why should you pregnancy-test every reproductive-age woman with pain, GI symptoms or collapse?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.back: Because ectopic presentations are commonly atypical, and a positive test with no intrauterine pregnancy is ectopic until proven otherwise; missing it risks fatal rupture.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.front: What signs indicate a ruptured/unstable ectopic pregnancy?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.back: Sudden severe pain, collapse and shock, with peritonism, shoulder-tip pain, tachycardia and hypotension.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.front: Why does shoulder-tip pain occur in a ruptured ectopic?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.back: Intraperitoneal blood irritates the diaphragm, causing referred shoulder-tip pain.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.front: What is the immediate management of a ruptured/unstable ectopic?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.back: Resuscitate (ABC, IV access, fluids/blood, crossmatch) and proceed to immediate surgery (laparoscopy/laparotomy) — usually salpingectomy.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.front: What are the key examination signs of a (stable) ectopic pregnancy?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.back: Cervical motion tenderness ('cervical excitation') and adnexal tenderness/mass.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.front: List the main risk factors for ectopic pregnancy.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.back:
• Previous ectopic (strongest)
  • PID/salpingitis (especially chlamydia)
  • tubal surgery/ligation
  • endometriosis
  • adhesions
  • IUD/IUS in situ
  • assisted reproduction (IVF)
  • smoking
  • and older age
(Anything that damages the tube.)

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.front: What is the first-line investigation once pregnancy is confirmed in suspected ectopic?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.back:
Transvaginal ultrasound — to locate the pregnancy; findings include
  • an adnexal mass/tubal sac
  • NO intrauterine pregnancy
  • and free fluid (blood) in the pouch of Douglas

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.front: What is a 'pregnancy of unknown location' (PUL)?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.back: A positive pregnancy test with NO pregnancy seen anywhere on transvaginal ultrasound — neither inside nor outside the uterus. If an adnexal mass IS seen, that is a probable ectopic, not a PUL.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.front: How are serial serum βhCG levels interpreted in a PUL?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.back:
Taken 48h apart:
  • a normal intrauterine pregnancy roughly DOUBLES
  • an ectopic or failing pregnancy rises slowly, plateaus, or falls

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.front: Where should a woman with a positive pregnancy test and pain/pelvic/cervical-motion tenderness be referred?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.back: Immediately to the Early Pregnancy Assessment Unit (EPAU).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.front: What are the criteria for EXPECTANT management of a stable ectopic?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.back: Clinically stable AND pain-free AND a tubal ectopic <35 mm AND no fetal heartbeat AND hCG 1000 IU/L or less AND able to attend follow-up — with monitoring by serial hCG. Expectant management may be CONSIDERED if hCG is 1000–1500 IU/L; 1500 is the methotrexate ceiling, not the expectant one.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.front: What are the criteria for MEDICAL management (methotrexate) of an ectopic?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.back:
• Stable
  • no significant pain
  • unruptured
  • mass <35 mm
  • no fetal heartbeat
  • hCG <1500 IU/L
  • no intrauterine pregnancy
  • and able to attend follow-up

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.front: How is methotrexate given and monitored in ectopic pregnancy?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.back: A single IM dose; serum hCG is monitored on days 4 and 7 for an adequate fall (~15% between days 4–7); repeat dose or surgery if the fall is inadequate.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.front: How does methotrexate treat an ectopic pregnancy, and what advice follows?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.back: It is a folate antagonist that stops trophoblast proliferation. Afterwards, avoid pregnancy for 3 months and take folic acid (it is teratogenic).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.front: What management options apply when hCG is 1500–5000 IU/L in a stable ectopic?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.back: A choice of methotrexate or surgery (if pain-free and able to follow up).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.front: What are the criteria mandating SURGICAL management of an ectopic?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.back:
• Significant pain
  • or mass ≥35 mm
  • or a fetal heartbeat
  • or hCG ≥5000 IU/L
  • or rupture/instability
  • or inability to attend follow-up

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.front: When is salpingectomy vs salpingotomy chosen?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.back: Salpingectomy (remove the tube) is first-line if the contralateral tube is healthy; salpingotomy (remove the pregnancy, preserve the tube) is used if there is an infertility risk (contralateral tube damaged), but ~1 in 5 need further treatment.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.front: What is the mnemonic to remember salpingectomy vs salpingotomy?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.back: SalpingECTOMY = remove the tube; salpingOTOMY = you've still GOT the tube (tube preserved).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.front: What are the anti-D rules for ectopic pregnancy management?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.back: Anti-D is NOT given for an ectopic pregnancy below 12 weeks — whether managed expectantly, medically or surgically (NICE). From 12⁺⁰ weeks, give anti-D immunoglobulin (at least 250 IU) to Rhesus-negative women having medical or surgical management. NICE says do NOT use a Kleihauer test here.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.front: What GI symptoms can occur with an ectopic due to pouch of Douglas blood?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.back: Dyschezia (pain on defaecation) and diarrhoea, from blood irritating the pouch of Douglas.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.front: How is miscarriage defined and classified?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.back:
Spontaneous loss of a pregnancy before 24 weeks (most <12 weeks), classified by
  • whether the cervical os is open/closed
  • whether products have been expelled
  • and whether the fetus is alive

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.front: What three questions frame a bleeding early pregnancy?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.back:
• (1) Is the OS open or closed?
  • (2) Have PRODUCTS passed (partially/fully)?
  • (3) Is the fetus ALIVE?

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.front: What does an open vs closed cervical os indicate about the miscarriage type?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.back:
• An OPEN os = miscarriage progressing (inevitable or incomplete)
  • a CLOSED os = threatened (viable) or missed (dead but retained), or complete (all passed)

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.front: What is the mnemonic for the open-os miscarriage types?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.back: 'OPEN YOUR I's' — an OPEN cervical os means INEVITABLE or INCOMPLETE miscarriage.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.front: Describe a threatened miscarriage.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.back: Closed os, painless light bleeding, and a live fetus.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.front: Describe an inevitable miscarriage.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.back: Open os, heavy bleeding with clots and pain, with an intrauterine sac still present and products not yet passed. Cardiac activity may still be seen — it is the OPEN os that makes the loss unavoidable.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.front: Describe an incomplete miscarriage.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.back: Open os with only some products passed (retained products of conception), and ongoing pain and bleeding.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.front: Describe a complete miscarriage.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.back: Closed os, little bleeding, with all products passed.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.front: Describe a missed (delayed) miscarriage.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.back: Closed os with a dead fetus retained; there are no symptoms of expulsion, pregnancy symptoms fade, and usually no pain.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.front: What is the key risk of an incomplete miscarriage?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.back: Retained products of conception → risk of ongoing bleeding and infection → needs medical or surgical clearance.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.front: How does the pain/bleeding sequence help distinguish ectopic from miscarriage?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.back: In ectopic, PAIN comes FIRST then bleeding; in miscarriage, bleeding typically comes first (± pain). Always confirm an intrauterine pregnancy on scan before assuming miscarriage.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.front: What is the first-line, diagnostic investigation for miscarriage?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.back: Transvaginal ultrasound — a crown-rump length (CRL) of 7 mm or more with NO cardiac activity indicates miscarriage (or a mean sac diameter ≥25 mm with no fetal pole), but a second opinion on viability and/or a repeat scan at least 7 days later is advised before confirming it.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.front: What should be done if ultrasound findings for viability are borderline/uncertain?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.back: Repeat the scan in about 7–14 days before confirming miscarriage.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.front: When is serum βhCG used in suspected miscarriage?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.back: When the pregnancy location is uncertain, to help exclude an ectopic pregnancy.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.front: What is the first-line management for most miscarriages?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.back: Expectant management — waiting 7–14 days for the miscarriage to complete, then repeating a pregnancy test/scan to confirm.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.front: When should medical or surgical management be preferred over expectant management?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.back:
• Increased risk of haemorrhage (late first trimester, coagulopathy, cannot have transfusion)
  • previous adverse/traumatic pregnancy experience
  • or evidence of infection
(or if unstable/haemorrhaging, do not wait).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.front: What is the medical regimen for a MISSED miscarriage?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.back: Oral mifepristone 200 mg (a progesterone-receptor antagonist that primes/softens the cervix), then 48h later misoprostol 800 mcg vaginally, orally or sublingually (a prostaglandin causing contractions/expulsion), unless the sac has already passed.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.front: What is the medical regimen for an INCOMPLETE miscarriage?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.back: A single dose of misoprostol 600 mcg (vaginal/oral/sublingual).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.front: Why was the management of missed miscarriage changed to mifepristone plus misoprostol?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.back: Trial evidence showed the combination is more effective than misoprostol alone, resulting in fewer surgical procedures.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.front: What supportive care and follow-up accompany medical management of miscarriage?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.back: Antiemetics and pain relief, and a pregnancy test at 3 weeks to confirm completion.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.front: What surgical options exist for miscarriage, and when are they used?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.back:
Manual vacuum aspiration (local anaesthetic, outpatient) or surgical management in theatre (general anaesthetic) — used if
  • the woman is unstable
  • expectant/medical management has failed
  • there is infection
  • or the woman prefers it

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.front: What are the anti-D rules in miscarriage management?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.back: Anti-D is NOT given for miscarriage or threatened miscarriage below 12 weeks, whatever the management (NICE). From 12⁺⁰ weeks, give anti-D immunoglobulin (at least 250 IU) to Rhesus-negative women — for medical or surgical management, and after any spontaneous miscarriage at or after 12 weeks.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.front: Roughly how common is miscarriage?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.back: About 1 in 5 pregnancies.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.front: What is gestational trophoblastic disease (GTD)?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.back:
A spectrum of conditions arising from abnormal proliferation of placental TROPHOBLAST tissue — from benign/premalignant molar pregnancies (complete and partial hydatidiform moles) to the malignant forms collectively called gestational trophoblastic neoplasia (GTN):
  • invasive mole,
  • choriocarcinoma, and
  • PSTT.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.front: Why is a markedly elevated hCG the defining feature of GTD, and what does it explain?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.back:
Because trophoblast produces hCG. The very high hCG explains
  • exaggerated pregnancy symptoms (severe hyperemesis)
  • early pre-eclampsia, and
  • hyperthyroidism (hCG structurally resembles TSH).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.front: What is the genetic basis of a COMPLETE mole?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.back: An empty egg fertilised by sperm → ALL PATERNAL chromosomes, usually 46,XX (diploid). There is NO fetal tissue, hCG is very high, and malignant potential is higher.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.front: What is the genetic basis of a PARTIAL mole?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.back: A normal egg fertilised by TWO sperm → three sets of chromosomes (triploid, e.g. 69,XXY). There is some fetal tissue (often a non-viable fetus), hCG is moderately raised, and malignant potential is lower.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.front: What is the GTD spectrum from benign to malignant?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.back: Hydatidiform mole (complete/partial, premalignant) → invasive mole (invades myometrium) → choriocarcinoma (malignant, can follow a mole/miscarriage/ectopic/normal pregnancy, metastasises to lung) → placental-site trophoblastic tumour (PSTT, rare).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.front: What defines gestational trophoblastic neoplasia (GTN)?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.back: The malignant end of the spectrum (invasive mole, choriocarcinoma, PSTT), diagnosed when hCG persists or rises after evacuation of a mole.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.front: What are the classic clinical features of a molar pregnancy?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.back:
• Painless bleeding in the first/early-second trimester
  • exaggerated pregnancy symptoms (e.g. hyperemesis)
  • a uterus that is very large for dates
  • and a very high hCG
hypertension and hyperthyroidism may occur, ± grape-like vesicles and theca lutein cysts.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.front: Why can hyperthyroidism occur in a molar pregnancy?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.back: Because the very high hCG structurally resembles TSH and can stimulate the thyroid.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.front: Give the reflex clinical picture of a molar pregnancy.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.back: First-trimester bleeding + uterus large for dates + very high hCG + snowstorm scan → molar pregnancy → evacuate + register + hCG follow-up.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.front: What is the characteristic ultrasound appearance of a complete mole?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.back: A 'snowstorm' or bunch-of-grapes appearance — numerous small anechoic spaces.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.front: What is the definitive diagnostic investigation for GTD?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.back: Histopathology of the evacuated products of conception.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.front: What is the method of choice for evacuating a complete mole?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.back: Suction curettage (urgent uterine evacuation); a partial mole with fetal parts may require medical evacuation. Products must be sent for histological examination.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.front: What precautions apply during evacuation of a molar pregnancy?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.back:
• Give anti-D if Rhesus-negative
  • and avoid oxytocics before evacuation completes (risk of embolisation of trophoblastic tissue).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.front: Why must a woman with GTD be registered with a specialist GTD centre?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.back: It is the UK standard of care, enabling serial hCG monitoring to detect persistent/malignant disease (progression to GTN).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.front: What follow-up is required after evacuation of a molar pregnancy?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.back: Serial hCG monitoring until it normalises (to detect persistent/malignant disease), plus effective contraception to avoid pregnancy during follow-up.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.front: Why should pregnancy be avoided during hCG follow-up after a mole?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.back: Because a new pregnancy's hCG would confuse the monitoring used to detect persistent/malignant disease.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.front: How is gestational trophoblastic neoplasia treated?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.back:
With chemotherapy —
  • low-risk GTN with single-agent methotrexate
  • high-risk GTN with multi-agent chemotherapy (EMA-CO).
GTN is highly chemo-sensitive.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.front: Why is GTN described as the most curable gynaecological malignancy?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.back: Because it is highly chemo-sensitive, with cure rates over 90–95%.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.front: What indicates that a molar pregnancy has progressed to GTN?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.back: Persistent or rising hCG after evacuation.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.front: Which pregnancy events can choriocarcinoma follow?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ea.back:
• A molar pregnancy,
  • a miscarriage,
  • an ectopic pregnancy,
  • or a normal pregnancy
it is malignant and characteristically metastasises to the lung.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Br.front: What is mastitis?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Br.back: Inflammation of the breast tissue — most commonly lactational — caused either by MILK STASIS (duct obstruction → milk accumulation) or by INFECTION (Staph aureus commonest). It presents as a painful, red, warm area of breast ± fever.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Br.front: Why does mastitis usually start as milk stasis rather than infection?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Br.back: When milk is not removed (poor latch, blocked duct, missed feeds, engorgement), it backs up and the duct/tissue inflames — initially a sterile/inflammatory process. If stasis persists, bacteria (Staph aureus) can superinfect it.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Br.front: What is the first-line treatment for all mastitis?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Br.back: Effective milk removal — continue breastfeeding (it is safe and therapeutic), with frequent feeding, good latch/positioning, and expressing if needed. Antibiotics are NOT first-line.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Br.front: What is the commonest organism in infective mastitis?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Br.back: Staphylococcus aureus.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Br.front: What typically allows bacteria to enter and cause infective mastitis?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Br.back: A nipple fissure/crack (often from a poor latch), which acts as a bacterial entry point.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Br.front: How does mastitis progress to a breast abscess, and what is the safety-net?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Br.back: It can progress to a breast abscess (a fluctuant, very tender collection of pus) — and this can happen despite antibiotics, not only when mastitis is untreated. So reassess at 48 hours if she is not improving (ultrasound for an abscess, send a milk culture), and admit if she is severely unwell or septic.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Br.front: Give the reflex approach to a painful, red, wedge-shaped area of breast in a breastfeeding woman.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Br.back: This is mastitis → keep feeding + effective milk removal → add antibiotics only if she is systemically unwell, has an infected nipple fissure, is not improving after 12–24h, or has a positive culture.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Br.front: Contrast inflammatory (milk stasis) and infective mastitis.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Br.back:
• Inflammatory: caused by milk not being removed (blocked duct/poor latch/engorgement), mild/no systemic symptoms, intact nipple, improves with effective milk removal, no antibiotics.
  • Infective: bacterial (Staph aureus) superinfection, fever/systemically unwell, often a nipple fissure, does not improve with milk removal alone, needs antibiotics.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Br.front: What are the clinical features of mastitis?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Br.back:
• Breast pain
  • focal, wedge-shaped/segmental erythema
  • local warmth and inflammation
  • ± nipple discharge and fever.
It is typically unilateral and focal/segmental, following the affected duct/lobule.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Br.front: How is mastitis diagnosed, and when is breast milk culture indicated?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Br.back: It is a clinical diagnosis. Breast milk culture is indicated if it is not improving, the woman is systemically unwell, it is recurrent, or it is being treated in hospital.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Br.front: When is ultrasound used in suspected mastitis?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Br.back: When a breast abscess (a fluctuant mass) is suspected.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Br.front: What is the malignancy caveat for 'mastitis'?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Br.back: 'Mastitis' that does NOT resolve with treatment (especially non-lactational or persistent) should prompt consideration of INFLAMMATORY BREAST CANCER and referral for assessment.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Br.front: What conservative measures are recommended for all mastitis?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Br.back:
• Continue breastfeeding with effective milk removal (feed frequently, good latch, express if needed)
  • breast massage
  • heat packs/warm showers
  • and analgesia (paracetamol/ibuprofen).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Br.front: What are the specific criteria for starting antibiotics in mastitis?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Br.back:
• Systemically unwell
  • an infected nipple fissure
  • symptoms not improving after 12–24h of effective milk removal
  • or a culture indicating infection.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Br.front: What is the first-line antibiotic for infective mastitis, its course, and the penicillin-allergic alternative?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Br.back: Flucloxacillin 500 mg QDS for 10–14 days; if penicillin-allergic, erythromycin 250–500 mg QDS or clarithromycin 500 mg BD for 10–14 days. Reassess at 48 hours if she is not improving.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Br.front: How is a breast abscess managed?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Br.back: Incision and drainage OR ultrasound-guided needle aspiration (increasingly first-line), plus antibiotics; continue expressing/feeding.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Br.front: Why should breastfeeding be continued during mastitis?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Br.back: Because removing milk IS the treatment — it relieves stasis and is safe and therapeutic for both mother and baby.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Br.front: What is Raynaud's of the nipple?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Br.back: Intermittent nipple pain with blanching, then cyanosis ± erythema, during or after feeding; managed by minimising cold exposure.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Br.front: What is breast engorgement and when does it occur?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Br.back: Bilateral firm, swollen, painful breasts, typically around days 3–5 postpartum; managed by feeding/expressing frequently.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Br.front: How does nipple candidiasis (thrush) relate to breastfeeding problems?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Br.back: It often occurs after antibiotics and can cause recurrent mastitis. Treat mother and baby simultaneously: miconazole 2% cream to the mother's nipples after every feed, plus miconazole oral gel to the baby's mouth (nystatin suspension if under 4 months), for at least 2 weeks.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Br.front: Is frequent feeding alone a sign of low milk supply?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Br.back: No — frequent feeding is not by itself a sign of low milk supply, and the mother can be reassured. But >10% weight loss in the first week needs a same-day clinical assessment: an expert feeding review PLUS assessment for dehydration and illness (hypernatraemic dehydration, jaundice, sepsis), with paediatric referral if unwell or not improving.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Br.front: What is the commonest cause of nipple pain in breastfeeding, and its management?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Br.back: Often a poor latch — managed by seeking positioning/latch advice.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Br.front: What is breast engorgement?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Br.back: Painful, over-full, swollen breasts in the early postnatal period, resulting from milk accumulation, interstitial oedema, and increased blood flow when the milk 'comes in'. It is typically bilateral, in the first few days after birth, and worst just before a feed.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Br.front: What is the core mechanism of breast engorgement?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Br.back: Supply outstrips removal in the early days — around days 2–5 postpartum the milk 'comes in' (lactogenesis II) and the breasts fill rapidly; if milk is not removed (infrequent feeds, poor latch), they become overfull, swollen, tense and painful.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Br.front: When does breast engorgement typically occur?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Br.back: In the first few days postpartum (around days 2–5), as the milk comes in.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Br.front: Why can engorgement be mistaken for early mastitis?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Br.back: Because it can cause breast redness and a transient low-grade fever; however, unlike mastitis it is bilateral, diffuse, and settles within about 24h with effective milk removal.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Br.front: Give the reflex clinical picture of breast engorgement.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Br.back: Bilateral, painful, swollen, full breasts in the first few days postpartum, worst before feeds → frequent effective feeding/expression.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Br.front: How does engorgement differ from mastitis in laterality and distribution?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Br.back: Engorgement is bilateral and diffuse (whole breast, both sides); mastitis is usually unilateral and focal/segmental (wedge-shaped).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Br.front: How does engorgement differ from mastitis in fever/course?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Br.back:
• Engorgement: any fever subsides within ~24h and it is self-limiting.
  • Mastitis: persistent fever, systemically unwell, and may need antibiotics.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Br.front: What clinical features suggest engorgement rather than mastitis?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Br.back:
• Bilateral breast pain in the first few days postpartum
  • worst before feeds
  • poor milk flow
  • difficult infant attachment
  • ± a transient fever and redness that settles quickly.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Br.front: Why does engorgement make attachment difficult, creating a vicious cycle?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Br.back: A swollen, tense breast flattens the nipple so the infant cannot attach → milk is not removed → more engorgement, which can down-regulate supply and progress to blocked ducts/mastitis.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Br.front: What are the complications of untreated engorgement?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Br.back:
• Blocked ducts leading to mastitis
  • difficulty breastfeeding
  • and reduced milk supply (unrelieved fullness down-regulates production).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Br.front: What is the mainstay of managing engorgement?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Br.back: Effective, frequent milk removal — continue breastfeeding, feeding frequently and on demand (do not restrict or delay feeds), with support for good latch/attachment.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Br.front: What is reverse pressure softening?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Br.back: Gently pressing on the areola to soften it so the infant can latch more easily when the breast is engorged and tense.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Br.front: What symptomatic relief measures help in engorgement?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Br.back:
• Analgesia (paracetamol/ibuprofen, safe in breastfeeding)
  • a warm compress/shower before a feed (to encourage let-down)
  • a cold compress after a feed (to reduce swelling)
  • ± gentle breast massage
  • and reassurance.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Br.front: Why use a warm compress before and a cold compress after feeds in engorgement?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Br.back: Warmth before a feed encourages let-down/milk flow, while cold after a feed reduces swelling and discomfort.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Br.front: Is breast engorgement self-limiting?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Br.back: Yes — it is benign and self-limiting, settling with effective milk removal; the woman can be reassured.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Br.front: What should be done if the breast is too full/tense for the baby to attach?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Br.back: Express a little milk to soften the breast/areola so the baby can attach and feed effectively.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Br.front: Why is continued frequent breastfeeding important in engorgement, beyond symptom relief?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Br.back: Because it relieves the fullness, maintains milk supply, and prevents progression to blocked ducts and mastitis.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Br.front: What should prompt reconsideration of mastitis rather than engorgement?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Br.back: A persistent fever or a unilateral, focal red (wedge-shaped) area of breast, or systemic illness that does not settle within ~24h.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Br.front: What is a galactocele?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Br.back: A benign, milk-filled RETENTION CYST of the breast, caused by occlusion of a lactiferous duct so milk builds up behind the blockage and is walled off into a cystic lesion. It is characteristically painless with no signs of infection.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Br.front: When does a galactocele typically occur?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Br.back: Typically in women who have recently STOPPED (or reduced) breastfeeding — milk removal falls but some milk is still produced, so a duct occludes and milk pools.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Br.front: What is the single key feature that distinguishes a galactocele from other lactational lumps?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Br.back: It is benign, PAINLESS and NON-infected — unlike mastitis (painful, red, hot, febrile) and breast abscess (painful, fluctuant, systemically unwell).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Br.front: Give the reflex clinical picture of a galactocele.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Br.back: A painless, smooth breast lump in a woman who has recently stopped breastfeeding, with no signs of infection.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Br.front: How does a galactocele differ from mastitis and abscess in pain and systemic features?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Br.back: Galactocele is painless with no infection/systemic upset; mastitis and abscess are painful with fever and systemic illness.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Br.front: How does the timing of a galactocele differ from mastitis?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Br.back: A galactocele typically appears AFTER stopping breastfeeding, whereas mastitis occurs DURING breastfeeding (and abscess is a complication of mastitis).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Br.front: What are the examination findings of a galactocele?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Br.back: A smooth, rounded, mobile, non-tender cystic lump; it may be fluctuant and may express milky fluid.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Br.front: How is a galactocele diagnosed?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Br.back: Largely clinically (a painless lump with recent lactation), supported by ultrasound showing a cystic lesion (± a fat-fluid level, since milk contains fat); aspiration yields milky fluid.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Br.front: What does aspiration of a galactocele yield, and why is this useful?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Br.back: Milky fluid — which is both diagnostic and therapeutic.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Br.front: What ultrasound feature may be seen in a galactocele?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Br.back: A cystic lesion, sometimes with a fat-fluid level (because milk contains fat).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Br.front: What is the breast-lump caution with a suspected galactocele?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Br.back: Any breast lump needs its diagnosis confirmed — if atypical, in an older woman, solid on ultrasound, or persistent, use triple assessment (clinical + imaging + biopsy) to exclude malignancy; do not assume every lactational lump is benign without confirmation.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Br.front: How is a typical galactocele managed?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Br.back: Reassurance — galactoceles are benign and often resolve spontaneously (especially once lactation fully ceases).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Br.front: When is needle aspiration used for a galactocele?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Br.back: If it is symptomatic, large, or for diagnostic confirmation; it yields milky fluid and may need repeating.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Br.front: When is excision of a galactocele considered?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Br.back: Rarely — reserved for recurrent cysts, diagnostic uncertainty, or non-resolution.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Br.front: What causes the milk build-up in a galactocele?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Br.back: Occlusion of a lactiferous duct, behind which milk accumulates and is walled off into a cyst.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Br.front: Why does a galactocele classically appear as breastfeeding winds down?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Br.back: Because milk removal decreases while some milk is still produced, so a duct can occlude and milk pools behind it, forming the cyst.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Br.front: Is a galactocele infected or associated with fever?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Br.back: No — it is characteristically non-infected and painless, with no fever or systemic upset (which is what distinguishes it from mastitis/abscess).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Br.front: What is the triple assessment used to exclude malignancy in a breast lump?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Br.back: Clinical examination, imaging (ultrasound ± mammography), and biopsy — used if a lump is atypical, persistent, or in an older woman.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.front: What are the common benign vulvovaginal/cervical conditions and the key organising principle?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.back: Atrophic vaginitis, Bartholin's & Nabothian cysts, and cervical ectropion — benign conditions that are usually clinical diagnoses but must be distinguished from sinister mimics (postmenopausal bleeding → endometrial cancer; post-coital bleeding → cervical cancer).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.front: What is atrophic vaginitis, and its modern name?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.back: Thinning, drying and inflammation of the vaginal/vulval/urethral tissues due to OESTROGEN DEFICIENCY (most commonly after the menopause). The modern term is genitourinary syndrome of menopause (GSM), reflecting that it affects the vulva, vagina, urethra and bladder.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.front: Why are these genital/urinary tissues affected by oestrogen deficiency?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.back: They are oestrogen-dependent — oestrogen maintains a thick, elastic, well-lubricated, glycogen-rich epithelium with an acidic pH (lactobacilli → lactic acid). When oestrogen falls, tissues thin, lose elasticity, dry out, and the pH rises (alkaline).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.front: What symptoms result from atrophic vaginitis/GSM?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.back:
• Vaginal dryness, itch, soreness and dyspareunia
  • post-coital bleeding/spotting and reduced lubrication
  • and urinary symptoms — urgency, frequency, dysuria and recurrent UTIs.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.front: Why is GSM described as chronic and progressive?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.back: Because, unlike hot flushes, it does not self-resolve — it persists and worsens without treatment and recurs when treatment stops, so it needs ongoing management.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.front: Why was the term 'atrophic vaginitis' replaced by 'genitourinary syndrome of menopause'?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.back: Because oestrogen deficiency also causes urinary symptoms and recurrent UTIs (the urethra and bladder trigone are oestrogen-sensitive too), not just vaginal changes.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.front: List causes of the oestrogen deficiency underlying GSM.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.back:
• Menopause (commonest)
  • also premature ovarian insufficiency
  • post-oophorectomy
  • breastfeeding (lactation)
  • anti-oestrogen drugs (GnRH agonists, aromatase inhibitors, tamoxifen)
  • and post-chemotherapy/radiotherapy.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.front: Give the reflex clinical picture of atrophic vaginitis/GSM.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.back: A post-menopausal woman with vaginal dryness, dyspareunia, or recurrent UTIs → moisturisers + topical vaginal oestrogen.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.front: What are the examination findings in atrophic vaginitis?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.back:
• A pale, thin, dry vaginal epithelium with loss of rugae (smooth)
  • reduced elasticity
  • a narrowed/shortened vagina
  • petechiae/friability/contact bleeding
  • and a pale/atrophic vulva
  • vaginal pH is raised/alkaline.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.front: How is atrophic vaginitis diagnosed?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.back: It is a clinical diagnosis, usually needing no tests; exclude infection (candida, BV, STIs) if there is discharge, and send a urine culture if there are UTI symptoms.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.front: What is the crucial differential to exclude in a post-menopausal woman with bleeding attributed to atrophy?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.back: Endometrial cancer — post-menopausal bleeding must be investigated (2-week-wait referral if aged 55 or over, considered under 55, plus transvaginal ultrasound for endometrial thickness ± biopsy) before attributing bleeding to atrophy.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.front: What are the first-line/non-hormonal treatments for atrophic vaginitis?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.back: Vaginal moisturisers (regular, e.g. hyaluronic-acid based) and lubricants (for intercourse) — first-line for mild symptoms or when oestrogen is contraindicated/declined.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.front: What is the mainstay treatment for atrophic vaginitis, and its safety profile?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.back:
Low-dose TOPICAL vaginal oestrogen (cream, pessary, or ring) —
  • it directly restores the epithelium
  • has minimal systemic absorption
  • can be used long-term
  • and needs NO progestogen.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.front: How long does topical vaginal oestrogen take to work, and what happens if it is stopped?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.back: It takes about 3 months for full benefit, and symptoms recur when treatment is stopped (as the condition is chronic).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.front: Why is no progestogen needed with topical vaginal oestrogen (unlike systemic HRT)?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.back: Because systemic absorption is minimal, so there is no significant stimulation of the endometrium requiring progestogenic endometrial protection.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.front: How does systemic HRT relate to GSM management?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.back: If a woman also has systemic menopausal symptoms (e.g. flushes), systemic HRT helps GSM too; vaginal oestrogen can be added if genitourinary symptoms persist despite systemic HRT.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.front: What are the alternative treatments for GSM beyond oestrogen?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.back:
• Vaginal DHEA (prasterone)
  • and ospemifene (an oral SERM).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.front: How is GSM managed in a woman with breast cancer, especially on aromatase inhibitors?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.back: Non-hormonal options (moisturisers/lubricants) first; vaginal oestrogen only after discussion with oncology.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.front: Roughly how common is atrophic vaginitis/GSM after menopause, and why does it matter to ask about it?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.back: It affects more than 50% of post-menopausal women but is massively under-reported, so clinicians should proactively ask about it.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.front: What do Bartholin's and Nabothian cysts have in common, and how do they differ in site?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.back: Both are common, benign mucus-retention cysts arising from blockage of a mucus-secreting gland/duct with trapped mucus. Bartholin's cysts are at the VULVA (vaginal opening); Nabothian cysts are on the CERVIX.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.front: Give the reflex clue for distinguishing a Bartholin's from a Nabothian cyst.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.back:
• A unilateral cyst/swelling at the vaginal opening = Bartholin's
  • a smooth whitish bump on the cervix = Nabothian.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.front: Where are the Bartholin's (greater vestibular) glands located and what is their function?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.back: Bilaterally at the vaginal introitus (approximately 4 and 8 o'clock positions); they secrete mucus for lubrication.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.front: How does a Bartholin's cyst form, and how does an abscess develop?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.back: The Bartholin's duct blocks, causing mucus retention and a cyst; if the cyst becomes infected, it forms an abscess.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.front: Describe the typical features of a Bartholin's cyst (uninfected).
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.back: A unilateral, fluid-filled swelling 1–4 cm near the vaginal opening; often soft and painless or only mildly uncomfortable.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.front: Describe the features of a Bartholin's abscess.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.back: Hot, tender, red, painful and rapidly enlarging.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.front: What is the commonest cause of a Bartholin's abscess, and what should be considered?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.back: E. coli is the commonest cause (usually polymicrobial); consider STI testing (gonorrhoea/chlamydia).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.front: How is a Bartholin's cyst (uninfected) managed?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.back: Conservatively — hygiene, analgesia and warm compresses; many resolve.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.front: How is a Bartholin's abscess managed?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.back: Antibiotics plus a swab (culture) and surgical drainage — a Word catheter (a balloon catheter creating an epithelialised tract) or marsupialisation (suturing the cyst edges open, used for recurrence).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.front: What is a Word catheter and its purpose in Bartholin's abscess?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.back: A small balloon catheter inserted after drainage to keep the cavity open so it forms an epithelialised tract, reducing recurrence.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.front: What is marsupialisation?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.back: A surgical procedure suturing the edges of the drained Bartholin's cyst/abscess open to create a permanent opening — used especially for recurrent cases.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.front: What is the malignancy caveat for a Bartholin's mass?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.back: In a woman over ~40 years, consider biopsy/excision to exclude a (rare) Bartholin's gland carcinoma.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.front: How does a Nabothian cyst form?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.back: Squamous epithelium of the ectocervix grows over the mucus-producing columnar epithelium of the endocervix (squamous metaplasia at the transformation zone), trapping mucus underneath and forming a cyst.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.front: What triggers Nabothian cyst formation?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.back: It follows childbirth, minor trauma, or cervicitis.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.front: Describe the typical appearance and symptoms of a Nabothian cyst.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.back: Smooth, rounded, whitish/yellow bumps on the cervix near the os, usually found incidentally on speculum examination and typically asymptomatic.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.front: How is a Nabothian cyst managed?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.back: Reassurance — they are benign and persist harmlessly, needing no treatment; colposcopy or biopsy/excision only if the diagnosis is uncertain or to exclude other pathology.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.front: Are Bartholin's and Nabothian cysts usually symptomatic?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.back: Both are usually harmless and often incidental; the clinical importance is recognising them as benign (and managing a Bartholin's abscess if it becomes infected).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.front: Why might a Nabothian cyst need colposcopy?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.back: If the diagnosis is uncertain — to confirm it is benign and exclude other cervical pathology.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.front: Give the reflex management summary for a hot, tender, red unilateral swelling at the vaginal opening.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.back: This is a Bartholin's abscess → antibiotics + swab + Word catheter or marsupialisation.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.front: What is cervical ectropion (ectopy)?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.back: A benign condition where the COLUMNAR epithelium of the endocervix extends OUT onto the ectocervix, exposing the delicate glandular lining on the outer cervix. It is NOT a true erosion/ulcer despite the old name 'erosion'.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.front: What are the two epithelia of the cervix and where are they?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.back:
• The ectocervix (outer) is tough stratified SQUAMOUS epithelium (pale pink)
  • the endocervix (canal) is delicate, mucus-secreting COLUMNAR epithelium (red, glandular).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.front: Why does cervical ectropion develop, and in which states?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.back: High-oestrogen states move the squamocolumnar junction outward, exposing fragile columnar epithelium on the ectocervix — seen in puberty/adolescence, combined pill use, and pregnancy.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.front: Why does exposed columnar epithelium cause post-coital bleeding and discharge?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.back: Columnar epithelium is thin, vascular and mucus-producing, so it bleeds easily on contact (post-coital bleeding) and produces increased mucus discharge.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.front: What is the transformation zone?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.back: The squamocolumnar junction — a dynamic zone that moves with oestrogen; exposed columnar epithelium undergoes squamous metaplasia over time.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.front: Give the reflex clinical picture of cervical ectropion.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.back: Post-coital bleeding + increased clear discharge in a young pill-user or pregnant woman, with a red velvety ring around the os — but exclude cervical cancer/STIs first.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.front: What is the typical appearance of a cervical ectropion on speculum examination?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.back: A red, velvety ring around the external os that bleeds easily on contact.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.front: What are the clinical features of cervical ectropion?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.back:
Often asymptomatic; when symptomatic —
  • post-coital bleeding (classic contact bleeding)
  • intermenstrual bleeding
  • increased non-offensive clear mucus discharge
  • ± dyspareunia.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.front: Which conditions must be excluded before attributing symptoms to cervical ectropion?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.back: Cervical cancer — examine with a speculum first: a suspicious-looking cervix means an urgent 2-week-wait referral, NOT a smear (screening is not diagnostic, and a normal or recent smear does not exclude cancer). Also exclude CIN (colposcopy), infection/STIs (chlamydia/gonorrhoea swabs) and pregnancy; consider cervical polyps.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.front: What is the critical safety point about post-coital bleeding?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.back:
Never assume post-coital bleeding is 'just ectropion'.
  • A suspicious-looking cervix goes on the 2-week-wait pathway straight away — a normal or recent smear does not exclude cancer and must not delay referral
  • A normal-looking cervix with persistent symptoms warrants colposcopy
  • Always exclude STIs too.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.front: When does cervical ectropion regress?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.back: After the menopause or on stopping the combined oral contraceptive pill (as the oestrogen driver is removed).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.front: How is an asymptomatic cervical ectropion managed?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.back: Reassurance and no treatment — it is benign and often regresses after menopause or stopping the pill.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.front: How is a symptomatic cervical ectropion managed (after excluding sinister causes)?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.back: Change contraception (stop/switch the combined pill to remove the oestrogen driver) or ablate the columnar epithelium (cryotherapy, cautery, silver nitrate, or diathermy) for persistent symptoms.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.front: How is symptomatic cervical ectropion managed in pregnancy?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.back: Usually conservatively, as it regresses after delivery.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.front: Which contraceptive is associated with cervical ectropion, and how does stopping it help?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.back: The combined oral contraceptive pill (oestrogen-containing); stopping or switching it removes the oestrogen driver and can improve symptoms.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.front: Is cervical ectropion premalignant?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.back: No — it is a normal, benign, oestrogen-driven finding; the key task is excluding serious causes (cervical cancer/CIN, STIs) before attributing symptoms to it.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.front: Why is the old term 'cervical erosion' misleading?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.back: Because there is no true erosion or ulcer — it is simply endocervical (columnar) lining located on the outer cervix.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.front: Which ablative options are used for persistent symptomatic cervical ectropion?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.back: Cryotherapy, cautery, silver nitrate, or diathermy applied to the columnar epithelium.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.front: In which three physiological/hormonal situations is cervical ectropion most commonly seen?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.back: Puberty/adolescence, combined pill use, and pregnancy — all high-oestrogen states.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.front: What are the three common benign uterine/pelvic conditions and how are they distinguished?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.back:
• Fibroids (firm masses, bulk symptoms/menorrhagia)
  • endometriosis (cyclical pain, dyspareunia, subfertility — deposits outside the uterus)
  • and adenomyosis (endometrium within the myometrium → bulky, tender uterus).
They are distinguished by history and imaging.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.front: What are uterine fibroids (leiomyomas)?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.back: Benign, oestrogen- and progesterone-DEPENDENT smooth-muscle tumours of the myometrium — the commonest benign uterine tumour and the commonest pelvic tumour in women. They are often multiple and range from tiny to very large.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.front: Why does the hormone-dependence of fibroids explain their behaviour?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.back: Because they grow in the reproductive years and in pregnancy (high oestrogen) and REGRESS after the menopause (oestrogen withdrawal); this is why management can be conservative near menopause and why anti-oestrogen therapy (GnRH agonists) shrinks them.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.front: Which demographic factors are associated with fibroids?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.back: They are very common (especially in the 30s–40s) and are more frequent and larger in Black women; they are often asymptomatic.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.front: Give the reflex clinical picture of uterine fibroids.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.back: Heavy menstrual bleeding + a bulky, irregular ('knobbly') uterus + pressure symptoms in a reproductive-age woman → ultrasound → treat by symptoms, fertility wishes and size.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.front: How does the location of a fibroid determine its symptoms?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.back:
• Submucosal → heavy menstrual bleeding + subfertility/miscarriage (distorts the cavity)
  • intramural → bleeding + bulk symptoms
  • subserosal → bulk/pressure symptoms (bladder/bowel)
  • pedunculated → can tort (twist) causing acute pain
  • cervical → pressure/obstruction.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.front: Which fibroid location most causes heavy bleeding and fertility problems, and why?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.back: Submucosal fibroids — because they bulge into the uterine cavity under the endometrium, distorting the cavity, they are the biggest cause of fibroid-related heavy bleeding and subfertility/miscarriage.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.front: What is the commonest location of fibroids?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.back: Intramural — within the myometrial wall (causing bleeding and bulk symptoms).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.front: What can happen to a pedunculated fibroid?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.back: It can undergo torsion (twist on its stalk), causing acute pain; a submucosal pedunculated fibroid may present as a 'fibroid polyp'.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.front: What is the commonest symptom of fibroids, and its consequence?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.back: Heavy menstrual bleeding, which can cause iron-deficiency anaemia.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.front: What bulk/pressure symptoms can fibroids cause?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.back:
• Abdominal swelling/mass
  • urinary frequency or retention
  • and constipation.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.front: What is the characteristic examination finding in fibroids?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.back: A firm, enlarged, irregular ('knobbly'), non-tender uterus.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.front: What is the first-line investigation for fibroids?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.back: Transvaginal (± transabdominal) ultrasound — to assess number, size and location. Hysteroscopy assesses submucosal/cavity fibroids, MRI maps before surgery/embolisation, and FBC/ferritin assess anaemia.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.front: What is the key size threshold guiding fibroid management, and why?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.back: The <3 cm vs ≥3 cm split — medical therapy is less effective for larger (≥3 cm) fibroids, so bulk/large fibroids more often need procedural options.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.front: What is the first-line treatment for fibroid-related heavy bleeding with small (<3 cm) fibroids?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.back: The levonorgestrel intrauterine system (LNG-IUS/Mirena), provided the uterine cavity is not distorted. If a submucosal fibroid IS distorting the cavity the LNG-IUS is unsuitable — consider hysteroscopic removal (myomectomy) instead.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.front: What non-hormonal options treat fibroid-related heavy bleeding?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.back: Tranexamic acid 1 g orally three times daily during menstruation (avoid in active or previous VTE) and NSAIDs such as mefenamic acid 500 mg three times daily; hormonal options include the combined pill or cyclical progestogens.
