conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.front: How do GnRH agonists (e.g. goserelin) help with large fibroids, and what limits their use?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.back: They induce a temporary menopausal state that shrinks fibroids, useful short-term especially pre-operatively; use is limited to ≤6 months (with add-back HRT) because of menopausal side effects/bone loss.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.front: What procedural options exist for large (≥3 cm) or bulk-symptom fibroids?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.back:
• GnRH agonists (pre-op shrinkage)
  • uterine artery embolisation (uterine-sparing)
  • myomectomy (removes fibroids, preserves fertility)
  • hysterectomy (definitive)
  • and endometrial ablation for bleeding.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.front: Which fibroid treatment is preferred if fertility is desired?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.back: Myomectomy — it removes fibroids while preserving the uterus/fertility; uterine artery embolisation and hysterectomy are generally avoided when fertility is wanted.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.front: Why is ulipristal acetate now restricted in fibroid treatment?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.back: Because of a risk of serious liver injury (MHRA warning) — it is now only for intermittent treatment when surgery/UAE are unsuitable, failed or declined.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.front: What is red (carneous) degeneration of a fibroid?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.back: When a fibroid outgrows its blood supply (especially in the second trimester of pregnancy), causing infarction/haemorrhage → acute severe abdominal pain, low-grade fever, vomiting and localised tenderness.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.front: How is red degeneration of a fibroid managed?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.back: Conservatively — analgesia, rest and hydration; it is self-limiting.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.front: What obstetric problems can fibroids cause in pregnancy?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.back:
• Malpresentation
  • obstructed labour
  • postpartum haemorrhage (poor uterine contraction)
  • and miscarriage (as well as red degeneration).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.front: Are fibroids premalignant, and what features suggest leiomyosarcoma?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.back: Fibroids are benign and malignant transformation (leiomyosarcoma) is very rare (<1%). Suspect it with rapid growth, growth AFTER the menopause, or pain/systemic features.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.front: What is endometriosis?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.back: Endometrial-like tissue OUTSIDE the uterine cavity (in the pelvis and beyond) — an oestrogen-dependent, chronic inflammatory condition causing pelvic pain, dysmenorrhoea, dyspareunia and subfertility.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.front: What is an endometrioma, and what is endometrium within the myometrium called?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.back: An endometrioma is an endometriotic ovarian cyst ('chocolate cyst'). Endometrial tissue within the myometrium is adenomyosis (a related, 'internal' condition).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.front: What is the core pathophysiological concept of endometriosis?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.back: Ectopic endometrium still responds to the menstrual cycle — it proliferates, breaks down and bleeds each cycle, but the blood cannot escape, causing cyclical inflammation, fibrosis, adhesions and scarring.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.front: Why is endometriosis pain typically cyclical, becoming chronic over time?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.back: The deposits bleed with menstruation, causing cyclical inflammation; over time, fibrosis and adhesions develop, so the pain becomes constant/chronic.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.front: Give the reflex symptom cluster of endometriosis.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.back: Cyclical pelvic pain + dysmenorrhoea + deep dyspareunia + subfertility in a reproductive-age woman.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.front: Why does severity of symptoms correlate poorly with disease extent in endometriosis?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.back: Tiny deposits can cause severe pain, while large endometriomas may be silent — so symptom severity does not reliably reflect the amount of disease.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.front: What causes deep dyspareunia in endometriosis?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.back: Deposits on the uterosacral ligaments and in the pouch of Douglas.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.front: What symptoms suggest bowel involvement in endometriosis?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.back: Dyschezia (painful defaecation) ± cyclical rectal bleeding, from bowel/rectovaginal deposits.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.front: What symptoms suggest bladder involvement in endometriosis?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.back: Dysuria ± cyclical haematuria, from bladder deposits.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.front: Why does endometriosis cause subfertility?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.back: Adhesions distort pelvic anatomy and inflammation impairs implantation, so it is a major cause of subfertility.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.front: Why does endometriosis regress after menopause and respond to hormonal suppression?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.back: Because it is oestrogen-dependent — reducing oestrogen (menopause or hormonal suppression) reduces disease activity.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.front: What might examination show in endometriosis, and what is a key caveat?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.back:
It may be NORMAL (a normal exam does not exclude endometriosis). If abnormal:
  • tender uterosacral nodules/pouch of Douglas
  • a fixed retroverted uterus (adhesions)
  • adnexal masses (endometriomas)
  • or bluish deposits in the posterior fornix.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.front: What imaging should be offered to all women with suspected endometriosis, and its limitation?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.back: Transvaginal ultrasound — offered to all, even if examination is normal (detects endometriomas and deep disease). A NORMAL ultrasound does NOT exclude endometriosis, as superficial peritoneal disease is not seen.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.front: When is MRI used in endometriosis?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.back: For suspected DEEP disease involving the bowel, bladder or ureter.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.front: What is the gold-standard investigation for endometriosis, and what does it show?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.back: Laparoscopy with direct visualisation ± biopsy — the only way to definitively confirm or exclude it. Findings include 'powder-burn' spots, red/vesicular lesions, adhesions and endometriomas.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.front: Should treatment be delayed until laparoscopy confirms endometriosis?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.back: No — treat EMPIRICALLY; do not delay treatment waiting for laparoscopy. (A normal systematic laparoscopy makes endometriosis unlikely.)

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.front: What is the first-line analgesia for endometriosis pain?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.back: NSAIDs ± paracetamol, as a 3-month trial.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.front: What is first-line hormonal treatment for endometriosis pain?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.back: The combined oral contraceptive pill or progestogens (± continuous/back-to-back use); the LNG-IUS also reduces bleeding and pain.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.front: What hormonal options are used for refractory endometriosis?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.back: GnRH agonists (e.g. goserelin — a temporary menopausal state, ≤6 months with add-back HRT) and GnRH antagonists (relugolix/linzagolix).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.front: What surgical options exist for endometriosis?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.back:
• Laparoscopic excision or ablation of deposits plus adhesiolysis (for refractory pain or diagnosis-plus-treatment)
  • ovarian cystectomy for an endometrioma (balanced against ovarian reserve)
  • and specialist MDT surgery for deep disease.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.front: What is the definitive surgical treatment for severe refractory endometriosis when fertility is not desired?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.back: Hysterectomy ± bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy (removing the oestrogen source).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.front: Why must hormonal treatments not be used in women trying to conceive?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.back: Because all hormonal treatments for endometriosis are contraceptive and do NOT improve fertility.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.front: How is subfertility due to endometriosis managed?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.back: With laparoscopic surgery (excision/ablation, endometrioma cystectomy), which can improve spontaneous pregnancy rates, and assisted conception (IVF) as needed — not hormonal suppression.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.front: List the main complications of endometriosis.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.back:
• Chronic pelvic pain
  • subfertility
  • endometriomas ('chocolate cysts')
  • dense adhesions ('frozen pelvis', bowel obstruction)
  • quality-of-life/mental-health impact
  • and a small associated risk of clear-cell/endometrioid ovarian cancer.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.front: What is adenomyosis?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.back: Endometrial tissue (glands + stroma) WITHIN the myometrium ('endometriosis interna'), causing an enlarged, bulky, 'boggy' uterus with heavy, painful periods.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.front: What is the core concept of adenomyosis?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.back: Endometrium in the wrong layer — endometrial tissue grows down into the uterine muscle. Being oestrogen-responsive, it bleeds cyclically within the muscle, causing heavy menstrual bleeding and dysmenorrhoea/chronic pelvic pain.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.front: What are the two clinical hallmarks of adenomyosis?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.back: (1) Heavy menstrual bleeding (an enlarged, poorly-contracting uterus) and (2) painful periods (dysmenorrhoea) with chronic pelvic pain.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.front: What is the characteristic examination finding in adenomyosis?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.back: A diffusely enlarged, 'bulky', tender, 'boggy' (soft), symmetrical uterus.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.front: Who is the classic patient with adenomyosis?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.back: A multiparous woman in her 40s (± previous uterine surgery such as caesarean or D&C); it often co-exists with fibroids and endometriosis.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.front: Why does adenomyosis regress after the menopause?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.back: Because it is oestrogen-dependent — the fall in oestrogen after menopause reduces disease activity.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.front: How does the uterus in adenomyosis differ from that in fibroids on examination?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.back:
• Adenomyosis: diffusely enlarged, soft/boggy, tender, symmetrical
  • Fibroids: firm, irregular ('knobbly'), non-tender, asymmetrical.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.front: How does the pain pattern differ between adenomyosis and fibroids?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.back: Adenomyosis is typically painful (prominent dysmenorrhoea), whereas fibroids are often painless (presenting with bleeding/bulk).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.front: How does adenomyosis differ from endometriosis?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.back: Adenomyosis is endometrium IN the myometrium (internal → bulky tender uterus); endometriosis is endometrium OUTSIDE the uterus (pelvis → dyspareunia, adhesions, endometriomas).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.front: What type of dysmenorrhoea occurs in adenomyosis and its timing?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.back: Secondary dysmenorrhoea — the pain characteristically starts 3–4 days before the period.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.front: What is the first-line investigation for adenomyosis?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.back: Transvaginal ultrasound — more accurate than transabdominal ultrasound, and of comparable accuracy to MRI, which is a useful adjunct and superior for assessing the junctional zone.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.front: What ultrasound features suggest adenomyosis?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.back:
• A globally enlarged uterus
  • myometrial cysts
  • an ill-defined/thickened junctional zone
  • and 'venetian-blind' shadowing.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.front: What is the definitive diagnosis of adenomyosis?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.back: Histology after hysterectomy — although modern imaging (transvaginal ultrasound/MRI) now allows a clinical diagnosis.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.front: What is the first-line treatment for adenomyosis (heavy bleeding + pain)?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.back: The levonorgestrel intrauterine system (LNG-IUS/Mirena) — it thins the endometrium and treats both bleeding and pain.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.front: What non-hormonal options are useful in adenomyosis, especially when trying to conceive?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.back: Tranexamic acid and NSAIDs — useful for bleeding ± pain and non-hormonal, so appropriate when the woman is trying to conceive.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.front: What hormonal options (other than LNG-IUS) are used in adenomyosis?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.back: The combined oral contraceptive pill or progestogens (e.g. dienogest) to suppress the ectopic endometrium; GnRH agonists are second-line (temporary menopausal state, short-term/pre-op with add-back HRT).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.front: What uterine-sparing procedures are options for adenomyosis?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.back: Uterine artery embolisation (UAE) and endometrial ablation (for bleeding).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.front: What is the definitive cure for adenomyosis?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.back: Hysterectomy — for severe refractory disease when fertility is not desired.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.front: Give the reflex clinical picture of adenomyosis.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.back: Heavy, painful periods with a diffusely enlarged, tender, boggy uterus in a multiparous woman in her 40s.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.front: What complication can heavy menstrual bleeding in adenomyosis cause?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Be.back: Iron-deficiency anaemia — so an FBC should be checked.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.front: How is antepartum haemorrhage (APH) defined?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.back: Bleeding from the genital tract from 24 weeks of gestation onwards. The two major causes are placenta praevia and placental abruption; vasa praevia and the placenta accreta spectrum are rarer but critical.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.front: What single question best organises the assessment of APH?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.back: Is the bleeding PAINLESS with a SOFT non-tender uterus (suggesting praevia) or PAINFUL with a TENDER 'woody' uterus (suggesting abruption)?

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.front: What immediate steps apply to any APH with maternal/fetal compromise?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.back:
• Resuscitate (ABC)
  • do NOT perform a vaginal examination until praevia is excluded (a speculum is safe, a digital exam is not)
  • give anti-D if Rhesus-negative
  • and involve senior obstetrics.
Do not be reassured by a normal blood pressure — pregnancy masks blood loss.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.front: What is placenta praevia?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.back: A placenta lying wholly or partly in the LOWER uterine segment, at or covering the internal cervical os — in the path of delivery. Its hallmark is PAINLESS antepartum haemorrhage in the second half of pregnancy.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.front: Why does placenta praevia cause bleeding?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.back: As the lower segment stretches and the cervix effaces later in pregnancy, the low-lying placenta shears off, causing painless, unprovoked vaginal bleeding (with a soft, non-tender uterus).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.front: Why may placenta praevia require caesarean delivery?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.back: Because a placenta covering the os blocks the exit, making vaginal delivery unsafe — so caesarean is needed.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.front: What is the 'golden rule' in suspected placenta praevia?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.back: Do NOT perform a digital vaginal examination — it can provoke catastrophic haemorrhage. Diagnose by ultrasound instead.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.front: Give the reflex clinical picture of placenta praevia.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.back: Painless vaginal bleeding in later pregnancy with a soft, non-tender uterus → no vaginal exam → transvaginal ultrasound → caesarean if praevia.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.front: Contrast the pain and uterus in praevia vs abruption.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.back:
• Praevia: PAINLESS bleeding with a soft, non-tender uterus.
  • Abruption: PAINFUL (constant) bleeding with a tense, 'woody' hard, tender uterus.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.front: Contrast the bleeding and shock in praevia vs abruption.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.back:
• Praevia: visible/revealed bleeding, with shock broadly proportional to the visible loss.
  • Abruption: bleeding may be concealed, with shock OUT of proportion to visible loss.
Caveat for both — a young pregnant woman compensates, so blood pressure can stay normal until 1–1.5 litres have been lost; tachycardia comes first and hypotension is a late sign.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.front: Contrast the fetal heart and coagulation in praevia vs abruption.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.back:
• Praevia: fetal heart usually normal, coagulation problems rare.
  • Abruption: fetus often distressed, and DIC can occur.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.front: What is a 'herald bleed' in placenta praevia?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.back: A small warning bleed that may precede a larger haemorrhage in placenta praevia.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.front: What is the modern (RCOG) terminology for placental position, replacing grades I–IV?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.back:
• LOW-LYING placenta = placental edge <20 mm from the internal os (not covering)
  • PLACENTA PRAEVIA = placenta covers/overlies the internal os.
(Old grades I–II ≈ low-lying; III–IV ≈ praevia.)

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.front: List the main risk factors for placenta praevia.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.back:
• Previous caesarean/uterine scar (dose-dependent)
  • multiparity
  • multiple pregnancy
  • older maternal age
  • previous praevia
  • IVF
  • and smoking.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.front: Why does placenta praevia with a previous caesarean raise particular concern?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.back: Because it increases the risk of the placenta accreta spectrum (abnormal placental invasion into the caesarean scar), which carries a major postpartum haemorrhage risk.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.front: What clinical features (besides painless bleeding) suggest placenta praevia?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.back:
• A soft, non-tender uterus
  • usually normal fetal heart
  • and malpresentation or a high, non-engaged head (the low placenta blocks engagement)
  • shock proportional to visible loss.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.front: What is the first-line/gold-standard investigation for placental position, and why?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.back: Transvaginal ultrasound — it is safe and more accurate than transabdominal ultrasound for confirming placental position. Praevia is often first picked up incidentally at the 20-week anomaly scan.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.front: What investigations accompany an actively bleeding woman with suspected praevia?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.back:
• A speculum (not digital) exam may assess bleeding
  • bloods including FBC, group & save/crossmatch and clotting
  • plus anti-D if Rhesus-negative.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.front: How is an incidental low placenta at the 20-week scan managed?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.back: Rescan at 32 weeks — most low placentas 'migrate' upward and resolve; a final scan around 36 weeks is done if it persists, to plan delivery. No activity/intercourse restriction is needed unless bleeding occurs.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.front: How is persistent placenta praevia delivered?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.back: By elective caesarean at 36–37 weeks (current RCOG, uncomplicated), with an experienced obstetrician and anaesthetist present; consider antenatal corticosteroids if early delivery is likely.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.front: Can a low-lying placenta allow vaginal delivery?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.back: A low-lying placenta with the edge clear of the os may allow a trial of vaginal delivery, but a placenta covering the os requires caesarean.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.front: How is active bleeding from placenta praevia managed?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.back:
• Admit
  • ABC with large-bore IV access, bloods/crossmatch, fluids/blood, and maternal + fetal monitoring
  • if the mother cannot be stabilised, is labouring, or is at term → emergency caesarean
  • anti-D if Rhesus-negative
  • steroids if preterm.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.front: What should happen if a woman with known praevia labours before her elective section?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.back: Emergency caesarean.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.front: Why is postpartum haemorrhage a particular risk after praevia?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.back: Because the lower uterine segment (where the placenta was implanted) contracts poorly, so it does not achieve haemostasis as effectively as the upper segment.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.front: List the main complications of placenta praevia.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.back:
• Antepartum and postpartum haemorrhage (poorly-contracting lower segment)
  • need for transfusion/hysterectomy
  • placenta accreta spectrum (especially with prior caesarean)
  • preterm birth
  • and malpresentation.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.front: What is placental abruption?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.back: Premature SEPARATION of a NORMALLY-sited placenta from the uterine wall, causing maternal haemorrhage into the space between placenta and uterus. It classically presents as PAINFUL antepartum haemorrhage with a tender, 'woody'-hard uterus.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.front: How does abruption differ conceptually from placenta praevia?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.back: Abruption is a problem of premature DETACHMENT of a normally-sited placenta, whereas praevia is a problem of placental LOCATION (low-lying/over the os).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.front: Why does placental abruption cause a painful, 'woody'-hard, tender uterus?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.back: Bleeding into the decidua basalis forms a haematoma that irritates the myometrium, which contracts tonically — producing constant pain and a tense, woody, tender uterus.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.front: Why can shock be 'out of proportion' to visible bleeding in abruption?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.back: Because bleeding may be CONCEALED (trapped behind the placenta), so the visible external loss under-represents the true blood loss — a key safety concept.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.front: What are the three main consequences of placental abruption?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.back:
• (1) Pain with a woody-hard tender uterus
  • (2) potentially concealed bleeding with shock out of proportion to visible loss
  • and (3) fetal compromise plus maternal DIC.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.front: Give the reflex clinical picture of placental abruption.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.back: Painful vaginal bleeding with a tense, tender, woody uterus and shock out of proportion to visible loss → resuscitate and deliver. It is an obstetric emergency.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.front: Contrast pain and uterine findings in abruption vs praevia.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.back:
• Abruption: PAINFUL (constant) with a tender, tense, 'woody'-hard uterus.
  • Praevia: PAINLESS with a soft, non-tender uterus.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.front: Contrast fetal heart, lie and coagulation in abruption vs praevia.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.back:
• Abruption: fetal heart often absent/distressed, NORMAL lie, DIC can occur.
  • Praevia: fetal heart usually normal, malpresentation common, coagulation problems rare.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.front: What is the difference between revealed and concealed abruption?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.back:
• Revealed: blood escapes through the cervix as visible vaginal bleeding.
  • Concealed: blood is trapped retroplacentally with little/no visible bleeding — dangerous, as the true loss is hidden and shock is out of proportion.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.front: What is the clinical trap of concealed abruption?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.back: A woman with severe abdominal pain and signs of shock but little or no visible bleeding can still have a major concealed abruption — do not be reassured by minimal external blood.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.front: Roughly what proportion of abruptions are concealed vs revealed?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.back: About 20–35% are concealed and 65–80% are revealed.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.front: What does the ABRUPTION mnemonic stand for?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.back:
• A – previous Abruption (strongest single risk)
  • B – Blood pressure (hypertension/pre-eclampsia)
  • R – Ruptured membranes
  • U – Uterine injury/trauma
  • P – Polyhydramnios
  • T – Twins/multiple gestation
  • I – Infection (chorioamnionitis)
  • O – Older age (>35)
  • N – Narcotics (cocaine/amphetamines) + smoking.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.front: What is the single strongest risk factor for placental abruption?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.back: A previous placental abruption.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.front: Which risk factors for abruption are the classically-tested ('high-yield triad') causes?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.back:
• Hypertension/pre-eclampsia
  • trauma
  • and cocaine/smoking.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.front: Why is placental abruption a clinical diagnosis rather than an ultrasound one?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.back: Because ultrasound has poor sensitivity (~24%) and does NOT exclude abruption; a normal scan cannot rule it out. Ultrasound is used mainly to exclude praevia.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.front: Which blood tests are important in suspected placental abruption?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.back:
• FBC
  • clotting (for DIC)
  • U&E (for AKI)
  • fibrinogen
  • and group & save/crossmatch.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.front: What is the role of the Kleihauer test in abruption?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.back: In ALL Rhesus-negative women with an antepartum haemorrhage, the Kleihauer test quantifies fetomaternal haemorrhage to guide the anti-D dose.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.front: What monitoring is used for the fetus in placental abruption?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.back: Continuous cardiotocography (CTG).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.front: What are the principles of initial management of placental abruption?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.back:
It is an obstetric emergency:
  • resuscitate the mother (ABC, two large-bore cannulae, IV fluids/blood, crossmatch, catheterise for urine output)
  • involve senior obstetric/anaesthetic/haematology teams
  • treat DIC with blood products
  • continuous CTG
  • and give anti-D if Rhesus-negative.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.front: How is abruption managed if the fetus is alive but distressed (any gestation)?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.back: Immediate caesarean section.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.front: How is abruption managed if the fetus is alive, >36 weeks, with no distress?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.back: Deliver vaginally (induce/aim for vaginal birth).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.front: How is abruption managed if the fetus is alive, <36 weeks, with no distress?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.back: Observe with antenatal corticosteroids and NO tocolysis; the threshold to deliver depends on gestation and maternal/fetal condition.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.front: How is abruption managed if the fetus has died?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.back: Induced VAGINAL delivery (avoiding caesarean where possible), while stabilising the mother and managing DIC.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.front: What is a Couvelaire uterus?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.back: When abruption blood infiltrates the myometrium, producing a bruised, boggy uterus that contracts poorly → postpartum haemorrhage, occasionally requiring hysterectomy.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.front: List the main maternal and fetal complications of placental abruption.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.back:
• Maternal: DIC, hypovolaemic shock, AKI/anuria, postpartum haemorrhage, Couvelaire uterus, death.
  • Fetal: hypoxia, intrauterine death, prematurity, and growth restriction (with chronic abruption).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.front: What is vasa praevia?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.back: Unprotected FETAL blood vessels running through the placental MEMBRANES, across or near the internal os, below the presenting part — unsupported by placental tissue or the cord's Wharton's jelly. Because they are unprotected, they rupture when the membranes break, causing fetal exsanguination.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.front: How does vasa praevia differ fundamentally from placenta praevia and abruption?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.back: In vasa praevia the bleeding is FETAL (the baby exsanguinates), whereas in praevia and abruption the bleeding is MATERNAL (the mother shocks).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.front: Why can even a small blood loss be catastrophic in vasa praevia?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.back: Because the fetal circulating blood volume is tiny (~80–100 ml/kg), so even a small bleed can rapidly exsanguinate and kill the fetus (bradycardia/death within minutes).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.front: Why is the mother NOT shocked in vasa praevia?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.back: Because the bleeding is fetal, not maternal — the small volume lost is from the baby's circulation, so the mother remains haemodynamically stable while the fetus deteriorates.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.front: What is the classic triad of acute vasa praevia?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.back: (1) Rupture of membranes → (2) painless vaginal bleeding → (3) fetal bradycardia/distress.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.front: How does the outcome of vasa praevia depend on the timing of diagnosis?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.back: If diagnosed antenatally and delivered by planned caesarean, survival is >95%. If it presents acutely (undiagnosed) at membrane rupture, fetal mortality is high (~60%).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.front: Give the reflex clinical picture of acute vasa praevia.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.back: Painless vaginal bleeding with fetal bradycardia immediately after the membranes rupture → emergency caesarean.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.front: What is Type I vasa praevia?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.back: Vasa praevia arising from a VELAMENTOUS cord insertion — the cord inserts into the membranes, so the vessels run unprotected through the membranes to the placenta.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.front: What is Type II vasa praevia?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.back: Vasa praevia arising from a vessel connecting the placenta with a SUCCENTURIATE (accessory) lobe — the bridging vessels cross the os.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.front: List the risk factors for vasa praevia (who to screen).
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.back:
• Velamentous cord insertion
  • a succenturiate/bilobed placenta
  • a low-lying placenta/placenta praevia in the second trimester
  • multiple pregnancy
  • and IVF/assisted conception.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.front: What is the diagnostic test for antenatal vasa praevia?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.back: Transvaginal ultrasound with COLOUR DOPPLER, showing fetal vessels crossing or lying near the internal os.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.front: What should prompt assessment of the cord insertion/vasa praevia at the anomaly scan?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.back: Finding a low-lying placenta at the anomaly scan should prompt assessment of the cord insertion (and screening for vasa praevia).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.front: How does acute (undiagnosed) vasa praevia present?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.back: At membrane rupture: painless, dark-red vaginal bleeding with acute fetal bradycardia/distress; occasionally pulsating fetal vessels are felt on vaginal examination through the membranes.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.front: How is acute vasa praevia diagnosed and managed?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.back: It is a clinical diagnosis (bleeding + fetal bradycardia at membrane rupture) — there is no time for tests; management is immediate (category 1) emergency caesarean, with neonatal resuscitation and likely neonatal transfusion.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.front: How is antenatally diagnosed vasa praevia managed?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.back:
• Consider third-trimester hospital admission
  • give antenatal corticosteroids (fetal lung maturity)
  • and perform an ELECTIVE caesarean at ~34–36 weeks, BEFORE labour and membrane rupture.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.front: Why is elective caesarean for vasa praevia timed at 34–36 weeks?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.back: To deliver the baby before labour and spontaneous membrane rupture (which would tear the vessels), balancing this against prematurity — corticosteroids are given for lung maturity.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.front: What neonatal care may be needed after acute vasa praevia?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.back: Neonatal resuscitation and likely neonatal transfusion, because the baby has lost blood from its own circulation.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.front: What is the survival difference between diagnosed and undiagnosed vasa praevia?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.back: Antenatally diagnosed and delivered electively: survival >95%. Undiagnosed with acute rupture: mortality ~60% (survival ~40%).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.front: Why are the fetal vessels in vasa praevia so vulnerable to rupture?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.back: Because they run through the membranes without the protection of placental tissue or the cord's Wharton's jelly, so they are easily torn when the membranes rupture.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.front: What is the overall management principle for vasa praevia?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.back: Antenatal DETECTION (screening high-risk women) followed by elective caesarean before labour — this is what converts a high-mortality condition into one with >95% survival.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.front: What is placenta accreta spectrum (PAS)?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.back: Abnormally ADHERENT or INVASIVE placentation, in which the placenta attaches through/into the myometrium because of a defective decidua basalis, so it fails to separate at delivery — risking catastrophic postpartum haemorrhage. It is a spectrum by depth: accreta → increta → percreta.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.front: What is the underlying pathophysiology of placenta accreta spectrum?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.back: A damaged or absent decidua basalis (the normal cleavage plane), usually over a previous uterine scar (caesarean). Without this cleavage plane the placenta is anchored into (or through) the myometrium and won't detach in the third stage, causing torrential haemorrhage.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.front: Define placenta accreta (the mnemonic and depth).
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.back: Accreta = 'ATTACH' — the placenta attaches to the myometrium surface (decidua absent) but does not invade into it.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.front: Define placenta increta.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.back: Increta = 'INVADE' — the placenta invades INTO the myometrium.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.front: Define placenta percreta.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.back: Percreta = 'PERCOLATES' — the placenta percolates THROUGH the myometrium and serosa, ± into adjacent organs such as the bladder.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.front: Which grade of PAS may involve the bladder and require urology input?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.back: Percreta — where the placenta penetrates through the serosa, potentially into the bladder or other adjacent organs, needing urology involvement and complex surgery.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.front: What is the key risk combination for placenta accreta spectrum?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.back: Placenta PRAEVIA plus a PREVIOUS CAESAREAN — a low placenta lying over the old lower-segment scar.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.front: List other risk factors for placenta accreta spectrum.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.back:
• Multiple caesareans (dose-dependent)
  • myomectomy
  • curettage or manual placental removal
  • older maternal age
  • high parity
  • IVF
  • and previous PAS.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.front: How does placenta accreta spectrum usually present antenatally?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.back: Usually asymptomatic — it is found on screening ultrasound in at-risk women. There may be antepartum bleeding if there is co-existing praevia.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.front: What happens if placenta accreta spectrum is undiagnosed until delivery?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.back: At delivery the placenta fails to separate, causing a retained placenta and massive postpartum haemorrhage.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.front: What is the primary screening/diagnostic investigation for PAS?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.back: Ultrasound — used to screen at-risk women (praevia + previous caesarean).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.front: What are the ultrasound hallmarks of placenta accreta spectrum?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.back:
• Myometrial thinning
  • abnormal placental lacunae ('moth-eaten'/'Swiss-cheese' spaces)
  • and neovascularisation between uterus and placenta (± loss of the clear zone and bladder-wall interruption).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.front: What is the role of MRI in placenta accreta spectrum?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.back: MRI complements ultrasound to assess the DEPTH and lateral extent of invasion — especially for a posterior placenta or suspected parametrial/bladder involvement; its diagnostic value is similar to expert ultrasound.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.front: Where should a woman with known placenta accreta spectrum be delivered?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.back: In a specialist PAS centre with an experienced multidisciplinary team — senior obstetrician, anaesthetist, urologist, interventional radiology, haematology, massive-transfusion capacity and neonatology.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.front: When is planned delivery timed for placenta accreta spectrum?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.back: A planned caesarean at around 35–36⁺⁶ weeks (before labour), with antenatal corticosteroids; earlier if bleeding occurs.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.front: What is the definitive surgical management of placenta accreta spectrum?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.back: Caesarean plus hysterectomy with the placenta LEFT IN SITU — deliver the baby through an incision that avoids the placenta, do NOT attempt to remove the placenta, and proceed to hysterectomy with the placenta still attached.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.front: Why must the placenta NOT be forcibly removed in placenta accreta spectrum?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.back: Because there is no cleavage plane — attempting removal tears the invaded myometrium and causes torrential haemorrhage.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.front: What preparations are made for the massive haemorrhage risk in PAS surgery?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.back:
• Crossmatched blood and a massive-transfusion protocol
  • cell salvage
  • and interventional radiology (e.g. internal iliac balloon occlusion) where available.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.front: When might conservative management (leaving the placenta in situ without hysterectomy) be considered in PAS?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.back: For fertility preservation in selected cases — but it carries risks of infection, delayed haemorrhage, and the later need for hysterectomy.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.front: What should women with PAS be consented for?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.back:
• Hysterectomy
  • massive transfusion
  • bladder/ureteric injury
  • and ICU admission.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.front: List the main complications of placenta accreta spectrum.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.back:
• Massive obstetric haemorrhage (dominant risk)
  • DIC
  • massive transfusion
  • hysterectomy (loss of fertility)
  • bladder/ureteric/bowel injury (especially percreta)
  • ICU admission
  • maternal death
  • and preterm birth.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.front: Give the reflex approach when placenta praevia is found with a previous caesarean.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.back: Screen for accreta antenatally (ultrasound ± MRI) and plan a specialist MDT caesarean-hysterectomy.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.front: What is androgen insensitivity syndrome (AIS) and its inheritance?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.back: An X-LINKED RECESSIVE disorder of end-organ RESISTANCE to testosterone, caused by a mutation in the androgen receptor gene on the X chromosome. A genotypically male (46,XY) individual develops a female phenotype. It is a disorder of sex development (DSD).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.front: What single molecular defect underlies AIS?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.back: A non-functioning androgen receptor — so although the testes produce testosterone, tissues cannot respond to androgens.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.front: Why do individuals with AIS have female external genitalia despite being 46,XY with functioning testes?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.back: Because the androgen receptor doesn't work, tissues cannot respond to testosterone, so the external genitalia default to the female pattern (no virilisation).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.front: Why do individuals with AIS develop breasts?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.back: Testosterone is aromatised to OESTROGEN, and oestrogen-responsive tissues still respond — driving breast development and a female habitus.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.front: Why do individuals with AIS have no uterus, cervix, upper vagina or fallopian tubes?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.back: The testes still produce anti-Müllerian hormone (AMH), which acts normally to suppress the Müllerian (female internal) structures.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.front: Why do individuals with AIS have neither ovaries nor a uterus?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.back: There are no ovaries because the gonads are testes (46,XY); and no uterus because AMH suppressed the Müllerian ducts — leaving a blind-ending vagina, no menstruation and infertility.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.front: Summarise the three hormone signals that explain the AIS phenotype.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.back:
• (1) Testosterone is made but not sensed → female external genitalia + scant hair
  • (2) AMH is present and acts → no uterus/cervix/upper vagina/tubes
  • (3) oestrogen (aromatised from testosterone) acts → breast development.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.front: What are the two forms of AIS?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.back:
• Complete AIS (CAIS) — a fully female phenotype
  • and partial AIS (PAIS) — ambiguous or undervirilised genitalia.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.front: How might AIS present in infancy/childhood?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.back: With bilateral inguinal hernias or groin swellings in an apparent girl that turn out to contain testes (undescended) — a key trigger to investigate.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.front: How does AIS typically present in adolescence?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.back: Primary amenorrhoea in a normally developed phenotypic female (breasts present), with scant pubic/axillary hair and a short/blind-ending vagina.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.front: Why is pubic and axillary hair scant in AIS?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.back: Because pubic and axillary hair growth is androgen-dependent, and androgens are not sensed — making scant hair a useful discriminator.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.front: Give the classic reflex description of AIS.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.back: A phenotypic female with primary amenorrhoea, absent uterus, breast development, scant pubic/axillary hair, and inguinal 'hernias' (testes) → karyotype 46,XY.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.front: How does AIS (CAIS) differ from Müllerian agenesis (MRKH) in primary amenorrhoea with an absent uterus?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.back:
• AIS: 46,XY, high (male-range) testosterone, scant pubic hair, gonads are testes
  • MRKH: 46,XX, female-range/normal testosterone, NORMAL pubic hair, ovaries present.
Karyotype, testosterone and pubic hair distinguish them.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.front: How does 5α-reductase deficiency differ from AIS?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.back: Both are 46,XY with absent uterus and high testosterone, but in 5α-reductase deficiency DHT is low and affected individuals virilise at puberty, whereas in AIS androgens are not sensed at all (no virilisation).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.front: What is the key confirmatory investigation in AIS?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.back: Karyotype showing 46,XY; androgen receptor gene sequencing confirms the mutation.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.front: What is the typical hormone profile in post-pubertal AIS?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.back:
• Testosterone in the normal/high MALE range
  • raised LH (no androgen negative feedback)
  • oestrogen present
  • AMH detectable.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.front: What do pelvic imaging (USS/MRI) findings show in AIS?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.back:
• Absent uterus and ovaries
  • testes in the abdomen or inguinal canal
  • and a blind-ending vagina.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.front: What is the overall management approach to AIS?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.back:
• Multidisciplinary care (endocrine/gynae/urology/psychology/genetics) with sensitive counselling
  • usually female sex of rearing in CAIS
  • gonadectomy (timing now usually deferred to post-puberty)
  • oestrogen replacement after gonadectomy
  • vaginal and psychological support.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.front: Why is gonadectomy now typically deferred until after puberty in AIS?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.back: Because the pre-pubertal malignancy risk of the intra-abdominal testes is low, and retaining the testes allows spontaneous puberty/feminisation via aromatisation; gonadectomy is a shared decision, with gonads often retained into early adulthood under surveillance.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.front: What is the malignancy risk from retained intra-abdominal testes in AIS?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.back: An increased risk of gonadal (germ-cell) malignancy that rises with age; modern estimates of frank malignancy are lower than older figures (~1–2%, premalignant change ~6%), almost all occurring post-puberty.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.front: Why is oestrogen replacement given after gonadectomy in AIS, and why is progesterone not needed?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.back: Oestrogen maintains secondary sexual characteristics and protects bone (preventing osteoporosis) and cardiovascular/metabolic health. Progesterone is not needed because there is no uterus/endometrium to protect.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.front: What additional supportive measures are important in AIS?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.back:
• Vaginal dilation or surgery if the vagina is short (for sexual function)
  • psychological support
  • genetic counselling (X-linked implications for relatives)
  • and infertility counselling (cannot carry a pregnancy).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.front: Why is fertility not possible in AIS?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__An.back: There is no uterus and no ovaries, so the individual cannot produce eggs or carry a pregnancy.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: What two parallel cycles make up the menstrual cycle, and what links them?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: The OVARIAN cycle (follicular → ovulation → luteal) and the UTERINE/endometrial cycle (proliferative → secretory → menstruation). They are linked by ovarian hormones — oestrogen and progesterone drive the uterine changes.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: Which axis governs the menstrual cycle and what is its overall feedback pattern?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: The hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal (HPG) axis, running cyclically. It is governed by NEGATIVE feedback throughout, except for one mid-cycle POSITIVE-feedback burst (high oestrogen) that triggers ovulation.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: What happens during the follicular phase (ovarian side)?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: FSH rises and stimulates follicle development (several recruited, one becomes dominant); the growing follicle's granulosa cells produce rising oestrogen.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: What is the uterine counterpart of the follicular phase, and which hormone drives it?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: The PROLIFERATIVE phase — oestrogen (from the developing follicle) causes endometrial proliferation/thickening and thins cervical mucus to make it fertile.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: Why does FSH fall slightly during the mid/late follicular phase?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: Rising oestrogen exerts negative feedback, lowering FSH; this helps select the single dominant follicle (which can survive the falling FSH).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: What triggers ovulation, and what is unique about the feedback involved?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: When oestrogen reaches a critically high level, feedback switches from negative to POSITIVE, triggering a massive LH surge (with a smaller FSH surge). This is the ONLY positive-feedback loop in the cycle and one of the few in endocrinology.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: How long after the LH surge begins does ovulation occur?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: The follicle ruptures and releases the egg approximately 24–36 hours after the LH surge begins.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: What happens during the luteal phase (ovarian side)?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: The ruptured follicle becomes the corpus luteum, which secretes progesterone (plus some oestrogen).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: What are the effects of progesterone in the luteal phase?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back:
• It produces a SECRETORY endometrium (glands secrete, preparing for implantation),
  • thickens cervical mucus,
  • and raises basal body temperature (an ovulation marker).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: What is the feedback effect of luteal-phase progesterone and oestrogen?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: They suppress FSH and LH (negative feedback), preventing the development of new follicles during the luteal phase.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: Why is the luteal phase a fixed length, and what is the clinical implication?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: The corpus luteum has a fixed lifespan, so the luteal phase is reliably ~14 days. Therefore cycle-length variation comes from the FOLLICULAR phase, not the luteal phase — useful for dating ovulation.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: What happens during menstruation if pregnancy does not occur?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: The corpus luteum regresses (~day 24–28), so progesterone and oestrogen fall; the endometrium can no longer be maintained and sheds (menstruation). The falling hormones release feedback, so FSH rises again to start the next cycle.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: Describe the FSH pattern across the cycle.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: FSH rises early (follicular phase), has a small ovulatory surge, and is suppressed during the luteal phase.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: Describe the LH pattern across the cycle.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: LH is low through the follicular phase, then shows a dramatic mid-cycle surge that triggers ovulation, and falls again in the luteal phase.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: Describe the oestrogen pattern across the cycle.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: Oestrogen rises through the follicular phase, peaks just before ovulation (triggering the LH surge), then has a second smaller rise during the luteal phase.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: Describe the progesterone pattern across the cycle.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: Progesterone is low in the follicular phase, rises in the luteal phase (from the corpus luteum), and falls if no pregnancy occurs — leading to menstruation.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: What raises basal body temperature after ovulation, and how is this used?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: Progesterone from the corpus luteum raises basal body temperature; a sustained temperature rise is used as a marker that ovulation has occurred.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: What happens hormonally if the egg is fertilised and implants?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: The embryo secretes hCG, which 'rescues' the corpus luteum so it keeps producing progesterone; the endometrium is maintained (no menstruation) and pregnancy continues.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: What is the role of hCG, and when does the placenta take over progesterone production?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: hCG maintains the corpus luteum (and is the basis of pregnancy tests). The placenta takes over progesterone production at around weeks 8–12.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: How does the combined oral contraceptive pill work in terms of the cycle?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: Its oestrogen and progesterone provide negative feedback, reducing FSH and LH, so there is no follicular development or ovulation.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: How does progesterone-only contraception work?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back:
• It thickens cervical mucus,
  • thins the endometrium,
  • and (depending on the type/dose) may inhibit ovulation.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: What hormonal changes occur at menopause?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: Follicle depletion leads to falling oestrogen and a marked rise in FSH (loss of negative feedback from the ovary).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: What is the hormonal picture in PCOS relevant to the cycle?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: A disrupted axis with a raised LH:FSH ratio and anovulation, producing irregular/absent cycles.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: Which two events should be anchored to understand the cycle?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back:
• (1) The mid-cycle oestrogen peak → LH surge → ovulation; and
  • (2) the luteal progesterone rise → secretory endometrium (then its fall → menstruation).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: What are the two broad purposes of maternal physiological adaptation in pregnancy?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: (1) To SUPPLY the fetus (increased cardiac output, blood volume, ventilation) and (2) to PREPARE for delivery and lactation — driven by pregnancy hormones (hCG, progesterone, oestrogen, hPL).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: Which organ becomes the main endocrine organ of pregnancy?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: The placenta — it takes over as the principal source of pregnancy hormones (progesterone, oestrogen, hPL) after the early corpus-luteum phase.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: What is the role of hCG in pregnancy?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: It maintains the corpus luteum early (sustaining progesterone) until the placenta takes over at ~weeks 8–12, and is the basis of pregnancy tests.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: What are progesterone's key roles in pregnancy?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back:
• Maintaining the endometrium/pregnancy,
  • relaxing smooth muscle (the unifying cause of many adaptations),
  • and preventing uterine contractions.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: Which single hormonal effect explains many pregnancy adaptations, and give examples?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back:
Progesterone-mediated SMOOTH MUSCLE RELAXATION — causing
  • vasodilation (↓SVR),
  • reduced gut motility (constipation/reflux),
  • and ureteric dilation (hydronephrosis).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: What is the role of human placental lactogen (hPL)?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: It increases maternal insulin resistance, diverting glucose to the fetus — the physiological basis of gestational diabetes.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: By how much does cardiac output rise in pregnancy and via what mechanisms?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: Cardiac output rises ~30–50%, through increased stroke volume and heart rate, to supply the uteroplacental circulation.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: By how much does plasma volume increase in pregnancy, and why?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: Plasma volume rises ~50%, driven by RAAS activation and fluid retention.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: What happens to systemic vascular resistance and blood pressure in pregnancy?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: Progesterone-mediated vasodilation lowers systemic vascular resistance, so BP falls in the 1st/2nd trimester and returns towards normal by term.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: Why is a rising blood pressure or hypertension abnormal in pregnancy?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: Because BP normally FALLS in early–mid pregnancy (vasodilation); a rising BP or hypertension is abnormal and should prompt consideration of pre-eclampsia.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: What is aortocaval compression and how is it managed?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: The gravid uterus compresses the IVC (and aorta) when the woman is supine, reducing venous return and causing hypotension (supine hypotensive syndrome). It is managed by nursing in the left lateral tilt.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: Explain the physiological (dilutional) anaemia of pregnancy.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: Plasma volume increases (~50%) more than red cell mass (~25%), so the blood is diluted, producing a physiological fall in haemoglobin — a normal dilutional anaemia, not iron deficiency.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: Why is pregnancy a hypercoagulable state, and what is the consequence?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: There are increased clotting factors, reduced fibrinolysis, and venous stasis (Virchow's triad), raising VTE risk — a leading cause of maternal death, hence the importance of prophylaxis.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: Why are iron and folate requirements increased in pregnancy?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: Fetal demand. Folic acid is given routinely (and prevents neural tube defects); iron is given only when deficiency or anaemia is identified, not routinely.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: Describe the respiratory adaptations of pregnancy.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: Progesterone increases tidal volume and hence minute ventilation, blowing off CO₂ to cause a mild (compensated) respiratory alkalosis; oxygen consumption rises with fetal/maternal demand.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: Why do many pregnant women feel breathless, and what must be excluded?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: Physiological breathlessness results from increased ventilation and the uterus splinting the diaphragm. Pulmonary embolism must be excluded given the increased VTE risk.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: What happens to GFR and serum creatinine/urea in pregnancy?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: Renal blood flow and GFR rise ~50%, lowering serum creatinine and urea — so a 'normal' creatinine may actually be relatively high for pregnancy.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: Why is there an increased risk of UTI/pyelonephritis in pregnancy?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: Physiological hydronephrosis (progesterone-induced ureteric relaxation plus uterine compression) causes urinary stasis, predisposing to UTI and pyelonephritis.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: Why does mild glycosuria occur in pregnancy?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: The renal threshold for glucose is lowered, so mild glycosuria can occur and is usually benign.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: What drives the insulin resistance of pregnancy, and what condition results if uncompensated?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: Insulin resistance is driven by hPL, progesterone and cortisol (diverting glucose to the fetus); if the maternal pancreas cannot compensate, gestational diabetes develops — typically in later trimesters when placental hormones peak.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: How does pregnancy affect the thyroid, and its clinical implication?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: Oestrogen raises thyroid-binding globulin, increasing the total thyroid hormone requirement — which is why levothyroxine doses often need increasing in pregnancy. Separately, hCG has weak TSH-like activity and can transiently stimulate a functioning thyroid.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: What GI adaptations occur in pregnancy and their mechanism?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back:
Progesterone relaxes smooth muscle →
  • reduced gut motility (constipation),
  • reduced lower oesophageal sphincter tone (reflux/heartburn),
  • and gallbladder stasis (gallstones);
nausea/vomiting is hCG-related.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: How is VTE prophylaxis/treatment managed in pregnancy, and why not warfarin/DOACs?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: Low molecular weight heparin (LMWH) is used, because warfarin is teratogenic and DOACs are not recommended in pregnancy.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: How do the renal/volume changes of pregnancy affect drug handling?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: Increased GFR raises drug clearance and the increased volume of distribution alters drug levels — both affecting dosing in pregnancy.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: What four organ functions does the placenta perform for the fetus?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back:
• Gas exchange (replacing the lungs)
  • nutrition (replacing the gut)
  • waste removal (replacing the kidneys)
  • and endocrine function (hCG, progesterone, oestrogen, hPL).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: How does the placenta achieve gas exchange, nutrition and waste removal?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back:
• O₂ passes to the fetus and CO₂ away down gradients
  • glucose crosses by facilitated diffusion, amino acids by active transport, and fatty acids to the fetus
  • urea/creatinine/CO₂ are cleared to maternal blood.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: What is the key structural principle of the placenta regarding maternal and fetal blood?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: Maternal and fetal blood come close but do NOT mix — they are separated by the placental membrane, across which exchange occurs by diffusion/transport.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: Which substances readily cross the placenta?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back:
• O₂, CO₂, nutrients and water
  • IgG antibodies (giving neonatal passive immunity)
  • many drugs (e.g. warfarin, alcohol)
  • some pathogens (TORCH)
  • and anti-D IgG.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: Which important substances do NOT cross the placenta well?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back:
• Maternal red cells (normally)
  • IgM (too large)
  • and heparin
— which is why heparin/LMWH is the anticoagulant of choice in pregnancy.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: Why is heparin/LMWH preferred over warfarin in pregnancy, in placental terms?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: Warfarin crosses the placenta and is teratogenic, whereas heparin does not cross — so LMWH is used for anticoagulation in pregnancy.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: Which antibody class crosses the placenta and what does it provide?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: IgG crosses the placenta, providing the neonate with passive immunity.IgM is too large to cross.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: Explain the placental basis of rhesus disease.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: Maternal anti-D IgG crosses the placenta and attacks fetal red cells, causing fetal haemolysis (haemolytic disease of the fetus/newborn).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: What are TORCH infections in the context of placental transfer?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: Pathogens that can cross the placenta to cause congenital infection — Toxoplasma, Rubella, CMV, and others (e.g. herpes/'other') — hence 'TORCH'.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: What is the structure of fetal haemoglobin (HbF) and its key property?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: HbF is 2α2γ and has a HIGHER oxygen affinity than adult HbA (a left-shifted O₂ dissociation curve).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: Why does HbF's higher oxygen affinity matter physiologically?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: It lets the fetus extract O₂ from maternal blood across the placenta — fetal Hb 'grabs' the O₂ that maternal Hb releases.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: Why do β-chain disorders like sickle cell and β-thalassaemia present after birth rather than in utero?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: Because HbF (which lacks β-chains) is gradually replaced by adult HbA after birth; as HbF wanes, the β-chain defects become manifest.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: Name the three fetal shunts and what each connects.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back:
• Ductus venosus (umbilical vein → IVC)
  • foramen ovale (right atrium → left atrium)
  • and ductus arteriosus (pulmonary artery → aorta).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: What is the purpose of the ductus venosus?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: It bypasses the liver, sending oxygenated placental blood from the umbilical vein straight to the IVC and heart.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: What is the purpose of the foramen ovale?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: It bypasses the lungs by shunting blood from the right atrium to the left atrium across the atrial septum.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: What is the purpose of the ductus arteriosus?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: It bypasses the lungs by diverting blood from the pulmonary artery to the aorta.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: What haemodynamic conditions drive the fetal shunt pattern?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: High pulmonary vascular resistance (fluid-filled, non-functional lungs) and low systemic vascular resistance (the large placental circulation) drive blood away from the lungs and through the shunts.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: Trace the path of oxygenated blood in the fetal circulation.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: Placenta → umbilical vein → ductus venosus (past the liver) → IVC → right atrium → most crosses the foramen ovale to the left heart → body/brain; blood in the pulmonary artery mostly crosses the ductus arteriosus to the aorta.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: What two events at birth transform the circulation?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back:
• The first breath inflates the lungs → pulmonary vascular resistance falls dramatically (blood flows to the lungs)
  • and cord clamping removes the low-resistance placenta → systemic vascular resistance rises.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: What does the foramen ovale become after birth, and what triggers its closure?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: It becomes the fossa ovalis; closure is triggered when left atrial pressure exceeds right atrial pressure, causing the flap to close.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: What does the ductus arteriosus become after birth, and what triggers its closure?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: It becomes the ligamentum arteriosum; closure is triggered by rising O₂ and falling prostaglandins, constricting it (over days).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: What does the ductus venosus become after birth?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: The ligamentum venosum, following the loss of umbilical blood flow.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: How do prostaglandins affect the ductus arteriosus, and what is the clinical application?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: Prostaglandins keep the ductus arteriosus OPEN in utero. Clinically, prostaglandin (PGE) is used to keep it open in duct-dependent congenital heart disease, while NSAIDs/indometacin (which reduce prostaglandins) close a patent ductus arteriosus.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: What is patent ductus arteriosus (PDA) and how is it managed pharmacologically?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: Failure of the ductus arteriosus to close, causing a left-to-right shunt. Indometacin (reducing prostaglandins) is used to close it; PGE is used to keep it open when a duct-dependent lesion is present.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: What is persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: Failure of the pulmonary vascular resistance to fall at birth, so the circulation does not transition normally to the lungs.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: What are the two hormonal arms of lactation and their distinct roles?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back:
• Prolactin (anterior pituitary) makes the milk (production/synthesis)
  • and oxytocin (posterior pituitary) ejects it (the let-down reflex, by contracting myoepithelial cells).
Both are sustained by the suckling stimulus.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: Which hormone is responsible for milk PRODUCTION, and from where?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: Prolactin, from the anterior pituitary — it drives milk synthesis in the alveolar cells.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: Which hormone is responsible for milk EJECTION (let-down), and from where?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: Oxytocin, from the posterior pituitary — it contracts the myoepithelial cells around the alveoli to eject milk into the ducts.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: How is the breast prepared for lactation during pregnancy?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: Placental oestrogen and progesterone develop the ducts and alveoli (glandular tissue), priming the breast for milk production.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: What is the 'pregnancy paradox' of lactation?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: Prolactin rises through pregnancy, but the high oestrogen and progesterone BLOCK prolactin's milk-producing action — so no milk is made during pregnancy despite the priming.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: What triggers milk production to begin after birth, and when does milk 'come in'?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: Delivery of the placenta causes oestrogen and progesterone to fall sharply, removing the block so prolactin can act; milk production begins around day 2–3 postpartum.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: What is colostrum?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: The protein- and antibody-rich (especially IgA) first milk, produced in the first few days before mature milk.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: Describe the suckling reflex and its role in milk supply.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: The baby suckling sends a sensory signal to the hypothalamus → increased prolactin (and oxytocin) → more milk made and ejected. This 'supply and demand' loop matches milk supply to the baby's demand.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: How is prolactin normally controlled by dopamine?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: Prolactin is under tonic INHIBITION by dopamine; suckling reduces this dopamine inhibition, allowing prolactin to rise.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: Why do dopamine antagonists (e.g. antipsychotics) raise prolactin?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: Because dopamine normally inhibits prolactin; blocking dopamine removes this inhibition, raising prolactin and potentially causing galactorrhoea.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: Which drugs are used to SUPPRESS lactation, and why do they work?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: Dopamine agonists — bromocriptine and cabergoline — because increasing dopamine activity suppresses prolactin and hence milk production.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: Describe the let-down (milk ejection) reflex pathway.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: Suckling → signal to the hypothalamus → posterior pituitary releases oxytocin → oxytocin contracts myoepithelial cells around the alveoli → milk is ejected into the ducts.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: How can the let-down reflex be triggered or inhibited by non-suckling factors?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: It can be triggered by a conditioned/neural stimulus such as the baby's cry or the sight of the baby, and inhibited by stress/pain (sympathetic activation)— which is why a relaxed environment aids breastfeeding.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: Besides milk ejection, what other effect does oxytocin have postpartum?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: It causes uterine contraction, helping the uterus involute after birth (and can cause 'afterpains' during breastfeeding).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: What is lactational amenorrhoea and its mechanism?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: High prolactin suppresses the HPG axis (↓GnRH → ↓LH/FSH), suppressing ovulation and causing amenorrhoea during breastfeeding— a natural but unreliable contraceptive effect.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: Why does breastfeeding delay the return of fertility postpartum?
