conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: Because high prolactin suppresses the HPG axis and ovulation (lactational amenorrhoea), delaying the return of menstruation and fertility, especially during exclusive breastfeeding.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: What immune protection does breast milk provide the neonate?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: Secretory IgA, which provides mucosal protection for the neonate's gut and respiratory tract — a form of natural passive immunity; colostrum is especially antibody-rich.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: Why is caution needed when prescribing drugs to a breastfeeding mother?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: Because many drugs pass into breast milk and can reach the infant, so prescribing during breastfeeding requires care over drug safety.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: In a non-pregnant person, what can cause hyperprolactinaemia with galactorrhoea and amenorrhoea?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: A prolactinoma or dopamine antagonists (e.g. antipsychotics) — raising prolactin, which causes galactorrhoea and suppresses the HPG axis (amenorrhoea).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.front: Summarise how supply is established and maintained in breastfeeding.
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.back: Suckling stimulates prolactin (production) and oxytocin (ejection); the more the baby feeds, the more milk is made and released — a demand-driven 'supply and demand' system.

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.front: Which cells produce β-hCG, and which test is first-line to confirm pregnancy?
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.back: β-hCG is produced by the syncytiotrophoblast. The qualitative URINE hCG (point-of-care) test is first-line to confirm pregnancy — highly sensitive, usually positive around the time of the missed period.

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.front: What is the 'discriminatory zone' for serum β-hCG?
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.back: Above a serum β-hCG of ~1500 IU/L an intrauterine pregnancy should normally be visible on transvaginal ultrasound. Above this level with an EMPTY uterus, suspect an ectopic pregnancy.

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.front: How does serum β-hCG behave in a normal early intrauterine pregnancy?
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.back: It roughly DOUBLES every ~48 hours. A suboptimal rise or plateau suggests a failing IUP or an ectopic pregnancy.

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.front: A woman has a serum β-hCG much higher than expected for her gestational dates. What should you think of?
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.back: Molar pregnancy (gestational trophoblastic disease) or a multiple (e.g. twin) pregnancy. Very high hCG also drives severe hyperemesis gravidarum and is a tumour marker in choriocarcinoma/germ-cell tumours.

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.front: Can a single β-hCG value confirm a viable or intrauterine pregnancy?
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.back: No. A single value cannot distinguish a viable IUP, a failing IUP, or an ectopic. It must be interpreted alongside ultrasound and, when needed, serial 48-hourly values.

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.front: What is the first-line imaging investigation for pain/bleeding in early pregnancy, and what two things does it establish?
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.back: Transvaginal ultrasound (TVUSS). It establishes LOCATION (intrauterine vs ectopic) and VIABILITY of the pregnancy.

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.front: State the RCOG-style TVUSS criteria for a non-viable pregnancy (miscarriage).
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.back:
• Mean sac diameter (MSD) ≥25 mm with NO visible fetal pole, OR
  • crown-rump length (CRL) ≥7 mm with NO fetal heartbeat.
If borderline/below threshold, repeat the scan after ~7 days before confirming.

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.front: In what order do normal early structures appear on TVUSS, and at roughly what gestation?
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.back:
• Gestational sac (~4.5-5 weeks, β-hCG ~1000-1500+), then
  • yolk sac (~5-5.5 weeks), then
  • fetal pole with a heartbeat (~6 weeks).

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.front: What is the classic TVUSS triad suggesting an ectopic pregnancy?
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.back:
• Empty uterus (no intrauterine sac despite positive test)
  • an adnexal mass separate from the ovary ('tubal ring'/'bagel' or complex mass)
  • free fluid in the pouch of Douglas.

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.front: What is a 'pregnancy of unknown location' (PUL) and how is it managed?
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.back: A positive pregnancy test but no pregnancy visible anywhere (uterus or adnexa) on TVUSS. Managed with serial serum β-hCG measurements to determine whether it is an early intrauterine pregnancy, a failing PUL, or an ectopic.

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.front: What is a pregnancy of unknown location (PUL)?
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.back: A positive pregnancy test with NO intrauterine and NO extrauterine pregnancy visible on transvaginal ultrasound (TVUSS). Serial serum β-hCG (two samples 48h apart) is used in stable women to characterise it as a developing IUP, a failing pregnancy, or a possible ectopic.

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.front: In a PUL, what does a serum β-hCG rise of >~63% over 48h suggest and what is the action?
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.back: Suggests (does not confirm) a likely developing intrauterine pregnancy. Action: arrange a repeat TVUSS, e.g. once hCG is above the discriminatory zone / around a week later.

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.front: In a PUL, what does a serum β-hCG fall of >~50% over 48h suggest and what is the action?
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.back: Suggests a failing PUL / likely miscarriage. Action: repeat a urine pregnancy test in about 2 weeks to confirm resolution.

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.front: Which 48h serial β-hCG pattern is most suspicious of an ectopic, and what is done?
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.back: A SUBOPTIMAL change — anything between a ~50% fall and a ~63% rise (a plateau or slow/abnormal rise). It is treated as ectopic until proven otherwise: refer to/review in the EPAU for senior review, further imaging and possible intervention.

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.front: When is serial β-hCG monitoring NOT appropriate in suspected ectopic pregnancy?
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.back: In any woman who is symptomatic or unstable — pain, syncope, shoulder-tip pain, peritonism or haemodynamic instability. She needs immediate assessment, resuscitation and urgent surgical review; clinical symptoms always override reassuring hCG numbers. Serial hCG is only for the stable, asymptomatic patient.

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.front: Who should receive anti-D immunoglobulin, and within what time frame after a sensitising event?
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.back: A NON-sensitised RhD-negative woman (no anti-D antibodies yet). Give within ~72 hours of any potentially sensitising event. Also at 28 weeks (RAADP) and postnatally if the baby is RhD-positive.

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.front: What does the Kleihauer (Kleihauer–Betke acid-elution) test measure, and why does it matter?
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.back: It quantifies the SIZE of the feto-maternal haemorrhage on a maternal blood film. Acid elutes maternal HbA (pale 'ghost' cells) while fetal HbF-containing cells stay dark pink and are counted. It determines whether the standard anti-D dose is sufficient or additional anti-D is needed for a large FMH.

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.front: Why is the FIRST sensitising RhD+ pregnancy usually unaffected while later ones are at risk?
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.back: During the first exposure the mother is only just mounting the anti-D IgG response, so little crosses to that fetus. In a SUBSEQUENT RhD+ pregnancy, established maternal anti-D IgG crosses the placenta and causes HDFN (fetal anaemia, hydrops, jaundice/kernicterus).

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.front: A booking antibody screen in an RhD-negative woman is positive for anti-D. Will anti-D immunoglobulin help?
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.back: No. She is already sensitised — anti-D cannot reverse established immunisation. She needs specialist fetal-medicine surveillance, e.g. MCA Doppler to detect fetal anaemia.

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.front: How does cell-free fetal DNA (cffDNA) genotyping refine anti-D prophylaxis?
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.back: It determines the fetal RhD type from maternal blood, allowing TARGETED antenatal prophylaxis — only RhD-negative mothers carrying an RhD-positive fetus are given anti-D, sparing those carrying an RhD-negative fetus.

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.front: What are the three management options for a confirmed miscarriage?
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.back:
• Expectant (wait 7–14 days),
  • medical (misoprostol ± mifepristone), or
  • surgical (MVA under LA / ERPC under GA).
Surgical is first-line with heavy bleeding, haemodynamic instability, infection or patient choice; give anti-D if surgically managed.

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.front: What criteria make a stable ectopic suitable for methotrexate rather than surgery?
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.back:
• Unruptured
  • minimal/no pain
  • no fetal heartbeat
  • mass <35 mm
  • βhCG <1500 (up to ~5000)
  • no IUP, and
  • able to attend follow-up (hCG on days 4 & 7, expecting ≥15% fall).
Otherwise surgery (salpingectomy, or salpingotomy if the other tube is damaged).

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.front: How is a molar pregnancy managed after diagnosis?
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.back:
• Suction evacuation with histology and registration at a GTD centre
  • serial βhCG until it normalises to detect persistent GTD/choriocarcinoma
  • advise avoiding pregnancy until hCG is normal.

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.front: When is the UK dating scan performed and what measurement dates the pregnancy?
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.back: ~10–14 weeks; the crown–rump length (CRL) is used to accurately date the pregnancy. It also confirms viability and detects multiple pregnancy and chorionicity. Beyond CRL ~84 mm, head circumference is used instead.

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.front: What are the components of the combined test and when is it offered?
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.back: Offered ~11–14 weeks. Combines maternal age + nuchal translucency (NT) on USS + serum β-hCG + PAPP-A, screening for trisomies 21 (Down), 18 (Edwards) and 13 (Patau).

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.front: What is the biochemical/ultrasound pattern of Down syndrome (T21) on the combined test?
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.back: ↑ Nuchal translucency (NT), ↑ β-hCG, and ↓ PAPP-A.

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.front: What test is offered for Down syndrome screening if a woman books too late for the combined test, and what are its markers?
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.back:
The quadruple test (offered ~14–20 weeks). Markers:
  • serum AFP
  • β-hCG
  • unconjugated oestriol (uE3)
  • and inhibin A

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.front: After a higher-chance screening result, how is a diagnosis confirmed and where does NIPT fit?
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.back: NIPT (cell-free fetal DNA) is highly sensitive advanced screening but NOT diagnostic. Definitive diagnosis requires karyotyping via chorionic villus sampling (CVS ~11–14w) or amniocentesis (from ~15w).

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.front: What does the mnemonic DR C BRAVADO stand for in CTG interpretation?
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.back:
• Define Risk
  • Contractions (per 10 min)
  • Baseline RAte
  • Variability
  • Accelerations
  • Decelerations
  • Overall impression
A structured framework to interpret every CTG systematically.

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.front: Normal ranges on a CTG: baseline rate, variability, and what defines an acceleration?
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.back:
• Baseline 110–160 bpm
  • variability 5–25 bpm
  • acceleration = rise ≥15 bpm lasting ≥15 s
Accelerations are reassuring.

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.front: Differentiate early, variable and late decelerations by mechanism.
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.back:
• Early = mirror the contraction, due to head compression (benign)
  • Variable = vary in timing/shape, due to cord compression
  • Late = trough occurs after the contraction peak, due to uteroplacental insufficiency / fetal hypoxia (pathological)

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.front: Which CTG combination is the classic sign of fetal hypoxia?
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.back: Late decelerations plus reduced variability (<5 bpm). Also worrying: prolonged deceleration >3 min or prolonged bradycardia.

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.front: Initial management of a pathological CTG?
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.back:
• Conservative measures (left lateral position, IV fluids, stop oxytocin, treat cause)
  • senior obstetric review
  • consider fetal blood sampling (scalp pH/lactate) where appropriate
  • if unresolved, expedite delivery (instrumental or emergency caesarean)
A single ominous feature (e.g. prolonged bradycardia) may mandate immediate delivery.

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.front: How is SGA defined, and how does it differ from FGR?
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.back:
• SGA (small-for-gestational-age) = estimated fetal weight or abdominal circumference <10th centile — may be constitutionally small and healthy
  • FGR (fetal growth restriction) = failure to reach growth potential, usually due to placental insufficiency, with abnormal Dopplers, static growth or centile crossing, and/or oligohydramnios
FGR is the pathological, high-risk group; not all SGA babies are growth-restricted.

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.front: Which three biometric measurements make up a fetal growth scan, and what do they combine to give?
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.back: Head circumference (HC), abdominal circumference (AC), and femur length (FL) are combined into an estimated fetal weight (EFW), plotted on customised/population growth charts. Liquor volume (AFI or deepest pool) is also assessed. AC is the most sensitive single marker of asymmetric growth restriction.

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.front: Describe the umbilical artery Doppler waveform progression with worsening placental insufficiency.
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.back: Normal forward flow with positive end-diastolic flow (EDF) → raised pulsatility index (still forward diastolic flow) → absent end-diastolic flow (AEDF) → reversed end-diastolic flow (REDF). Increasing resistance/PI at each step; AEDF and REDF indicate severe compromise with high stillbirth risk.

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.front: What is the significance of absent or reversed end-diastolic flow (AEDF/REDF) on umbilical artery Doppler?
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.back: It indicates severe placental insufficiency and a high risk of stillbirth. It is a strong indication for delivery — needs urgent fetal-medicine review, corticosteroids for lung maturity if preterm, and planned early delivery, balancing prematurity against intrauterine death risk.

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.front: What do MCA and ductus venosus Dopplers add in severe FGR?
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.back:
• Middle cerebral artery (MCA) Doppler shows a falling PI as blood redistributes to the brain ('brain-sparing') — a sign of fetal hypoxic adaptation
  • Ductus venosus Doppler (a-wave) reflects cardiac decompensation and helps time delivery in severe early-onset FGR

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.front: Which test diagnoses gestational diabetes, and what are the two diagnostic thresholds?
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.back:
The 75g oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT). Diagnose GDM if EITHER:
  • fasting venous plasma glucose ≥ 5.6 mmol/L
  • OR 2-hour glucose ≥ 7.8 mmol/L
(mnemonic "5, 6, 7, 8").

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.front: When in pregnancy is the OGTT performed, and what triggers it?
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.back:
Usually at 24–28 weeks (earlier, soon after booking, if previous GDM). Triggered by risk factors:
  • BMI >30
  • previous GDM
  • previous macrosomic baby ≥4.5 kg
  • first-degree relative with diabetes
  • high-risk ethnicity (South Asian, Black Caribbean, Middle Eastern)
  • or detected glycosuria

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.front: Outline the stepwise management of GDM based on fasting glucose.
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.back:
• If fasting <7 mmol/L: trial diet & exercise first; add metformin, then insulin if targets not met
  • If fasting ≥7 mmol/L at diagnosis: start insulin immediately (± metformin)

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.front: List the key fetal/neonatal complications of untreated GDM.
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.back:
• Macrosomia (→ shoulder dystocia)
  • polyhydramnios
  • neonatal hypoglycaemia (fetal hyperinsulinaemia)
  • and increased risk of stillbirth

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.front: What is the pathophysiology of GDM and the long-term maternal implication?
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.back: Carbohydrate intolerance first recognised in pregnancy due to the diabetogenic/insulin-resistance effect of placental hormones. It usually resolves after delivery but confers a lasting risk of type 2 diabetes — offer postnatal fasting glucose/HbA1c and lifelong follow-up.

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.front: What defines the proteinuria threshold in pre-eclampsia by PCR and ACR?
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.back:
Significant proteinuria =
  • urine protein:creatinine ratio (PCR) ≥30 mg/mmol
  • OR albumin:creatinine ratio (ACR) ≥8 mg/mmol
A dipstick of ≥1+ prompts this quantification; 24-hour collection is now rarely used.

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.front: In pre-eclampsia, what happens to PlGF and the sFlt-1:PlGF ratio, and why?
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.back: PlGF (placental growth factor, pro-angiogenic) is LOW; sFlt-1 (anti-angiogenic) is HIGH, so the sFlt-1:PlGF ratio is RAISED. This reflects abnormal spiral-artery remodelling and placental ischaemia driving maternal endothelial dysfunction.

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.front: How is PlGF-based testing used in suspected pre-eclampsia, and in what gestational window?
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.back: NICE recommends PlGF or sFlt-1:PlGF ratio between ~20 and ~35–37 weeks, used chiefly to RULE OUT pre-eclampsia — a normal PlGF has high negative predictive value, excluding disease needing delivery in the next 1–2 weeks.

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.front: What is the definitive treatment of pre-eclampsia, and what is magnesium sulphate for?
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.back: Definitive cure is delivery of the placenta. Magnesium sulphate prevents and treats eclamptic seizures (not blood pressure). Labetalol is first-line antihypertensive; aspirin from 12 weeks is preventive in high-risk women.

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.front: List red-flag severe features of pre-eclampsia mandating urgent review.
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.back:
• Severe hypertension
  • severe headache
  • visual disturbance
  • epigastric/RUQ pain
  • vomiting
  • brisk reflexes/clonus
  • rapidly progressive oedema
  • HELLP syndrome (haemolysis, elevated liver enzymes, low platelets)
  • and eclampsia (seizures)

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.front: Give the fetal-scalp-pH thresholds and their actions.
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.back:
• ≥7.25 normal
  • 7.21–7.24 borderline → repeat in ~30 min
  • ≤7.20 abnormal → expedite delivery
Fetal scalp stimulation producing an acceleration is reassuring and may avoid FBS.

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.front: How is symphysis-fundal height used, and what triggers a growth scan?
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.back: Measure SFH from ~24 weeks and plot on a customised (GROW) chart. SFH <10th centile, static, or crossing centiles → refer for a growth scan + umbilical artery Doppler.

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.front: What combined-test biochemistry pattern suggests Edwards (T18) or Patau (T13) rather than Down (T21)?
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.back:
All three show raised nuchal translucency.
  • Down (T21): high βhCG, low PAPP-A
  • Edwards/Patau (T18/T13): low βhCG AND low PAPP-A

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.front: What is the definition of PPROM?
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.back: Preterm Prelabour Rupture Of Membranes — rupture of the fetal membranes before 37 weeks gestation AND before the onset of labour. It risks ascending infection (chorioamnionitis), cord prolapse, oligohydramnios and preterm labour.

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.front: What is the first-line investigation for suspected PPROM, and what are you looking for?
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.back: A sterile speculum examination, looking for a pool of amniotic fluid in the posterior fornix (or fluid leaking from the os on coughing/Valsalva). Digital vaginal examination is avoided unless the woman is in active labour, as it increases infection risk.

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.front: Which bedside biochemical tests confirm equivocal PPROM, and what do they detect?
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.back:
• PAMG-1 (placental alpha-microglobulin-1, e.g. AmniSure)
  • and IGFBP-1 (insulin-like growth factor binding protein-1, e.g. Actim PROM).
Both detect amniotic-fluid proteins in vaginal fluid. Older nitrazine/pH and ferning tests are less reliable.

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.front: Which antibiotic is given in confirmed PPROM, and which is contraindicated?
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.back: Oral erythromycin for 10 days (or until labour) reduces chorioamnionitis and prolongs pregnancy. Co-amoxiclav is contraindicated because it increases the risk of neonatal necrotising enterocolitis.

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.front: What are the features of chorioamnionitis and how does it change management of PPROM?
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.back:
• Maternal fever/tachycardia
  • fetal tachycardia
  • uterine tenderness
  • offensive discharge
  • raised CRP/WCC.
It is an emergency requiring prompt broad-spectrum IV antibiotics and delivery regardless of gestation; tocolysis is avoided.

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.front: What is fetal fibronectin and why does its presence in cervicovaginal secretions matter?
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.back: A glycoprotein at the choriodecidual interface acting as 'biological glue'. It leaks into cervicovaginal secretions when the interface is disrupted and preterm labour is imminent, so a swab helps predict (mainly rule out) preterm birth.

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.front: What is the main clinical value of a NEGATIVE fetal fibronectin test in threatened preterm labour?
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.back: High negative predictive value — preterm birth within ~1–2 weeks is very unlikely, allowing safe reassurance and avoiding unnecessary admission, steroids, tocolysis and transfer. A positive test is much less specific.

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.front: On transvaginal ultrasound, what cervical length findings make imminent preterm labour unlikely vs raise the risk?
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.back: Cervical length ≥~15 mm makes imminent preterm labour unlikely; a short cervix (e.g. <15 mm, or <25 mm in some contexts), often with funnelling of the internal os, raises the risk.

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.front: List three situations that make a fetal fibronectin test invalid.
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.back:
• Recent vaginal bleeding
  • sexual intercourse within ~24 hours
  • and ruptured membranes.
The swab must also be taken before digital examination, lubricant or ultrasound gel.

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.front: What time-critical interventions does genuine established preterm labour <~34 weeks require?
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.back:
• Antenatal corticosteroids (fetal lung maturity)
  • magnesium sulphate (neuroprotection, <30–34 weeks)
  • and consideration of tocolysis (e.g. nifedipine) to buy time for steroids and in-utero transfer.
Predictive tests must not delay treating a woman in advanced labour.

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.front: What is the single most useful diagnostic test for suspected obstetric cholestasis (ICP)?
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.back: Serum bile acids (raised) — the key test, sent alongside LFTs. A raised bile acid level with no alternative cause confirms ICP.

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.front: Describe the classic itch of obstetric cholestasis.
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.back: Intense pruritus, typically of the palms and soles, worse at night, in the third trimester, characteristically WITHOUT a rash (only excoriations may be seen). Jaundice is uncommon.

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.front: What is the main fetal risk in obstetric cholestasis, and what level marks the highest risk?
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.back: Stillbirth is the principal fetal danger (also preterm birth and meconium-stained liquor). Risk rises with peak bile acid level and is highest when bile acids are ≥100 micromol/L (severe disease).

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.front: Why is obstetric cholestasis called a diagnosis of exclusion, and what must be ruled out?
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.back:
Raised bile acids/LFTs have other causes that must be excluded first:
  • pre-eclampsia/HELLP
  • acute fatty liver of pregnancy
  • viral/autoimmune hepatitis
  • and gallstones/biliary obstruction.

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.front: Outline management and natural course of obstetric cholestasis.
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.back:
• Monitor bile acids/LFTs and fetus
  • emollients + antihistamine for sleep
  • ursodeoxycholic acid for symptoms (limited fetal-outcome evidence)
  • vitamin K if clotting deranged
  • planned early birth timed to peak bile acid severity (~35–37+ wks).
Resolves after delivery (recheck postnatally); recurs in future pregnancy and with oestrogen-containing contraception.

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.front: What are the five components of the Bishop score?
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.back:
• Cervical dilatation
  • effacement/length
  • consistency (firm→soft)
  • position (posterior→anterior)
  • and fetal station (relative to the ischial spines).
Higher total = more favourable/ripe cervix.

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.front: A woman has a Bishop score of 3. What is the next step in her induction?
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.back: Unfavourable cervix (≤6) → cervical ripening first with vaginal prostaglandin E2 (dinoprostone) or a mechanical balloon catheter, then reassess the Bishop score before amniotomy/oxytocin.

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.front: A woman has a Bishop score of 8. How would you proceed with induction?
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.back: Favourable cervix (≥7–8) → proceed to amniotomy (ARM) ± oxytocin infusion; ripening agents are not needed.

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.front: What is uterine hyperstimulation and how is it managed?
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.back:
Excessive/prolonged contractions (tachysystole) after prostaglandin or oxytocin, causing fetal distress (abnormal CTG) and rarely uterine rupture. Management:
  • remove the pessary/stop oxytocin
  • give tocolysis (e.g. terbutaline)
  • continuous CTG
  • and escalate; may need emergency caesarean.

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.front: Name three contraindications to vaginal induction of labour with prostaglandins.
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.back:
• Placenta praevia
  • transverse/oblique lie
  • and previous classical (upper-segment) caesarean section.
Others include cord presentation and active primary genital herpes.

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.front: Contrast placenta praevia and abruption on assessment and immediate management.
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.back:
• Praevia: low placenta on TVUS, painless bright bleeding, soft uterus → no PV exam, admit, deliver by LSCS
  • Abruption: clinical, painful woody/tender uterus, bleeding may be concealed → resuscitate and deliver.
Kleihauer doses anti-D in rhesus-negative women.

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.front: What are the 4 Ts of PPH and the escalation ladder?
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.back: Tone (commonest) > Trauma > Tissue > Thrombin. Escalate: massage/bimanual compression → uterotonics (oxytocin, ergometrine, carboprost, misoprostol) + tranexamic acid → balloon tamponade → surgery (B-Lynch, artery ligation, hysterectomy); activate the major haemorrhage protocol.

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.front: What does crossing the partogram action line mean and what do you do?
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.back: Slow progress in labour. Reassess, augment with ARM ± oxytocin, escalate to a senior and consider LSCS for failure to progress or obstructed labour.

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.front: What must every episode of postmenopausal bleeding (PMB) be regarded as until proven otherwise?
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.back: Endometrial cancer until proven otherwise. PMB warrants urgent (2-week-wait) referral, transvaginal ultrasound, and endometrial (Pipelle) biopsy if the endometrium is >4 mm or bleeding persists.

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.front: In the PMB pathway, what endometrial thickness on transvaginal ultrasound triggers an endometrial (Pipelle) biopsy?
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.back: An endometrial thickness >4 mm (or persistent/recurrent bleeding regardless of thickness) prompts endometrial sampling with a Pipelle.

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.front: Why does a normal or insufficient Pipelle biopsy NOT exclude endometrial cancer when bleeding persists?
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.back: The Pipelle is a blind procedure sampling only part of the cavity. It detects diffuse disease well but can miss focal lesions (polyps, focal cancer). Persistent bleeding requires hysteroscopy ± directed biopsy — the gold standard for focal pathology.

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.front: Which endometrial hyperplasia subtype is premalignant, and how does its management differ?
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.back: Atypical hyperplasia is premalignant, carrying a high risk of coexisting or progression to carcinoma; it is usually managed with hysterectomy. Hyperplasia without atypia has low malignant potential and is often treated with progestogens (e.g. LNG-IUS).

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.front: List the key risk factors for endometrial cancer/hyperplasia (unopposed oestrogen states).
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.back:
• Obesity
  • nulliparity
  • early menarche/late menopause
  • PCOS
  • tamoxifen
  • oestrogen-only HRT
  • Lynch syndrome
  • and type 2 diabetes.
Combined HRT and the LNG-IUS are protective.

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.front: What is the first-line investigation for postmenopausal bleeding, and what does it measure?
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.back: Transvaginal ultrasound (TVUS) measuring endometrial thickness (the endometrial stripe / double-layer thickness). It is a triage test that decides who needs endometrial sampling.

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.front: In a postmenopausal woman with bleeding, what endometrial thickness cut-off is used and what does each side mean?
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.back:
• ≤4 mm: high negative predictive value, endometrial cancer very unlikely (reassure/observe).
  • >4 mm (thickened): requires endometrial biopsy (Pipelle) ± hysteroscopy.

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.front: A postmenopausal woman has a thin (3 mm) endometrium but continues to have recurrent bleeding. What is the correct management?
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.back: Proceed to endometrial biopsy ± hysteroscopy anyway. A thin stripe does not exclude focal pathology, and persistent/recurrent PMB mandates further evaluation regardless of thickness. PMB is endometrial cancer until proven otherwise.

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.front: Why is endometrial thickness on TVUS unreliable in women taking tamoxifen, and how are they assessed if they bleed?
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.back: Tamoxifen causes subendometrial cystic changes that falsely thicken/distort the measurement. Bleeding on tamoxifen is investigated by hysteroscopy ± biopsy, not by the ultrasound stripe.

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.front: Besides measuring the endometrial stripe, what structural pathology can TVUS detect in the PMB work-up?
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.back:
• Fibroids
  • endometrial polyps (often needing saline infusion sonography/hysteroscopy to characterise)
  • and adnexal/ovarian pathology.
Note the fixed 4 mm cut-off does not apply in premenopausal women (thickness varies across the cycle).

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.front: In the NICE ovarian cancer pathway, what CA-125 threshold triggers an ultrasound of the abdomen and pelvis?
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.back: CA-125 ≥35 IU/mL — measured first in a woman with persistent symptoms (bloating, early satiety, pelvic/abdominal pain, urinary/bowel change) or age >50; if ≥35, arrange abdomino-pelvic USS.

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.front: State the Risk of Malignancy Index (RMI) formula and its three components.
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.back:
RMI = U × M × CA-125.
  • U = ultrasound score (0–1 feature → U=1; 2+ features → U=3).
  • M = menopausal status (premenopausal → M=1; postmenopausal → M=3).
  • CA-125 = serum value in IU/mL.

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.front: Which five ultrasound features score a point in the RMI ultrasound component, and what RMI value prompts gynae-oncology referral?
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.back:
• Multilocular cyst
  • solid areas
  • bilateral lesions
  • ascites
  • and intra-abdominal metastases.
An RMI >250 prompts referral to a specialist gynaecological oncology MDT/cancer centre.

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.front: Why is CA-125 not used alone/as a screening test for ovarian cancer?
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.back: It is non-specific — raised in many benign/physiological states (endometriosis, fibroids, menstruation, pregnancy, PID, ascites, liver disease) — and can be normal in early or some ovarian cancers. Hence it is used within a structured pathway (RMI).

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.front: In a woman under 40 with a suspected ovarian mass, which additional tumour markers should be measured and why?
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.back: AFP, β-hCG and LDH — to detect germ-cell tumours, which are relatively more common in young women and may be missed by CA-125 alone.

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.front: In the current UK cervical screening programme, what is tested first on the sample?
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.back: High-risk HPV (hrHPV, especially types 16 & 18). Cytology is only performed as reflex testing if hrHPV is positive (HPV primary screening).

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.front: What are the age ranges and intervals for cervical screening in England?
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.back:
Invited 25-64. The sample is tested for high-risk HPV first, with cytology only as a triage test. If HPV-negative, routine recall is every 5 years across the whole age range (England moved 25-49 from 3- to 5-yearly, matching 50-64 and Scotland and Wales).
  • HPV-positive with normal cytology is repeated at 12 months;
  • HPV-positive with abnormal cytology goes to colposcopy.

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.front: A woman is hrHPV positive but has normal reflex cytology. What next?
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.back: Repeat the HPV test in 12 months (surveillance). If still hrHPV positive at 12 and 24 months, refer for colposcopy.

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.front: How is CIN2/CIN3 (high-grade, pre-invasive disease) treated?
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.back: LLETZ — large loop excision of the transformation zone. CIN1 is usually monitored as it often regresses.

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.front: A 40-year-old has postcoital bleeding and a suspicious-looking cervix. What is the correct action?
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.back: Urgent gynaecology referral and examination (2-week-wait), NOT a screening smear. Screening is for asymptomatic women and does not exclude cancer in a symptomatic patient.

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.front: What is the imaging pitfall in ovarian torsion, and the correct action?
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.back: TVUSS/Doppler may show an enlarged oedematous ovary ± whirlpool sign, but a normal Doppler does NOT exclude torsion (dual blood supply). It is a clinical diagnosis → urgent diagnostic laparoscopy; do not delay for imaging.

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.front: Give the Rotterdam criteria and supporting investigations for PCOS.
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.back:
Rotterdam (2 of 3):
  • oligo/anovulation;
  • clinical/biochemical hyperandrogenism;
  • polycystic ovaries on TVUSS (≥20 follicles/ovary and/or volume >10 mL).
Bloods: raised free androgen index/testosterone, raised LH:FSH, low SHBG; exclude with TFTs, prolactin, 17-OHP. Screen metabolic risk (OGTT/HbA1c, lipids).

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.front: What staging imaging follows a positive gynae-cancer triage?
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.back:
• Raised RMI >250 → 2WW gynae-oncology + CT abdomen/pelvis.
  • Biopsy-confirmed endometrial cancer → MRI pelvis for local staging, then MDT.

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.front: What is the reference point for POP-Q staging?
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.back: The hymen, defined as plane 0. Points above the hymen are negative and points below are positive; the leading point's position relative to the hymen determines the stage.

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.front: Match each compartment to its prolapse: anterior, posterior, apical.
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.back:
• Anterior = cystocele (bladder) / urethrocele;
  • Posterior = rectocele (rectum) / enterocele (small bowel);
  • Apical/central = uterine prolapse or vaginal vault prolapse (post-hysterectomy).

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.front: Define POP-Q Stage 2 and Stage 4.
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.back:
• Stage 2 = leading point within 1 cm of the hymen (at the introitus).
  • Stage 4 = complete eversion/procidentia (full descent below the hymen).

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.front: How is prolapse best demonstrated on examination?
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.back: Left lateral position with a Sims speculum, asking the woman to bear down/cough/Valsalva to reveal maximum descent, examining each vaginal wall in turn.

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.front: Why can complete procidentia cause renal impairment?
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.back: Full eversion can kink the ureters, causing hydronephrosis and renal impairment (and can cause urinary retention or mucosal ulceration) — needs prompt reduction and urological/urogynae assessment.

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.front: When is a couple defined as subfertile, and when do you investigate earlier?
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.back: Failure to conceive after 1 year of regular unprotected intercourse. Investigate earlier (after 6 months) if the woman is ≥36, or there is a known cause/relevant history (e.g. amenorrhoea, previous PID, cryptorchidism). Investigate BOTH partners together.

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.front: What are the conditions for a semen analysis, and why repeat an abnormal sample at ~3 months?
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.back: Produced after 2–7 days abstinence and examined within ~1 hour. Repeat an abnormal sample after ~3 months because spermatogenesis takes ~74 days, so this confirms whether the abnormality is persistent rather than a transient dip (e.g. after febrile illness).

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.front: How and when do you time a mid-luteal (day-21) progesterone, and what result confirms ovulation?
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.back: Time it to 7 days before the expected next period (day 21 in a 28-day cycle, day 28 in a 35-day cycle). A raised progesterone, typically >30 nmol/L, confirms ovulation occurred.

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.front: Define oligozoospermia, asthenozoospermia, teratozoospermia and azoospermia.
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.back:
• Oligozoospermia = low sperm count;
  • Asthenozoospermia = reduced motility;
  • Teratozoospermia = abnormal morphology;
  • Azoospermia = no sperm in the ejaculate.

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.front: Which two pre-conception safety checks/interventions must be offered to every couple being investigated for subfertility?
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.back: Check rubella immunity (vaccinate if non-immune, avoid pregnancy for 1 month after) and start folic acid (400 mcg, or 5 mg if high-risk). Plus lifestyle: smoking cessation, alcohol reduction, weight optimisation.

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.front: What finding on HSG or HyCoSy confirms that a fallopian tube is patent?
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.back: Free spill of contrast from the fimbrial (distal) end into the peritoneal cavity.

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.front: Why are HSG and tubal patency tests performed in the follicular phase?
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.back: After menstruation and before ovulation to avoid irradiating / disrupting an early pregnancy (pregnancy must be excluded).

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.front: How does HyCoSy differ from HSG?
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.back: HyCoSy is ultrasound-based using a contrast/foam agent (or saline + air) — no ionising radiation and no iodinated contrast — assessing tubal patency and the uterine cavity; increasingly first-line. HSG uses X-ray/fluoroscopy with radio-opaque contrast.

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.front: What must be excluded/treated before tubal instrumentation, and why?
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.back: Exclude pregnancy and active pelvic infection; screen and treat chlamydia and give prophylactic antibiotics if indicated, because instrumentation can precipitate/flare pelvic inflammatory disease.

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.front: Why does a hydrosalpinx matter before IVF, and how is it managed?
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.back: A hydrosalpinx (dilated, fluid-filled blocked tube) reduces IVF success (toxic/embryotoxic reflux); treat before IVF, e.g. salpingectomy or proximal tubal occlusion.

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.front: What are Amsel's criteria for bacterial vaginosis, and how many are needed for diagnosis?
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.back:
3 of 4:
  • (1) thin white homogeneous discharge;
  • (2) clue cells on wet-mount microscopy;
  • (3) vaginal pH >4.5;
  • (4) positive whiff/amine test (fishy odour on adding KOH).

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.front: What are clue cells and which condition do they indicate?
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.back: Vaginal epithelial cells studded/coated with adherent bacteria (Gardnerella), giving a granular cytoplasm and obscured, stippled cell borders on wet mount. They indicate bacterial vaginosis.

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.front: What is the Nugent score and how is it used?
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.back:
A Gram-stain scoring system (0-10), the lab/research gold standard for BV, grading bacterial morphotypes (lactobacilli vs Gardnerella/anaerobes vs curved rods).
  • 0-3 normal
  • 4-6 intermediate
  • 7-10 = BV (higher = more anaerobes, fewer lactobacilli).

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.front: How does vaginal pH help distinguish candida from BV and trichomonas?
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.back: Candida usually has a NORMAL pH (<4.5), whereas both BV and Trichomonas vaginalis give a raised pH >4.5. pH is therefore a fast first discriminator, refined by microscopy and clinical features.

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.front: What are the classic microscopy and examination findings, and treatment, for Trichomonas vaginalis?
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.back:
• Wet mount shows motile flagellated protozoa;
  • examination may show a 'strawberry cervix' (punctate haemorrhages);
  • frothy yellow-green offensive discharge with pH >4.5.
It is an STI: treat with metronidazole plus full STI screen and partner notification/treatment.

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.front: A confirmed low mid-luteal progesterone (anovulation) — what is the next step?
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.back: Ovulation induction with letrozole (increasingly first-line) or clomifene citrate, with ultrasound follicle tracking and multiple-pregnancy counselling; escalate to gonadotrophins/specialist if it fails. First confirm true anovulation vs mistimed sampling.

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.front: What counselling accompanies metronidazole for BV or trichomonas?
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.back: Avoid alcohol during and for 48 hours after treatment (disulfiram-like reaction). Do NOT routinely treat asymptomatic BV — and pregnancy is not an indication to screen for or treat it. In trichomonas also treat the partner and screen for other STIs.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.question: In the UK, at what gestation does a pregnancy loss with no signs of life at birth count as a stillbirth rather than a miscarriage?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.explanation: In the UK a baby born with no signs of life from 24+0 weeks is a stillbirth and must be registered; loss before that is a miscarriage, with no legal registration. The threshold historically tracked viability.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.question: A woman at 30 weeks reports absent fetal movements and no fetal heart is heard on handheld Doppler. What is the appropriate step to confirm intrauterine fetal death?
options: Real-time ultrasound with colour Doppler of the fetal heart
Repeat handheld Doppler assessment after a further thirty minutes
Cardiotocography recorded over a twenty-minute period
Abdominal palpation by a second experienced midwife
Maternal serum beta-hCG measured and repeated at 48 hours
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.answer: Real-time ultrasound with colour Doppler of the fetal heart
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.explanation: Auscultation and handheld Doppler are not accurate enough — the maternal pulse or placental flow can mislead, and fetuses with inaudible heart sounds have been found alive. Real-time ultrasound is essential, with a second opinion wherever practicable.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.question: Which term describes the death of a liveborn baby within 28 days of birth?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.explanation: Neonatal death is the death of a liveborn baby within 28 days. The dividing line from stillbirth is simply whether the baby showed any signs of life at birth.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.question: For most cases of late intrauterine fetal death, what is the recommended mode of birth?
options: Expectant management until spontaneous labour only
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.explanation: Vaginal birth is recommended for most women: it is safer for her and better for future pregnancies. Caesarean is not the default, but it is a legitimate option to discuss, both for maternal indications and sometimes at her request.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.question: Which regimen is the usual method of induction of labour for late intrauterine fetal death?
options: Ergometrine followed by an oxytocin infusion
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.explanation: A combination of mifepristone and a prostaglandin is recommended first line. Misoprostol and oxytocin are not given simultaneously, and a previous caesarean calls for lower prostaglandin doses because of the risk of uterine rupture.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.question: A woman is diagnosed with an intrauterine fetal death at 32 weeks. Which test should be taken before the birth, and in whom?
options: A Kleihauer test, in every woman regardless of rhesus status
A Kleihauer test, but only if she is known to be rhesus-negative
A direct antiglobulin test on a maternal blood sample
A serum bile acid level to exclude obstetric cholestasis
An HbA1c to exclude undiagnosed maternal diabetes
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.answer: A Kleihauer test, in every woman regardless of rhesus status
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.explanation: The Kleihauer is taken in everyone, whatever her rhesus status, because feto-maternal haemorrhage is a potential cause of the death. It must be taken before the birth: delivery itself causes feto-maternal haemorrhage, so a later sample can be falsely high and cannot distinguish cause from effect. In rhesus-negative women it also guides the anti-D dose.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.question: Which coagulation-related complication should be specifically anticipated in a woman with a retained dead fetus, particularly after several weeks or with abruption?
options: Deep vein thrombosis of the calf veins
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.explanation: The risk runs at roughly 10% within four weeks of the death and about 30% beyond that, and abruption is the stronger driver. How macerated the baby looks does not predict it, so coagulation must actually be checked.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.question: Which pair of investigations has the highest yield for establishing the cause of a stillbirth?
options: Post-mortem examination together with placental histology
Maternal thrombophilia screen with red-cell antibody testing
Maternal HbA1c together with thyroid function testing
Umbilical artery Doppler with amniotic fluid index
Maternal infection screen with a full blood count
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.answer: Post-mortem examination together with placental histology
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.explanation: These two are complementary rather than alternatives, and together with the clinical history they find a probable cause in up to three-quarters of cases. Post-mortem needs written consent; if parents decline, less invasive alternatives such as post-mortem MRI should be offered.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.question: A woman with a confirmed IUFD is systemically well and asks to go home and wait rather than be induced immediately. Which finding would make expediting birth necessary rather than awaiting her choice?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.explanation: If she is well, with intact membranes and no pre-eclampsia, sepsis, abruption or coagulopathy, waiting is reasonable and most women labour spontaneously within about three weeks. Ruptured membranes raise the infection risk and are a reason to expedite, as are sepsis, pre-eclampsia, abruption and laboratory evidence of DIC.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.question: Which drug is offered to suppress lactation after a stillbirth, and what is the key contraindication?
options: Cabergoline, avoided in hypertension or pre-eclampsia
Cabergoline, avoided in a history of venous thromboembolism
Domperidone, avoided in significant renal impairment
Bromocriptine, which is preferred to cabergoline in the UK
Oxytocin, avoided in women with cardiac disease
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.answer: Cabergoline, avoided in hypertension or pre-eclampsia
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.explanation: Cabergoline is the dopamine agonist of choice and works well, but suppression should still be her choice — some women prefer to let lactation settle or to donate milk. Dopamine agonists are avoided in hypertension or pre-eclampsia, which matters here because pre-eclampsia is itself a cause of intrauterine death.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.question: Which of the following is a recognised risk factor for stillbirth?
options: A low booking body mass index
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.explanation: Recognised risk factors include a previous stillbirth, advanced maternal age, obesity, smoking, multiple pregnancy, fetal growth restriction and reduced fetal movements.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.question: Which ultrasound sign, reflecting overlapping fetal skull bones, indicates that fetal death occurred some time earlier?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.explanation: Collapse of the fetal skull with overlapping bones appears roughly four to seven days after death. Alongside gross skin oedema and intrafetal gas, it helps estimate when the death occurred and, importantly, prepares parents for how the baby will look at birth. The other signs listed are signs of early pregnancy.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.question: A junior doctor must break the news of a confirmed stillbirth. Which approach best reflects good bereavement care?
options: Tell them in a private space, unhurried, with senior support
Tell them quickly at the bedside
Wait until the full investigation results are available to explain
Ask the specialist bereavement midwife to break the news instead
Explain the likely cause first, then confirm that the baby has died
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.answer: Tell them in a private space, unhurried, with senior support
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.explanation: The words used at diagnosis are remembered for a lifetime. Break the news compassionately, in private, without haste and with senior involvement, then back it up in writing and involve a specialist bereavement midwife — who supports the family rather than substituting for the doctor's conversation.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.question: Which statement about the legal handling of a stillbirth in the UK is correct?
options: It is registered within 42 days in a separate stillbirth register
It is registered as both a live birth and a death within five days
A coroner must be informed and an inquest opened in every case
A medical examiner scrutinises the cause before it can be registered
No formal registration is required for a loss at any gestation
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.answer: It is registered within 42 days in a separate stillbirth register
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.explanation: A medical certificate of stillbirth is issued by a doctor or midwife present at the birth or who examined the baby, and registration follows in a separate register — there is no birth certificate and no death certificate. Stillbirths sit outside both the coroner and medical examiner systems, because in law the baby never had an independent life.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.question: What form of scrutiny follows a stillbirth in the UK, given that no coroner is involved?
options: A multidisciplinary review of care, in place of a coroner's inquest
A coroner's inquest held in public with the parents present in court
A police investigation whenever the cause cannot be established
An internal review conducted only if the parents make a complaint
No formal review, since the cause is established at post-mortem
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.answer: A multidisciplinary review of care, in place of a coroner's inquest
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.explanation: Every stillbirth triggers a mandatory standardised review of the care given, carried out by a multidisciplinary team. Parents' own perspective and questions must be sought and fed into it — for most families this is the only review of their baby's death that takes place.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.question: What should honestly be conveyed to bereaved parents about establishing a cause?
options: A cause is found in most, but a substantial minority stay unexplained
Every stillbirth has an identifiable cause once it is fully investigated
The cause is almost never established even after full investigation
The cause can usually be inferred from the handheld Doppler findings
Stillbirth is usually caused by something the mother did in pregnancy
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.answer: A cause is found in most, but a substantial minority stay unexplained
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.explanation: With full investigation — history, post-mortem and placental histology — a probable cause is found in up to three-quarters of late intrauterine deaths. Being straight about the remaining uncertainty matters, because it helps parents understand that they are not to blame.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fe.question: A fetus has an estimated fetal weight consistently on the 8th centile, with normal growth velocity, normal umbilical artery Doppler and normal liquor. The mother is petite. Which statement is most accurate?
options: The fetus is SGA but is not necessarily growth-restricted
The fetus meets the accepted definition of growth restriction
This is a large-for-gestational-age fetus for this gestation
Birth should be expedited once corticosteroids are complete
Doppler surveillance can safely be stopped
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fe.answer: The fetus is SGA but is not necessarily growth-restricted
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fe.explanation: SGA is a size label, and most SGA fetuses are constitutionally small. With normal growth velocity, normal Dopplers and normal liquor in a petite mother, this fetus is reaching its own potential. Growth restriction needs evidence of a pathological process, so surveillance continues but birth is not indicated.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fe.question: Which finding MOST suggests that a small fetus is truly growth-restricted rather than constitutionally small?
options: A falling growth velocity with abnormal umbilical artery Doppler
Short maternal stature with a low booking body mass index
A single estimated fetal weight measurement on the 9th centile
Polyhydramnios with an otherwise normal detailed anomaly scan
An abdominal circumference tracking steadily along the 20th centile
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fe.answer: A falling growth velocity with abnormal umbilical artery Doppler
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fe.explanation: Growth restriction is a failure to reach growth potential, so the signals are dynamic or functional: a falling velocity, or abnormal Dopplers. A single low measurement, a small mother, or a fetus tracking steadily along a lower centile all point to constitutional smallness. Polyhydramnios is not a feature.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fe.question: A growth scan shows a fetus with a low abdominal circumference but a relatively preserved head circumference. Which pattern and underlying cause does this suggest?
options: Asymmetric growth restriction from placental insufficiency
Symmetric growth restriction from a chromosomal abnormality
Macrosomia driven by undiagnosed maternal gestational diabetes
Symmetric growth restriction from congenital cytomegalovirus
A normal variant needing no further growth surveillance
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fe.answer: Asymmetric growth restriction from placental insufficiency
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fe.explanation: In asymmetric (head-sparing) growth restriction the fetus redistributes blood to the brain, so the abdominal circumference falls first while head growth is relatively preserved. This is the classic placenta-mediated, later-onset pattern. A proportionately small fetus points instead to early chromosomal or infective causes.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fe.question: An early, severely and symmetrically small fetus is identified at 20 weeks. Which cause is MOST likely?
options: A chromosomal abnormality or a congenital infection
A prolonged pregnancy continuing beyond 42 weeks
Maternal smoking with otherwise normal placentation
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fe.answer: A chromosomal abnormality or a congenital infection
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fe.explanation: Proportionate, early-onset growth restriction points to a non-placental cause: a chromosomal or genetic anomaly, or a congenital infection. Placental causes such as pre-eclampsia and smoking typically produce later, head-sparing restriction, while diabetes and prolonged pregnancy are associated with large rather than small babies.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fe.question: Which is the single COMMONEST cause of fetal growth restriction?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fe.answer: Placental insufficiency
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fe.explanation: Placental insufficiency, associated with pre-eclampsia, maternal vascular disease and smoking, is the commonest cause of growth restriction. Congenital infection, chromosomal abnormality and antiphospholipid syndrome are all recognised but much less common. Note that the commonest reason a fetus is SGA at all is simply being constitutionally small.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fe.question: A woman has a major risk factor for a small-for-gestational-age baby. Her uterine artery Doppler in mid-pregnancy is normal and biometry is normal. How should she be monitored?
options: Serial growth scans with umbilical artery Doppler from around 32 weeks
Serial growth scans with umbilical artery Doppler from around 20 weeks
Symphysis-fundal height on a growth chart, with no routine scanning
A single growth scan arranged at 36 weeks with no earlier imaging
Daily fetal movement counting measured against a fixed threshold
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fe.answer: Serial growth scans with umbilical artery Doppler from around 32 weeks
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fe.explanation: Women at increased risk are offered serial growth scans with umbilical artery Doppler, and a mid-pregnancy uterine artery Doppler decides how early those start. A normal result allows them to begin at around 32 weeks; an abnormal one brings them forward to around 24-28 weeks. Fundal height alone is not reliable enough here.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fe.question: A low-risk woman has her symphysis-fundal height plotted at 30 weeks and it falls below the 10th centile. What is the appropriate next step?
options: Refer her for an ultrasound growth scan
Reassure her and simply remeasure in four weeks
Arrange induction of labour within the next week
Proceed to caesarean birth once steroids are given
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fe.answer: Refer her for an ultrasound growth scan
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fe.explanation: A fundal height below the 10th centile, or static growth, prompts referral for ultrasound assessment of growth, liquor and umbilical artery Doppler. The scan defines whether this is a constitutionally small fetus or a growth-restricted one, and only then do decisions about birth follow.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fe.question: During surveillance of an FGR fetus, the umbilical artery Doppler now shows reversed end-diastolic flow. What does this indicate?
options: Serious placental compromise requiring urgent review
A normal finding for the third trimester of pregnancy
A constitutionally small but entirely healthy fetus
Fetal macrosomia with raised cardiac output demands
Technical artefact that should simply be repeated later
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fe.answer: Serious placental compromise requiring urgent review
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fe.explanation: Placental resistance rises progressively, so end-diastolic flow falls, then disappears, then reverses. Absent or reversed end-diastolic flow signals serious placental compromise and triggers intensified surveillance and a decision about the timing of birth.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fe.question: Which Doppler assessment is used particularly to help TIME delivery in a preterm growth-restricted fetus, with an abnormal result being a late, ominous sign?
options: Ductus venosus Doppler with computerised CTG
Uterine artery Doppler at the booking visit
Middle cerebral artery Doppler used in isolation
Umbilical vein diameter at the cord insertion
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fe.answer: Ductus venosus Doppler with computerised CTG
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fe.explanation: The ductus venosus, used with computerised CTG, helps decide when to deliver a preterm growth-restricted fetus; an abnormal or reversed a-wave reflects cardiac decompensation and is a late sign. The middle cerebral artery shows redistribution but is not used on its own to trigger birth, and uterine artery Doppler is a risk-prediction tool earlier in pregnancy.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fe.question: Which intervention is used to PREVENT placenta-mediated growth restriction in women at high risk, and when must it be started to be effective?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fe.answer: Low-dose aspirin, started from 12 weeks
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fe.explanation: Low-dose aspirin reduces the risk of pre-eclampsia and placental disease in high-risk women. It is started from 12 weeks and must be in place before 16 weeks to work, so starting it late is of little value. Magnesium sulfate is used for neuroprotection around preterm birth, not for prevention.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fe.question: A growth-restricted fetus at 30 weeks develops reversed end-diastolic flow, and preterm delivery is planned. Which two adjuncts should be given?
options: Corticosteroids for lung maturity and magnesium sulfate
Low-dose aspirin together with high-dose folic acid supplementation
Broad-spectrum antibiotics and tocolysis to prolong the pregnancy
Subcutaneous insulin with metformin to optimise glycaemic control
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fe.answer: Corticosteroids for lung maturity and magnesium sulfate
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fe.explanation: When preterm birth is anticipated, antenatal corticosteroids promote fetal lung maturity and magnesium sulfate gives fetal neuroprotection. Tocolysis to prolong the pregnancy is inappropriate once birth is indicated for fetal compromise.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fe.question: A growth-restricted neonate develops jitteriness and a low blood glucose shortly after birth. What is the main reason FGR babies are prone to hypoglycaemia?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fe.answer: Reduced glycogen and fat stores
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fe.explanation: A growth-restricted fetus lays down little glycogen and fat, so the newborn has minimal substrate to draw on and becomes hypoglycaemic soon after birth. Large babies also become hypoglycaemic, but by a different route.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fe.question: The Barker hypothesis links fetal growth restriction to which long-term outcome?
options: Increased risk of adult cardiometabolic disease
Increased final adult height and skeletal mass
Reduced lifetime risk of type 2 diabetes mellitus
Protection against later ischaemic heart disease
No measurable effect on adult health outcomes
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fe.answer: Increased risk of adult cardiometabolic disease
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fe.explanation: Fetal programming proposes that an adverse intrauterine environment permanently alters physiology, predisposing to hypertension, type 2 diabetes and ischaemic heart disease in adult life. Growth-restricted babies are also at higher risk of neurodevelopmental difficulty.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fe.question: A fetus has an estimated fetal weight above the 90th centile. Which maternal condition should be actively excluded as the key cause?
options: Chronic kidney disease with proteinuric decline
Pre-eclampsia arising in the third trimester
Systemic lupus erythematosus in active flare
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fe.answer: Diabetes, either gestational or pre-existing
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fe.explanation: Maternal hyperglycaemia crosses the placenta and drives fetal hyperinsulinaemia, which acts as a growth factor. The fat is laid down truncally, which is why the shoulders outgrow the head. The other conditions listed all impair placental function and are associated with small rather than large babies.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fe.question: Which complication is the most feared during the vaginal delivery of a macrosomic infant?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fe.answer: Shoulder dystocia
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fe.explanation: A large baby markedly increases the risk of shoulder dystocia, which can cause brachial plexus injury and birth asphyxia. The risk is compounded by maternal diabetes, because fetal fat is deposited preferentially across the shoulders and trunk.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fe.question: A large baby is born to a mother with poorly controlled gestational diabetes. Why is this neonate at risk of hypoglycaemia?
options: Depleted hepatic glycogen and fat stores
Reduced subcutaneous fat deposition in the uterus
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fe.answer: Fetal hyperinsulinaemia persisting after birth
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fe.explanation: Chronic exposure to high maternal glucose drives the fetal pancreas to oversecrete insulin. When the placental glucose supply stops abruptly at birth, that high insulin level persists for some hours and drives the blood glucose down.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ur.question: A postmenopausal woman describes a feeling of 'something coming down' in the vagina, worse at the end of the day, with a visible bulge. What is the diagnosis?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ur.explanation: A bearing-down sensation with a vaginal bulge, worse on standing/end of day, is characteristic of pelvic organ prolapse.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ur.question: A woman has descent of the bladder into the anterior vaginal wall with urinary symptoms. What is this called?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ur.explanation: Descent of the bladder into the anterior vaginal wall is a cystocele, associated with urinary symptoms; a rectocele involves the posterior wall/rectum.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ur.question: Which is the biggest risk factor for pelvic organ prolapse?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ur.explanation: Vaginal delivery and multiparity (especially instrumental/prolonged deliveries and large babies) are the biggest risk factors; age/menopause, obesity and raised intra-abdominal pressure also contribute.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ur.question: A woman with a posterior vaginal wall prolapse reports constipation and needing to splint to empty her bowels. What type of prolapse is this?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ur.explanation: A rectocele (rectum descending into the posterior vaginal wall) is associated with constipation, incomplete evacuation and splinting.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ur.question: What is the first-line management for a woman with mild, symptomatic prolapse?
options: Conservative measures including pelvic floor muscle training
A vaginal pessary as first choice always
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ur.answer: Conservative measures including pelvic floor muscle training
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ur.explanation: Conservative measures (weight loss, treating constipation/cough, PFMT ≥16 weeks, topical oestrogen) are first-line, especially for mild (POP-Q stage 1–2) prolapse.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ur.question: How often should a ring pessary be changed to prevent complications?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ur.explanation: A vaginal pessary should be removed/changed at least every 6 months to prevent erosion, discharge, bleeding and fistula formation.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ur.question: A woman with a symptomatic cystocele who has failed conservative treatment opts for surgery. Which procedure is appropriate?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ur.explanation: An anterior colporrhaphy (anterior repair, without mesh) is used for a cystocele; posterior colporrhaphy is for a rectocele.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ur.question: A woman develops a vault prolapse several years after a hysterectomy. Which surgical procedure is appropriate?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ur.explanation: Vault prolapse (top of the vagina after hysterectomy) is treated with sacrocolpopexy or sacrospinous fixation.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ur.question: What is the current UK position on transvaginal mesh for prolapse repair?
options: It is first-line for all repairs
It is recommended for cystocele repair
It is mandatory for vault prolapse
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ur.explanation: Transvaginal mesh is highly restricted/paused in the UK (research-only per NICE) because of serious complications; native-tissue repairs are first-line.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ur.question: How is asymptomatic pelvic organ prolapse managed?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ur.explanation: Asymptomatic prolapse needs no treatment; observation is reasonable, with lifestyle advice.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ur.question: A woman with symptomatic uterine prolapse wishes to preserve her uterus. Which surgical option is appropriate?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ur.explanation: Sacrohysteropexy is a uterus-preserving procedure for uterine prolapse; vaginal hysterectomy is the alternative when preservation is not desired.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ur.question: Which examination technique helps demonstrate a prolapse that is not visible at rest?
options: Examining while the woman bears down (± standing)
Examining only when supine and relaxed
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ur.answer: Examining while the woman bears down (± standing)
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ur.explanation: Prolapse may only show when the woman bears down or stands, so examination is performed in these positions (a Sims speculum helps visualise each wall).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ur.question: A frail elderly woman with significant prolapse who does not wish to retain sexual function is offered which definitive procedure?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ur.explanation: Colpocleisis (vaginal closure) is an option for frail women not wishing to retain sexual function, being a simpler, effective procedure.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Te.question: Under which legal ground are the vast majority of abortions in England performed?
options: Ground C (risk to the woman's health)
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Te.answer: Ground C (risk to the woman's health)
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Te.explanation: Ground C — a greater risk to the woman's physical/mental health than termination — is used for the vast majority of abortions and applies up to <24 weeks.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Te.question: Which abortion ground has NO upper gestational time limit?
options: Ground E (substantial risk of serious fetal abnormality)
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Te.answer: Ground E (substantial risk of serious fetal abnormality)
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Te.explanation: Grounds A (risk to life), B (grave permanent injury) and E (serious fetal abnormality) have no upper time limit; C and D apply <24 weeks.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Te.question: How many registered medical practitioners must agree to a non-emergency abortion?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Te.explanation: Two registered medical practitioners must agree in good faith that a legal ground is met; one is sufficient in an emergency to save life or prevent grave permanent injury.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Te.question: What is the mechanism of mifepristone in medical termination of pregnancy?
options: It is a prostaglandin that causes contractions
An anti-progesterone that breaks down the decidua
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Te.answer: An anti-progesterone that breaks down the decidua
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Te.explanation: Mifepristone is an anti-progesterone; it blocks progesterone, breaking down the decidua and sensitising the uterus, after which misoprostol is given to expel the pregnancy.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Te.question: In medical TOP, when is misoprostol typically given after mifepristone?
options: At the same time as the follow-up test
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Te.explanation: Misoprostol (a prostaglandin analogue causing uterine contractions) is given 24–48 hours after mifepristone.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Te.question: Which surgical method is used for TOP up to about 14 weeks?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Te.explanation: Vacuum aspiration (manual or electric) is used up to ~14 weeks; dilatation & evacuation (D&E) is used for later gestations, with cervical priming beforehand.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Te.question: A woman has a positive urine pregnancy test 5 weeks after a medical TOP. What does this suggest?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Te.explanation: A urine test can stay positive up to ~4 weeks after TOP; a positive test beyond 4 weeks suggests incomplete abortion or persistent trophoblast, warranting investigation (retained products/GTD).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Te.question: How is the success of a medical TOP best confirmed?
options: A urine test the next day
A multi-level urine pregnancy test at ~2 weeks
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Te.answer: A multi-level urine pregnancy test at ~2 weeks
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Te.explanation: Success is confirmed with a self-performed follow-up pregnancy test at about 2 weeks — a multi-level or low-sensitivity urine test. A quantitative serum β-hCG is not routine and is reserved for selected cases.
