conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Te.question: A RhD-negative woman has a surgical TOP. What should she receive?
options: No anti-D as it is not needed
Anti-D only if she is over 10 weeks
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Te.explanation: Anti-D is given to RhD-negative women having a surgical abortion, and for medical abortion after 10 weeks; it is no longer needed for early medical abortion before 10 weeks.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Te.question: What is the current provision for early medical abortion via telemedicine?
options: Both pills must be taken in hospital
Both pills at home after a remote consultation
Only mifepristone can be taken at home
It is allowed up to 24 weeks at home
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Te.answer: Both pills at home after a remote consultation
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Te.explanation: Since the COVID-era provisions were made permanent, early medical abortion up to 9⁺⁶ weeks can follow a remote consultation, with both mifepristone and misoprostol taken at home.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Te.question: Which contraceptive can be inserted immediately after a surgical TOP?
options: Only after a negative pregnancy test at 4 weeks
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Te.explanation: An IUD/IUS can be inserted immediately after surgical evacuation; implants/injections/pills can be started at the time of medical TOP.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Te.question: Which is a recognised complication specific to surgical (rather than medical) TOP?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Te.explanation: Uterine perforation and cervical trauma are complications specific to surgical TOP; retained products, infection, haemorrhage and failed termination can occur with either method.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Te.question: Which assessment is recommended before a termination of pregnancy (NICE)?
options: A full autoimmune and thrombophilia screen
Confirm and date the pregnancy, group and Rhesus, FBC, STI screen
No assessment is needed before the procedure
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Te.answer: Confirm and date the pregnancy, group and Rhesus, FBC, STI screen
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Te.explanation: Before TOP, the pregnancy is confirmed and dated, blood group/Rhesus and FBC are checked, STI screening is done, options discussed non-judgementally, and contraception planned.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Re.question: Why can reduced fetal movements be a warning sign of fetal compromise?
options: The fetus moves less as it grows larger
Reduced movements indicate imminent normal delivery
A chronically hypoxic fetus reduces movement to conserve oxygen
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Re.answer: A chronically hypoxic fetus reduces movement to conserve oxygen
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Re.explanation: A chronically hypoxic fetus redistributes blood to vital organs and reduces movement to lower oxygen consumption, so RFM is an important (if non-specific) marker of fetal condition.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Re.question: At what gestation is quickening (first perception of fetal movements) usually felt?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Re.explanation: Quickening is usually felt around 18–20 weeks (earlier in multiparous women).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Re.question: Which statement about fetal movements at the end of pregnancy is correct?
options: Movements plateau after ~32 weeks and should NOT reduce
There is a fixed normal number of movements
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Re.answer: Movements plateau after ~32 weeks and should NOT reduce
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Re.explanation: Movements increase until ~32 weeks then plateau; they should not reduce at the end of pregnancy — the idea that late movements decrease is a myth.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Re.question: A woman at 30 weeks reports reduced movements. On handheld Doppler, no fetal heartbeat is heard. What is the immediate next step?
options: Send home with a kick chart
Arrange a growth scan in 2 weeks
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Re.explanation: If no fetal heartbeat is detected on handheld Doppler, an immediate ultrasound is performed to confirm viability.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Re.question: A woman at 32 weeks reports reduced movements and a fetal heartbeat is confirmed. What is the next step?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Re.explanation: With a confirmed heartbeat, a CTG (≥20 minutes) is done to assess fetal wellbeing; ultrasound follows if concern persists or risk factors are present.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Re.question: What advice should be given to a woman worried about reduced fetal movements?
options: Wait until the next day and re-count
Use a home Doppler for reassurance
Increase caffeine to stimulate the baby
Attend the maternity unit immediately for assessment
Count movements for 2 hours before contacting anyone
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Re.answer: Attend the maternity unit immediately for assessment
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Re.explanation: She should attend for assessment immediately. Counting movements against a fixed cut-off before presenting is no longer recommended — there is insufficient evidence for it and it builds delay into the pathway. She should not wait until the next day or rely on a home Doppler.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Re.question: Which condition is most strongly associated with reduced fetal movements as a concerning cause?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Re.explanation: FGR/SGA is a concerning cause linked with ~29% of RFM cases; anterior placenta, obesity, distraction and sedatives are benign causes of reduced perception.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Re.question: A woman reports she has never felt fetal movements by 24 weeks. What is the appropriate action?
options: Refer to a fetal medicine unit
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Re.answer: Refer to a fetal medicine unit
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Re.explanation: If movements have never been felt by 24 weeks, referral to a fetal medicine unit is indicated, with the heartbeat confirmed on handheld Doppler.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Re.question: What does the trial evidence show about formal fetal movement awareness packages?
options: They eliminated the need for CTG
No reduction in stillbirth, more interventions
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Re.answer: No reduction in stillbirth, more interventions
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Re.explanation: A formal awareness-of-movements package did not significantly reduce stillbirth and increased interventions, so routine formal kick-counting is not recommended.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Re.question: A woman with RFM has a normal CTG and normal growth scan. What is the appropriate management?
options: Reassure, advising immediate re-presentation if RFM recurs
Weekly CTG for the rest of pregnancy
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Re.answer: Reassure, advising immediate re-presentation if RFM recurs
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Re.explanation: If investigations are normal, reassure and advise the woman to re-present immediately if RFM recurs; recurrent RFM warrants ultrasound and closer surveillance.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Re.question: Which is a benign cause of reduced perception of fetal movements?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Re.explanation: An anterior placenta (<28 weeks) cushions movements and reduces perception; the others are concerning/pathological causes.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Re.question: Why is recurrent reduced fetal movements clinically important?
options: It warrants ultrasound and closer surveillance
It confirms the baby is well
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Re.answer: It warrants ultrasound and closer surveillance
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Re.explanation: Recurrent RFM is itself a risk factor, so it warrants ultrasound, closer surveillance and a lower threshold for a delivery discussion near term.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Re.question: A woman with RFM is found to have an SGA fetus with abnormal umbilical artery Doppler. How should she be managed?
options: As fetal growth restriction, with timed delivery
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Re.answer: As fetal growth restriction, with timed delivery
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Re.explanation: RFM with SGA, abnormal Doppler or abnormal liquor is managed as fetal growth restriction (RCOG), with increased surveillance and timed delivery.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.question: A woman at 30 weeks reports a gush of vaginal fluid. Speculum shows pooling of fluid in the posterior fornix. What is the diagnosis?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.explanation: Rupture of membranes before labour before 37 weeks, confirmed by pooling of amniotic fluid in the posterior fornix on sterile speculum, is PPROM.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.question: Which examination should be AVOIDED in suspected PPROM?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.explanation: A digital vaginal examination is avoided in suspected PPROM — it introduces infection and shortens the latency period. A sterile speculum is the examination of choice.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.question: What prophylactic antibiotic is given in PPROM?
options: Oral erythromycin 250 mg QDS for 10 days
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.answer: Oral erythromycin 250 mg QDS for 10 days
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.explanation: Erythromycin 250 mg QDS for 10 days reduces chorioamnionitis and delays delivery in PPROM; co-amoxiclav is avoided due to neonatal NEC risk.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.question: Which antibiotic is contraindicated in PPROM due to a risk of neonatal necrotising enterocolitis?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.explanation: Co-amoxiclav is associated with neonatal necrotising enterocolitis in PPROM and is avoided; erythromycin is used instead.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.question: A woman with stable PPROM at 31 weeks has no signs of infection. What is the recommended timing of birth?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.explanation: Current RCOG guidance favours expectant management to 37⁺⁰ weeks in stable PPROM (better outcomes than early birth); deliver early only for infection/fetal compromise.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.question: A woman with PPROM develops a fever, maternal and fetal tachycardia, and a raised CRP. What is the appropriate management?
options: Discharge home with oral antibiotics and a review in 48 hours
IV broad-spectrum antibiotics and expedite birth (chorioamnionitis)
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.answer: IV broad-spectrum antibiotics and expedite birth (chorioamnionitis)
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.explanation: Signs of chorioamnionitis (maternal fever/tachycardia, fetal tachycardia, raised CRP) mean maternal sepsis. Start IV broad-spectrum antibiotics immediately without waiting for cultures, and expedite birth regardless of gestation.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.question: If no pooling of fluid is seen on speculum in suspected PPROM, which test can confirm the diagnosis?
options: PAMG-1 or IGFBP-1 on vaginal fluid
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.answer: PAMG-1 or IGFBP-1 on vaginal fluid
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.explanation: If pooling is not seen, biochemical tests (PAMG-1/IGFBP-1) on vaginal fluid help confirm PPROM; ultrasound may show supportive oligohydramnios.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.question: Which intervention is NOT recommended in PPROM?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.explanation: Tocolysis is not recommended in PPROM (no clear benefit and may mask infection); steroids, erythromycin, MgSO₄ and infection monitoring are used.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.question: Up to what gestation are antenatal corticosteroids offered in PPROM?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.explanation: Antenatal corticosteroids are offered at 24⁺⁰–33⁺⁶ weeks and considered at 34⁺⁰–35⁺⁶, to reduce neonatal RDS, IVH, NEC and death.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.question: Which fetal complication results specifically from severe, early oligohydramnios in PPROM?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.explanation: Severe/early oligohydramnios can cause cord/limb compression and pulmonary hypoplasia (Potter sequence if very early), alongside cord prolapse and prematurity.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.question: When is magnesium sulphate offered in PPROM, and for what purpose?
options: At any gestation to prevent infection
Only after 34 weeks, to reduce infection
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.explanation: IV magnesium sulphate is given for fetal neuroprotection (reducing cerebral palsy) at 24⁺⁰–29⁺⁶ weeks (considered to 33⁺⁶) when birth is expected within 24 hours.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.question: What is the main maternal complication of PPROM?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.explanation: Chorioamnionitis is the main maternal complication of PPROM (cause or consequence), along with postpartum endometritis and sepsis.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.question: A woman at 29 weeks has regular painful contractions with cervical change, and clinical assessment suggests preterm labour. What is the appropriate management?
options: Wait for a fetal fibronectin result
Send home with advice to return if contractions persist
Treat with corticosteroids ± tocolysis without needing further tests
Give co-amoxiclav and continue expectant management
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.answer: Treat with corticosteroids ± tocolysis without needing further tests
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.explanation: At ≤29⁺⁶ weeks, if clinical assessment suggests preterm labour, treat with steroids ± tocolysis without requiring further diagnostic tests.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.question: A woman at 31 weeks has suspected preterm labour with intact membranes and an uncertain diagnosis. Which test helps predict birth within 48 hours?
options: Both cervical length and fibronectin together
Transvaginal cervical length OR fetal fibronectin
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.answer: Transvaginal cervical length OR fetal fibronectin
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.explanation: At ≥30 weeks, either transvaginal cervical length (>15 mm unlikely) OR fetal fibronectin (≥50 ng/mL positive) is used — but not both together.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.question: Which is the strongest risk factor for preterm labour?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.explanation: A previous preterm birth (and late miscarriage) is the strongest risk factor; multiple pregnancy, PPROM, infection and cervical incompetence also increase risk.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.question: What is the first-line tocolytic for preterm labour, and its aim?
options: Nifedipine — to improve neonatal outcomes long-term
Nifedipine — to delay birth ~48 hours for steroids and in-utero transfer
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.answer: Nifedipine — to delay birth ~48 hours for steroids and in-utero transfer
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.explanation: Nifedipine is first-line tocolysis (26⁺⁰–33⁺⁶ weeks, intact membranes), aiming to delay birth ~48h for corticosteroids to work and to allow in-utero transfer; it does not improve outcomes alone.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.question: Antenatal corticosteroids in preterm labour reduce which complications, and up to what gestation are they offered?
options: RDS, IVH, NEC and death; up to 33⁺⁶ weeks
Only jaundice and hypothermia; up to 40 weeks
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.answer: RDS, IVH, NEC and death; up to 33⁺⁶ weeks
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.explanation: Corticosteroids accelerate fetal lung maturity, reducing RDS, IVH, NEC and neonatal death. They are offered at 24⁺⁰–33⁺⁶ weeks and considered at 34⁺⁰–35⁺⁶.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.question: Magnesium sulphate is given in preterm labour for which purpose?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.explanation: IV magnesium sulphate is given for fetal neuroprotection (reducing cerebral palsy) when birth is expected within 24h at 24⁺⁰–29⁺⁶ weeks (considered to 33⁺⁶).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.question: When should antibiotics (erythromycin) be given in preterm labour?
options: In all cases of preterm labour
Only if the membranes have ruptured (PPROM)
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.answer: Only if the membranes have ruptured (PPROM)
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.explanation: Erythromycin is given only if the membranes have ruptured (PPROM); it is not given in preterm labour with intact membranes.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.question: A magnesium sulphate infusion causes loss of deep tendon reflexes and respiratory depression. What is the antidote?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.explanation: Magnesium toxicity (loss of reflexes → respiratory depression) is treated with IV calcium gluconate; reflexes, respiratory rate and urine output are monitored.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.question: Which complication of prematurity is caused by over-oxygenation in infants born before 32 weeks?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.explanation: Retinopathy of prematurity results from over-oxygenation causing abnormal retinal neovascularisation, in infants born <32 weeks.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.question: How is preterm birth prevented in a woman with a previous preterm birth and a short cervix?
options: A choice of vaginal progesterone or cervical cerclage
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.answer: A choice of vaginal progesterone or cervical cerclage
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.explanation: High-risk women (previous preterm birth, short cervix) are offered a choice of vaginal progesterone or cervical cerclage — the two are alternatives rather than a combination.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.question: Which respiratory complication of prematurity results from surfactant deficiency?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.explanation: RDS results from surfactant deficiency in the preterm lung; chronic lung disease (bronchopulmonary dysplasia) can follow.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.question: A fetal fibronectin swab is planned in a woman with suspected preterm labour. When should it be taken?
options: Only if the cervix is closed
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pr.explanation: The fetal fibronectin swab must be taken before any digital vaginal examination, as digital examination alters the result.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.question: A woman bleeds 1500 mL from the genital tract 2 hours after a vaginal delivery, and her uterus feels soft and 'boggy'. What is the most likely cause?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.explanation: A soft, boggy uterus that won't contract indicates uterine atony (Tone) — the commonest cause of PPH (~70%).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.question: What is the definition of postpartum haemorrhage by blood loss?
options: ≥500 mL from the genital tract after delivery
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.answer: ≥500 mL from the genital tract after delivery
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.explanation: PPH is defined as blood loss ≥500 mL from the genital tract after delivery; major PPH is >1000 mL or any volume with shock.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.question: What is the FIRST-line intervention to stop bleeding in atonic PPH?
options: Uterine massage ('rub up' the fundus) and empty the bladder
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.answer: Uterine massage ('rub up' the fundus) and empty the bladder
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.explanation: Mechanical measures are first-line — 'rub up' the fundus (uterine massage) and empty the bladder — while resuscitation and medical measures proceed alongside. Bimanual compression is a separate, more forceful manoeuvre used if bleeding continues.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.question: Which uterotonic is contraindicated in a woman with pre-eclampsia during PPH?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.explanation: Ergometrine is contraindicated in hypertension/pre-eclampsia; carboprost is avoided in asthma.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.question: Which uterotonic should be avoided in a woman with asthma during PPH?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.explanation: Carboprost (PGF2α) can cause bronchospasm and is avoided in asthma; ergometrine is avoided in hypertension.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.question: Which drug reduces death from PPH when given early?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.explanation: Tranexamic acid 1 g IV given early (within 3 hours) reduces death from PPH, so it is given early in all significant PPH.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.question: A woman presents with heavy vaginal bleeding and fever 10 days after delivery. What is the likely cause of this secondary PPH?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.explanation: Secondary PPH (24 hours to 12 weeks postpartum) is typically due to retained placental tissue or endometritis; treat with antibiotics ± evacuation of retained products, guided by ultrasound.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.question: Which is the biggest single predictor of postpartum haemorrhage?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.explanation: A previous PPH is the biggest single predictor; an overdistended uterus, pre-eclampsia, praevia/accreta and emergency caesarean also increase risk.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.question: Which intervention at delivery reduces PPH risk for all women?
options: Active management of the third stage with prophylactic IM oxytocin
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.answer: Active management of the third stage with prophylactic IM oxytocin
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.explanation: Active third-stage management with prophylactic IM oxytocin 10 IU reduces PPH by ~60% and is used for all births, since most PPH occurs without risk factors.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.question: If mechanical and medical measures fail to control atonic PPH, which tamponade device is used?
options: A Foley catheter in the bladder
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.explanation: An intrauterine (Bakri) balloon provides tamponade; further options escalate to B-Lynch suture, artery ligation/embolisation, and hysterectomy as a last resort.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.question: A woman who had a severe PPH later fails to lactate and has amenorrhoea. What is the diagnosis?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.explanation: Severe PPH causing hypovolaemic shock can cause pituitary necrosis (Sheehan's syndrome), classically with failed lactation (low prolactin) and amenorrhoea (low gonadotrophins).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.question: Which of the 4 T's refers to retained placenta or membranes as a cause of PPH?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.explanation: 'Tissue' refers to retained placenta or membranes, which prevent effective uterine contraction; Tone is atony, Trauma is tears/rupture, Thrombin is coagulopathy.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.question: A woman is bleeding <500 mL after delivery with no shock, and the bleeding is settling. What is this most likely to be?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.explanation: Bleeding <500 mL with no shock is likely normal lochia (postpartum discharge reducing over ~6 weeks); persistent bleeding beyond 6 weeks warrants ultrasound for retained products.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.question: A woman 5 days postpartum has a fever of 38.5°C, lower abdominal pain, a tender uterus and offensive lochia. What is the most likely diagnosis?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.explanation: Fever with uterine tenderness and offensive lochia postpartum is classic endometritis — the commonest cause of puerperal pyrexia.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.question: What is the first-line antibiotic regimen for postpartum endometritis?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.explanation: IV clindamycin + gentamicin is first-line for endometritis, continued until the woman is afebrile for >24 hours.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.question: Which is the biggest risk factor for postpartum endometritis?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.explanation: Caesarean section is the biggest risk factor for endometritis; prolonged ROM/labour, retained products and multiple vaginal exams also increase risk.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.question: A febrile postpartum woman is hypotensive and tachycardic with a raised lactate. What is the appropriate immediate management?
options: Initiate the Sepsis Six and escalate urgently
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.answer: Initiate the Sepsis Six and escalate urgently
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.explanation: Sepsis with organ dysfunction or septic shock requires immediate initiation of the Sepsis Six and urgent escalation (RCOG), alongside identifying and treating the source.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.question: Which organism causing genital tract sepsis is particularly virulent and rapidly progressive postpartum?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.explanation: Group A Streptococcus is a highly virulent, rapidly-progressive genital-tract pathogen postpartum, warranting a low threshold for aggressive treatment and infection control.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.question: A woman 3 days after caesarean has a fever and erythema with discharge from her abdominal wound. What is the likely source of her puerperal pyrexia?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.explanation: Erythema and discharge from a caesarean wound indicate a wound infection as the source; a systematic 'where is the source?' approach is used.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.question: How long is IV treatment for endometritis typically continued?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.explanation: IV clindamycin + gentamicin is continued until the woman is afebrile for >24 hours, and oral continuation is usually not needed.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.question: A febrile postpartum woman has dysuria, frequency and loin pain. Which source should be investigated?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.explanation: Dysuria, frequency and loin pain point to a UTI/pyelonephritis; an MSU is sent and appropriate antibiotics given.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.question: Why is clindamycin added in severe Group A streptococcal genital tract sepsis?
options: For its antitoxin effect (reducing toxin production)
Because it is the only effective antibiotic
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.answer: For its antitoxin effect (reducing toxin production)
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.explanation: Clindamycin is added for its antitoxin effect against Group A Strep, alongside broad cover such as piperacillin-tazobactam or a carbapenem.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.question: What is the traditional temperature threshold defining puerperal pyrexia, and its timing?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.explanation: Puerperal pyrexia is traditionally a temperature ≥38°C in the first 14 days after delivery (some definitions extend across the puerperium to 6 weeks).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.question: A postpartum woman has a fever with a unilateral tender, red, swollen breast. What is the likely source?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.explanation: A unilateral tender, red, swollen breast indicates mastitis as the source of the fever; it is managed with milk removal ± antibiotics.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.question: Which investigation is most appropriate if retained products of conception are suspected as a cause of postpartum endometritis?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.explanation: Pelvic ultrasound is used to assess for retained products/pelvic collection; evacuation of retained products (ERPC) may be needed if tissue is driving the infection.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.question: A postpartum woman has a low-grade fever with calf swelling and breathlessness. Which source must be considered?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.explanation: Calf swelling and breathlessness with a low-grade fever raise concern for VTE (DVT/PE); Doppler/CTPA and anticoagulation are considered.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.question: A woman develops confusion, mania, and delusions centred on her baby 8 days after delivery. What is the diagnosis and appropriate management?
options: Puerperal psychosis — urgent psychiatric admission (Mother & Baby Unit)
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.answer: Puerperal psychosis — urgent psychiatric admission (Mother & Baby Unit)
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.explanation: Rapid-onset psychosis, mania, and delusions (often about the baby) within 2–3 weeks of birth is puerperal psychosis — a psychiatric emergency requiring urgent admission, ideally to a Mother & Baby Unit.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.question: Puerperal psychosis is most strongly associated with which underlying condition?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.explanation: Puerperal psychosis is strongly linked to bipolar disorder; a personal/family history of bipolar or previous puerperal psychosis is the biggest risk factor.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.question: A woman is tearful, anxious and irritable on day 4 postpartum, with mild labile mood. What is the diagnosis and management?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.explanation: Baby blues (~60–70%, days 3–7) is mild and self-limiting, managed with reassurance and support, not medication.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.question: Which screening tool is used for postnatal depression?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.explanation: The EPDS (10-item, max 30; ≥13 suggests likely depressive illness) is used to screen for postnatal depression.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.question: Which SSRI is preferred for a breastfeeding woman with postnatal depression, and which is avoided?
options: Prefer sertraline (paroxetine an alternative); avoid fluoxetine
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.answer: Prefer sertraline (paroxetine an alternative); avoid fluoxetine
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.explanation: Sertraline is preferred first-line in breastfeeding (lowest infant exposure), with paroxetine an acceptable alternative; fluoxetine is avoided because its long half-life leads to infant accumulation.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.question: What is the preferred setting for admitting a woman with puerperal psychosis?
options: A general adult psychiatric ward without the baby
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.explanation: Admission to a Mother & Baby Unit is preferred, as it keeps mother and baby together to support bonding while maintaining safety.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.question: Which pharmacological treatments are used in puerperal psychosis?
options: Antipsychotics + a mood stabiliser (lithium), ± benzodiazepines; ECT if severe
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.answer: Antipsychotics + a mood stabiliser (lithium), ± benzodiazepines; ECT if severe
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.explanation: Puerperal psychosis is treated with antipsychotics (olanzapine/quetiapine), a mood stabiliser (lithium), short-term benzodiazepines for agitation, and ECT if severe or resistant. Lithium is not recommended while breastfeeding — it passes into milk and can cause infant toxicity — so feeding options are discussed and an alternative considered.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.question: What must be assessed and managed urgently in a woman with puerperal psychosis?
options: Risk to the mother (suicide) and to the baby (harm/neglect)
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.answer: Risk to the mother (suicide) and to the baby (harm/neglect)
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.explanation: Risk to the mother (suicide) and baby (harm/neglect) must be assessed and managed urgently in puerperal psychosis.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.question: Which is a recognised risk factor for puerperal psychosis?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.explanation: Previous puerperal psychosis (and a personal/family history of bipolar disorder, primiparity, and stopping psychiatric medication in pregnancy) are risk factors.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.question: What should be ruled out when assessing a woman with suspected puerperal psychosis?
options: Nothing — the diagnosis is always clear
Organic causes such as infection, thyroid disease and medication effects
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.answer: Organic causes such as infection, thyroid disease and medication effects
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.explanation: Organic causes (infection, thyroid disorder, medication) must be excluded when assessing suspected puerperal psychosis.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.question: A woman has low mood, anhedonia, poor sleep and guilt starting 6 weeks postpartum. What is the diagnosis and first-line management?
options: Postnatal depression — CBT (± SSRI if needed)
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.answer: Postnatal depression — CBT (± SSRI if needed)
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.explanation: Low mood, anhedonia and guilt starting within the first months is postnatal depression, managed with CBT first-line and an SSRI if needed.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.question: What is the prognosis of puerperal psychosis with treatment?
options: Generally good, but with high recurrence in future pregnancies
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.answer: Generally good, but with high recurrence in future pregnancies
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.explanation: With prompt treatment most women recover fully, but recurrence in future pregnancies is high, so pre-conception counselling and a perinatal mental health plan are important.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.question: What is the typical onset time of puerperal psychosis after delivery?
options: Within 2-3 weeks (often within the first few days)
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.answer: Within 2-3 weeks (often within the first few days)
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.explanation: Puerperal psychosis typically has an abrupt onset within ~2–3 weeks of birth, often within the first few days.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.question: A woman 3 months postpartum has palpitations, tremor and anxiety; TFTs show ↑T4 and ↓TSH. Radioiodine uptake is low. What is the diagnosis?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.explanation: A thyrotoxic phase within months of delivery with LOW radioiodine uptake indicates the destructive thyrotoxicosis of postpartum thyroiditis, not Graves' (which has high uptake).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.question: How should the thyrotoxic phase of postpartum thyroiditis be managed?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.explanation: The thyrotoxic phase is destructive release, so it is managed symptomatically with propranolol; antithyroid drugs (which block synthesis) are not used.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.question: Why are antithyroid drugs (e.g. carbimazole) not used in postpartum thyroiditis?
options: The thyroid is leaking stored hormone, not overproducing it
They are ineffective against TPO antibodies
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.answer: The thyroid is leaking stored hormone, not overproducing it
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.explanation: PPT is a destructive thyroiditis (hormone release from a damaged gland), so antithyroid drugs, which block hormone synthesis, do not address the problem.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.question: Which antibodies are characteristic of postpartum thyroiditis?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.explanation: TPO antibodies are present in ~90% of PPT and predict its development; TRAb are characteristic of Graves' disease.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.question: Which feature distinguishes postpartum thyroiditis from Graves' disease?
options: Low radioiodine uptake in PPT vs high uptake in Graves'
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.answer: Low radioiodine uptake in PPT vs high uptake in Graves'
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.explanation: PPT (destructive) has LOW radioiodine uptake and TPO antibodies with no eye signs; Graves' (stimulatory) has HIGH uptake, TRAb, and may have eye disease.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.question: What is the classic triphasic course of postpartum thyroiditis?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.explanation: The classic pattern is thyrotoxic → hypothyroid → euthyroid, though not every woman goes through all three phases.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.question: A woman 6 months postpartum has fatigue and cold intolerance with ↓T4 and ↑TSH, in keeping with the hypothyroid phase of PPT. How is she managed if symptomatic?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.explanation: The hypothyroid phase is treated with levothyroxine if symptomatic (or if trying to conceive), then tapered at ~6–12 months as it is usually transient.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.question: Which follow-up is recommended after postpartum thyroiditis, and why?
options: Annual TSH monitoring, as up to ~50% develop permanent hypothyroidism
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.answer: Annual TSH monitoring, as up to ~50% develop permanent hypothyroidism
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.explanation: Up to ~50% of women with PPT develop permanent hypothyroidism in later years, so annual TSH monitoring is advised.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.question: Which factor increases the risk of postpartum thyroiditis?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.explanation: Type 1 diabetes, previous PPT, and a personal/family history of autoimmune thyroid disease increase the risk of postpartum thyroiditis.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.question: What predicts which women will develop postpartum thyroiditis?
options: A low free T4 in pregnancy
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.explanation: TPO-positivity in pregnancy predicts PPT — about 50% of TPO-positive women develop it.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.question: Why is postpartum thyroiditis frequently missed?
options: It causes no symptoms at all
Symptoms are attributed to normal postnatal fatigue/stress
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.answer: Symptoms are attributed to normal postnatal fatigue/stress
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.explanation: PPT is easily missed because its symptoms are often dismissed as normal postnatal fatigue/stress.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.question: A woman with postpartum thyrotoxicosis is breastfeeding. Which treatment is safe for symptom control?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.explanation: Propranolol is safe in breastfeeding and controls the adrenergic symptoms of the thyrotoxic phase; antithyroid drugs and radioiodine are not appropriate for PPT.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.question: What is the recurrence risk of postpartum thyroiditis in future pregnancies?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Po.explanation: Postpartum thyroiditis has a high recurrence rate (~20–70%) in future pregnancies.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.question: A 22-year-old sexually active woman has bilateral lower abdominal pain, deep dyspareunia, and cervical motion tenderness on examination. What is the most likely diagnosis?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.answer: Pelvic inflammatory disease
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.explanation: Bilateral lower abdominal pain with cervical motion tenderness in a young sexually active woman is classic PID (ascending infection).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.question: What is the most common causative organism of PID?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.answer: Chlamydia trachomatis
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.explanation: Chlamydia trachomatis is the commonest cause of PID (often asymptomatic/insidious); gonorrhoea causes more severe disease.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.question: What is the first-line antibiotic regimen for PID (BASHH)?
options: Oral ofloxacin 400 mg BD + metronidazole 400 mg BD for 14 days
Single-dose azithromycin 1 g with no further treatment
IM ceftriaxone 1 g + doxycycline 100 mg BD + metronidazole 400 mg BD, both for 14 days
Oral amoxicillin 500 mg TDS for 7 days with review
IV benzylpenicillin 1.2 g QDS until afebrile
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.answer: IM ceftriaxone 1 g + doxycycline 100 mg BD + metronidazole 400 mg BD, both for 14 days
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.explanation: First-line is IM ceftriaxone 1 g + doxycycline 100 mg BD for 14 days + metronidazole 400 mg BD for 14 days; fluoroquinolone regimens are now second-line.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.question: Why are fluoroquinolones (ofloxacin/moxifloxacin) now second-line for PID?
options: They are contraindicated in all women
They cause fewer side effects than ceftriaxone
Safety advice on tendon and neurological effects
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.answer: Safety advice on tendon and neurological effects
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.explanation: Following MHRA safety advice about serious adverse effects, fluoroquinolones became second-line, with the ceftriaxone-based regimen preferred first-line.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.question: Which investigation must always be performed in a sexually active woman with suspected PID?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.answer: A pregnancy test (β-hCG)
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.explanation: A pregnancy test must be done to exclude ectopic pregnancy, the must-not-miss differential, before diagnosing PID.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.question: A woman with a suspected PID has a swab microscopy showing no pus cells. What does this suggest?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.answer: PID is unlikely
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.explanation: The absence of pus cells on microscopy makes PID unlikely — a useful rule-out, though PID remains a clinical diagnosis.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.question: A woman develops right upper quadrant pain in the context of PID, with 'violin-string' perihepatic adhesions. What is this complication?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.answer: Fitz-Hugh-Curtis syndrome (perihepatitis)
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.explanation: Perihepatitis with RUQ pain and violin-string adhesions is Fitz-Hugh-Curtis syndrome, a classic complication of chlamydial/gonococcal PID.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.question: A woman with a copper IUD develops mild PID. How should the device be managed?
options: It must always be removed immediately
It should be replaced with a new one
It can usually be left in situ
It should be removed only after treatment
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.answer: It can usually be left in situ
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.explanation: In mild PID the IUD can usually be left in situ; removal is considered in severe cases or if there is no improvement within 48–72 hours.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.question: Which feature would make quinolone-based PID treatment inadvisable?
options: A high likelihood of gonococcal PID
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.answer: A high likelihood of gonococcal PID
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.explanation: Quinolones are avoided when gonococcal PID is likely (partner with gonorrhoea, severe disease, contact abroad) because of high quinolone resistance in gonorrhoea.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.question: Which is a recognised long-term complication of PID?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.answer: Infertility from tubal scarring
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.explanation: Tubal scarring from PID causes infertility (risk rising with each episode), ectopic pregnancy and chronic pelvic pain.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.question: Why should PID be treated empirically without waiting for swab results?
options: It is never caused by an STI
It is a clinical diagnosis with serious complications
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.answer: It is a clinical diagnosis with serious complications
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.explanation: PID is a clinical diagnosis with a low treatment threshold, because a negative swab does not exclude it and delayed treatment risks serious complications (infertility, ectopic, chronic pain).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.question: When should a woman with PID be admitted for IV antibiotics?
options: A surgical emergency cannot be excluded, or severe disease
Only if she has an IUD
Never — PID is always managed in the community
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.answer: A surgical emergency cannot be excluded, or severe disease
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.explanation: Inpatient/IV treatment is indicated for severe disease, tubo-ovarian abscess, pregnancy, failure of oral therapy, or inability to tolerate oral treatment.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.question: A woman treated for PID should also receive which of the following?
options: GUM referral for contact tracing and partner treatment
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.answer: GUM referral for contact tracing and partner treatment
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.explanation: PID management includes GUM referral for contact tracing and partner treatment, plus advice to avoid intercourse until treatment is completed and screening for other STIs.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.question: A woman has a thin, white, homogenous vaginal discharge with a fishy odour but no itching. The vaginal pH is 5.0. What is the most likely diagnosis?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.answer: Bacterial vaginosis
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.explanation: Thin, white, homogenous, fishy discharge with a raised pH and no itch is characteristic of bacterial vaginosis.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.question: What is the underlying cause of bacterial vaginosis?
options: Loss of lactobacilli with anaerobic overgrowth
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.answer: Loss of lactobacilli with anaerobic overgrowth
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.explanation: BV results from loss of protective lactobacilli, raising the vaginal pH and allowing anaerobic overgrowth (chiefly Gardnerella vaginalis).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.question: Which of Amsel's criteria is a microscopy finding characteristic of BV?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.answer: Clue cells
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.explanation: Clue cells (epithelial cells studded with adherent bacteria) are the microscopy hallmark of BV; pseudohyphae suggest candida and motile flagellates suggest trichomonas.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.question: How many of Amsel's four criteria are needed to diagnose BV?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.answer: 3 of 4
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.explanation: BV is diagnosed if ≥3 of the 4 Amsel's criteria (thin discharge, pH >4.5, clue cells, positive whiff test) are present.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.question: What is the first-line treatment for symptomatic bacterial vaginosis?
options: Oral metronidazole 400 mg twice daily for 5-7 days
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.answer: Oral metronidazole 400 mg twice daily for 5-7 days
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.explanation: Oral metronidazole 400 mg BD for 5–7 days is first-line; alternatives include a 2 g single dose or topical metronidazole/clindamycin.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.question: A woman is prescribed metronidazole for BV. What advice should she be given?
options: Take it with alcohol to improve absorption
Avoid alcohol during and for ~48h after treatment
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.answer: Avoid alcohol during and for ~48h after treatment
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.explanation: Metronidazole is associated with a disulfiram-like reaction with alcohol, so patients are advised to avoid alcohol during and for ~48h after treatment.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.question: Is bacterial vaginosis a sexually transmitted infection, and should partners be treated?
options: It is an STI, and partners must be treated
It is not an STI, and partners are not routinely treated
It is an STI, but partners are not treated
It is not an STI, but partners must be treated
It only occurs after sexual contact
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.answer: It is not an STI, and partners are not routinely treated
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.explanation: BV is not an STI (it is a flora disturbance), and treating male partners does not reduce recurrence, so partners are not routinely treated.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.question: Which pregnancy complication is associated with bacterial vaginosis?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.answer: Preterm birth
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.explanation: BV in pregnancy is associated with miscarriage, preterm birth, PROM, chorioamnionitis, low birth weight and postpartum endometritis.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.question: Which preventive advice reduces recurrence of BV?
options: Avoid vaginal douching and internal soaps
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.answer: Avoid vaginal douching and internal soaps
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.explanation: Avoiding douching and internal soaps/shower gels preserves the protective lactobacilli and reduces BV; recurrence is common.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.question: A pregnant woman has symptomatic BV. What is the appropriate treatment?
options: Oral metronidazole (avoiding the 2 g single dose) or topical treatment
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.answer: Oral metronidazole (avoiding the 2 g single dose) or topical treatment
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.explanation: Symptomatic BV in pregnancy is treated (given adverse outcomes) with oral metronidazole (avoiding the high-dose single 2 g regimen) or topical treatment; metronidazole is considered low-risk.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.question: Why does the fishy odour of BV worsen after intercourse or menstruation?
options: Blood is acidic and neutralises the discharge
Alkaline semen and blood raise the vaginal pH, releasing amines
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.answer: Alkaline semen and blood raise the vaginal pH, releasing amines
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.explanation: Alkaline semen and menstrual blood raise the vaginal pH, releasing the fishy amine odour, so it is worse after sex/menstruation.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.question: Which feature distinguishes BV from vulvovaginal candidiasis?
options: BV causes intense itching and soreness
BV: minimal itch, thin fishy discharge
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.answer: BV: minimal itch, thin fishy discharge
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.explanation: BV causes a thin, fishy, homogenous discharge with minimal itch and a raised pH, whereas candida causes a thick, curdy, intensely itchy discharge with a normal pH.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.question: Which increased risk is associated with BV due to the raised vaginal pH and loss of protection?
options: Acquiring sexually transmitted infections including HIV
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.answer: Acquiring sexually transmitted infections including HIV
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.explanation: The raised pH and loss of lactobacilli in BV increase the risk of acquiring STIs, including HIV.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.question: A woman has a frothy, yellow-green, offensive vaginal discharge with vulval itching and dysuria. Examination shows punctate cervical haemorrhages. What is the diagnosis?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.answer: Trichomoniasis
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.explanation: Frothy yellow-green offensive discharge with itch and a 'strawberry cervix' (punctate cervical haemorrhages) is classic trichomoniasis.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.question: What type of organism causes trichomoniasis?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.answer: A flagellated protozoan parasite
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.explanation: Trichomonas vaginalis is a motile, flagellated protozoan parasite — a sexually transmitted infection.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.question: Which feature most distinguishes trichomoniasis from bacterial vaginosis in management?
options: It has a normal vaginal pH
It is an STI, so partners must be treated and contact-traced
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.answer: It is an STI, so partners must be treated and contact-traced
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.explanation: Both raise vaginal pH and can smell fishy, but trichomonas is an STI requiring partner treatment/contact tracing, whereas BV is a flora disturbance where partners are not treated.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.question: What is the first-line treatment for trichomoniasis?
options: Oral metronidazole 400-500 mg twice daily for 5-7 days
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.answer: Oral metronidazole 400-500 mg twice daily for 5-7 days
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.explanation: Oral metronidazole 400–500 mg BD for 5–7 days is first-line; a 2 g single dose is an alternative but less favoured (and avoided in pregnancy).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.question: How is trichomoniasis best diagnosed in a woman?
options: Charcoal swab for microscopy, or NAAT
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.answer: Charcoal swab for microscopy, or NAAT
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.explanation: A charcoal swab from the posterior fornix shows motile trophozoites on microscopy; NAAT is the most sensitive test. A Pap smear is not diagnostic.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.question: Why is a Pap smear not relied upon to diagnose trichomoniasis?
options: It gives false positives and negatives
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.answer: It gives false positives and negatives
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.explanation: Trichomonas may be an incidental Pap finding, but the Pap is not diagnostic (false positives/negatives), so a proper test is needed to confirm.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.question: A man's partner is diagnosed with trichomoniasis. He is asymptomatic. What is the appropriate management?
options: No treatment, as he is asymptomatic
Treat only if he develops symptoms
Treat him and arrange contact tracing (it is an STI)
Test him and treat only if he is positive
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.answer: Treat him and arrange contact tracing (it is an STI)
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.explanation: Trichomonas is an STI, so partners are treated and contact-traced regardless of symptoms (men are often asymptomatic but can transmit it).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.question: Which pregnancy complication is associated with trichomoniasis?
options: Preterm birth and low birth weight
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.answer: Preterm birth and low birth weight
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.explanation: Trichomoniasis in pregnancy is linked to preterm birth and low birth weight; it also increases HIV transmission risk.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.question: How should trichomoniasis be treated in pregnancy?
options: Oral metronidazole, avoiding the 2 g single dose
A single 2 g metronidazole dose preferred
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.answer: Oral metronidazole, avoiding the 2 g single dose
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.explanation: Oral metronidazole is used in pregnancy (avoiding the high-dose 2 g single regimen); topical/gel treatment is not effective for trichomonas.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.question: Which vaginal pH finding is typical of trichomoniasis?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.answer: >4.5 (raised)
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.explanation: Trichomoniasis (like BV) raises the vaginal pH above 4.5; candida has a normal pH (<4.5).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.question: A woman is diagnosed with trichomoniasis. What additional step is recommended?
options: Screen for other STIs (chlamydia, gonorrhoea, HIV)
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.answer: Screen for other STIs (chlamydia, gonorrhoea, HIV)
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.explanation: Co-infection is common, so screening for other STIs (chlamydia, gonorrhoea, HIV) is recommended, along with partner treatment and GUM referral.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.question: Which advice accompanies metronidazole treatment for trichomoniasis?
options: Avoid alcohol during and shortly after treatment
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.answer: Avoid alcohol during and shortly after treatment
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.explanation: Metronidazole causes a disulfiram-like reaction with alcohol, so alcohol should be avoided during and shortly after treatment.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.question: What is the significance of asymptomatic trichomonas infection?
options: It means no treatment is needed
Asymptomatic infection is not detectable by NAAT
It is not a true infection
Carriers act as a reservoir for transmission
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.answer: Carriers act as a reservoir for transmission
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Pe.explanation: Up to ~50% of infections are asymptomatic (men usually), forming a reservoir for ongoing transmission, which is why partner treatment/contact tracing matter.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ov.question: A 24-year-old with a known 5 cm ovarian cyst presents with sudden severe right pelvic pain and vomiting. What is the most likely diagnosis?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ov.explanation: Sudden severe unilateral pelvic pain with vomiting in a woman with an ovarian cyst is ovarian torsion until proven otherwise.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ov.question: Which investigation must always be performed first in a woman with suspected ovarian torsion?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ov.explanation: A pregnancy test is always done first to exclude ectopic pregnancy, the must-not-miss differential.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ov.question: An ultrasound in a woman with severe pelvic pain shows normal Doppler flow to the ovary. What is the correct interpretation?
options: It makes an ovarian cyst the more likely cause
Normal Doppler does NOT exclude torsion
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ov.answer: Normal Doppler does NOT exclude torsion
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ov.explanation: Venous obstruction precedes arterial compromise in torsion, so Doppler flow may be normal/present in up to ~50% of cases; normal Doppler does not exclude torsion.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ov.question: Which structures does the ovary twist around in ovarian torsion?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ov.explanation: The ovary twists on the infundibulopelvic (suspensory) ligament (carrying the vessels) and the utero-ovarian ligament.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ov.question: At laparoscopy, a torted premenopausal ovary looks blue-black and ischaemic. What is the preferred management?
options: Detorsion and conservation of the ovary
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ov.answer: Detorsion and conservation of the ovary
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ov.explanation: Ovarian conservation with detorsion is preferred in premenopausal women even if the ovary looks ischaemic, as visual viability assessment is unreliable and blackened ovaries often recover.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ov.question: Which ultrasound finding is characteristic of ovarian torsion?
options: A gestational sac in the tube
An enlarged, oedematous ovary with a whirlpool sign
A normal-sized ovary with brisk flow
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ov.answer: An enlarged, oedematous ovary with a whirlpool sign
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ov.explanation: Torsion shows an enlarged, oedematous ovary, peripherally displaced follicles (stromal oedema pushes them to the rim), a whirlpool sign from the twisted pedicle, and free fluid.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ov.question: Which group characteristically torses a NORMAL (non-enlarged) ovary?
options: Pregnant women with corpus luteum cysts
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ov.explanation: Prepubertal girls, with long ovarian ligaments and mobile ovaries, can torse a normal ovary; adults usually torse an enlarged/abnormal ovary.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ov.question: Which is the biggest risk factor for ovarian torsion?
options: An ovarian cyst or mass, especially a dermoid
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ov.answer: An ovarian cyst or mass, especially a dermoid
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ov.explanation: An ovarian cyst/mass (especially dermoid cysts and cysts ~5 cm or larger) is the biggest risk factor, acting as a lever point.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ov.question: When is oophorectomy indicated in ovarian torsion?
options: Any torted ovary in a young woman
A frankly necrotic ovary or a suspicious mass
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ov.answer: A frankly necrotic ovary or a suspicious mass
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ov.explanation: Oophorectomy is reserved for a truly necrotic/non-viable ovary or a suspicious mass (possible malignancy), particularly in postmenopausal women; otherwise the ovary is conserved.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ov.question: A woman with equivocal ultrasound findings has a high clinical suspicion of ovarian torsion. What is the appropriate next step?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ov.explanation: If clinical suspicion is high despite equivocal imaging, diagnostic laparoscopy is undertaken, as the definitive diagnosis is made at surgery and delay risks ovarian loss.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ov.question: Which procedure may be added to prevent recurrence in torsion of a normal ovary with long ligaments?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ov.explanation: Oophoropexy (fixing the ovary) is used for recurrent torsion or torsion of a normal ovary with long ligaments; cystectomy addresses an underlying cyst.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ov.question: Why does delayed diagnosis of ovarian torsion matter?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ov.explanation: Delayed detorsion allows progression from venous congestion to arterial ischaemia and infarction, causing loss of ovarian tissue and fertility consequences — so timing is critical.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ov.question: A pregnant woman with ovulation-induced enlarged ovaries develops sudden unilateral pelvic pain. Besides OHSS, which complication must be considered?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ov.explanation: Enlarged ovaries (from OHSS/ovulation induction or pregnancy) are prone to torsion; sudden unilateral pelvic pain should prompt consideration of ovarian torsion.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.question: How many antenatal appointments are recommended for an uncomplicated nulliparous pregnancy (NICE)?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.explanation: NICE recommends 10 appointments for nulliparous women and 7 for parous women in uncomplicated pregnancies.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.question: At what gestation is the fetal anomaly scan performed?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.explanation: The anomaly scan is done at 18–20⁺⁶ weeks; the dating scan is at 10–13⁺⁶ weeks and the combined test at 11–13⁺⁶ weeks.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.question: Which test is no longer part of the booking blood panel?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.explanation: Rubella screening has been removed from the booking bloods; HIV, hepatitis B and syphilis screening continue.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.question: A woman with epilepsy taking antiepileptic drugs is planning pregnancy. What dose of folic acid should she take?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.explanation: High-dose (5 mg) folic acid is recommended for women with epilepsy on antiepileptics (and obesity, NTD history, diabetes, coeliac, thalassaemia trait); the standard dose is 400 micrograms.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.question: What vitamin D dose is recommended for all pregnant women?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.explanation: All pregnant women are advised to take vitamin D 10 micrograms daily (note the unit is micrograms).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.question: Why should pregnant women avoid liver and high-dose vitamin A?
options: Vitamin A is teratogenic in high doses
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.answer: Vitamin A is teratogenic in high doses
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.explanation: High-dose vitamin A (>700 mcg) is teratogenic, and liver is very high in vitamin A, so both are avoided in pregnancy.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.question: When are the two antenatal anti-D doses given to a RhD-negative woman?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.explanation: Routine antenatal anti-D prophylaxis is given at 28 and 34 weeks (or as a single dose), plus postnatally if the baby is RhD-positive.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.question: At which appointment is presentation checked and ECV offered if the baby is breech?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.explanation: Presentation is checked at 36 weeks, and ECV is offered if the baby is breech.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.question: A woman at 30 weeks has a new BP of 150/95. What is the appropriate action?
options: Start labetalol at home without referral
Ignore, as BP always rises in pregnancy
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.explanation: New BP ≥140/90 after 20 weeks warrants referral within 24 hours; ≥160/110 needs same-day assessment. (BP normally falls in the first half of pregnancy.)

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.question: What does the combined test screen for, and what does it include?
options: Down's, Edwards' and Patau's — NT, βhCG and PAPP-A
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.answer: Down's, Edwards' and Patau's — NT, βhCG and PAPP-A
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.explanation: The combined test (11⁺²–14⁺¹ weeks) screens for trisomy 21, 18 and 13 — Down's, Edwards' and Patau's — using nuchal translucency, βhCG and PAPP-A.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.question: Which supplement is NOT routinely offered to all pregnant women?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.explanation: Iron is not routinely offered — only if the woman is anaemic; folic acid (to 12 weeks) and vitamin D are recommended for all.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.question: From what gestation is symphysis-fundal height measured and plotted?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.explanation: Symphysis-fundal height is plotted from 24–28 weeks to monitor growth; a small measurement prompts a growth scan.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.question: How is the onset of labour diagnosed?
options: Irregular contractions with no cervical change
Regular painful contractions with progressive cervical change
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.answer: Regular painful contractions with progressive cervical change
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.explanation: Labour is diagnosed by regular painful uterine contractions producing progressive cervical change (effacement and dilatation), distinguishing it from Braxton Hicks.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.question: A term woman has irregular contractions every 20 minutes with no cervical change and is otherwise well. What is the appropriate management?
options: Reassure and send home (Braxton Hicks/false labour)
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.answer: Reassure and send home (Braxton Hicks/false labour)
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.explanation: Irregular contractions without progressive cervical change are Braxton Hicks/false labour; a term, well woman can be reassured and sent home.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.question: The first stage of labour extends from onset to which point?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.explanation: The first stage runs from onset to full dilatation (10 cm), with a latent phase up to ~4 cm and an active phase from ~4 cm.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.question: Which management of the third stage of labour reduces postpartum haemorrhage (NICE)?
options: Active management (IM oxytocin + controlled cord traction)
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.answer: Active management (IM oxytocin + controlled cord traction)
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.explanation: Active third-stage management (a prophylactic uterotonic such as IM oxytocin plus controlled cord traction and delayed cord clamping) reduces PPH risk.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.question: Which is the correct order of the first three cardinal movements of labour?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.explanation: The cardinal movements begin engagement → descent → flexion, then internal rotation → extension → restitution → external rotation → expulsion.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.question: Which is the commonest, and correctable, cause of failure to progress in labour?
options: Power (inadequate uterine contractions) — corrected with oxytocin
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.answer: Power (inadequate uterine contractions) — corrected with oxytocin
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.explanation: Inadequate contractions ('Power') are the commonest cause of failure to progress and can be corrected with oxytocin; Passage and Passenger are the other two P's.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.question: What is used to graphically monitor progress in labour?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.explanation: A partogram graphically records cervical dilatation vs time, contractions, fetal heart and maternal observations, flagging when progress crosses the alert/action line.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.question: In a low-risk labour, how is the fetal heart monitored?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.explanation: Low-risk labour uses intermittent auscultation; continuous CTG is used if there are risk factors or concerns.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.question: At approximately what rate does the cervix dilate in the active first stage of labour?
options: It does not dilate in the active phase
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.explanation: In the active first stage the cervix dilates approximately 0.5–1 cm per hour.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.question: During which stage of labour do the cardinal movements (mechanism of labour) occur?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.explanation: The mechanism of labour (cardinal movements) occurs during the second stage, from full dilatation to delivery of the baby.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.question: Which analgesic option is the strongest listed for labour pain?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.explanation: Analgesia in labour escalates from non-pharmacological measures to Entonox to epidural, the last being the strongest.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.question: A 'show' during pregnancy refers to which of the following?
options: Passage of the blood-stained mucus plug
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.answer: Passage of the blood-stained mucus plug
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.explanation: A 'show' is passage of the blood-stained cervical mucus plug, one of the signs associated with the onset of labour.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.question: A nulliparous woman has been actively pushing for 2 hours without delivery. How is this described?
options: Diagnosed delay in the second stage
Normal progress for a first labour
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.answer: Diagnosed delay in the second stage
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.explanation: In a nulliparous woman, delay in the active second stage is suspected after 1 hour of active pushing and diagnosed after 2 hours. It prompts senior review and consideration of assisted vaginal birth.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.question: A parous woman has been actively pushing for 35 minutes. What is the correct interpretation?
options: Delay in the first stage of labour
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.explanation: In a parous woman, delay in the active second stage is suspected after 30 minutes and diagnosed after 1 hour. At 35 minutes the delay is suspected, prompting review rather than immediate delivery.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.question: A woman opted for physiological management of the third stage. The placenta has not delivered 45 minutes after the birth. What should happen?
options: Diagnose a prolonged third stage and do nothing
Give a further dose of misoprostol
Return her to the first stage
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.explanation: Physiological third stage is prolonged if not completed within 60 minutes, but it is converted to active management sooner if there is haemorrhage or the woman requests it. At 45 minutes with no progress, conversion is appropriate.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.question: A placenta has not delivered 35 minutes after birth despite active management. What does this represent?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.explanation: With active management the third stage is prolonged if not completed within 30 minutes. This is a retained placenta, and the main risk is postpartum haemorrhage because the uterus cannot contract down.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.question: A woman in established labour has dilated from 4 cm to 5 cm over 4 hours. How is this described?
options: Delay in the established first stage
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.answer: Delay in the established first stage
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__No.explanation: Delay in the established first stage is less than 2 cm of dilatation in 4 hours. One centimetre in 4 hours meets that definition and prompts assessment of the three Ps.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Mu.question: Which factor primarily determines the risk profile and management of a twin pregnancy?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Mu.explanation: Chorionicity — not zygosity — determines management, because it decides whether the twins share a circulation.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Mu.question: A first-trimester ultrasound shows a lambda (λ)/'twin peak' sign at the membrane junction. What does this indicate?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Mu.explanation: The lambda/twin peak sign (thick membrane with a wedge of placenta) indicates a dichorionic pregnancy; the T-sign indicates monochorionic.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Mu.question: Which twin type carries the highest risk due to cord entanglement, and how is it delivered?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Mu.explanation: MCMA twins (one placenta, one sac) are at highest risk from cord entanglement and are delivered by caesarean at 32+0 to 33+6 weeks.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Mu.question: A monochorionic twin pregnancy develops one twin with oligohydramnios and growth restriction and the other with polyhydramnios and polycythaemia. What is the diagnosis?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Mu.explanation: Unbalanced blood flow across placental anastomoses causes TTTS — the donor (oligohydramnios, anaemic, growth-restricted) and recipient (polyhydramnios, polycythaemic).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Mu.question: How is twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome treated?
options: Fetoscopic laser ablation of the communicating placental vessels
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Mu.answer: Fetoscopic laser ablation of the communicating placental vessels
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Mu.explanation: TTTS is treated with fetoscopic laser ablation of the shared communicating placental vessels.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Mu.question: Which surveillance schedule is recommended for a monochorionic twin pregnancy?
options: Fortnightly ultrasound from 16 weeks to screen for TTTS/TAPS/sFGR
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Mu.answer: Fortnightly ultrasound from 16 weeks to screen for TTTS/TAPS/sFGR
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Mu.explanation: Monochorionic twins need fortnightly ultrasound from 16 weeks (amniotic fluid/Doppler) to screen for TTTS/TAPS/sFGR; dichorionic twins are scanned less intensively (~4-weekly).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Mu.question: What is the planned timing of birth for an uncomplicated DCDA twin pregnancy?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Mu.explanation: Uncomplicated DCDA twins are delivered at 37+0 weeks; MCDA at 36+0 weeks; MCMA at 32+0 to 33+6 weeks by caesarean.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Mu.question: Which is the dominant fetal risk in twin pregnancy?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Mu.explanation: Preterm birth is the dominant risk — about 60% of twins deliver before 37 weeks.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Mu.question: A twin pregnancy is in labour with twin 1 in a cephalic presentation. What mode of delivery can be offered?
options: Forceps delivery of both without monitoring
Vaginal birth (with 2 obstetricians, continuous CTG, epidural advised)
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Mu.answer: Vaginal birth (with 2 obstetricians, continuous CTG, epidural advised)
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Mu.explanation: If twin 1 is cephalic, vaginal birth can be offered with 2 obstetricians present, continuous CTG and epidural often advised; caesarean is for non-cephalic twin 1 or MCMA.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Mu.question: Which statement about zygosity and chorionicity is correct?
options: All dizygotic twins are DCDA; monozygotic can be any
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Mu.answer: All dizygotic twins are DCDA; monozygotic can be any
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Mu.explanation: Dizygotic twins are always DCDA; monozygotic twins can be any chorionicity depending on the timing of the split.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Mu.question: Which prophylactic medication is offered in twin pregnancy to reduce pre-eclampsia risk?
