conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.explanation: A neglected transverse lie leads to obstructed labour and, ultimately, uterine rupture — the feared end-point.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.question: Which is a limitation of ECV for unstable/abnormal lie?
options: ECV is contraindicated in all abnormal lies
ECV can only be done under general anaesthetic
The lie tends to revert, so ECV alone is often insufficient
ECV causes cord prolapse in most cases
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.answer: The lie tends to revert, so ECV alone is often insufficient
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.explanation: Abnormal/unstable lie tends to revert after ECV, so ECV alone is often insufficient; elective caesarean is used for persistent abnormal lie.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.question: What is 'stabilising induction' for selected unstable lie?
options: ECV then immediate amniotomy and oxytocin in theatre
Induction with prostaglandins in a midwife-led unit
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.answer: ECV then immediate amniotomy and oxytocin in theatre
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.explanation: Stabilising induction is a specialist option: ECV to cephalic then immediate amniotomy and oxytocin, done in theatre with caesarean standby.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.question: How is the fetal lie defined?
options: The relationship of the presenting part to the pelvis
The position of the fetal head
The relationship of the fetal long axis to the uterine long axis
The station of the presenting part
The attitude of the fetal head
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.answer: The relationship of the fetal long axis to the uterine long axis
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.explanation: Lie is the relationship of the fetal long axis to the uterine long axis; normal is longitudinal, and transverse/oblique are abnormal.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.question: On abdominal examination of a woman at term, neither the head nor buttocks is felt at the fundus or pelvis, and the fetus is felt lying across. What is the likely lie?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.answer: Transverse lie
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.explanation: Neither pole at the fundus/pelvis with the fetus felt lying across suggests a transverse lie, confirmed on ultrasound.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.question: Why should amniotomy be avoided with a high/mobile presenting part in an abnormal lie?
options: It risks cord or arm prolapse
It always fails to rupture the membranes
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.answer: It risks cord or arm prolapse
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Ma.explanation: Amniotomy with a high/mobile presenting part risks cord or arm prolapse, so it is avoided in abnormal lie.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.question: A woman is being assessed for induction of labour and has a Bishop score of 4. What is the appropriate first step?
options: Cervical ripening with vaginal dinoprostone (or mechanical)
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.answer: Cervical ripening with vaginal dinoprostone (or mechanical)
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.explanation: A Bishop score ≤6 (unfavourable) requires cervical ripening first (dinoprostone/misoprostol or mechanical); ARM + oxytocin is reserved for a favourable cervix.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.question: A woman has a Bishop score of 9 and a cephalic presentation. What is the appropriate method of induction?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.explanation: A favourable cervix (Bishop >6) is managed with amniotomy plus oxytocin, titrated to about 4 contractions per 10 minutes.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.question: What is the commonest indication for induction of labour, and when is it offered?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.explanation: Prolonged pregnancy is the commonest indication; induction is offered at 41–42 weeks to reduce stillbirth risk.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.question: During an oxytocin induction, the CTG shows fetal distress with 7 contractions in 10 minutes. What is the diagnosis and management?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.explanation: Excessive contractions with fetal distress indicate uterine hyperstimulation; management is to stop or remove the agent, consider tocolysis (terbutaline 250 micrograms subcutaneously), continue CTG, and escalate.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.question: Which is the standard first-line pharmacological agent for cervical ripening?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.explanation: Vaginal dinoprostone (PGE2) is the standard first-line ripening agent; low-dose oral misoprostol is an alternative, and mechanical methods are used when prostaglandins are unsuitable.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.question: A woman with a previous caesarean scar requires cervical ripening for induction. Which method is often preferred, and why?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.explanation: With a previous caesarean, mechanical methods (balloon) are often preferred as they cause less hyperstimulation than prostaglandins, reducing uterine-rupture risk.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.question: Which is a recognised contraindication to induction of labour (favouring caesarean)?
options: Prelabour rupture of membranes at term
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.explanation: Placenta praevia (and vasa praevia, cord presentation, transverse lie, classical caesarean, active primary genital herpes) contraindicate vaginal delivery/induction; the others are indications for IOL.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.question: Which complication is a specific risk of amniotomy during induction, especially with a high presenting part?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.explanation: Amniotomy with a high, poorly-applied presenting part risks cord prolapse, as the cord can descend below the presenting part.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.question: What contraction rate is targeted when titrating oxytocin during induction?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.explanation: Oxytocin is titrated to about 4 contractions per 10 minutes; more frequent contractions risk hyperstimulation and fetal distress.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.question: A membrane sweep is best described as which of the following?
options: An adjunct offered from ~39-41 weeks, not formal induction
A method of cervical ripening equivalent to dinoprostone
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.answer: An adjunct offered from ~39-41 weeks, not formal induction
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.explanation: A membrane sweep is an adjunct offered from ~39–41 weeks to promote spontaneous labour, distinct from formal induction methods.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.question: What monitoring is essential during active induction with prostaglandins or oxytocin?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.explanation: Continuous CTG is used during active induction to detect fetal distress and uterine hyperstimulation.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.question: An induction fails to establish labour despite ripening and oxytocin. What is the appropriate next step?
options: Re-attempt ripening or proceed to caesarean section
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.answer: Re-attempt ripening or proceed to caesarean section
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.explanation: Failed induction is managed by re-attempting cervical ripening or proceeding to caesarean section.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.question: Which statement about the Bishop score is correct?
options: A score of 6 or less means the cervix is favourable
≤6 is unfavourable and needs ripening first
A high score means caesarean is needed
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.answer: ≤6 is unfavourable and needs ripening first
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.explanation: The Bishop score (dilatation, effacement, consistency, position, station) determines readiness: ≤6 unfavourable (ripen first), >6 favourable (ARM + oxytocin).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.question: A woman in labour develops a cord prolapse with fetal bradycardia. Which category of caesarean and what decision-to-delivery target apply?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.explanation: Cord prolapse with an immediate threat to the baby is a Category 1 (crash) caesarean, with a decision-to-delivery target of 30 minutes.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.question: What is the decision-to-delivery target for a Category 2 caesarean?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.explanation: Category 2 (compromise not immediately life-threatening) has a 75-minute audit target, though acute fetal compromise is pushed toward 30 minutes where possible.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.question: Which type of caesarean incision is used in ~99% of cases and carries a lower future rupture risk?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.explanation: The lower segment transverse (LSCS) incision is used in ~99% of caesareans and has a lower future rupture risk, less bleeding and better healing than a classical incision.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.question: Which structure is NOT cut during a caesarean section?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.explanation: The rectus abdominis is separated at the linea alba and retracted laterally, not cut; the sheath, peritoneum and uterus are incised.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.question: A woman had a previous classical (vertical) caesarean. Regarding VBAC, what is correct?
options: VBAC has the same rupture risk as after LSCS
She should be induced with prostaglandins
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.explanation: A previous classical scar (or previous uterine rupture) contraindicates VBAC because of the high uterine rupture risk; VBAC is appropriate after a single previous lower-segment caesarean at ≥37 weeks.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.question: What is the main serious risk of attempting VBAC?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.explanation: Uterine rupture is the feared complication of VBAC (~0.5% absolute risk, higher than elective repeat caesarean); VBAC success is ~72–75%.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.question: Which is a placental indication for caesarean section?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.explanation: Placenta praevia — the placenta covering the internal os — along with accreta and vasa praevia, is a placental indication for caesarean. The grade I–IV and major/minor terms are no longer used. The others are not, in themselves, indications for caesarean.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.question: Why does the risk of placenta praevia/accreta increase with each caesarean section?
options: The placenta can implant abnormally over the uterine scar
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.answer: The placenta can implant abnormally over the uterine scar
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.explanation: Abnormal placental implantation over the uterine scar increases the risk of praevia and accreta with each successive caesarean.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.question: Routine postoperative thromboprophylaxis after caesarean is given to prevent which complication?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.explanation: Caesarean increases VTE risk, so thromboprophylaxis is essential; other complications include haemorrhage, infection, ileus and organ injury.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.question: A CTG shows persistent fetal bradycardia with suspected uterine rupture. What category of caesarean is indicated?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.explanation: Suspected uterine rupture with fetal bradycardia is an immediate threat to life — a Category 1 caesarean with a 30-minute target.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.question: Planned VBAC is most appropriate in which situation?
options: Two previous caesareans with a vertical scar
A single previous lower-segment caesarean at ≥37 weeks
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.answer: A single previous lower-segment caesarean at ≥37 weeks
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.explanation: VBAC is appropriate with a single previous lower-segment caesarean at ≥37 weeks; previous rupture or a classical scar contraindicate it.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.question: Which neonatal complication is more common after caesarean (especially elective, pre-labour)?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.explanation: Transient tachypnoea of the newborn is more common after caesarean (retained lung fluid), and iatrogenic prematurity can occur if dates are wrong.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.question: Which is a recognised indication for a classical (vertical) caesarean incision rather than LSCS?
options: A previous LSCS with a favourable cervix
Anterior placenta praevia/accreta or very preterm delivery
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.answer: Anterior placenta praevia/accreta or very preterm delivery
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.explanation: Classical incisions are reserved for situations such as very preterm delivery, some transverse lies, anterior praevia/accreta, or obstructing fibroids, where the lower segment is inaccessible/unsuitable.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.question: A tear after vaginal delivery involves the perineal muscle but not the anal sphincter. What degree is it, and how is it managed?
options: Second degree — sutured on the ward
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.answer: Second degree — sutured on the ward
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.explanation: A tear involving the perineal muscle but sparing the anal sphincter is second-degree and is sutured on the ward; sphincter involvement (3rd/4th degree, OASIS) requires theatre.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.question: A tear involves the anal sphincter complex and the rectal mucosa. What degree is it?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.explanation: A tear involving the anal sphincter complex plus the rectal (anorectal) mucosa is a fourth-degree tear; third-degree involves the sphincter without the rectal mucosa.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.question: What does the term OASIS refer to?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.explanation: OASIS (obstetric anal sphincter injury) comprises third- and fourth-degree tears; these are repaired in theatre, whereas 1st/2nd degree are managed on the ward.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.question: A third-degree tear involves more than 50% of the external anal sphincter thickness but not the internal sphincter. How is it subclassified?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.explanation: 3a is <50% of EAS, 3b is >50% of EAS, and 3c is EAS plus IAS torn; here >50% EAS with intact IAS is 3b.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.question: Which is the strongest risk factor for OASIS?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.explanation: Primigravida/first vaginal birth is the strongest risk factor (OASIS ~6% in primips vs ~1.7% in multips).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.question: A rectal mucosal tear is found with an intact anal sphincter. How should this be classified?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.explanation: A buttonhole tear (rectal mucosa torn, sphincter intact) is a separate entity documented separately — it is NOT a fourth-degree tear/OASIS.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.question: Where should a third- or fourth-degree perineal tear be repaired?
options: On the ward under local anaesthesia
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.explanation: OASIS (3rd/4th degree) is repaired in theatre by a trained clinician under regional/general anaesthesia; 1st/2nd degree are managed on the ward.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.question: Which instrumental delivery is associated with a higher risk of OASIS?
options: Neither — the risk is the same for both
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.explanation: Forceps delivery carries a higher OASIS risk than ventouse; instrumental delivery overall is a risk factor.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.question: What is the appropriate post-OASIS bowel management?
options: Nil by mouth for a week
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.explanation: After OASIS repair, laxatives are used to reduce wound dehiscence; a routine bulking agent is avoided. Broad-spectrum antibiotics, physiotherapy and a rectal exam are also part of care.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.question: Which type of episiotomy is recommended to help prevent OASIS?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.explanation: A mediolateral episiotomy (~60° from the midline) is used where indicated to reduce OASIS, especially in instrumental delivery; midline episiotomy increases OASIS risk.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.question: What is the feared long-term complication of a third/fourth-degree perineal tear?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.explanation: Faecal urgency/incontinence is the feared long-term complication of OASIS; flatus incontinence, dyspareunia and rectovaginal fistula (4th degree) can also occur.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.question: A first-degree perineal tear is identified after delivery. What is the appropriate management?
options: Suture unless the skin edges are well opposed
Immediate caesarean for the next birth
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.answer: Suture unless the skin edges are well opposed
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.explanation: A first-degree tear involves skin/superficial tissue only. It often heals without suturing when the skin edges are well opposed; suture it if they are not, or if it is bleeding. It does not need theatre, sphincter repair, or a change to the next birth plan.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.question: When uncertain whether a tear is 3a or 3b, what should the clinician do?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.explanation: If in doubt about the grade of a third-degree tear, classify it higher to ensure appropriate repair and follow-up.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.question: A woman is fully dilated with an abnormal CTG. The head is 1/5 palpable, the position is occipito-anterior, membranes are ruptured and she has an epidural. What must be done immediately before an assisted vaginal birth?
options: Empty the bladder with a catheter
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.answer: Empty the bladder with a catheter
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.explanation: The 'S' of FORCEPS is sphincter — the bladder must be emptied by catheterisation. A full bladder obstructs descent and risks bladder injury during the procedure.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.question: During an assisted vaginal birth, which prerequisite concerns the station of the head?
options: The head must be above the pelvic brim
Station must be at least 3 cm above the spines
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.explanation: The head must be engaged — no more than 1/5 palpable abdominally, with the station at or below the ischial spines. An unengaged head is a contraindication.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.question: A ventouse delivery has failed after three pulls with no descent. What is the appropriate next step?
options: Repeat the ventouse with a larger cup
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.explanation: Sequential instruments must be avoided — swapping a failed ventouse for forceps sharply increases intracranial and subgaleal haemorrhage. A failed instrument goes to caesarean.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.question: Which instrument carries the higher risk of obstetric anal sphincter injury?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.explanation: Forceps carries a higher risk of third- and fourth-degree tears than ventouse and is the leading instrumental risk factor for OASIS. Ventouse causes less maternal trauma but fails more often.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.question: Which instrument is more likely to fail to deliver the baby?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.explanation: Ventouse is more likely to fail than forceps. The trade-off is that it causes less maternal trauma — ventouse spares the mother, forceps spares the baby.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.question: A baby delivered by difficult ventouse develops a boggy swelling that crosses the suture lines, with pallor and tachycardia. What is the diagnosis?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.explanation: A swelling that crosses suture lines with signs of shock is a subgaleal haemorrhage — blood between the aponeurosis and periosteum, a space that can hold the neonate's entire blood volume. A cephalhaematoma is subperiosteal and does not cross sutures.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.question: Which feature distinguishes a cephalhaematoma from a subgaleal haemorrhage?
options: It does not cross suture lines
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.answer: It does not cross suture lines
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.explanation: A cephalhaematoma is subperiosteal, so it is limited by the suture lines and is self-limiting. A subgaleal haemorrhage crosses them and can be fatal.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.question: A woman needs assisted delivery at 30 weeks' gestation. Which instrument should be avoided?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.explanation: Ventouse should be avoided below 32 weeks and used with caution between 32⁺⁰ and 36⁺⁰ weeks because of subgaleal and intracranial haemorrhage risk. Forceps is preferred at preterm gestations.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.question: A multiparous woman is fully dilated with intact membranes and a cephalic presentation at station 0. Is she suitable for assisted vaginal birth?
options: No — the membranes must be ruptured first
No — assisted birth needs a nulliparous woman
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.answer: No — the membranes must be ruptured first
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.explanation: Ruptured membranes are one of the FORCEPS prerequisites. All must be met; if any is missing, delivery should be by caesarean.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.question: Why is an assisted vaginal birth sometimes performed as a 'trial in theatre'?
options: So caesarean can follow immediately if it fails
It is a legal requirement for all cases
To allow a general anaesthetic to be used
Because forceps cannot be used elsewhere
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.answer: So caesarean can follow immediately if it fails
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.explanation: When failure is more likely — mid-cavity or occipito-posterior position, a suspected big baby, high BMI — the attempt is made in theatre so that caesarean can proceed immediately without delay.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.question: What prophylaxis is recommended after an assisted vaginal birth?
options: Topical antiseptic to the perineum only
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.explanation: A single prophylactic dose of co-amoxiclav after assisted vaginal birth roughly halves maternal infection and is now recommended (RCOG).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.question: A woman with severe cardiac disease reaches full dilatation. Why might assisted vaginal birth be offered?
options: To avoid the cardiovascular strain of pushing
Because caesarean is contraindicated in cardiac disease
To reduce the risk of fetal jaundice
Because forceps lowers maternal blood pressure
To shorten the first stage of labour
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.answer: To avoid the cardiovascular strain of pushing
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.explanation: Prolonged Valsalva during active pushing places significant strain on the maternal cardiovascular system, so assisted birth is offered in maternal cardiac disease, severe hypertension, myasthenia gravis and spinal cord injury.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.question: An assisted vaginal birth is being planned but the fetal position cannot be determined on vaginal examination. What should be done?
options: Use ultrasound to determine the position
Abandon all plans for vaginal birth
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.answer: Use ultrasound to determine the position
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__La.explanation: The position must be known before an instrument is applied, because placement depends on it and misplacement causes injury. If vaginal examination is uncertain, ultrasound should be used.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.question: Immediately after artificial rupture of membranes in a woman with a high presenting part, the CTG shows sudden fetal bradycardia. What is the most important next step?
options: Give maternal oxygen and re-check in 30 minutes
Perform a vaginal examination to exclude cord prolapse
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.answer: Perform a vaginal examination to exclude cord prolapse
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.explanation: Sudden fetal bradycardia after ARM (especially with a high presenting part) should prompt a vaginal examination to exclude cord prolapse.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.question: A woman has a palpable pulsating cord in the vagina after her membranes rupture, with fetal bradycardia. Which is the most appropriate immediate management?
options: Elevate the presenting part off the cord and arrange emergency caesarean
Push the cord back inside the uterus
Replace the membranes and continue expectant management
Sit the woman upright to encourage descent
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.answer: Elevate the presenting part off the cord and arrange emergency caesarean
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.explanation: Cord prolapse is managed by relieving cord compression (elevate the presenting part, positioning ± bladder filling), stopping oxytocin, and category 1 caesarean; the cord must not be forcibly replaced.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.question: What distinguishes cord prolapse from cord presentation?
options: Cord prolapse occurs with the membranes still intact
Prolapse follows membrane rupture; presentation precedes it
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.answer: Prolapse follows membrane rupture; presentation precedes it
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.explanation: Cord prolapse requires ruptured membranes (the cord descends past/alongside the presenting part); with intact membranes the same anatomy is cord presentation, a warning sign.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.question: Why should the umbilical cord not be handled excessively or forcibly replaced in cord prolapse?
options: It increases the risk of cord avulsion
It allows the membranes to reseal
Handling and cold provoke cord vasospasm
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.answer: Handling and cold provoke cord vasospasm
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.explanation: Handling and cold provoke cord vasospasm, further cutting off fetal blood flow; the cord is kept warm/moist and not replaced, while pressure is relieved and delivery expedited.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.question: What is the default mode of delivery for cord prolapse when the cervix is not fully dilated?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.explanation: The default is a category 1 emergency caesarean (delivery within 30 minutes); instrumental vaginal delivery is used only if the cervix is fully dilated and delivery is imminent.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.question: Which technique can relieve cord compression when delivery or transfer is delayed in cord prolapse?
options: Applying steady fundal pressure to push the cord back
Filling the bladder with warm saline via a Foley catheter
Lying the woman flat on her back
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.answer: Filling the bladder with warm saline via a Foley catheter
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.explanation: Bladder filling with ~500 mL warm saline elevates the presenting part off the cord and is useful if delivery/transfer is delayed (empty before delivery).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.question: Which is a recognised risk factor for cord prolapse?
options: Post-term pregnancy with an engaged head
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.explanation: Abnormal lie (transverse/unstable), breech, prematurity, polyhydramnios, twins, a high presenting part and ARM predispose to cord prolapse, as a poorly-applied presenting part leaves a gap.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.question: A midwife at a home birth finds a cord prolapse. What should she advise while awaiting the ambulance?
options: Push the cord back and continue at home
Encourage active pushing to speed delivery at home
Knee-chest position, call 999, elevate the presenting part
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.answer: Knee-chest position, call 999, elevate the presenting part
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.explanation: In the community, advise a knee-chest position, call 999, and elevate the presenting part; midwives carry a Foley catheter for bladder filling.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.question: Which position is preferred for ambulance transfer of a woman with cord prolapse?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.explanation: Exaggerated Sims is preferred for transfer because the knee-chest position is unsafe in a moving ambulance.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.question: What medication should be stopped, and what may be considered, in cord prolapse with a delay to delivery?
options: Stop oxytocin; consider tocolysis (terbutaline 0.25 mg SC)
Give ergometrine to expedite the third stage
Start magnesium sulfate to prevent seizures
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.answer: Stop oxytocin; consider tocolysis (terbutaline 0.25 mg SC)
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.explanation: Oxytocin is stopped and tocolysis (terbutaline 0.25 mg subcutaneously) considered if there is fetal compromise and delivery is delayed, to reduce contractions compressing the cord.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.question: What is the central danger to the fetus in cord prolapse?
options: Uterine rupture along a previous scar
Cord compression and vasospasm causing hypoxia
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.answer: Cord compression and vasospasm causing hypoxia
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.explanation: The central danger is cord compression and vasospasm cutting off fetal blood flow, causing hypoxia that can lead to hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy, cerebral palsy or death.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.question: In which situation is instrumental vaginal delivery (rather than caesarean) appropriate for cord prolapse?
options: When the cervix is fully dilated and delivery is imminent
When the woman is only 4 cm dilated
When the presenting part is high
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.answer: When the cervix is fully dilated and delivery is imminent
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.explanation: Instrumental vaginal delivery is appropriate only when the cervix is fully dilated and delivery is imminent; otherwise category 1 caesarean is the default.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.question: A CTG shows variable decelerations shortly after spontaneous rupture of membranes in a woman with polyhydramnios. What complication should be actively excluded?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.explanation: Variable decelerations/bradycardia after ROM — especially with polyhydramnios (a risk factor) — should prompt a vaginal exam to exclude cord prolapse.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.question: After the fetal head delivers, it retracts tightly against the perineum and the shoulders fail to deliver with routine traction. What is the first-line manoeuvre?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.explanation: The turtle-neck sign indicates shoulder dystocia; McRoberts' (hyperflexing the hips) is first-line, ~90% effective and least invasive, typically combined with suprapubic pressure.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.question: Which action is contraindicated in shoulder dystocia?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.explanation: Fundal pressure worsens the impaction and risks uterine rupture; suprapubic (not fundal) pressure is used, along with McRoberts' and internal manoeuvres.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.question: Excessive downward traction on the fetal head during shoulder dystocia most commonly causes which injury?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.explanation: Excessive/downward traction is the main cause of brachial plexus injury (Erb's palsy, C5–C6, 'waiter's tip'); only routine axial traction should be used.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.question: What does the 'H' in the HELPERR mnemonic stand for?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.explanation: HELPERR: H = call for Help, E = Evaluate for episiotomy, L = Legs (McRoberts'), P = suprapubic Pressure, E = Enter (internal rotation), R = Remove posterior arm, R = Roll (all-fours).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.question: Which manoeuvre involves rotating the fetal shoulders and is performed with a hand inserted vaginally?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.explanation: Internal rotation manoeuvres — Rubin II and Woods' screw — are performed with a vaginal hand to rotate/reduce the shoulder diameter; McRoberts' and suprapubic pressure are external.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.question: Which single factor is the most important associated risk factor for shoulder dystocia?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.explanation: Maternal diabetes (with associated macrosomia) is the most important associated risk factor, though most shoulder dystocia is unpredictable.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.question: A neonate after shoulder dystocia holds the arm adducted and internally rotated with the forearm pronated ('waiter's tip'). What is the diagnosis?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.explanation: The 'waiter's tip' posture is Erb's palsy (C5–C6), a common brachial plexus injury after shoulder dystocia that usually resolves; Klumpke's (C8–T1) gives a claw hand.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.question: Which is the last-resort manoeuvre involving replacing the fetal head into the uterus for emergency caesarean?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.explanation: The Zavanelli manoeuvre (replacing the head into the uterus then caesarean) is a last resort if all other manoeuvres fail, along with cleidotomy/symphysiotomy.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.question: Which manoeuvre in shoulder dystocia is highly effective by reducing the shoulder diameter?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.explanation: Delivering the posterior arm sweeps it across the chest, reducing the diameter and freeing the impaction — a highly effective manoeuvre.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.question: What are the main MATERNAL complications of shoulder dystocia?
options: Uterine inversion and amniotic fluid embolism
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.explanation: The main maternal risks are postpartum haemorrhage and perineal tears; symphyseal separation/femoral neuropathy can also occur from McRoberts'.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.question: Which statement about predicting shoulder dystocia is correct?
options: It can be reliably predicted from risk factors
All macrosomic babies have shoulder dystocia
Prediction alone justifies caesarean for all at-risk women
It never occurs in diabetic mothers
Most cases are unpredictable, so every attendant must be prepared
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.answer: Most cases are unpredictable, so every attendant must be prepared
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.explanation: Most shoulder dystocia is unpredictable; risk factors are weak predictors, so every birth attendant must be ready, and prediction alone does not justify routine induction/caesarean. The exception is a woman with diabetes and suspected macrosomia (estimated fetal weight >4.5 kg), where planned caesarean should be considered.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.question: What is the role of episiotomy in managing shoulder dystocia?
options: It creates room for internal manoeuvres, not bony relief
It replaces the need for McRoberts' and suprapubic pressure
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.answer: It creates room for internal manoeuvres, not bony relief
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.explanation: Episiotomy does not relieve the bony impaction itself but creates space to perform internal (vaginal) rotation and posterior-arm manoeuvres.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.question: Which documentation is essential after a shoulder dystocia?
options: Manoeuvres used, but not their order or timings
The birth weight and Apgar scores alone
Which shoulder was anterior, but not the timings or staff present
Times of head and body delivery, manoeuvres in order, and staff present
The maternal blood loss and perineal tear degree only
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.answer: Times of head and body delivery, manoeuvres in order, and staff present
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.explanation: Because of the medicolegal significance, the time of head/body delivery, manoeuvres performed and their order, which shoulder was anterior, cord gases, and staff present must all be documented.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.question: A pregnant woman with HIV has a viral load of <50 copies/mL at 36 weeks. What mode of delivery is appropriate?
options: Delivery must be delayed until viral load rises
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.explanation: An undetectable viral load (<50) makes vaginal birth safe; planned caesarean is reserved for higher viral loads (≥400, or consider at 50–399).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.question: A pregnant woman with HIV has a viral load of 800 copies/mL at 36 weeks. What is recommended?
options: Await spontaneous labour with no intervention
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.explanation: A viral load ≥400 copies/mL warrants a planned caesarean, plus combination neonatal PEP.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.question: How is HIV screening offered to pregnant women in the UK?
options: Only to women with risk factors
To all women at booking on an opt-out basis
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.answer: To all women at booking on an opt-out basis
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.explanation: HIV testing is offered to all pregnant women at booking on an opt-out basis, alongside hepatitis B and syphilis.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.question: Which pregnant women with HIV should receive antiretroviral therapy?
options: Only those with a low CD4 count
Only those with a high viral load
None — ART is deferred until after delivery
All of them, regardless of CD4 or viral load
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.answer: All of them, regardless of CD4 or viral load
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.explanation: All pregnant women with HIV take combination ART for life, regardless of CD4 count or viral load, to suppress the virus and prevent transmission.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.question: When should an HIV-exposed neonate receive post-exposure prophylaxis?
options: Only if the baby tests positive
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.explanation: Every HIV-exposed infant receives antiretroviral PEP within 4 hours of birth — zidovudine monotherapy if the mother is suppressed, or combination PEP if higher-risk.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.question: How should an HIV-exposed infant be diagnosed in the early months of life?
options: Viral load in the mother only
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.explanation: HIV PCR is used because maternal antibodies persist in the infant for ~18 months, making antibody testing unreliable early on.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.question: What is the UK default recommendation for infant feeding when the mother has HIV?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.explanation: Formula feeding is the UK default as it eliminates the breastfeeding transmission route; breastfeeding is supported only if strict suppression/monitoring criteria are met.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.question: At which point is the risk of vertical HIV transmission greatest?
options: In utero in the first trimester
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.explanation: The intrapartum period (exposure to maternal blood/secretions at delivery) carries the biggest transmission risk, which is why viral suppression and delivery planning are central.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.question: Which procedure should be avoided during labour in a woman with HIV who is not virally suppressed?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.explanation: Fetal scalp electrodes, fetal blood sampling and instrumental delivery are avoided if the mother is not suppressed, as they increase fetal exposure to maternal blood.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.question: A woman with HIV is already on effective ART when she becomes pregnant. What should happen to her treatment?
options: Stop ART during the first trimester
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.explanation: A woman on effective ART at conception should continue it; newly diagnosed women start ART as soon as possible.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.question: Under BHIVA guidance, breastfeeding may be supported in a woman with HIV only if which conditions are met?
options: Any viral load, provided the baby receives PEP for 4 weeks
Sustained viral load <50, adherence and monthly monitoring
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.answer: Sustained viral load <50, adherence and monthly monitoring
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.explanation: Breastfeeding is supported only if the mother is fully suppressed (<50), adherent, engaged with the MDT, and has monthly viral-load monitoring of mother and baby; formula remains the default.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.question: A pregnant woman with HIV has a viral load of 200 copies/mL at 36 weeks. What is the recommended approach to delivery?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.explanation: A viral load of 50–399 copies/mL falls in the intermediate band where caesarean is considered, with higher-risk neonatal PEP.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.question: What intrapartum treatment is given when a caesarean is performed for viral-load reasons in HIV?
options: Oral zidovudine for the baby only
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.explanation: An intrapartum IV zidovudine infusion is used when caesarean is done for viral-load reasons or in higher-risk labour.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.question: Which combination is a typical antiretroviral regimen in pregnancy?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.explanation: A typical regimen is tenofovir + emtricitabine (or abacavir + lamivudine) plus a third agent, often dolutegravir; zidovudine monotherapy is used for low-risk neonatal PEP, not maternal treatment.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.question: A pregnant woman at 16 weeks with no history of chickenpox is exposed to a child with chickenpox. What is the first step?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.explanation: The first step is to determine susceptibility with urgent VZV IgG; if seronegative, post-exposure prophylaxis is arranged.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.question: A susceptible pregnant woman is exposed to chickenpox but has no rash. According to current UKHSA/RCOG guidance, what is the preferred post-exposure prophylaxis?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.explanation: Post-exposure prophylaxis is now antiviral-first — oral aciclovir 800 mg QDS from days 7–14 after exposure; VZIG is reserved for those unable to take oral antivirals.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.question: A pregnant woman at 30 weeks develops a chickenpox rash 12 hours ago. What is the appropriate treatment?
options: Oral aciclovir 800 mg five times daily for 7 days
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.answer: Oral aciclovir 800 mg five times daily for 7 days
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.explanation: Once the rash has appeared, aciclovir is the treatment — 800 mg five times daily for 7 days orally if within 24h of onset and ≥20 weeks. Immunoglobulin has no benefit once the rash is out.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.question: Why is VZIG not given to a pregnant woman who has already developed a chickenpox rash?
options: VZIG causes the rash to spread
It is prophylactic and useless once the rash is out
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.answer: It is prophylactic and useless once the rash is out
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.explanation: VZIG is a prophylactic, not a treatment; it has no benefit once the rash appears, so established chickenpox is treated with aciclovir.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.question: Maternal chickenpox before 28 weeks (especially <20 weeks) carries which fetal risk?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.explanation: Infection before 28 weeks carries a small (~1%) risk of fetal varicella syndrome; neonatal varicella is the risk around delivery.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.question: Which is a recognised feature of fetal varicella syndrome?
options: Dermatomal skin scarring with limb hypoplasia
Sensorineural deafness with cataracts and cardiac defects
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.answer: Dermatomal skin scarring with limb hypoplasia
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.explanation: Fetal varicella syndrome features dermatomal skin scarring, limb hypoplasia, eye defects and neurological abnormalities; the deafness/cataract/cardiac triad is congenital rubella.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.question: Which maternal complication of varicella in pregnancy is the main cause of mortality?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.explanation: Varicella pneumonia is a major cause of maternal mortality, with risk rising with gestation, smoking and immunosuppression.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.question: A mother develops a chickenpox rash 3 days before delivery. What should the neonate receive?
options: Nothing, as maternal antibody will protect it
Oral aciclovir alone, with no immunoglobulin
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.explanation: A maternal rash from 7 days before to 7 days after delivery exposes the neonate before protective antibody develops, so the baby is given aciclovir plus IV varicella-zoster immunoglobulin. VZIG has been withdrawn in the UK, so an IV varicella-zoster immunoglobulin preparation is used, or normal IVIG if that cannot be sourced.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.question: Which vaccine-related fact about varicella is important in pregnancy?
options: The varicella vaccine should be given routinely in pregnancy
The varicella vaccine is live and contraindicated in pregnancy
The vaccine is safe in the first trimester
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.answer: The varicella vaccine is live and contraindicated in pregnancy
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.explanation: The varicella vaccine is a live attenuated vaccine and is contraindicated in pregnancy.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.question: A pregnant woman with severe chickenpox has dense rash and respiratory symptoms. What is the appropriate management?
options: Reassure and review in the community in 48 hours
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.explanation: Severe varicella (pneumonia, neurological signs, dense rash) requires admission and IV aciclovir.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.question: When should a detailed ultrasound be performed to look for fetal varicella syndrome after maternal infection?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.explanation: A detailed ultrasound is performed about 5 weeks after maternal infection to look for FVS features; referral to fetal medicine is made.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.question: A pregnant woman gives a clear history of having had chickenpox as a child. She is exposed to a case. What is the appropriate action?
options: Check VZV IgG and give VZIG
Reassure — she is immune, no action needed
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.answer: Reassure — she is immune, no action needed
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.explanation: A reliable prior history of chickenpox (or 2 vaccine doses) indicates immunity, so reassurance is appropriate with no further action.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.question: How long should a pregnant woman with chickenpox avoid contact with other pregnant women and neonates?
options: Until the lesions have crusted over (~5 days)
There is no need to isolate
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.answer: Until the lesions have crusted over (~5 days)
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.explanation: She should isolate until the lesions have crusted over (~5 days), as she is infectious until then.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.question: Which fetal/neonatal outcome is associated with maternal chickenpox occurring between 28 weeks and term (not around delivery)?
options: Shingles in infancy, but usually well at birth
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.answer: Shingles in infancy, but usually well at birth
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.explanation: Infection between 28 weeks and term usually leaves the baby well at birth, though it may develop shingles in infancy; FVS is an earlier risk and neonatal varicella a perinatal one.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.question: A woman contracts rubella at 8 weeks' gestation. What is the approximate risk to the fetus, and what counselling is appropriate?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.explanation: First-trimester rubella (<8–10 weeks) affects up to ~90% of fetuses with severe multiple defects; counselling includes the option of termination via fetal medicine.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.question: What is the classic triad of congenital rubella syndrome?
options: Sensorineural deafness, cataracts, and congenital heart disease (PDA)
Limb hypoplasia, skin scarring, and eye defects
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.answer: Sensorineural deafness, cataracts, and congenital heart disease (PDA)
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.explanation: The CRS triad is sensorineural deafness + congenital cataracts + congenital heart disease (classically patent ductus arteriosus).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.question: Which congenital heart lesion is classically associated with congenital rubella syndrome?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.explanation: Patent ductus arteriosus (and pulmonary artery stenosis) is the classic congenital heart lesion in congenital rubella syndrome.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.question: What is the treatment for rubella infection in pregnancy?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.explanation: There is no antiviral treatment for rubella; management is supportive with counselling on fetal risk, and prevention relies on pre-pregnancy MMR.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.question: Why is MMR not given during pregnancy?
options: It is a live vaccine and is contraindicated in pregnancy
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.answer: It is a live vaccine and is contraindicated in pregnancy
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.explanation: MMR is a live attenuated vaccine and is contraindicated in pregnancy; non-immune women are vaccinated postnatally, avoiding conception for 1 month.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.question: A non-immune woman has just delivered. Regarding rubella prevention, what should be done?
options: Give MMR only if she is not breastfeeding
Give MMR in the next pregnancy's first trimester
Offer MMR postnatally, advising to avoid conception for 1 month
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.answer: Offer MMR postnatally, advising to avoid conception for 1 month
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.explanation: Non-immune women are offered MMR postnatally (it can be given while breastfeeding), advising them to avoid conception for 1 month afterwards.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.question: A pregnant woman has a fine maculopapular rash spreading from the face and tender lymph nodes behind the ears. Which infection is suggested?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.explanation: A fine maculopapular rash (face → trunk) with characteristic postauricular/suboccipital lymphadenopathy suggests rubella.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.question: Which statement about antenatal rubella screening in the UK is correct?
options: It remains part of the routine booking blood panel
It is done in the third trimester
It has stopped — it does not protect the current pregnancy
It is offered only to non-immune women
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.answer: It has stopped — it does not protect the current pregnancy
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.explanation: Antenatal rubella susceptibility screening has stopped in England — it does not protect the current pregnancy and rubella is now very rare. HIV, hepatitis B and syphilis screening continue.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.question: At which gestation does the risk of congenital rubella syndrome become essentially negligible?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.explanation: Risk is highest in the first trimester and becomes very low after 16–20 weeks, with defects essentially not seen after 20 weeks.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.question: How is rubella confirmed serologically in a pregnant woman with a suspicious rash?
options: IgM = acute infection; IgG = past immunity
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.answer: IgM = acute infection; IgG = past immunity
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.explanation: Rubella serology uses IgM (acute infection) and IgG (past infection/immunity), with paired sera/avidity to confirm timing; public health is notified.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.question: Which congenital infection is characterised by hydrocephalus, intracranial calcification and chorioretinitis?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.explanation: Toxoplasmosis classically causes hydrocephalus, intracranial calcification and chorioretinitis; rubella causes cataracts/PDA/deafness and CMV periventricular calcification/deafness/microcephaly.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.question: A pregnant woman contracts rubella at 24 weeks. What is the appropriate counselling regarding congenital rubella syndrome?
options: Reassure — CRS is essentially not seen after 20 weeks
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.answer: Reassure — CRS is essentially not seen after 20 weeks
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.explanation: After 20 weeks, congenital rubella syndrome is essentially not seen, so reassurance regarding CRS is appropriate.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.question: Which feature is shared between congenital rubella and congenital CMV?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.explanation: The 'blueberry muffin' rash (dermal haematopoiesis) is seen in both congenital rubella and CMV.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.question: What is the cornerstone of preventing congenital rubella syndrome at population level?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.explanation: Population prevention relies on childhood MMR (2 doses) and vaccinating women of uncertain immunity before conception.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.question: A woman's previous baby had invasive Group B Streptococcal disease. What is the appropriate management in this pregnancy?
options: Offer intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis (no swab needed)
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.answer: Offer intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis (no swab needed)
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.explanation: A previous baby with invasive GBS disease is an indication to offer IAP in labour, without needing a swab.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.question: Why is Group B Streptococcus prophylaxis given intrapartum rather than antenatally?
options: Antenatal antibiotics cause antibiotic resistance in the fetus
Only intrapartum antibiotics stop colonisation during birth
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.answer: Only intrapartum antibiotics stop colonisation during birth
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.explanation: GBS prophylaxis works only intrapartum — antenatal treatment of vaginal carriage does not prevent early-onset GBS disease, because recolonisation occurs before birth.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.question: What is the first-line intrapartum antibiotic for GBS prophylaxis?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.explanation: IV benzylpenicillin is first-line, given as soon as labour starts and repeated 4-hourly until delivery.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.question: Which describes the UK approach to Group B Streptococcus in pregnancy?
options: Antenatal oral antibiotics for all carriers
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.explanation: The UK uses a risk-factor-based approach to IAP rather than universal screening; the USA uses universal swab screening at 35–37 weeks.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.question: Which type of GBS disease is prevented by intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.explanation: IAP prevents early-onset GBS disease (vertical, in the first days of life); late-onset disease is not targeted by this strategy.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.question: GBS is detected on a urine culture (bacteriuria) at 20 weeks. What is the correct management?
options: Treat now, and offer intrapartum prophylaxis
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.answer: Treat now, and offer intrapartum prophylaxis
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.explanation: GBS bacteriuria in the current pregnancy should be treated at diagnosis and also triggers intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.question: A woman with severe penicillin allergy (anaphylaxis) requires GBS intrapartum prophylaxis. Which antibiotic is appropriate?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.explanation: For severe penicillin allergy (anaphylaxis), vancomycin is used; a cephalosporin is used for non-severe allergy, and clindamycin is no longer recommended due to resistance.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.question: Which of the following is a recognised indication to offer intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis for GBS?
options: A normal term labour with no risk factors
A planned caesarean with intact membranes
Maternal GBS carriage in a friend
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.explanation: Preterm labour, intrapartum fever ≥38°C, GBS in the current pregnancy, prolonged rupture of membranes, and a previous baby with GBS disease are indications for IAP.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.question: Is intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis needed for a planned pre-labour caesarean with intact membranes in a GBS carrier?
options: Only if the baby is preterm
No, because there is no passage through the birth canal
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.answer: No, because there is no passage through the birth canal
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.explanation: No IAP is needed for a planned caesarean with intact membranes before labour, as the baby does not pass through the colonised birth canal.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.question: A neonate is born to a mother who received adequate intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis and is clinically well. What is the appropriate management?
options: A full septic screen and antibiotics regardless
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.explanation: A well baby whose mother received adequate IAP — an appropriate antibiotic given at least 4 hours before birth — has routine observation; investigation and antibiotics are for babies with inadequate or no IAP plus risk factors, or signs of infection.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.question: Early-onset GBS disease most characteristically presents with which features?
options: Sepsis and respiratory distress in the first days
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.answer: Sepsis and respiratory distress in the first days
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.explanation: Early-onset GBS disease presents in the first days of life with sepsis, pneumonia and respiratory distress; late-onset disease more often causes meningitis.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.question: Why is clindamycin no longer recommended for GBS intrapartum prophylaxis?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.explanation: Clindamycin is no longer recommended because of rising GBS resistance; vancomycin is used for severe penicillin allergy instead.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.question: A woman was known to be colonised with GBS in a previous pregnancy. What are her options this pregnancy?
options: IAP this labour, OR late-pregnancy testing (ECM) with IAP if positive
No action, as it was a previous pregnancy
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.answer: IAP this labour, OR late-pregnancy testing (ECM) with IAP if positive
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__In.explanation: Known GBS colonisation in a previous pregnancy means offering either IAP this labour or testing (enriched culture medium) in late pregnancy with IAP if positive.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.question: A woman at 32 weeks has BP 150/95 on two occasions and a urine protein:creatinine ratio of 45 mg/mmol. What is the diagnosis?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.explanation: New hypertension ≥140/90 after 20 weeks plus proteinuria (PCR ≥30) defines pre-eclampsia; without proteinuria/organ features it would be gestational hypertension.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.question: What is the definitive treatment of pre-eclampsia?
options: Delivery of the fetus and placenta
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.answer: Delivery of the fetus and placenta
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.explanation: Because the placenta drives the disease, delivery of the fetus and placenta is the definitive cure; other measures temporise for fetal maturity.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.question: Which drug is first-line for treating hypertension in pre-eclampsia?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.explanation: Labetalol is first-line; nifedipine is second-line (e.g. in asthma) and methyldopa third-line. ACE inhibitors/ARBs are contraindicated in pregnancy.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.question: A woman with severe pre-eclampsia has a tonic-clonic seizure. Which drug is the treatment of choice?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.explanation: Magnesium sulfate both treats and prevents eclamptic seizures and is superior to diazepam/phenytoin.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.question: A woman on magnesium sulfate loses her deep tendon reflexes. What does this indicate and what is the antidote?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.explanation: Loss of deep tendon reflexes is the first sign of magnesium toxicity (progressing to respiratory/cardiac depression); the antidote is IV calcium gluconate.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.question: Which antihypertensive class is contraindicated in pregnancy due to fetal renal damage and oligohydramnios?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.explanation: ACE inhibitors and ARBs are contraindicated in pregnancy because they cause fetal renal damage and oligohydramnios — a classic trap. Thiazide diuretics are also avoided, as they reduce an already-contracted plasma volume.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.question: A nulliparous 41-year-old with a BMI of 37 is pregnant. Regarding pre-eclampsia prophylaxis, what is appropriate?
options: Aspirin from 12 weeks (two or more moderate-risk factors)
Aspirin only if she develops hypertension
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.answer: Aspirin from 12 weeks (two or more moderate-risk factors)
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.explanation: She has ≥2 moderate-risk factors (nulliparity, age ≥40, BMI ≥35), so aspirin 75–150 mg from 12 weeks until birth is indicated.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.question: Which of the following is a HIGH-risk factor that alone warrants aspirin prophylaxis for pre-eclampsia?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.explanation: A single high-risk factor (e.g. chronic hypertension, previous hypertensive pregnancy, CKD, diabetes, autoimmune disease) warrants aspirin; the others listed are moderate-risk (need two).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.question: A woman with pre-eclampsia develops RUQ pain, nausea, and blood tests show haemolysis, raised liver enzymes and low platelets. What is the diagnosis?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.explanation: Haemolysis, Elevated Liver enzymes and Low Platelets with RUQ pain define HELLP syndrome, a severe complication of pre-eclampsia requiring stabilisation and delivery.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.question: Which finding is a severe/impending-eclampsia red flag in pre-eclampsia?
options: Clonus with severe headache and visual disturbance
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.answer: Clonus with severe headache and visual disturbance
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.explanation: Severe headache, visual disturbance, epigastric/RUQ pain, brisk reflexes/clonus and BP ≥160/110 are severe features signalling impending eclampsia.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.question: A woman develops a tonic-clonic seizure 2 days after delivery, having had pre-eclampsia. What does this illustrate?
options: This must be epilepsy unrelated to pregnancy
BP monitoring can stop after delivery
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.explanation: Eclamptic seizures can occur antenatally, intrapartum or postnatally, so BP monitoring and vigilance must continue after delivery.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.question: What is the target blood pressure when treating pre-eclampsia?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.explanation: The target blood pressure in pre-eclampsia is ≤135/85 mmHg.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.question: A woman presents with hypertension and proteinuria at 14 weeks' gestation. What should this prompt?
options: Consideration of chronic hypertension or another cause (e.g. molar pregnancy), as pre-eclampsia is defined after 20 weeks
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.answer: Consideration of chronic hypertension or another cause (e.g. molar pregnancy), as pre-eclampsia is defined after 20 weeks
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.explanation: Pre-eclampsia is defined by new hypertension after 20 weeks; hypertension before 20 weeks suggests chronic/pre-existing hypertension or another cause such as a molar pregnancy.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.question: How does PLGF-based testing help in suspected pre-eclampsia (20–36⁺⁶ weeks)?
options: It helps rule out pre-eclampsia (low PLGF supports the diagnosis)
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.answer: It helps rule out pre-eclampsia (low PLGF supports the diagnosis)
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.explanation: PLGF is a pro-angiogenic factor made by the placenta; it falls in pre-eclampsia. Testing between 20 and 36⁺⁶ weeks is used mainly to RULE OUT the disease — a normal level makes pre-eclampsia in the next 14 days very unlikely, while a low level supports the diagnosis.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.question: A woman with a normal booking BP is found to have BP 148/94 at 30 weeks on two occasions, with a clear urine dipstick and normal bloods. What is the diagnosis?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.explanation: New hypertension after 20 weeks with no proteinuria and no organ dysfunction is gestational hypertension; proteinuria/organ features would make it pre-eclampsia.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.question: A woman with gestational hypertension develops proteinuria (PCR 40) at a later visit. What has happened?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.explanation: The development of proteinuria (or organ dysfunction) means gestational hypertension has progressed to pre-eclampsia — which is why dipstick at every visit is key.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.question: Which is the single most important test at each antenatal visit for a woman with gestational hypertension?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.explanation: Urine dipstick/PCR at each visit is the key test to detect the transition to pre-eclampsia (new proteinuria).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.question: What is the first-line antihypertensive for gestational hypertension?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.explanation: Labetalol is first-line (as in pre-eclampsia); nifedipine is second-line and methyldopa third-line. ACE inhibitors/ARBs are contraindicated.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.question: How does gestational hypertension typically behave after delivery?
options: It converts to chronic kidney disease
It usually resolves after birth, typically within 6 weeks
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.answer: It usually resolves after birth, typically within 6 weeks
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.explanation: Gestational hypertension usually resolves after birth, typically within 6 weeks, unlike chronic hypertension which persists. If BP is still raised at the 6–8 week postnatal review, investigate for a secondary cause.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.question: A woman has BP 145/92 at her booking visit at 12 weeks. What is the most likely diagnosis?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.explanation: Hypertension present before 20 weeks (e.g. at booking) is chronic (pre-existing) hypertension, not gestational hypertension, which arises after 20 weeks.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.question: Approximately what proportion of women with gestational hypertension progress to pre-eclampsia?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.explanation: Up to about a quarter (~15–25%) of women with gestational hypertension go on to develop pre-eclampsia.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.question: What is the target blood pressure when treating gestational hypertension?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.explanation: The target blood pressure is ≤135/85 mmHg, the same as in pre-eclampsia.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.question: Which antihypertensive is contraindicated in gestational hypertension?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.explanation: ACE inhibitors (and ARBs) are contraindicated in pregnancy due to fetal renal damage; labetalol, nifedipine and methyldopa are used.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.question: A woman had gestational hypertension in her first pregnancy and is now pregnant again. What prophylaxis is indicated?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.explanation: A hypertensive disorder in a previous pregnancy is a high-risk factor for pre-eclampsia, so aspirin 75–150 mg from 12 weeks is indicated in a subsequent pregnancy.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.question: Which long-term health issue is gestational hypertension associated with?
options: Increased future risk of chronic hypertension and cardiovascular disease
Chronic kidney failure in all women
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.answer: Increased future risk of chronic hypertension and cardiovascular disease
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.explanation: Gestational hypertension flags a higher lifetime risk of chronic hypertension and cardiovascular disease, warranting long-term follow-up.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.question: When is earlier delivery considered in a woman with gestational hypertension?
options: If it progresses to pre-eclampsia or BP becomes uncontrolled
As soon as it is diagnosed
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.answer: If it progresses to pre-eclampsia or BP becomes uncontrolled
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.explanation: Where BP is controlled and there are no complications, pregnancy continues to term; earlier delivery is considered if pre-eclampsia develops or BP is uncontrolled.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.question: How is severe gestational hypertension defined by blood pressure?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.explanation: Severe gestational hypertension is BP ≥160/110 mmHg; mild-moderate is up to <160/110, graded as for pre-eclampsia.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.question: Which feature would exclude a diagnosis of gestational hypertension in a woman with high BP after 20 weeks?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Hy.explanation: Gestational hypertension is defined by the absence of proteinuria and organ dysfunction; significant proteinuria (PCR ≥30) would reclassify it as pre-eclampsia.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.question: A 62-year-old woman presents with a single episode of postmenopausal bleeding. What is the most appropriate initial action?
options: Arrange a routine cervical smear only
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.explanation: Postmenopausal bleeding is endometrial cancer until proven otherwise; a woman ≥55 with PMB warrants 2-week-wait referral for TVUS ± biopsy.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.question: On the PMB pathway, transvaginal ultrasound shows an endometrial thickness of 3 mm. What does this indicate?
options: Reassuring — low likelihood of endometrial cancer
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.answer: Reassuring — low likelihood of endometrial cancer
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.explanation: An endometrial thickness ≤4 mm is reassuring with >99% negative predictive value; >4 mm would prompt biopsy. The exception is a woman on tamoxifen, in whom the measurement is unreliable and hysteroscopy ± biopsy is done regardless.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.question: Which factor increases endometrial cancer risk through unopposed oestrogen?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.explanation: Obesity increases risk because adipose tissue aromatises androgens to oestrogen; the COCP, Mirena, multiparity and (anti-oestrogenic) smoking are protective/reduce risk.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.question: A woman on tamoxifen for breast cancer develops postmenopausal bleeding. Why is this concerning?
options: Tamoxifen has no effect on the endometrium
Tamoxifen is protective against all gynae cancers
Bleeding on tamoxifen is always benign
It is pro-oestrogenic on the endometrium
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.answer: It is pro-oestrogenic on the endometrium
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.explanation: Tamoxifen is anti-oestrogenic in the breast but pro-oestrogenic on the endometrium, raising endometrial cancer risk; PMB on tamoxifen needs investigation.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.question: What is the first-line outpatient tissue diagnosis for suspected endometrial cancer with a thickened endometrium?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.explanation: An outpatient Pipelle endometrial biopsy is first-line for tissue diagnosis; hysteroscopy with directed biopsy follows if inadequate or a focal lesion is present.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.question: A 45-year-old woman is diagnosed with endometrial cancer. Which hereditary condition should be considered?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.explanation: Endometrial cancer in a younger patient should prompt consideration of Lynch syndrome, MMR testing, and colorectal cancer screening.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.question: Which histological type is characteristic of Type 2 (non-endometrioid) endometrial cancer?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.explanation: Type 2 endometrial cancers are serous, clear cell or carcinosarcoma — oestrogen-independent, aggressive, and often p53-mutated, affecting older/thinner women.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.question: What is the surgical cornerstone for early-stage endometrial cancer?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.explanation: Total hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy (± lymph node assessment) is the cornerstone treatment for early-stage endometrial cancer.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.question: A young woman with early, low-grade endometrial cancer wishes to preserve fertility. Which option may be considered?
options: High-dose progestogen or LNG-IUS with surveillance
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.answer: High-dose progestogen or LNG-IUS with surveillance
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.explanation: Fertility-sparing progestogen therapy (high-dose oral or LNG-IUS) with close surveillance may be considered in selected young women with early, low-grade disease or atypical hyperplasia.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.question: Which of the following is protective against endometrial cancer?
options: Oestrogen-only HRT in a woman with a uterus
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.explanation: The LNG-IUS (Mirena) and COCP are protective (progestogenic/anti-proliferative), whereas oestrogen-only HRT, tamoxifen, obesity and nulliparity increase risk.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.question: A woman presents with endometrial cancer that is confined to the uterus on staging. Which imaging best assesses myometrial invasion?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.explanation: MRI pelvis assesses depth of myometrial invasion; CT is used to look for distant spread once malignancy is confirmed.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.question: How is atypical endometrial hyperplasia (the precursor of Type 1 endometrial cancer) definitively managed?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.explanation: Total hysterectomy is definitive for atypical endometrial hyperplasia; LNG-IUS/progestogen with surveillance is used if fertility is desired or the woman is unfit for surgery.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.question: Which statement contrasts endometrial with ovarian cancer prognosis?
options: Endometrial cancer usually presents late with a poor prognosis
Both usually present at an advanced stage
Endometrial presents early with bleeding; ovarian late
Endometrial cancer has no early symptoms
Ovarian cancer usually presents with early bleeding
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.answer: Endometrial presents early with bleeding; ovarian late
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.explanation: Endometrial cancer typically presents early via bleeding, giving a good prognosis — the opposite of ovarian cancer, which usually presents late with vague symptoms.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.question: A woman <55 presents with postmenopausal bleeding. What does NICE advise regarding referral?
options: Only refer if bleeding recurs three times
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.explanation: NICE advises a 2WW referral for any woman ≥55 with PMB and to consider a 2WW referral in women <55 with PMB.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Gy.question: A 58-year-old woman has 3 months of persistent bloating, early satiety and urinary frequency. What is the most appropriate first investigation?
