conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.explanation: The ductus venosus shunts oxygenated umbilical venous blood past the liver directly to the IVC.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.question: Which fetal shunt connects the right atrium to the left atrium, bypassing the lungs?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.explanation: The foramen ovale shunts blood from the right atrium to the left atrium, bypassing the fluid-filled fetal lungs.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.question: What primarily drives blood away from the lungs in the fetal circulation?
options: Low pulmonary resistance with high systemic resistance
Active pumping by the fetal lungs
Closure of the ductus arteriosus in utero
High oxygen tension in the pulmonary artery
High pulmonary vascular resistance with low systemic (placental) resistance
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.answer: High pulmonary vascular resistance with low systemic (placental) resistance
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.explanation: Fluid-filled fetal lungs create high pulmonary vascular resistance, while the large placental circulation gives low systemic resistance, so blood is driven through the shunts away from the lungs.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.question: At birth, what change causes the foramen ovale to close?
options: Right atrial pressure rises above left
Left atrial pressure rises above right
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.answer: Left atrial pressure rises above right
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.explanation: After the first breath, pulmonary blood flow increases and left atrial pressure exceeds right atrial pressure, closing the flap of the foramen ovale (→ fossa ovalis).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.question: What triggers closure of the ductus arteriosus after birth?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.explanation: Increased arterial O₂ and reduced prostaglandins after birth cause the ductus arteriosus to constrict and close over days (→ ligamentum arteriosum).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.question: A neonate has a duct-dependent congenital heart lesion. Which drug is used to keep the ductus arteriosus open until surgery?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.explanation: Prostaglandins keep the ductus arteriosus patent; PGE is given to maintain ductal patency in duct-dependent lesions until definitive treatment.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.question: A preterm infant has a symptomatic patent ductus arteriosus. Which pharmacological agent is used to close it?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.explanation: NSAIDs such as indometacin or ibuprofen reduce prostaglandins and promote closure of a patent ductus arteriosus.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.question: Which group of infections can cross the placenta to cause congenital infection?
options: Only bloodborne viruses that infect red cells
None — the placenta is an absolute barrier
Only sexually transmitted infections acquired at delivery
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.explanation: TORCH pathogens (Toxoplasma, Rubella, CMV, and others) can cross the placenta and cause congenital infection.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.question: In rhesus disease, what crosses the placenta to cause fetal red cell haemolysis?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.explanation: Maternal anti-D IgG crosses the placenta and binds fetal RhD-positive red cells, causing haemolytic disease of the fetus/newborn.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.question: Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn results from failure of which normal transition at birth?
options: The rise in systemic vascular resistance
The fall in pulmonary vascular resistance
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.answer: The fall in pulmonary vascular resistance
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.explanation: If pulmonary vascular resistance fails to fall at birth, the circulation cannot transition to the lungs, causing persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.question: Which statement about maternal-fetal blood at the placenta is correct?
options: They come close but do not mix
Maternal and fetal blood mix freely
Fetal blood is filtered directly into maternal arteries
Maternal red cells routinely enter the fetus
Exchange occurs only through the umbilical arteries
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.answer: They come close but do not mix
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.explanation: At the placenta, maternal and fetal blood are separated by the placental membrane and do not normally mix; exchange occurs by diffusion/transport across it.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.question: Which fetal structure becomes the ligamentum arteriosum after birth?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.explanation: The ductus arteriosus becomes the ligamentum arteriosum; the ductus venosus becomes the ligamentum venosum and the foramen ovale becomes the fossa ovalis.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.question: Which hormone is responsible for milk production, and which for milk ejection (let-down)?
options: Oxytocin produces milk; prolactin ejects it
Oestrogen produces milk; progesterone ejects it
hCG produces milk; oxytocin ejects it
Prolactin produces milk; oxytocin ejects it
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.answer: Prolactin produces milk; oxytocin ejects it
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.explanation: Prolactin (anterior pituitary) drives milk synthesis, while oxytocin (posterior pituitary) causes let-down by contracting myoepithelial cells.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.question: Why does milk not flow during pregnancy despite rising prolactin?
options: High oestrogen and progesterone block prolactin's milk-producing action
Oxytocin is not produced until birth
The breast has no glandular tissue until birth
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.answer: High oestrogen and progesterone block prolactin's milk-producing action
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.explanation: During pregnancy the high placental oestrogen and progesterone block prolactin's action on the breast, so milk is not produced despite priming.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.question: A woman notices her milk 'comes in' about 2–3 days after delivery. What triggers this?
options: A surge in oestrogen after birth
The first suckle immediately produces mature milk
Oestrogen and progesterone fall after the placenta delivers
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.answer: Oestrogen and progesterone fall after the placenta delivers
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.explanation: Delivery of the placenta causes oestrogen and progesterone to fall, removing the block on prolactin so milk production begins around day 2–3.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.question: The let-down reflex ejects milk via which hormone and mechanism?
options: Oxytocin contracting myoepithelial cells around the alveoli
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.answer: Oxytocin contracting myoepithelial cells around the alveoli
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.explanation: Oxytocin causes contraction of the myoepithelial cells around the alveoli, ejecting milk into the ducts (the let-down reflex).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.question: How does the suckling reflex maintain milk supply?
options: Suckling suppresses prolactin to conserve milk
Suckling has no effect on hormone levels
Suckling raises prolactin and oxytocin, so supply matches demand
Suckling raises oestrogen to make more milk
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.answer: Suckling raises prolactin and oxytocin, so supply matches demand
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.explanation: Suckling signals the hypothalamus to increase prolactin (production) and oxytocin (ejection), creating a demand-driven 'supply and demand' system.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.question: A new mother is prescribed an antipsychotic (a dopamine antagonist) and develops galactorrhoea. What is the mechanism?
options: The drug stimulates the posterior pituitary
Blocking dopamine removes its inhibition of prolactin, raising prolactin
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.answer: Blocking dopamine removes its inhibition of prolactin, raising prolactin
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.explanation: Prolactin is under tonic dopamine inhibition; a dopamine antagonist removes this inhibition, raising prolactin and causing galactorrhoea.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.question: Which drug class is used to suppress lactation?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.explanation: Dopamine agonists such as cabergoline or bromocriptine suppress prolactin and thus milk production, and are used to suppress lactation.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.question: What is the mechanism of lactational amenorrhoea?
options: Oestrogen from milk suppresses the pituitary
High prolactin suppresses the HPG axis, inhibiting ovulation
Progesterone from the breast blocks ovulation
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.answer: High prolactin suppresses the HPG axis, inhibiting ovulation
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.explanation: High prolactin during breastfeeding suppresses GnRH and hence LH/FSH, inhibiting ovulation and causing lactational amenorrhoea (a natural, if unreliable, contraceptive effect).

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.question: During breastfeeding a woman experiences cramping uterine 'afterpains'. Which hormone is responsible?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.explanation: Oxytocin released during breastfeeding contracts the uterus, aiding involution and causing afterpains.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.question: Which immunoglobulin in breast milk provides mucosal (passive) immunity to the neonate?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.explanation: Breast milk (especially colostrum) provides secretory IgA, giving mucosal protection to the neonate's gut and respiratory tract — natural passive immunity.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.question: Why can stress or pain impair breastfeeding?
options: It raises oestrogen to block milk
It causes the placenta to retain hormones
Sympathetic activation inhibits oxytocin release, impairing let-down
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.answer: Sympathetic activation inhibits oxytocin release, impairing let-down
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.explanation: Stress/pain (sympathetic activation) inhibits oxytocin release and hence the let-down reflex, which is why a relaxed environment helps breastfeeding.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.question: What is colostrum?
options: Mature milk produced after several weeks
The protein- and antibody-rich first milk produced in the first few days
The fluid that primes the ducts in pregnancy
Milk produced only if the baby is preterm
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.answer: The protein- and antibody-rich first milk produced in the first few days
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.explanation: Colostrum is the antibody-rich (especially IgA) first milk produced in the first few days before mature milk comes in.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.question: A non-pregnant, non-breastfeeding woman presents with galactorrhoea and amenorrhoea. Which is a likely cause?
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.explanation: Hyperprolactinaemia — e.g. from a prolactinoma or dopamine antagonists — causes galactorrhoea and suppresses the HPG axis, producing amenorrhoea.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.question: The let-down reflex can be triggered even before the baby latches. Which stimulus best explains this?
options: The sight or cry of the baby
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.answer: The sight or cry of the baby
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.explanation: Let-down is partly a conditioned/neural reflex — the baby's cry or sight can trigger oxytocin release and milk ejection before suckling.

conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.question: Which statement about prescribing for a breastfeeding mother is correct?
options: Only intravenous drugs enter breast milk
Many drugs pass into breast milk, so drug safety must be considered
Breast milk destroys all drugs before the infant is exposed
Drug safety in breastfeeding is identical to pregnancy in every case
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.answer: Many drugs pass into breast milk, so drug safety must be considered
conditions__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY__Fo.explanation: Many drugs pass into breast milk and can reach the infant, so prescribing while breastfeeding requires attention to drug safety.

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.question: A 26-year-old woman presents with 6 weeks of amenorrhoea, left iliac fossa pain and light vaginal bleeding. Urine hCG is positive. Transvaginal ultrasound shows an empty uterus and her serum β-hCG is 2100 IU/L. What is the most appropriate interpretation?
options: Reassure her that this is a normal early intrauterine pregnancy and rescan in two weeks
The positive urine test is likely a false positive and should be repeated
The empty uterus with β-hCG above the discriminatory zone is highly suspicious for an ectopic pregnancy
This indicates a complete miscarriage and no further action is needed
The β-hCG is too low to be significant and can be ignored
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.answer: The empty uterus with β-hCG above the discriminatory zone is highly suspicious for an ectopic pregnancy
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.explanation: With serum β-hCG (2100 IU/L) above the discriminatory zone of ~1500 IU/L, an intrauterine pregnancy should normally be visible on TVUSS. An empty uterus at this level, especially with pain and bleeding, strongly suggests an ectopic pregnancy and mandates urgent early-pregnancy assessment. It is never reassured away on a single value.

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.question: A woman is being investigated for a pregnancy of unknown location (positive test, nothing seen on scan). Which single feature of serum β-hCG best supports a normally developing intrauterine pregnancy?
options: A value above 100,000 IU/L on a single test
A β-hCG that halves over 48 hours
A very high value that is greater than expected for dates
A single positive qualitative urine test
A β-hCG that roughly doubles over 48 hours
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.answer: A β-hCG that roughly doubles over 48 hours
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.explanation: A normal early intrauterine pregnancy shows serum β-hCG roughly doubling every ~48 hours. A halving trend suggests a failing pregnancy/miscarriage, a very high value suggests molar or multiple pregnancy, and no single value can confirm location or viability — hence serial measurement in PUL.

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.question: A 30-year-old with 9 weeks amenorrhoea has severe vomiting, a uterus larger than expected for dates, and a serum β-hCG markedly higher than expected. What is the most likely diagnosis?
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.answer: Molar pregnancy (gestational trophoblastic disease)
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.explanation: A markedly elevated β-hCG (higher than expected for dates), a large-for-dates uterus and hyperemesis are classic for a molar pregnancy. Very high hCG points to molar or multiple pregnancy; the excess hCG also drives the severe vomiting. Ultrasound (snowstorm appearance) and histology confirm the diagnosis.

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.question: A 27-year-old woman with a positive pregnancy test and a last menstrual period 7 weeks ago undergoes TVUSS for light bleeding. It shows an intrauterine gestational sac containing a fetal pole with a crown-rump length of 9 mm but no visible fetal heartbeat. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Diagnose a viable intrauterine pregnancy and reassure
Diagnose miscarriage (non-viable pregnancy) and discuss management options
Repeat the scan in 7 days before making any diagnosis
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.answer: Diagnose miscarriage (non-viable pregnancy) and discuss management options
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.explanation: A CRL ≥7 mm with no fetal heartbeat meets the RCOG threshold for a non-viable pregnancy (miscarriage). Because the CRL exceeds 7 mm the diagnosis can be made; a repeat scan would only be needed if the CRL were <7 mm or findings were borderline. The pregnancy is clearly intrauterine, so ectopic-focused steps (laparoscopy, serial β-hCG for PUL) are not indicated.

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.question: A 31-year-old woman presents with left iliac fossa pain and a positive pregnancy test. She is tachycardic (HR 122), hypotensive (BP 88/54) and looks pale and unwell. Bedside assessment suggests a possible ruptured ectopic. What is the most appropriate immediate management?
options: Resuscitate (ABC, large-bore IV access, cross-match) and proceed to emergency surgery
Arrange an urgent formal transvaginal ultrasound before doing anything else
Wait for the serum β-hCG result to confirm the diagnosis
Give a single dose of intramuscular methotrexate
Admit for observation and repeat β-hCG in 48 hours
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.answer: Resuscitate (ABC, large-bore IV access, cross-match) and proceed to emergency surgery
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.explanation: A haemodynamically unstable woman with a positive pregnancy test and suspected ruptured ectopic is a surgical emergency. Management is immediate resuscitation and emergency surgery (usually laparoscopic or open salpingectomy) WITHOUT waiting for scans or serial bloods. Methotrexate and expectant management require a stable patient and are contraindicated here.

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.question: A 24-year-old woman with a positive pregnancy test and 6 weeks' amenorrhoea has a TVUSS. The uterine cavity is empty, and there is a 3 cm mass in the right adnexa separate from the right ovary with a bright echogenic ring around a central hypoechoic centre ('bagel' sign), plus a small amount of free fluid in the pouch of Douglas. She is currently haemodynamically stable. What does this TVUSS appearance most strongly indicate?
options: A corpus luteum cyst of pregnancy
A pregnancy of unknown location with no localising features
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.answer: A tubal ectopic pregnancy
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.explanation: An empty uterus with a positive test, an adnexal 'tubal ring/bagel' mass separate from the ovary, and free fluid in the pouch of Douglas is the classic triad of a tubal ectopic pregnancy. A molar pregnancy shows an intrauterine 'snowstorm/cluster of grapes' pattern; a corpus luteum lies within the ovary and moves with it; and PUL by definition has no localising features — here a localising adnexal mass IS seen, so it is not PUL.

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.question: A 27-year-old woman with a positive pregnancy test and mild lower abdominal discomfort has a TVUSS showing no intrauterine or adnexal pregnancy. She is haemodynamically stable and pain settles. Her serum β-hCG is 480 mIU/mL, and a repeat 48h later is 520 mIU/mL. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Reassure and discharge with a routine dating scan at 12 weeks
Repeat a urine pregnancy test in 2 weeks
Repeat the β-hCG in a further 7 days from primary care
Refer for EPAU senior review with further imaging as a possible ectopic
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.answer: Refer for EPAU senior review with further imaging as a possible ectopic
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.explanation: The change from 480 to 520 (~8% rise) is a suboptimal change — between a ~50% fall and a ~63% rise. In a PUL this plateau is the pattern most suspicious of an ectopic, so she needs EPAU/senior review and further imaging, not reassurance or a delayed repeat. She is stable, so immediate surgery is not yet indicated.

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.question: A stable woman with a PUL has serum β-hCG of 1800 mIU/mL, falling to 700 mIU/mL 48h later. She has no pain or bleeding of concern. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Repeat a urine pregnancy test in about 2 weeks to confirm resolution
Start serial daily β-hCG monitoring in hospital
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.answer: Repeat a urine pregnancy test in about 2 weeks to confirm resolution
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.explanation: A fall of >50% over 48h (1800 → 700 is ~61% fall) suggests a failing PUL / likely miscarriage. Standard management is a repeat urine pregnancy test in about 2 weeks to confirm the pregnancy has resolved. Methotrexate and laparoscopy are for confirmed ectopic disease, not a resolving PUL.

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.question: A 31-year-old woman is being monitored with serial β-hCG for a PUL. While awaiting her 48h repeat level she presents acutely with severe right iliac fossa pain, right shoulder-tip pain, and a heart rate of 122 with BP 96/58. What is the most appropriate immediate action?
options: Wait for the scheduled 48h β-hCG before deciding
Arrange an outpatient TVUSS for the following morning
Reassure, as her earlier β-hCG trend was not clearly abnormal
Resuscitate and arrange urgent senior/surgical review for likely ruptured ectopic
Give methotrexate and discharge with EPAU follow-up
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.answer: Resuscitate and arrange urgent senior/surgical review for likely ruptured ectopic
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.explanation: Shoulder-tip pain, peritonism and haemodynamic instability point to a ruptured ectopic. Clinical symptoms always override reassuring or pending β-hCG numbers. She needs immediate resuscitation (ABC, IV access, fluids/blood, group and save/crossmatch) and urgent surgical review for emergency salpingectomy — not to wait for the algorithm. Methotrexate is contraindicated in an unstable/ruptured ectopic.

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.question: A 29-year-old RhD-negative woman at 30 weeks' gestation attends after a road traffic collision with abdominal trauma. Her booking antibody screen was negative and she received routine anti-D at 28 weeks. Which investigation most directly determines whether her current anti-D dose is adequate?
options: Direct antiglobulin test on the neonate
Middle cerebral artery (MCA) peak systolic velocity Doppler
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.answer: Kleihauer–Betke acid-elution test
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.explanation: After a potentially sensitising event beyond 20 weeks, the Kleihauer test quantifies the size of the feto-maternal haemorrhage to check whether the standard anti-D dose covers the bleed or whether additional anti-D is required. MCA Doppler assesses established fetal anaemia (in an already-sensitised woman), the neonatal DAT is postnatal, and cffDNA types the fetus rather than sizing a bleed.

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.question: An RhD-negative primigravida has a positive anti-D antibody screen at booking, consistent with prior sensitisation. What is the most appropriate management with respect to this pregnancy?
options: Give anti-D immunoglobulin now to prevent HDFN
Give anti-D immunoglobulin only at 28 weeks
Perform serial MCA Doppler for fetal anaemia surveillance
Withhold all intervention as the first pregnancy is always unaffected
Perform a Kleihauer test to decide the anti-D dose
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.answer: Perform serial MCA Doppler for fetal anaemia surveillance
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.explanation: Once a mother is already sensitised (anti-D antibodies present), anti-D immunoglobulin cannot reverse immunisation and has no role. Management is specialist fetal-medicine surveillance, using MCA peak systolic velocity Doppler to detect and monitor fetal anaemia. The 'first pregnancy is spared' rule applies to the pregnancy that CAUSES sensitisation, not to a pregnancy where sensitisation already exists.

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.question: Which single statement about anti-D immunoglobulin prophylaxis is correct?
options: It is given to RhD-positive mothers carrying an RhD-negative fetus
It reverses sensitisation once maternal anti-D antibodies are present
It should be delayed until after delivery in all cases
It is only indicated if the Kleihauer test is positive
It works by mopping up fetal RhD-positive cells before the mother mounts an immune response
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.answer: It works by mopping up fetal RhD-positive cells before the mother mounts an immune response
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.explanation: Anti-D immunoglobulin binds and clears fetal RhD-positive cells from the maternal circulation before an active maternal immune response can develop, preventing sensitisation. It is given to non-sensitised RhD-negative women (not RhD-positive mothers), cannot reverse existing sensitisation, and is given prophylactically after sensitising events, at 28 weeks (RAADP) and postnatally — not only when the Kleihauer is positive.

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.question: A stable woman has an unruptured 22 mm tubal ectopic with no fetal heartbeat and a βhCG of 1200 IU/L, and can attend follow-up. What is the most appropriate management?
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.answer: Methotrexate with serial βhCG follow-up
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.explanation: She meets methotrexate criteria: unruptured, asymptomatic/minimal pain, mass <35 mm, no fetal heartbeat, βhCG <1500 and able to attend follow-up (hCG days 4 and 7, expecting a ≥15% fall). Surgery is reserved for larger masses, higher βhCG, pain, heartbeat, or inability to follow up.

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.question: A woman attends for her first ultrasound at 12 weeks' gestation. The sonographer measures a specific parameter to accurately establish the gestational age and expected date of delivery. Which measurement is used?
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.answer: Crown–rump length
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.explanation: At the dating scan (~10–14 weeks) the crown–rump length (CRL) is the standard measurement used to accurately date the pregnancy. Once CRL exceeds ~84 mm (beyond ~14 weeks), head circumference/biparietal diameter is used. Nuchal translucency screens for aneuploidy, not dating; femur and abdominal circumference are used for later growth assessment.

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.question: A 38-year-old woman has a combined test at 12 weeks. Which set of results is most consistent with a higher chance of trisomy 21 (Down syndrome)?
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.answer: ↑ NT, ↑ β-hCG, ↓ PAPP-A
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.explanation: The classic Down syndrome pattern on the combined test is increased nuchal translucency, increased β-hCG and decreased PAPP-A (combined with maternal age). Edwards and Patau syndromes typically show low β-hCG and low PAPP-A.

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.question: A woman first books for antenatal care at 17 weeks' gestation, having missed the window for the combined test. Which test should be offered for Down syndrome screening?
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.answer: Quadruple test
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.explanation: When the combined-test window (~11–14 weeks) is missed, the quadruple test (serum AFP, β-hCG, unconjugated oestriol/uE3 and inhibin A) is offered ~15–20 weeks. NT is only reliable at 11–14 weeks; CVS and amniocentesis are diagnostic tests offered after a higher-chance screening result, not first-line screening.

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.question: A 29-year-old in established labour, augmented with oxytocin, has continuous CTG. Over 20 minutes there are repetitive decelerations whose lowest point consistently occurs after the peak of each contraction, with baseline variability reduced to <5 bpm. What is the most likely underlying process?
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.answer: Uteroplacental insufficiency causing fetal hypoxia
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.explanation: Late decelerations (nadir after the contraction peak) combined with reduced variability indicate uteroplacental insufficiency and fetal hypoxia — the pathological pattern. Head compression causes early decelerations and cord compression causes variable decelerations, neither of which is described here.

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.question: Which single CTG feature is considered reassuring and a sign of fetal wellbeing?
options: Variability of 2 bpm sustained for 60 minutes
Decelerations occurring after each contraction peak
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.answer: Accelerations of ≥15 bpm lasting ≥15 seconds
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.explanation: Accelerations (transient rises ≥15 bpm for ≥15 s) are reassuring. A baseline of 175 is tachycardia, variability of 2 bpm is reduced, late decelerations are pathological, and a deceleration lasting >3 min is a prolonged deceleration requiring urgent action.

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.question: A low-risk primigravida progresses normally in labour with no meconium, normal observations and reassuring intermittent auscultation. Which is the most appropriate form of fetal monitoring?
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.answer: Intermittent auscultation
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.explanation: In low-risk labour with no risk factors, intermittent auscultation is recommended. Continuous CTG is reserved for risk factors (e.g. meconium, sepsis/pyrexia, oxytocin, abnormal auscultation, hypertension, bleeding). Routine continuous CTG in low-risk labour increases intervention without improving outcomes, reflecting CTG's low specificity.

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.question: A 32-year-old woman at 30 weeks' gestation has a growth scan showing EFW on the 4th centile, having previously tracked the 40th centile. Umbilical artery Doppler shows absent end-diastolic flow and liquor is reduced. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Reassure and repeat the growth scan in 3 weeks
Advise fetal movement monitoring only and routine follow-up
Commence oral iron and rescan in 4 weeks
Urgent fetal-medicine review with corticosteroids and consideration of planned early delivery
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.answer: Urgent fetal-medicine review with corticosteroids and consideration of planned early delivery
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.explanation: Centile crossing from the 40th to the 4th centile with absent end-diastolic flow and oligohydramnios indicates fetal growth restriction from severe placental insufficiency, not constitutional smallness. Absent EDF carries a high stillbirth risk and is a strong indication to escalate: urgent fetal-medicine input, antenatal corticosteroids for lung maturity, and planned early delivery balancing prematurity against intrauterine death. Delaying with a routine 3-4 week rescan or discharging as SGA would be unsafe.

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.question: Which single ultrasound finding most reliably distinguishes fetal growth restriction (FGR) from a constitutionally small-for-gestational-age (SGA) fetus?
options: Estimated fetal weight below the 10th centile
Abnormal umbilical artery Doppler with static growth or centile crossing
A single deepest liquor pool of 3 cm
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.answer: Abnormal umbilical artery Doppler with static growth or centile crossing
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.explanation: An EFW <10th centile defines SGA but does not distinguish healthy constitutional smallness from pathology. FGR is identified by evidence of placental insufficiency and failure to meet growth potential — abnormal umbilical artery Doppler, static growth, or centile crossing (often with oligohydramnios). A normal deepest pool and a normal HC are reassuring, not discriminating, and FL alone does not establish FGR.

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.question: During umbilical artery Doppler assessment of a growth-restricted fetus, the waveform shows forward flow in systole but blood flowing backwards during diastole. Which statement best describes this finding?
options: It is a normal variant of umbilical artery flow in the third trimester
It indicates brain-sparing redistribution and is reassuring
It reflects low placental resistance and normal function
It represents reversed end-diastolic flow, an ominous sign of severe placental compromise
It is diagnostic of fetal anaemia requiring intrauterine transfusion
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.answer: It represents reversed end-diastolic flow, an ominous sign of severe placental compromise
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.explanation: Reversed end-diastolic flow (REDF) means diastolic flow is directed backward due to critically high placental resistance — a late, ominous sign of severe placental insufficiency and impending fetal decompensation, warranting delivery. It is never a normal variant or a sign of low resistance. Brain-sparing is assessed on MCA Doppler (falling MCA PI), not umbilical reversal. Fetal anaemia is suggested by a raised MCA peak systolic velocity, not umbilical REDF.

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.question: A 31-year-old woman with a BMI of 33 undergoes a 75g OGTT at 26 weeks' gestation. Her fasting venous plasma glucose is 5.9 mmol/L and her 2-hour value is 7.1 mmol/L. What is the most appropriate interpretation?
options: Gestational diabetes, because the fasting glucose is ≥5.6 mmol/L
Impaired glucose tolerance only — repeat OGTT in 4 weeks
Gestational diabetes, but only because the 2-hour value is abnormal
Test invalid — both values must be abnormal to diagnose GDM
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.answer: Gestational diabetes, because the fasting glucose is ≥5.6 mmol/L
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.explanation: NICE diagnoses GDM if EITHER threshold is met: fasting ≥5.6 mmol/L OR 2-hour ≥7.8 mmol/L. Here the fasting value (5.9) exceeds 5.6, so GDM is diagnosed even though the 2-hour value (7.1) is below 7.8. Only one abnormal value is required.

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.question: A 29-year-old woman is newly diagnosed with gestational diabetes at 27 weeks. Her fasting glucose at diagnosis is 7.4 mmol/L. What is the most appropriate initial management?
options: Trial of diet and exercise alone for 2 weeks
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.answer: Start insulin
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.explanation: When the fasting glucose at diagnosis is ≥7 mmol/L, NICE advises starting insulin immediately (± metformin) rather than a lifestyle trial. Diet/exercise first-line, then metformin, then insulin, is the pathway only when fasting is <7 mmol/L.

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.question: A neonate born to a mother with poorly controlled gestational diabetes is noted to be large for gestational age. Which immediate neonatal complication is most characteristic and should be actively monitored for after birth?
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.answer: Hypoglycaemia
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.explanation: Maternal hyperglycaemia drives fetal hyperinsulinaemia; after the cord is cut the maternal glucose supply stops but the neonate's high insulin persists, causing neonatal hypoglycaemia. Macrosomia (predisposing to shoulder dystocia) and neonatal hypoglycaemia are the classic combination tested in GDM.

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.question: A 31-year-old at 30 weeks has BP 148/96 and dipstick protein 2+. Which single investigation best confirms significant proteinuria?
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.answer: Urine protein:creatinine ratio (PCR)
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.explanation: A dipstick of ≥1+ prompts quantification. A spot PCR ≥30 mg/mmol (or ACR ≥8 mg/mmol) confirms significant proteinuria and is preferred over the outdated 24-hour collection. Serum creatinine, osmolality and MSU do not quantify proteinuria; repeating the dipstick adds nothing.

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.question: A woman at 28 weeks has suspected pre-eclampsia. Her PlGF result is normal. What does this most usefully indicate?
options: Confirms pre-eclampsia and mandates immediate delivery
Helps rule OUT pre-eclampsia needing delivery in the next 1–2 weeks
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.answer: Helps rule OUT pre-eclampsia needing delivery in the next 1–2 weeks
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.explanation: PlGF-based testing has a high negative predictive value. A normal PlGF between ~20 and 35–37 weeks helps exclude pre-eclampsia requiring delivery imminently. PlGF is LOW (not normal) in established pre-eclampsia, so a normal result does not confirm disease, HELLP, FGR or diabetes.

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.question: A 34-year-old at 33 weeks with pre-eclampsia develops a severe frontal headache, epigastric pain and brisk clonus. BP is 172/112. What is the most appropriate immediate priority alongside BP control?
options: Reassure and review in one week
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.answer: Give intravenous magnesium sulphate
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.explanation: These are severe features with impending eclampsia; magnesium sulphate is given to prevent seizures alongside urgent BP control and senior review, with delivery considered as the definitive treatment. Aspirin is preventive (from 12 weeks), not acute; PlGF/outpatient review and metformin are inappropriate in this emergency.

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.question: During labour a pathological CTG prompts fetal blood sampling; the scalp pH is 7.19. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Give maternal oxygen and observe for 2 hours
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.answer: Expedite delivery
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.explanation: A fetal scalp pH ≤7.20 is abnormal and indicates significant hypoxia, mandating expedited delivery. A borderline pH (7.21–7.24) would be repeated in ~30 minutes; ≥7.25 is normal.

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.question: A 30-year-old woman at 31 weeks gestation reports a sudden gush of clear fluid per vaginum 2 hours ago. She is afebrile and comfortable, with a soft, non-tender uterus and normal fetal heart rate. What is the most appropriate next step to confirm the diagnosis?
options: Digital vaginal examination to assess cervical dilatation
Sterile speculum examination looking for pooling of amniotic fluid in the posterior fornix
Transvaginal ultrasound to measure cervical length
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.answer: Sterile speculum examination looking for pooling of amniotic fluid in the posterior fornix
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.explanation: PPROM is a clinical diagnosis. A sterile speculum examination looking for a pool of amniotic fluid in the posterior fornix is the correct first step. Digital vaginal examination is avoided as it increases the risk of ascending infection. There is no indication for immediate delivery in a stable woman with no signs of infection or fetal compromise.

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.question: A woman at 29 weeks reports possible leaking of fluid, but sterile speculum examination does not clearly show pooling and the history is equivocal. Which investigation best confirms or excludes ruptured membranes?
options: Ferning of a cervical mucus sample under microscopy
Vaginal fluid PAMG-1 or IGFBP-1 bedside test
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.answer: Vaginal fluid PAMG-1 or IGFBP-1 bedside test
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.explanation: When pooling is not seen and doubt remains, a bedside test detecting amniotic-fluid proteins — PAMG-1 (AmniSure) or IGFBP-1 (Actim PROM) — is the most reliable confirmatory test. Nitrazine/pH and ferning tests are less reliable with more false positives. A digital exam is avoided in PPROM, and beta-hCG is not the standard bedside marker used here.

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.question: A woman with confirmed PPROM at 32 weeks develops a temperature of 38.4°C, maternal tachycardia, uterine tenderness and an offensive vaginal discharge; the CTG shows fetal tachycardia and CRP is markedly raised. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Continue expectant management and repeat CRP in 24 hours
Broad-spectrum IV antibiotics and expedite delivery regardless of gestation
Start oral erythromycin and discharge home
Commence tocolysis to prolong the pregnancy
Give a further course of antenatal corticosteroids and observe
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.answer: Broad-spectrum IV antibiotics and expedite delivery regardless of gestation
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.explanation: These features indicate chorioamnionitis, an obstetric emergency. Management is prompt broad-spectrum IV antibiotics and delivery regardless of gestation. Tocolysis is contraindicated in the presence of infection, and expectant management would risk maternal sepsis and fetal compromise.

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.question: A 29-year-old woman at 30 weeks presents with 3 hours of regular painful contractions. Membranes are intact, there is no bleeding, and the cervix is 2 cm long and closed on speculum. A fetal fibronectin swab is negative. What is the most appropriate interpretation?
options: A positive result would have confirmed she is definitely in preterm labour
She should immediately receive tocolysis and be transferred regardless of the result
The test is invalid because she is symptomatic
The negative result makes delivery within the next 1–2 weeks unlikely, supporting reassurance and avoiding unnecessary intervention
A negative result mandates cervical cerclage
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.answer: The negative result makes delivery within the next 1–2 weeks unlikely, supporting reassurance and avoiding unnecessary intervention
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.explanation: fFN is valued for its high negative predictive value. A negative test in a woman with threatened preterm labour makes imminent preterm birth unlikely, so it is used to rule out preterm delivery and avoid unnecessary admission, steroids, tocolysis and transfer. A positive test is far less specific and does not confirm labour.

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.question: A woman with threatened preterm labour is having a fetal fibronectin swab taken. Which factor would make the result unreliable/invalid?
options: A history of one previous term delivery
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.answer: Sexual intercourse the previous evening
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.explanation: Recent intercourse (within ~24 h), vaginal bleeding, and ruptured membranes all invalidate fFN, as does contamination with lubricant or ultrasound gel or a preceding digital exam. The other options do not affect test validity.

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.question: A 27-year-old at 28 weeks has painful contractions and a transvaginal cervical length of 8 mm with funnelling of the internal os; fFN is positive. She is now contracting every 2–3 minutes and the cervix is 4 cm dilated. What is the most appropriate immediate management priority?
options: Repeat the fetal fibronectin test in 24 hours before acting
Discharge with outpatient follow-up as most women do not deliver preterm
Give antenatal corticosteroids and magnesium sulphate, and arrange care without letting the tests delay treatment
Start prophylactic vaginal progesterone as the priority
Insert a rescue cervical cerclage at 4 cm dilatation
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.answer: Give antenatal corticosteroids and magnesium sulphate, and arrange care without letting the tests delay treatment
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.explanation: This woman is in genuine established, advanced preterm labour. Predictive tests are irrelevant here and must not delay treatment. She needs antenatal corticosteroids for lung maturity, magnesium sulphate for neuroprotection, and consideration of tocolysis/in-utero transfer as appropriate. Progesterone is preventive in asymptomatic high-risk women, and cerclage is not appropriate at 4 cm dilatation in active labour.

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.question: Which statement best describes how transvaginal cervical length is used in a woman with previous spontaneous preterm birth?
options: It is only useful once the membranes have ruptured
A long cervix indicates a higher risk of preterm birth
It replaces the need for any preventive treatment
Cervical length below 40 mm is always abnormal and requires cerclage
Serial screening for a short cervix identifies women who may benefit from progesterone or cerclage
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.answer: Serial screening for a short cervix identifies women who may benefit from progesterone or cerclage
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.explanation: In high-risk women (e.g. previous preterm birth), transvaginal cervical length screening detects a shortening cervix, which raises preterm birth risk and can guide preventive treatment with vaginal progesterone and/or cervical cerclage. A short (not long) cervix indicates higher risk, and it is used with intact membranes.

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.question: A 31-year-old woman at 34 weeks' gestation reports 2 weeks of intense itching of her palms and soles that is worst at night. On examination there is no rash, only a few scratch marks on her forearms. She is normotensive with no proteinuria. Which single investigation is most likely to confirm the diagnosis?
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.answer: Serum bile acids
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.explanation: The picture — third-trimester nocturnal itch of the palms and soles with no rash, and no features of pre-eclampsia — is classic for intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy. Serum bile acids are the key confirmatory test (typically with deranged LFTs). The other tests help exclude alternatives (HELLP, autoimmune liver disease, acute fatty liver) but do not confirm ICP.

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.question: A 29-year-old woman at 36 weeks is diagnosed with obstetric cholestasis. Her peak serum bile acid level is 120 micromol/L. Which complication is she at greatest increased risk of, and which most influences management?
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.answer: Stillbirth
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.explanation: The principal fetal danger in ICP is stillbirth, and the risk rises with the peak bile acid level, being highest when bile acids are ≥100 micromol/L (severe disease). This drives increased fetal surveillance and consideration of planned early birth. ICP does not cause maternal cirrhosis and is not linked to the other listed complications.

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.question: A 33-year-old woman at 33 weeks presents with itching and deranged LFTs. Her BP is 158/104 mmHg, urine dipstick shows 3+ protein, and her platelet count is 88 x10^9/L. Which is the most important next consideration before labelling this as obstetric cholestasis?
options: Exclude pre-eclampsia/HELLP as the cause of the deranged LFTs
Reassure and repeat LFTs in 4 weeks
Prescribe a sedating antihistamine and discharge
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.answer: Exclude pre-eclampsia/HELLP as the cause of the deranged LFTs
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.explanation: Obstetric cholestasis is a diagnosis of exclusion. Hypertension, significant proteinuria and thrombocytopenia point to pre-eclampsia/HELLP, which can also derange LFTs and is immediately dangerous — this must be identified and managed rather than mislabelled as ICP. Acute fatty liver of pregnancy is another mimic to exclude. Only after excluding these should ICP be diagnosed and treated.

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.question: A 40+5 week primigravida is admitted for induction of labour. On vaginal examination her cervix is posterior, firm, 1 cm long, closed, with the head at −3 station, giving a Bishop score of 2. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Amniotomy followed by an oxytocin infusion
Immediate caesarean section for failed induction
Vaginal prostaglandin E2 (dinoprostone) and reassess the Bishop score
Start a high-dose oxytocin infusion alone
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.answer: Vaginal prostaglandin E2 (dinoprostone) and reassess the Bishop score
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.explanation: A Bishop score of 2 indicates an unfavourable (unripe) cervix, so cervical ripening with vaginal prostaglandin (or a balloon catheter) is required before amniotomy/oxytocin, with reassessment of the score afterwards. Amniotomy is not feasible or advised with a closed, uneffaced cervix, and there is no indication yet for caesarean.

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.question: Two hours after insertion of a dinoprostone pessary for induction, a woman develops contractions occurring 7 times in 10 minutes and the CTG shows recurrent late decelerations with a fetal bradycardia. What is the most important immediate management step?
options: Remove the vaginal prostaglandin pessary and consider tocolysis
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.answer: Remove the vaginal prostaglandin pessary and consider tocolysis
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.explanation: This is uterine hyperstimulation (tachysystole) with fetal compromise. The priority is to remove the causative agent (the prostaglandin pessary), maintain continuous CTG, and give tocolysis such as terbutaline. Escalation for possible emergency caesarean follows if the fetal heart does not recover. Increasing oxytocin or amniotomy would worsen the situation.

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.question: Which of the following is a component of the Bishop score used to assess cervical favourability before induction of labour?
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.answer: Cervical dilatation
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.explanation: The Bishop score comprises five features found on vaginal examination: cervical dilatation, effacement/length, consistency, position, and fetal station. BMI, estimated fetal weight, amniotic fluid index, and fetal fibronectin are not part of it (fetal fibronectin is used in preterm labour prediction, not the Bishop score).

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.question: A woman at 34 weeks has painless, bright-red vaginal bleeding; a previous scan showed a low-lying placenta. What must you avoid?
options: A digital or speculum vaginal examination
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.answer: A digital or speculum vaginal examination
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.explanation: With suspected placenta praevia a vaginal (digital or speculum) examination can provoke catastrophic haemorrhage and must be avoided until praevia is excluded on ultrasound. Resuscitation measures, CTG and cross-match are all appropriate.

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.question: Immediately after delivery a woman has a brisk postpartum haemorrhage; the uterus is soft and boggy. After calling for help and starting resuscitation, what is the most appropriate first specific step?
options: Uterine massage / bimanual compression and a uterotonic (e.g. oxytocin)
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.answer: Uterine massage / bimanual compression and a uterotonic (e.g. oxytocin)
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.explanation: A soft, boggy uterus indicates atony (Tone) — the commonest cause. First-line is uterine massage/bimanual compression with uterotonics (oxytocin, then ergometrine/carboprost) plus tranexamic acid, escalating to balloon tamponade and surgery if bleeding continues.

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.question: A 64-year-old woman presents with a single episode of postmenopausal bleeding. She is obese and has type 2 diabetes. Transvaginal ultrasound shows an endometrial thickness of 9 mm. What is the most appropriate next investigation?
options: Reassure and discharge as a single episode
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.answer: Endometrial (Pipelle) biopsy
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.explanation: PMB with an endometrium >4 mm mandates endometrial sampling to exclude cancer/hyperplasia; the first-line test is a Pipelle biopsy. Her obesity and T2DM are unopposed-oestrogen risk factors. A single episode is never grounds for discharge, and imaging/CA-125 are not the appropriate first step.

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.question: A 58-year-old woman has recurrent postmenopausal bleeding. TVUS shows a thickened endometrium and a Pipelle biopsy returns 'insufficient sample for diagnosis.' What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Reassure her that the biopsy was normal
Commence tranexamic acid and review in a year
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.answer: Hysteroscopy with directed biopsy
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.explanation: An insufficient or normal Pipelle does not exclude cancer when bleeding persists, because the blind, partial sample can miss focal lesions. Recurrent PMB requires hysteroscopy ± directed biopsy, the gold standard for focal pathology. Oestrogen-only HRT would worsen risk, and delay/reassurance is unsafe.

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.question: A Pipelle biopsy in a 61-year-old with PMB reports 'atypical endometrial hyperplasia.' Which statement is correct regarding this finding?
options: It is a benign finding requiring no follow-up
It is premalignant and usually managed with hysterectomy
It is best treated with oestrogen-only HRT
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.answer: It is premalignant and usually managed with hysterectomy
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.explanation: Atypical hyperplasia is premalignant with a substantial risk of coexisting or progression to endometrial carcinoma, so total hysterectomy is usually recommended (fertility-sparing progestogen therapy only in selected cases). It does not exclude cancer, and oestrogen would worsen it.

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.question: A 63-year-old woman presents with a single episode of postmenopausal bleeding that has now settled. She is not on hormonal therapy and has no other symptoms. Transvaginal ultrasound shows a smooth endometrial stripe measured at 3 mm with no focal lesion, fibroids or adnexal abnormality. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Proceed directly to hysteroscopy and dilatation & curettage
Reassure and safety-net, no immediate endometrial sampling required
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.answer: Reassure and safety-net, no immediate endometrial sampling required
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.explanation: In postmenopausal bleeding an endometrial thickness ≤4 mm has a high negative predictive value for endometrial cancer, so with a single settled bleed and a thin, normal stripe the woman can be reassured and safety-netted. She must be told to re-present if bleeding recurs, as persistent/recurrent PMB warrants biopsy regardless of thickness.

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.question: A 68-year-old woman with breast cancer on tamoxifen reports two episodes of vaginal bleeding. Transvaginal ultrasound reports the endometrium as 9 mm with cystic subendometrial change. What is the single most appropriate investigation?
options: Reassure, as tamoxifen commonly thickens the endometrium
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.answer: Hysteroscopy with endometrial biopsy
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.explanation: Tamoxifen produces subendometrial cystic changes that make the ultrasound endometrial measurement unreliable, so the 4 mm cut-off cannot be used. A woman on tamoxifen who bleeds should be assessed directly by hysteroscopy with biopsy to obtain tissue and directly visualise the cavity.

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.question: A 59-year-old woman is referred with recurrent postmenopausal bleeding over three months. Transvaginal ultrasound shows an endometrial thickness of 2.5 mm and no other abnormality. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Discharge with reassurance as the endometrium is ≤4 mm
Prescribe tranexamic acid and review in 6 months
Proceed to endometrial biopsy ± hysteroscopy despite the thin endometrium
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.answer: Proceed to endometrial biopsy ± hysteroscopy despite the thin endometrium
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.explanation: A thin endometrial stripe reassures about diffuse disease but does not exclude focal pathology such as a polyp or focal carcinoma. Persistent or recurrent postmenopausal bleeding mandates biopsy and/or hysteroscopy even when the endometrium is ≤4 mm, because PMB is endometrial cancer until proven otherwise.

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.question: A 58-year-old postmenopausal woman reports 3 months of persistent bloating and early satiety. Serum CA-125 is 90 IU/mL. Transvaginal ultrasound shows a multilocular cyst with solid areas and a moderate volume of ascites. Using RMI = U × M × CA-125, what is her RMI and the correct action?
options: RMI 90 — reassure and repeat CA-125 in 3 months
RMI 90 — discharge as likely benign functional cyst
RMI 270 — measure AFP, β-hCG and LDH before any referral
RMI 810 — refer to a specialist gynaecological oncology MDT
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.answer: RMI 810 — refer to a specialist gynaecological oncology MDT
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.explanation: Three ultrasound features (multilocular, solid areas, ascites) give U=3; postmenopausal gives M=3; CA-125 = 90. RMI = 3 × 3 × 90 = 810. Being well above the >250 threshold, she should be referred to a gynae-oncology MDT/cancer centre. Germ-cell markers are indicated in women <40, not here.

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.question: A 52-year-old woman presents to her GP with 6 weeks of new, persistent abdominal bloating, loss of appetite and urinary frequency. She has no prior bowel history. What is the most appropriate first-line investigation?
options: Reassure and treat empirically as irritable bowel syndrome
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.answer: Serum CA-125
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.explanation: New persistent symptoms in a woman over 50 should not be attributed to IBS as a new diagnosis. NICE advises measuring serum CA-125 first; if ≥35 IU/mL, proceed to abdomino-pelvic ultrasound. Empirical IBS treatment risks missing ovarian cancer; CT/laparoscopy are not first-line, and germ-cell markers are reserved for women under 40.

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.question: A 24-year-old woman is found to have a 9 cm solid right ovarian mass on ultrasound. In addition to CA-125, which set of investigations is most important given her age?
options: Repeat CA-125 in 6 weeks with no further markers
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.answer: AFP, β-hCG and LDH
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.explanation: In women under 40 with a suspected ovarian mass, germ-cell tumours are relatively common and may not raise CA-125. AFP, β-hCG and LDH help detect germ-cell tumours (e.g. yolk-sac tumour, dysgerminoma, choriocarcinoma). CEA/CA 19-9 are gastrointestinal markers and the other options are not the priority here.

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.question: A 32-year-old woman attends for routine cervical screening. Her liquid-based cytology sample is tested and found to be high-risk HPV positive; reflex cytology is reported as normal. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Repeat the HPV test in 12 months
Return to routine recall in 3 years
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.answer: Repeat the HPV test in 12 months
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.explanation: hrHPV positive with normal cytology is managed by surveillance: repeat HPV testing at 12 months. Most infections clear, so immediate colposcopy would be over-investigation. Colposcopy is indicated if she remains hrHPV positive at 12 and 24 months, or if cytology is abnormal.

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.question: A 45-year-old woman presents to her GP with a 3-month history of postcoital bleeding. On speculum examination the cervix looks irregular and friable. Her last cervical screening 18 months ago was normal. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Reassure her, as her recent screening was normal
Repeat a cervical screening smear now
Urgent 2-week-wait referral to gynaecology for examination
Test the sample for high-risk HPV
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.answer: Urgent 2-week-wait referral to gynaecology for examination
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.explanation: Screening is for asymptomatic women and a normal result does not exclude cancer in a symptomatic patient. Postcoital bleeding with a suspicious cervix requires urgent referral and examination, not a screening smear.

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.question: Which statement best explains why the UK moved to HPV primary screening rather than cytology-first screening?
options: Cytology is more expensive than HPV testing
HPV testing removes the need for colposcopy
HPV testing allows screening to stop at age 40
HPV testing is more sensitive because persistent high-risk HPV infection causes virtually all cervical cancer
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.answer: HPV testing is more sensitive because persistent high-risk HPV infection causes virtually all cervical cancer
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.explanation: Nearly all cervical cancers arise from persistent high-risk HPV infection, so testing for hrHPV first is a more sensitive way to identify women at risk. Cytology is then used reflexively (only if hrHPV positive) to triage who needs colposcopy.

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.question: At colposcopy a lesion turns dense white after application of a solution, with sharp borders in the transformation zone. Biopsy confirms CIN3. Which solution produced this appearance, and what is the appropriate treatment?
options: Acetic acid; repeat smear in 12 months
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.answer: Acetic acid; LLETZ
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.explanation: Acetic acid produces acetowhite change in abnormal epithelium. CIN3 is high-grade, pre-invasive disease and is treated with LLETZ (large loop excision of the transformation zone). Lugol's iodine is an adjunct where abnormal areas fail to take up the stain.

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.question: A young woman has sudden severe unilateral pelvic pain and vomiting with an adnexal mass; TVUSS Doppler shows preserved arterial flow. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Reassure — preserved Doppler flow excludes torsion
A trial of analgesia and discharge
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.answer: Urgent diagnostic laparoscopy
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.explanation: Ovarian torsion is a clinical diagnosis; because of the ovary’s dual blood supply, preserved Doppler flow does NOT exclude it. Suspected torsion warrants urgent diagnostic laparoscopy for detorsion ± cystectomy to salvage the ovary.

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.question: Which set of findings satisfies the Rotterdam criteria for PCOS?
options: Two of: oligo/anovulation, hyperandrogenism, and polycystic ovaries on ultrasound
A raised CA-125 with an adnexal mass
A single raised LH level alone
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.answer: Two of: oligo/anovulation, hyperandrogenism, and polycystic ovaries on ultrasound
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.explanation: PCOS is diagnosed by the Rotterdam criteria: any two of oligo/anovulation, clinical or biochemical hyperandrogenism, and polycystic ovarian morphology on ultrasound, once mimics (thyroid disease, hyperprolactinaemia, late-onset CAH) are excluded.

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.question: A 68-year-old woman describes a bulge at the vaginal opening. On examination in the left lateral position with Valsalva, the most dependent point of the prolapse lies at the level of the introitus, within 1 cm of the hymen. What is the POP-Q stage?
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.answer: Stage 2
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.explanation: Stage 2 is defined as the leading point lying within 1 cm above or below the hymen (i.e. at the introitus). Stage 1 is >1 cm above the hymen, Stage 3 is >1 cm below but not complete, and Stage 4 is complete procidentia.

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.question: A multiparous woman reports having to press on the back wall of her vagina to fully empty her bowels. Which prolapse is most likely responsible?
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.answer: Rectocele
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.explanation: A posterior compartment rectocele allows stool to pocket in the anterior rectal bulge; patients characteristically 'splint' (apply digital pressure to the posterior vaginal wall/perineum) to defecate. A cystocele/urethrocele is anterior and causes urinary symptoms; uterine/vault prolapse is apical.

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.question: An 80-year-old woman presents with a fully everted uterine prolapse (procidentia) and reduced urine output. Blood tests show an acutely raised creatinine. Which complication most likely explains her renal impairment?
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.answer: Ureteric kinking causing hydronephrosis
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.explanation: Complete procidentia can drag on and kink the distal ureters, obstructing outflow and producing bilateral hydronephrosis with a rising creatinine. This is a reason for prompt reduction of the prolapse and urgent urological/urogynaecology assessment. Mucosal erosion causes bleeding/discharge but not renal failure.

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.question: A 29-year-old woman with regular 35-day cycles is being investigated for subfertility. Her GP wants to confirm she is ovulating with a serum progesterone. On which cycle day should the sample ideally be taken?
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.answer: Day 28
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.explanation: Mid-luteal progesterone must be taken 7 days before the expected next period, not fixed at day 21. In a 35-day cycle, the next period is expected around day 35, so the sample is taken around day 28. Day 21 would sample too early (still follicular) and risk a falsely low result.

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.question: A 33-year-old man's semen analysis shows a normal count and morphology but only 25% progressive motility. What is the single most appropriate next step?
options: Repeat the semen analysis in about 3 months
Start empirical clomifene for the male
Reassure and take no further action as this is normal
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.answer: Repeat the semen analysis in about 3 months
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.explanation: Progressive motility of 25% is below the WHO lower limit (≥30%), so the sample is abnormal. A single abnormal result should be confirmed by repeating at ~3 months, because spermatogenesis takes ~72 days and a transient factor (e.g. recent illness) can cause a temporary dip. Karyotype/microdeletion work-up is reserved for confirmed severe abnormalities such as azoospermia.

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.question: A couple attend after 14 months of trying to conceive. The man's semen analysis, repeated twice, confirms azoospermia. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Reassure and advise a further 12 months of natural conception attempts
Prescribe the man a course of antibiotics for presumed infection
Refer to a specialist for endocrine and genetic work-up
Arrange a hysterosalpingogram for the female partner as the priority
Start the couple directly on intrauterine insemination
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.answer: Refer to a specialist for endocrine and genetic work-up
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.explanation: Confirmed azoospermia is a red flag requiring specialist referral for further evaluation, including endocrine profiling (FSH/LH/testosterone) and genetic testing (karyotype, Y-microdeletions, and CFTR mutations where congenital absence of the vas is suspected). Continued natural attempts or empirical antibiotics are inappropriate, and tubal patency testing is not the priority when there is a confirmed severe male factor.

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.question: A 29-year-old woman with 18 months of primary subfertility has a normal partner semen analysis and confirmed ovulation. She has no history of pelvic infection or surgery. Which is the most appropriate first-line investigation of tubal patency?
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.answer: Hysterosalpingography or HyCoSy
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.explanation: For a woman with no known comorbidity, a non-invasive outpatient test (HSG or HyCoSy) is first-line once semen analysis is normal. Laparoscopy and dye is reserved for suspected tubal/pelvic pathology. Hysteroscopy assesses the cavity but not tubal patency; endometrial biopsy and CA-125 do not assess patency.

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.question: Before arranging a hysterosalpingogram in a subfertile woman, which step is most important to reduce the risk of iatrogenic pelvic inflammatory disease?
options: Give a course of oral steroids
Screen for and treat Chlamydia trachomatis and give prophylactic antibiotics if indicated
Perform the test in the luteal phase
Start combined oral contraception for one cycle
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.answer: Screen for and treat Chlamydia trachomatis and give prophylactic antibiotics if indicated
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.explanation: Transcervical instrumentation can flare a lower-genital-tract infection into PID. Chlamydia screening/treatment plus prophylactic antibiotics where indicated is the key safety step. The test is done in the follicular (not luteal) phase to avoid an early pregnancy; the other options are irrelevant.

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.question: An HSG in a 33-year-old woman shows contrast filling the uterine cavity and pooling within a distended, sausage-shaped right tube with no peritoneal spill on that side. She is being planned for IVF. What is the most appropriate management of this finding before IVF?
options: No action; proceed directly to IVF
Salpingectomy (or proximal tubal occlusion) of the affected tube before IVF
Repeat HSG in 6 months and reassess
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.answer: Salpingectomy (or proximal tubal occlusion) of the affected tube before IVF
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.explanation: The appearances describe a hydrosalpinx (dilated, non-spilling tube). A hydrosalpinx reduces IVF success rates, so treatment — typically salpingectomy or proximal tubal occlusion — is recommended before proceeding to IVF. Doing nothing lowers success; hysterectomy is grossly inappropriate; antibiotics or delay do not address the mechanical/embryotoxic problem.

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.question: A 29-year-old woman presents with a thin, greyish, fishy-smelling vaginal discharge but no itch or soreness. Vaginal pH is 5.0, and adding potassium hydroxide releases a strong fishy odour. Wet-mount microscopy shows epithelial cells with granular cytoplasm and obscured borders. Which is the single most appropriate treatment?
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.answer: Oral metronidazole
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.explanation: The thin grey fishy discharge, pH >4.5, positive whiff test and clue cells satisfy Amsel's criteria (3 of 4) for bacterial vaginosis. First-line treatment is metronidazole (oral or topical). Azoles treat candida; ceftriaxone treats gonorrhoea; aciclovir treats herpes.

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.question: A 24-year-old woman has an offensive, frothy, yellow-green vaginal discharge. Speculum examination reveals punctate haemorrhages over the cervix ('strawberry cervix') and vaginal pH is 5.5. Wet-mount microscopy shows motile flagellated organisms. In addition to metronidazole, which action is most important?
options: Reassure that no further investigation is needed
Offer a full STI screen and partner notification
Repeat vaginal pH testing in one week
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.answer: Offer a full STI screen and partner notification
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.explanation: The findings are diagnostic of Trichomonas vaginalis, a sexually transmitted infection. Beyond metronidazole, management must include a full STI screen (chlamydia, gonorrhoea, HIV, syphilis) and partner notification/treatment. Antifungals are irrelevant, and this is not a self-limiting condition to be reassured away.

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.question: A medical student is asked to distinguish the two BV diagnostic tools. Which statement correctly characterises the Nugent score?
options: It requires three of four clinical criteria to be positive
It measures vaginal pH using an indicator strip
It detects amine release after adding potassium hydroxide
It relies on visualising motile flagellated protozoa
It is a Gram-stain scoring system (0-10) used as the laboratory gold standard
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.answer: It is a Gram-stain scoring system (0-10) used as the laboratory gold standard
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.explanation: The Nugent score grades bacterial morphotypes on a Gram-stained smear from 0-10 (7-10 = BV) and is the lab/research gold standard. The 'three of four' clinical criteria, pH testing and the amine/whiff test are components of Amsel's criteria; motile flagellates indicate trichomonas.

investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.question: A woman with subfertility has a repeat mid-luteal (day-21-adjusted) progesterone of 12 nmol/L, confirming anovulation, with normal prolactin and thyroid function. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Ovulation induction with letrozole or clomifene and follicle tracking
Reassurance and review in one year
Start the combined oral contraceptive pill
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.answer: Ovulation induction with letrozole or clomifene and follicle tracking
investigations__OBSTETRICS & GYNAECOLOGY.explanation: A low mid-luteal progesterone on repeat confirms anovulation. With normal prolactin/thyroid, ovulation induction with letrozole (increasingly first-line) or clomifene, plus ultrasound follicle tracking and multiple-pregnancy counselling, is the appropriate next step.
